name: Helmut Malek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 60553/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) on 30 June 2000. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The First Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case was taken over by an Investigating Commissioner in August 1995. The Disciplinary Council decided to open the main proceedings on 3 June 1996. The applicant’s spouse and the two police officers submitted that they could not appear at that date. The case was adjourned and the file concerning the administrative criminal proceedings against the applicant was sent to the Vienna Federal Police Directorate. The file at issue had meanwhile been transmitted to an other administrative authority. The hearing was cancelled and the case was remitted to the Disciplinary council. The appeal was dismissed and the application was dismissed. The application was settled by the Vienna Court of Appeal. The judge found the applicant not guilty of all charges. The Disciplinary Council found that the applicant had misbehaved towards intervening police officers during a traffic control by threatening them with job-related troubles in case they charged him with traffic offences. The applicant was convicted and ordered to pay an additional fine of ATS 10,000 as he had already been order to pay ATS 25,000 in four other sets of disciplinary proceedings. He appealed against the decision but the Appeals Board dismissed his appeal. He complained, inter alia, about the length of the proceedings and claimed that the disciplinary authorities had failed to take the excessive length into account as a mitigating circumstance. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint on 29 February 2000.

The case was brought against the Republic of Austria under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Austrian national, Mr Helmut Malek. The case originated in an application (no. 60553/00) lodged with the Court on 30 June 2000. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Government decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government in 2002. In August 1995, after the case had been taken over by another Investigating Commissioner, the latter agreed with the Vienna Federal Police Directorate (Bundespolizeidirektion) to question the police officers involved in the traffic control at issue. On 3 November 1995 he filed letters rogatory with the Donaustadt District Court (Bezirksgericht) which were subsequently transferred to the Josefstadt District Court. On 13 December 1995 the two police officers were questioned. On 8 February 1996 the Investigating commissioner submitted his report to the Disciplinary Council. On 24 February 1997 the Constitutional Court, in proceedings unrelated to the present one’s, issued a decision concerning the composition of the Dis disciplinary Council. The applicant challenged two members of the Disciplinary Council for bias and submitted that he was prevented from appearing. The only witness heard was one of the two police officers, the other witnesses and the applicant submitted that they were not able to appear. The applicant was convicted and ordered to pay an additional fine of ATS 10,000. He complained, inter alia, about the length of the proceedings and claimed that the disciplinary authorities had failed to take the excessive length into account as a mitigating circumstance. He was struck off the bar roll on 6 April 2000. The application was dismissed by the Constitutional Court on 29 February 2000 and the appeal was dismissed on 14 June 1999.

train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) 11 Turkish nationals, including the first applicant, filed the application on 20 November 2001. The applicants were represented by Mr Şeyho Saya, who is a lawyer practising in Adıyaman. The Turkish Government was represented by their Agent. On 6 September 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicants filed criminal complaints with the Adıyaman Public Prosecutor against those police officers who had allegedly used excessive force during their arrest. The applicants appealed against this decision. In their appeal petition, they invoked a breach of Article 11 of the Convention, arguing that the police interference had breached their freedom of assembly. On 14 June 2001 the Supreme Administrative Council upheld the decision of the Administrative Council to not bring criminal proceedings against the accused officers. In reaching his decision, the Public Prosecutor stated that the demonstrators had been stopped by the police, although they had been walking silently along the pavement, without presenting a danger to the public or engaging in any violent activities. The police were under an obligation to warn the group out loud to disperse. However, it was observed from the recording of the incident that they had failed to do so. In consequence, the public prosecutor held that the accused had not violated Law no. 2911. the Assemblies and Marches Act (Law no. 2501) The case was settled out of court by the court of appeal at the end of February. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty by reason of misadventure. The judge ruled that the police had not committed a breach of the law by failing to warn them out loud that they were in trouble.

The applicant was living with his family in Germany, where his father was an Army Corporal serving in the Support Unit of the Rhine Garrison. On 8 February 1994 the applicant was charged with the murder of a young civilian woman. The German authorities waived jurisdiction pursuant to the NATO Status of Forces Agreement 1951 (see paragraph 21 below). The applicant was returned to Germany in time for his court-martial which commenced on 21 April 1995. Despite his father’s return, the applicant remained subject to military law as the proceedings had already commenced. The applicant returned to England in April 1994 where he was detained. His father was discharged from the army in November 1994. The trial ended with the applicant’s conviction on 3 May 1995. In accordance with the provisions of the Army Act 1995, the verdict of the court-martial was confirmed by a Confirming Officer. The applicant appealed to the Courts-Martial Appeal Court, which had the power to quash the conviction if it considered it unsafe. name: Danuta Durasik
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 6735/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant claimed compensation and a monthly pension for damage she had sustained as a result of a medical treatment at the Zgierz Hospital. The trial court found no fault on the part of the doctors concerned and accordingly dismissed the liability of the State Treasury for the damage. The court found, inter alia, that the doctors had failed to act diligently; consequently, the State Treasury was liable for the damage sustained by the applicant. The trial court again dismissed the action. The appellate court partly allowed the appeal and awarded the applicant PLN 4,000 in compensation. On 29 January 2002 the applicant lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) rejected her cassation Appeal on 29 October 2002. The appeal was dismissed on 25 January 2003. The case was heard at the Court of Appeal of the Polish Republic. The applicant appealed against the judgment on 9 October 2001.

train_texts: The case originated in four applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were accused of being members of an illegal armed organisation, namely the TIKP (the Revolutionary Communists’ Union of Turkey) They were also accused of carrying out activities on behalf of the TikB, such as taking part in demonstrations on 1 May and 8 March (Women’s Day) during which they had chanted slogans and distributed TIKB leaflets. On 4 September 2001 the Court decided to join the applications, declared them partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the applicants’ right to a fair hearing to the Government. The applicants were members of the TIKP, but found guilty under Article 169 of the Criminal Code for aiding and abetting an illegal organisation. The first, second and third applicants were sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment, while the second applicant was sentenced to three years and nine months. The applicants appealed. The chief public prosecutor at the Court of Cassation submitted his opinion on the merits of the appeal on 24 December 1997. This opinion was not served on the applicants, but read out during the hearing which took place on 18 March 1998. The decision was pronounced on 10 June 1998 and the applicants’ request for rectification was further rejected.

It therefore relied on a fourth expert report which served as a conciliation report for a calculation of the amount due to the applicant. name: Richard Woźniak
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was remanded in custody by the Gdańsk Regional Court on suspicion of murder. The courts considered that the applicant had been charged with the commission of crimes for which he was liable to a sentence of imprisonment exceeding 8 years. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The application was dismissed on 18 January 2007. The judge ruled that the application was not supported by the evidence. The decision was made to dismiss the application. From 20 March 2002 until 9 May 2002 and from 17 February 2003 until 18 March 2003 the applicant served prison sentences imposed in other sets of criminal proceedings against him. During the investigation and the trial the applicant filed several unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against the decisions prolonging his detention. The Gdańsk Regional Court found that the necessary pieces of evidence had been obtained and the case was at its final stage, so there was no need to prolong the applicant’s detention. He was released on 14 May 2007 and the proceedings are pending. The applicant was sentenced to 6-years’ imprisonment in respect of some of the charges.

name: Arnold Fragner
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18283/06) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the proceedings concerning his doctor's fees had not been dealt with within a reasonable time. He claimed payment for these treatments from the Lower Austrian Health Insurance Board. The Board refused to pay the fees claimed as the applicant is not a specialist doctor but a general practitioner. It was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1). The case was decided in favour of the applicant. The applicant applied for the transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) to the Regional Appeals Commission (Landesberufungskommission) before the Joint Arbitration Committee (Paritätische Schiedskommmission) on 4 September 1996. Because of a tie vote, it could not take a binding decision. The applicant filed a complaint with Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) and on 13 October 1999 that court quashed the Appeals Commission's decision. A further hearing, this time in public, took place on 26 November 2003. The Appeals Commission dismissed the applicant's claim on 10 December 2004. The applicant complained to the Constitutional Court, alleging a breach of the principle of equal treatment. The Constitutional Court found no violation of the right to a fair trial and upheld the contested decision. It held that the assessors of the Regional Appeals Commission were independent in exercising their function and no circumstances giving rise to doubts about their impartiality and independence had arisen in the present case. This decision was served on counsel on 29 November 2005. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal on 27 September 2005 and the decision was handed down on 27 October 2005. It ruled that the Appeals Commission was independent and that the decision had been made in a fair and impartial manner.

name: Dorothea Vogt
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 11 March 1994 and by the German Government on 29 March 1994. It originated in an application (no. 17851/91) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national, Mrs Dorothea Vogt, on 13 February 1991. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and also, in the case of the Commission's request, of Article 14. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 February 1995. The Grand Chamber comprised as ex officio members the President and the Vice-President, Mr Bernhardt, who in this case was already sitting as national judge. The names of the remaining ten judges were drawn by lot by the President in the presence of the Registrar on 27 January 1995, namely Mr F. Gölcüklü, Mr R. Macdonald, Mr A. Spielmann, Mr J. De Meyer, Mr I. Foighel, Mr M.A. Lopes Rocha, Mr D. Gotchev and Mr P. Kuris. Mrs Vogt was a member of the German Communist Party (Deutsche Kommunistische Partei - “DKP’) She studied literature and languages at the University of Marburg/Lahn for six years. In November 1975 she sat the examination to become a secondary-school teacher (wissenschaftliche Prüfung für das Lehramt an Gymnasien) She did her teaching practice from February 1976 to June 1977 at Fulda in the Land of Hesse. On 1 February 1979, before the end of her probationary period, she was appointed a permanent civil servant (Beamtin auf Lebenszeit) The applicant had failed to comply with the duty of loyalty to the Constitution (“duty of political loyalty“ - politische Treuepflicht) that she owed as a civil servant under section 61 (2) of the Lower Saxony Civil Service Act (Niedersächsisches Beamtengesetz - see paragraph 28 below). She had, it was said, engaged in various political activities on behalf of the DKP since the autumn of 1980 and in particular had stood as a DKP candidate in the 1982 elections to the Landtag. The proceedings were stayed in order to widen the investigations to include further instances of the applicant's political activity that had come to light in the meantime. By an order of 12 August 1986 the Weser-Ems regional council notified the applicant that she had been temporarily suspended from her post. “Although you knew the views of your superiors and the case-law of the disciplinary courts you have nevertheless, over a considerable period of time, deliberately violated your duty of oyalty. For a permanent civil servant that is anextraordinarily serious breach of duty.“ The applicant, who by her own account has been a member of the DKP since 1972, argued that her conduct could not amount to a failure to fulfil her duties as a civil servant. She had always carried out such activity within the law and within the limits laid down in the Constitution. Her action to promote peace within the Federal Republic of Germany and in its external relations was in no way indicative of an anti-constitutional stance. The institution of disciplinary proceedings against civil servants on account of their political activities on behalf of a party that had not been banned breached International Labour Organisation (ILO) Convention No. 111 concerning discrimination in respect of employment and occupation. It also violated Article 10 (art. 10) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Disciplinary Division found that the applicant had failed to comply with her duty of political loyalty and ordered her dismissal as a disciplinary measure. It granted her a sum equivalent to 75 per cent of her pension entitlement at that date, to be paid for a six-month period. The DKP's aims, as described in the Mannheim programme of 21 October 1978 (see paragraph 22 below), were clearly opposed to the free democratic constitutional system of the Federal Republic of Germany. Mrs Vogt was dismissed for having betrayed the relationship of trust between herself and her employer. She had repeatedly indicated that she intended to continue her political activities for the DKP despite the warnings she had received. The fact that she had done her work satisfactorily for many years was immaterial. The Disciplinary Division finally ordered that Mrs Vogt should be paid 75 per cent of her pension allowance for a period of six months. The applicant lodged an appeal against the above judgment with the Lower Saxony Disciplinary Court, reiterating her previous arguments (see paragraph 18 above). In a judgment of 31 October 1989 the Dis disciplinary court dismissed Mrs VogT's appeal and upheld the Administrative Court's judgment in all respects. The court held that the applicant's reference to Article 5 para. 1 of the Basic Law, which secured the right to freedom of expression, was not relevant. Mrs Vogt's conduct had been unlawful. She necessarily espoused anti-constitutional aims and had therefore to be considered to be opposed to the Constitution herself. It was not possible to support both systems at the same time. Even though she sought above all to support the constitutional system, she was opposed to it herself. The court also found that the party continued to be guided by the principles of Marx, Engels and Lenin. The fact that the Constitutional Court. had not banned the DKP did not prevent other courts from finding that the. party was anti- constitutional. The DKP's aims were admittedly not all anti-constitutional; some of them were compatible with the Basic Law. However, civil servants could not, as a means of furthering their own political objectives, make use of a party with anti- constitutional aims and help it to come to power. to achieve some of theDKP's short-term objectives such as reducing unemployment, promoting peace and eliminating so-called Berufsverbote (prohibitions on pursuing various occupations), this did not mean that her conduct was not culpable. In its judgment banning the former Communist Party (KPD) (BVerfGE 5, p. 85), the Federal Constitutional Court held that the 'tactics of conflict' employed by the former KPD were incompatible with the free democratic constitutional system. The court also considered that the applicant's commitment to changing the DKP's policies could not exculpate her. The political loyalty owed by civil servants entailed a duty for them to dissociate themselves unequivocally from groups which criticised or cast aspersions on the State and the existing constitutional system. The court added that such a breach of duty was especially serious in the case of a teacher, who was supposed to teach the children entrusted to her care the fundamental values of the Constitution. Her dismissal had therefore been justified, since a civil servant who thus persisted in breaching her duties and refusing to see reason was no longer capable of serving the State. The court added that a radical change in a civil servant's attitude could affect its assessment of the seriousness of professional misconduct. It followed that a more lenient disciplinary measure, aimed at persuading her to abandon her political activities within the DKP, was bound to fail. Her otherwise blameless conduct in carrying out her teaching tasks did not change the situation in any way, since the basis of trust that was essential for her to continue as a civil service was lacking. The applicant's dismissal had therefore not amounted to a breach of the principle of proportionality as regards her constitutional rights, the court said. The court decided on 7 August 1990 not to entertain the constitutional complaint, on the ground that it had insufficient prospects of success. From 1987 to 1991 the applicant worked as a playwright and drama teacher at the North Lower Saxony regional theatre (Landesbühne) in Wilhelmshaven. From 1 February 1991 she was reinstated in her post as a teacher for the LowerSaxony education authority. The Land government had beforehand repealed the decree on the employment of extremists in the Lower Saxonic civil service (Ministerpräsidentenbeschluß - also known as the Radikalenerlaß - see paragraph 32 below) and had published regulations for dealing with “earlier cases“ (see paragraph 33 below)

The Disciplinary Division held that the applicant had failed to comply with her duty of political loyalty and ordered her dismissal as a disciplinary measure. It granted her a sum equivalent to 75 per cent of her pension entitlement at that date, to be paid for a six-month period. She had repeatedly indicated that she intended to continue her political activities for the DKP despite the warnings she had received. The Disciplinary Division finally ordered that Mrs Vogt should be paid 75 per cent of her pension allowance for a period of six months. It did so in recognition of the fact that apart from her breach of the duty of loyalty Mrs VogT had always performed her duties unexceptionably and enthusiastically and needed some income to be protected from immediate hardship. The court also considered that the applicant's commitment to changing the DKP's policies could not exculpate her. Mrs Dorothea Vogt, a German national born in 1949, lives in Jever in the Land of Lower Saxony. She studied literature and languages at the University of Marburg/Lahn for six years. In November 1975 she sat the examination to become a secondary-school teacher (wissenschaftliche Prüfung für das Lehramt an Gymnasien). It granted her a sum equivalent to 75 per cent of her pension entitlement at that date, to be paid for a six-month period. This rule did not apply to measures, such as disciplinary proceedings, which initially had a different purpose and restricted the freedom to stand for election to, and to sit as a member of, parliament only as an indirect and unavoidable consequence of their implementation. The applicant had moreover carried out her political activities despite being familiar with the case-law establishing that active membership of the DKP was incompatible with the duty ofpolitical loyalty. The Disciplinary Division finally ordered that Mrs Vogt should be paid 75 per cent of her pension allowance for a period of six months. The DKP's political aims were incompatible with that system. By holding such a senior political post within the DKP, she necessarily espoused anti-constitutional aims and had therefore to be considered to be opposed to the Constitution herself, although she proclaimed her attachment to the Basic Law. It was not possible to support both systems at the same time. Even though Mrs Vogd sought above all to support above all the constitutional system, she had failed to satisfy the requirements of Article 5 para. . 5 of the Basic law, taken together with section 61 (2) of the Lower Saxony Civil Service Act. Under those provisions, civil servants must at all times bear witness to the free democratic constitutional system. The DKP's aims were admittedly not all anti-constitutional; some of them were compatible with the Basic Law. However, civil servants could not, as a means of furthering their own political objectives, make use of a party with anti- constitutional aims and help it to come to power. The Federal Disciplinary Court referred to the following observations made by the Federal Administrative Court (Bundesverwaltungsgericht) in a judgment of 20 January 1987: “It appears doubtful whether the view of the Constitution espoused by the official and described above reflects accurately the principles enshrined in the Basic law. It is not necessary to resolve that question here" The court also considered that the applicant's commitment to changing the DKP's policies could not exculpate her. The attitude of civil servants who, even if they campaigned within DKP for the renunciation of aims that were contrary to the Constitution, showed outside the party, through the political offices they held, that they unreservedly supported its programme and policy, was incompatible with such a duty. The court added that such a breach of duty was especially serious in the case of a teacher who was supposed to teach the children entrusted to her care the fundamental values of the Constitution. The State was under a duty to dismiss teachers who played an active role in an anti-constitutional organisation. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 7505/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that while performing his military service he had lost the sight in his left eye as a result of the military authorities’ failure to provide him with prompt and appropriate medical assistance. On 16 December 2014 the Chamber decided, under Rule 54 § 2 (c) of the Rules of Court, to invite the parties to submit further written observations on the admissibility of the applicant’s complaint. The patient had to have several operations to cure his eye condition. He was finally able to see a doctor for the first time in more than a month. The patient was awarded $30,000 in compensation for his eye problems. He is still waiting for a prosthetic eye to be fitted for him. He has also been awarded $15,000 for pain and suffering he suffered as a result of the surgery. The eye condition is now under control, but he is still unable to see well enough to work. He also has to have regular eye tests to make sure he is getting the right amount of light through his eyes. He must also have regular eyewear for the rest of his life. During the proceedings the administrative court appointed three university professors from the ophthalmology department of Gazi University’s Faculty of Medicine as experts with a view to clarifying whether there had been any medical malpractice in the case. Their expert report drawn up on 6 April 2005 concluded: “Our medical opinion, based on our examination of the plaintiff's allegations, is as follows: ‘We are of the opinion that there were no delays, shortcomings, mistakes or negligence in the steps taken in transferring the patient to the hospital, diagnosing the problem, treating the problem or treating the patient’’ In his written opinion submitted to the Supreme Military Administrative Court, the public prosecutor stated that the applicant should be awarded compensation either for the authorities’ negligence or if such negligence was established. The applicant claimed that he had been unable to see a doctor in the regiment infirmary because there had not been a doctor there during that time. The Supreme Military Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s claim by a majority of four to one and held that no fault could be attributed to the military authorities in the treatment of the applicant. The applicant requested a rectification of the administrative court's decision. The court refused the applicant's rectification request on 21 September 2005. According to a medical report of 9 October 2009 issued by the Haseki Hospital, the applicant was deemed to be suffering from a permanent disability. It was indicated that his ability to work had been reduced by 41% as a result of the disability.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36042/97) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission on Human Rights. The applicant alleged that British social-security legislation discriminated against him and his late wife on grounds of sex. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 11 May 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted. Widows' benefits are based on the assumption that women are more likely than men to have been financially dependent on their spouse's earnings. The benefits themselves are concentrated on those widows who are perceived to have the greatest problems. Most widowers of working age will have been in employment before the death of their wives. They will not have the same degree of difficulty in supporting themselves as widows. Women on average earn less than men. So even for women who have been working, the financial loss on widowhood is likely to be significantly more than for men. The Government says that the extension of the benefits on the same basis to widowers would mean substantial extra expenditure in paying maintenance benefit. To make existing widows' benefits provisions available to widowers would add an estimated GBP 490 million to the annual Social Security budget. The Government is of the opinion that at a time when all areas of public expenditure are having to be carefully considered, this is simply not a best use of scarce resources. In making these points, the Government says that it is in no way minimising the sad problems faced by widowers, in particular those left with small children to care for. For them there are already available benefits such as Child Benefit and One Parent Benefit, together with the range of income-related benefits, for example, Income Support for those not in full time work.

name: Cahit Akçam
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court ruled in favour of the applicant, and against the Republic of Turkey in the case. The case was settled at the High Court of Justice in Strasbourg. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way). On 20 February 1981 the Ankara Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law court convicted the applicant of membership. It sentenced the applicant to 16 years’ imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in the civil service and placed him under judicial guardianship. The case was automatically referred to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay). The criminal proceedings are still pending before the latter court.

Martínez, Delegate; (c) the applicant. On 24 September 1996 the Court removed the documents in question from the file (Rule 37 para. 1). The Court heard addresses by the applicant, the applicant himself, Mr Schürmann and Mr Boilat. Guy Ankerl and his wife moved into a flat on the second floor of no. 3, rue Saint-Léger, Geneva in 1978. He subleased the flat from a property-management company, Régie Immobilière SA, itself the tenant of a property company, SI Chrysanthemum SA. On 14 July 1987 Naef allegedly sent receipts relating to the payment of rent from April to July of that year and specified that in collecting the sums in question they were not recognising the existence of any direct legal relationship between Mr Ankersl and the owner of the building. The applicant then applied to the Rents and Leases Conciliation Board for an extension of the agreement, but no settlement having been reached. The applicant and his wife had an interview with Mr Linder, the director of GPR Degenève, on 22 April 1988. Chrysanthemum brought an action for possession in the Canton of Geneva Court of First Instance, alleging that the applicant was occupying the premises unlawfully. Mr Ankerl argued that the court had no jurisdiction ratione materiae, maintaining that he had an orally agreed lease from the plaintiff. The court thus had to determine whether the conduct of the protagonists amounted to an agreement to enter into a lease after the termination of the subtenancy. Only the first two were heard as witnesses on oath. Mr Dominique Veuillet: We knew that Mr Ankerl was in de facto occupation of the premises. In 1986 or 1987 he came to see me and told me that his position vis-à-vis Régie Immobilière was a rather special one. The defendant asked that we should draw up a lease in his name. He told me he did not wish to proceed in the matter and did not give me the reasons. ... I sent the file to our lawyer, who must have informed him of the shareholder’s position. I myself handed the file over to another property-management company on 31 December 1987. Mr Ruffieux and Mr Ankerl were asked to leave their flat in 1989. They were told they could occupy a newly built flat at the top of the house or a second-floor flat. Mr Ruffieuz: "Mr Linder never asked us to look for a flat elsewhere and he did not indicate that we had to leave within a given time" Mr Linder: "I did not realise that it was a subtenancy. I had consulted a lawyer before signing it. I did not want us to agree to it. He is up to date with the rent. I would not have been opposed to a settlement at the outset but relations with him have become difficult" Mr Linder, an employee of the new management, told the Court that he had had an interview with Mr Ankerl and had made it clear to him that in his view Mr AnKERl did not have a lease. No lease has been signed since the termination of the sublease. The Court reaches the conclusion that, in the circumstances of this case, no lease was entered into orally (the existence of an oral agreement has not been proved) or even implied by the clear conduct of the parties. The court below did not infer from those statements that the witness had indicated to the appellant that he would have to leave the flat. ... The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation. It originated in an application (no. 17748/91) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 10 December 1990. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr L. Wildhaber, the elected judge of Swiss nationality (Art 43) and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. The applicant and the Government were asked to provide documents by 5 April 1996. The Government informed the Registrar on 3 April 1996 that it was “not possible to accede to [the] request’. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 May 1996. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr P. Boillat, Head of the European Law and International Affairs Section, Federal Office of Justice, Agent, Mr A.D. Schmidt, former judge in the Canton of Geneva, Counsel. For the Commission Mr F. Martínez, Delegate; (c) the applicant. Guy Ankerl and his wife moved into a flat on the second floor of no. 3, rue Saint-Léger, Geneva in 1978. He subleased the flat from a property-management company, Régie Immobilière SA (“RégieImmobiliere“), itself the tenant of a property company, SI Chrysanthemum SA. The company was in liquidation in 1987 and requested to terminate the subtenancy agreement. The applicant applied to the Rents and Leases Conciliation Board for an extension of the agreement but no settlement had been reached. He maintains that he paid the rent into the company's bank account. Chrysanthemum brought an action for possession in the Canton of Geneva Court of First Instance. Mr Ankerl argued that the court had no jurisdiction ratione materiae, maintaining that he had an orally agreed lease from the plaintiff. The court thus had to determine whether the conduct of the protagonists amounted to an agreement to enter into a lease after the termination of the subtenancy. Only the first two were heard as witnesses on oath. The hearing was held on 19 May 1989. It heard Mr Linder (GPR Degenève), Mr Veuillet (Naef) and Mrs Ankerr; Mr Ruffieux and the applicant also gave evidence. Mr Dominique Veuillet: We knew that Mr Ankerl was in de facto occupation of the premises. In 1986 or 1987 he told me that his position vis-à-vis Régie Immobilière was a rather special one. The defendant asked that we should draw up a lease in his name. At the same time he had asked us to collect the rent direct from him. ... I myself handed the file over to another property-management company on 31 December 1987, and at that time, as far as we had described in our letter of 14 July 1987 ... It is true that on 14 November 1986 we had informed him about the proposed works in the building. We replied that the works might perhaps inconvenience us but that we wanted to stay. Mr Ruffieux: Mr Linder never asked us to look for a flat elsewhere and he did not indicate that we had to leave within a given time. Mr Ankerl: When I concluded the lease with Régie Immobilière, I did not realise that it was a subtenancy. The court held that there was no lease agreement between the parties and ordered Mr AnKERl to move all property and persons from the flat and restore it to the plaintiffs in good condition.“On 12 October 1989 the Court held that the tenant, RégieImmobilièr SA, had asked Naef to collect the rent direct from Mr Ankerser. This arrangement was accepted, the payments being received as an indemnity for unlawful occupation, as appears from a letter of 14 July 1987,” the judgment reads. Mr Linder, an employee of the new management, told the Court that he had had an interview with Mr Ankerl. Mr Ruffieux, the director and shareholder of the plaintiffs, said he had never agreed, and did not wish to agree, to enter into a lease with the defendant. The Court reaches the conclusion that, in the circumstances of this case, no lease was entered into orally (the existence of an oral agreement has not been proved) or even implied by the clear conduct of the parties. ... In law the only issue which it is necessary to resolve is whether the defendant, since his sublease was terminated, has been given a lease by the landlord. In the instant case no lease has been signed since the termination of the sublease. Guy Ankerl was denied a lease by Chrysanthemum SA for flat at no. 3, rue Saint-Léger, second floor. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal against the decision. The Canton of Geneva Court of Justice dismissed an appeal by Mr Anker l on the following grounds: “The Court cannot but agree with the court below that there was no contractual relationship between the landlord, Chrysantemum SA, and Guy Ankersl. ... It must be held that the defendant is on the premises unlawfully. Article 641 para. 2 [of the Civil Code] applies in this case ...“ The First Civil Division of the Federal Court delivered its judgment on 3 October 1990. It declared inadmissible - in particular - the complaint based on a violation of Articles 6 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. “... On a public-law appeal, the Federal court will consider only the complaints adequately pleaded,” it said.“ ... If the appellant’s argument, which is not very clear, has been understood correctly, the cantonal appellate court inadmissibly took into account the interview that Mr Linder had with the appellant in April 1988 in the presence of the appellant's wife, in that it completely ignored her statements’ The appellant did not, moreover, show in what way the cantonal appellate court had unsustainably interpreted the statements made by the sworn witness Jean-Gabriel Linder. The present appeal is manifestly ill-founded, and it must accordingly be dismissed in so far as it is admissible.“Mr and Mrs Ankerl left the flat in issue on 16 October 1991. The applicant’s departure is vindicated by the Supreme Court of Switzerland. ’s statement into consideration.’. The court below did not infer from those statements that the witness had indicated to the appellant that he would have to leave the flat.

It originated in an application (no. 17748/91) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swiss national, Mr Guy Ankerl, on 10 December 1990. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The President of the Court, Mr R. Ryssdal, drew by lot the names of the other seven members. The Court heard the case in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 May 1996. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr P. Boillat, Head of the European Law and International Affairs Section, Federal Office of Justice, Agent, Mr A.D. Schmidt, former judge in the Canton of Geneva, Counsel. For the Commission Mr F. Martínez, Delegate; (c) the applicant. The Court heard addresses by the applicant himself, Mr Schürmann and Mr Boill at. Mr Ankerl protested against the fact that the documents filed out of time by the Government had nonetheless been placed in the case file. Guy Ankerl and his wife moved into a flat on the second floor of no. 3, rue Saint-Léger, Geneva in 1978. He subleased the flat from a property-management company, Régie Immobilière SA (“Régie Immobsilière“), itself the tenant of a property company, SI Chrysanthemum SA. In the autumn of 1985 Mr Ruffieux became Chrysantheum’s main shareholder. In a letter of 8 May 1987 Naef gave Régie, which was in liquidation, notice to quit the flat. The applicant then applied to the Rents and Leases Conciliation Board for an extension of the agreement. Chrysanthemum brought an action for possession in the Canton of Geneva Court of First Instance, alleging that the applicant was occupying the premises unlawfully. Mr Ankerl argued that the court had no jurisdiction ratione materiae, maintaining that he had an orally agreed lease from the plaintiff. The court had to determine whether the conduct of the protagonists amounted to an agreement to enter into a lease after the termination of the subtenancy. Only the first two were heard as witnesses on oath. The transcript of the testimony reads as follows: “...Mr Jean-Gabriel Linder ... When I resumed [the management of the building in March 1988], Mr Ankersl was occupying premises but he had no written or oral lease or even a tacit one.” Mr Dominique Veuillet said: 'We knew that Mr Ankerl was in de facto occupation of the premises' He said he heard of an agreement that had earlier been made between Naef and Mr Ankerserl to the effect that he should pay the rent direct to Naef. Mr Linder added that at all events the process would be a long one, because the architect’s plans had not been approved by the Public Works Department. He also told us that during the building work we could occupy another flat in the block and that after the works we could move to another flat. The court found in favour of the tenants and ordered the landlord to pay back the rent. Landlord: I knew from the beginning that Mr Ankerl was occupying the premises. Mr Ruffieux: I would not have been opposed to a settlement at the outset. The court held that there was no lease agreement between the parties. The judge ordered Mr Ankersl to move all property and persons from the flat and restore it to the plaintiffs in good condition.“On 12 October 1989 the court held. that there were no lease agreements between the. parties and ordered Mr. Ankerls to move. all property. and persons out of the flat. The. court ordered him to. move all of the property and people from the apartment and restore. it to. the plaintiffs, as appears from a letter of 14 July 1987. Mr Ruffieux said he had never agreed, and did not wish to agree, to enter into a lease with the defendant. Mr Ankerl had been supplied personally with GPR Degenève’s account number and wrote to that company on 29 February 1988 to inform them that in future he would pay the rent into their account. The Court reaches the conclusion that, in the circumstances of this case, no lease was entered into orally (the existence of an oral agreement has not been proved) or even implied by the clear conduct of the parties. The only issue which it is necessary to resolve is whether the defendant, since his sublease was terminated, has been given a lease. Guy Ankerl appealed against the termination of his head lease. Canton of Geneva Court of Justice dismissed appeal on the grounds that there was no contractual relationship between the landlord, Chrysanthemum SA, and Guy Ankeral. It must be held that the defendant is on the premises unlawfully. Article 641 para. 2 [of the Civil Code] applies in this case ...“                  ‘I have no right to remain in the flat.’’. ‘I am the owner of the flat and I do not have any right to stay in it. ...’ ‘The landlord is entitled to raise his ownership against a subtenant and to rely on Article 6 41 para.2 [of The Civil Code], in the absence of any legal relationship between. the parties’ The First Civil Division of the Federal Court delivered its judgment on 3 October 1990. It declared inadmissible - in particular - the complaint based on a violation of Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention (art. 6, art. 14) of which the appellant makes a bald assertion without providing any explanation. “... On a public-law appeal, the. Federal Court will consider only the complaints adequately pleaded ... the notice of appeal must contain, inter alia, a. succinct statement of the constitutional rights or legal principles violated, specifying in. what the breach consists. ... In many respects, the present appeal does not comply with this requirement that reasons must be given.“ The appeal is manifestly ill-founded, and it must accordingly be dismissed in so far as it is admissible. The appellant did not, moreover, show in what way the cantonal appellate court had unsustainably interpreted the statements made by the sworn witness Jean-Gabriel Linder. The court below did not infer from those statements that the witness had indicated to the appellant that he would have to leave the flat. It merely found that Mr Linder `confirmed that he. would pass on to the landlord Guy Ankerl’s wish to enter into a new lease’. ... The present appeal is Manifestly Ill-founded.

name: Ezgin Engin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 6194/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Ezgin Engin (“the applicant”) was arrested and taken into custody on suspicion of being involved in the activities of an illegal organisation known as the DHKP-C (the Revolutionary People's Liberation Party) The applicant was brought before a single judge at the Istanbul State Security Court who ordered his pre-trial detention. The case against the applicant was subsequently resumed before the Istanbul Assize Court. The applicant is currently detained in the Kocaeli F Type Prison pending the criminal proceedings against him. The first-instance courts examined the applicant's continued detention at the end of every hearing. Each time the courts ordered his continued detention having regard to the state of evidence and the content of the file. The courts ruled that he should be held until he could be heard in court again. The case was adjourned until the next hearing on September 13. The judge ruled that the case should be heard again on September 19. The last hearing was held on September 14. The hearing concluded on September 17. The court ruled the appeal could be continued until September 21. The appeal was denied and the case was returned to the court of cassation.

On 25 December 2003 the applicant was convicted for a second time on the same charge and sentenced to life imprisonment. On 10 September 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The case is still pending before the Istanbul Assize Court. Throughout the proceedings, the first-instance courts examined the applicant's continued detention at the end of every hearing. Each time the courts ordered his continued detention having regard to the state of evidence and the content of the file. The case was adjourned to a later date to consider the application for bail. The application was denied and the case was returned to the High Court for further proceedings. The appeal has been adjourned until a later time to consider whether the applicant should be granted bail. It was also denied that the case should be transferred to the Supreme Court for a further hearing. The High Court ruled that the application should be remanded to the Court of Appeal.

The case originated in an application (no. 39678/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been denied a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal. By a decision of 2 December 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. In particular, it retained the applicant's complaint concerning the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the Diyarbakır State Security Court which tried and convicted him and declared inadmissible the remainder of his complaints. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. The applicant was charged with treason under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. On 3 July 1998 the Diyarbakır State Security Court convicted the applicant of treason and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The applicant's sentence was automatically referred to the Court of Cassation for appeal. On 27 October 1999 the court upheld the judgment and the applicant was sentenced to life in prison. He was released from prison on December 25, 2002. He is currently being held in a prison in the city of Yerevan, in the province of Bursa. He has been charged with involvement in other terrorist activities but has not yet been convicted of any crime.

name: Torsten Leander
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9248/81) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission on 2 November 1980 under Article 25. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Sweden recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. R. Ryssdal. President of the Chamber ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Swedish Government (‘the Government’), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant regarding the need for a written procedure. He directed that the lawyer and, should he so decide, the Agent should each have until 4 February 1986 to file a memorial. The applicant’s memorial was received at the registry on 3 February. On 3 April 1986, after consulting, through. the Registrar and the Agent, the Delegates and the applicant, the President directed that oral proceedings should open on 26 May 1986. On 28 April, the Commission communicated to the Registrar a number of documents whose production he had requested on the instructions of the President. On 12 May, certain additional documents furnished by the applicant were received. Torsten Leander was employed as a temporary technician at the Naval Museum at Karlskrona in the south of Sweden. The museum is adjacent to a restricted military security zone. The Government argued that the Director of the Museum had committed two mistakes in employing Mr. Leander before a personnel control had been undertaken. The Commander-in-Chief of the Navy stated that the Museum possesses several storage rooms and historical objects within the area for the security of which the Chief of the Naval Base (örlogsbaschefen) is responsible. The Court ruled in favour of the Government in the case of Mr Leander against the Director and the Museum. The Chief of the Naval Base requested a personnel control. The applicant complained to the Government and requested that the assessment of the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy be cancelled. He pointed out in particular that he had left a permanent position in Dalarna, in the North of Sweden, on being told that he was accepted for employment at the Naval Museum. “The decision whether or not to employ you is taken in a procedure distinct from the present one’, the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces wrote to the applicant in 1979.“ “If your duties at the. Naval Museum will not necessitate that you have access to the naval installations at the Sailor’s. Base, the Commander in-Chief sees no reason to oppose your employment.” The Court heard that Mr. Leander may properly be employed by the Naval Museum provided that the holder of the appointment does not require access to the Naval Base. The employment of Mr Leander during this time, 15 August - 1 September 1979, did not involve any access toThe Naval Base, the Court heard. In view of the above, the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy decided not to accept the applicant. The opinion of the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces was accompanied by a secret annex, containing the information on Mr.Leander released by the National Police Board (rikspolisstyrelsen). This annex was never communicated to the applicant and has not been included in the material submitted to the Court. The judge said Leander had not been given the opportunity to make observations about his background under the Personnel Control Ordinance. The judge said the National Police Board did not see any cause to apply this provision in the case of the applicant as no special reasons were found, and also as the registering had been effected in accordance with the secret Royal Decree. The Government rejected the whole of Leander’s complaint and did not examine his request for a revised assessment of his person. Leander has lodged no appeal with the Government in respect of appointment. His request that the Government should declare him acceptable for the provisional employment concerned cannot therefore be examined. He had not belonged to any political party since 1976. His only criminal conviction stems from his time in military service and consisted of a fine of 10 Swedish Crowns for having been late for a military parade. During his military service, in 1971-72, he had been active in the soldiers’ union and a representative at the soldiers' union conference in 1972 which, according to him, had been infiltrated by the security police. The applicant asserted however that according to unanimous statements by responsible officials, none of the above-mentioned circumstances should have been the cause for the unfavourable outcome of the personnel control. He had also beenActive in the Swedish Building Workers’ Association and had travelled a couple of times in Eastern Europe.

The case originated in an application (no. 9248/81) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission on 2 November 1980 under Article 25. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Sweden recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed violations by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 10 and 13. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality, and Mr. R. Ryssdal. President of the Chamber ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Swedish Government (“the Government’), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant regarding the need for a written procedure. On 12 December 1985, he directed that the lawyer and, should he so decide, the Agent should each have until 4 February 1986 to file a memorial. The applicant’s memorial was received at the registry on 3 February. By letter the same day, the agent of the Government stated that the Government did not intend to file any memorial. On 21 March, the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegates would present his observations at the hearing. Torsten Leander was employed as a temporary technician at the Naval Museum at Karlskrona in the south of Sweden. He alleged that on 3 September he was told to leave his work pending the outcome of a personnel control which had to be carried out on him. The Government contended that in employing Mr. Leander the Director had committed two mistakes. The post was opened for application until 28 September 1979, but Mr Leander did not apply. The applicant wrote to the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy (chefen för marinen) requesting to be informed of the reasons why he could not be employed at the Museum. The Museum possesses several storage rooms and historical objects within the area for the security. “On 22 October 1979, the applicant complained to the Government and requested that the assessment of the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy be cancelled. He pointed out in particular that he had left a permanent position in Dalarna, in the North of Sweden, on being told that he was accepted for employment at the Naval Museum’s premises.“ In his original complaint, and also in a letter of 4 December 1979, Mr. Leander further requested that he be given information about the reasons for his not being accepted’. The decision whether or not to employ you is taken in a procedure distinct from the present one. The Court heard that Mr. Leander may properly be employed by the Naval Museum provided that the holder of the appointment does not require access to the Naval Base. The Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces considers that Mr Leander can be employed. The Court was told that the National Police Board (rikspolisstyrelsen) released information on Mr.Leander to the Government. The information was never communicated to the applicant and has not been included in the material submitted to the Court. In its reply of 22 February 1980, the Board proposed that the applicant’s complaints be dismissed. It added: “The entering of information in the register of the Board's Security Department is based mainly on a 1973 Royal Decree which is secret.” “Mr. Leander replied to this opinion in a letter of 11 March 1980 to the Government, in which he argued, inter alia, that the Board should have communicated to him, at least orally and subject to a duty of confidentiality, the information kept on him.” “The Government do not examine Leander’s request for a revised assessment of his person and take no measure in regard to any other part of his petition.“ “ Leander has lodged no appeal with the Government in respect of appointment. His request that the Government should declare him acceptable for the provisional employment concerned cannot therefore be examined. During his military service, in 1971-72, he had been active in the soldiers’ union. His only criminal conviction stems from his time in military service and consisted of a fine of 10 Swedish Crowns for having been late for a military parade. The applicant asserted however that, according to unanimous statements by responsible officials, none of the above-mentioned circumstances should have been the cause for the unfavourable outcome of the personnel control. He had also beenActive in the Swedish Building Workers’ Association and he had travelled a couple of times in Eastern Europe. His application was rejected by the Court of Appeal and he will appeal the decision. The case originated in an application (no. 9248/81) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission on 2 November 1980. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Sweden recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. R. Ryssdal. President of the Chamber ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Swedish Government (“the Government’), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant regarding the need for a written procedure. On 12 December 1985, he directed that the lawyer and, should he so decide, the Agent should each have until 4 February 1986 to file a memorial. The applicant’s memorial was received at the registry on 3 February. By letter the same day, the agent of the Government stated that the Government did not intend to file any memorial. On 21 March, the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegates would present his observations at the hearing. The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The applicant, Mr. Torsten Leander, is a Swedish citizen born in 1951 and a carpenter by profession. He started to work as a temporary replacement in a post of museum technician (vikarierande museitekniker) at the Naval Museum at Karlskrona in the south of Sweden. The museum is adjacent to the Karlskurra Naval Base which is a restricted military security zone. The applicant maintained before the Court that the intention was that he should work for ten months in this post, while its ordinary holder was on leave. He alleged that on 3 September he was told to leave his work pending the outcome of a personnel control which had to be carried out. “On 22 October 1979, the applicant complained to the Government and requested that the assessment of the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy be cancelled’ “If your duties at the Naval Museum will not. necessitate that you have access to the naval installations at the. Naval Base, the Chief of the Naval Base requested a personnel control. The control carried out has provided such grounds for the. Commander- in-Chief’s assessment of you from a security point of view that the decision. has been taken not to accept you.“ “The decision whether or not to employ you is taken in a procedure distinct from the present one’ The application for employment with the Naval Museum in 1979 did not involve any access to the Naval Base. The Commander-in-Chief of the Navy has said that he does not oppose such employment. In view of the above and the fact that Mr. Leander would have access to secret installations and information, he decided not to accept the applicant. The opinion of the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces was accompanied by a secret annex, containing the information on Mr Leander released by the National Police Board (rikspolisstyrelsen). This annex was never communicated to the applicant and has not been included in the material submitted to the Court. Government rejected the whole of the applicant’s complaint. In its operative parts, the decision read: “The question whether or not a person is suitable for certain employment can only be examined by the Government in the context of a complaint about the appointment to a post. Leander has lodged no appeal in respect of appointment. His request that the Government should declare him acceptable for the provisional employment concerned cannot therefore be examined.” Leander maintained before the Court that he still did not know the content of the secret information recorded on him. At the relevant time, he had not belonged to any political party since 1976. Earlier he had been a member of the Swedish Communist Party. He had been active in the soldiers’ union and a representative at a conference in 1972. His only criminal conviction stems from his time in military service and consisted of a fine of 10 Swedish Crowns for having been late for a military parade. The applicant asserted however that, according to unanimous statements by responsible officials, none of the above-mentioned circumstances should have been the cause for the unfavourable outcome of the personnel control. He had travelled a couple of times in Eastern Europe and had been involved in the Swedish Building Workers’ Association and had travelled to Eastern Europe as a result of his membership of these organisations. He was found guilty of misconduct in public office and sentenced to 12 months in prison.

name: Mustafa Nazif Dildar
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 77361/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, in particular, about the excessive length of the civil proceedings, the non-enforcement of the court decision, as well as the authorities’ subsequent delay in paying the additional compensation awarded by the domestic courts. name: Halil Kızılöz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32962/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court. The Court declared the remainder of the applicant’s complaints inadmissible. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. Mr Rıza Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr Feyyaz Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge. The applicant was arrested on 1 December 1980 in Ankara in possession of false identity cards and weapons. The applicant was suspected of membership of an illegal organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) The applicant denied the allegations but admitted that the weapons and bullets found in his possession belonged to him. He was remanded in custody until his trial in the Ankara Martial Law Court (sıkıyönetim mahkemesi) in 1985. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to 13 years and 4 months’ imprisonment and permanently debarred him from working. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) The case was reviewed and reduced to ten years' imprisonment. The case involved employment in the civil service for offences under Article 168 § 1 of the Criminal Code and Article 17 of Law no. 1402. The applicant was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of £3,000. The appeal was rejected on 2 November 1995. The decision was quashed on 3 November 1996. The judge ruled that the applicant was entitled to appeal the decision. The verdict was overturned on 6 November 1997. The ruling was upheld on 9 November 1998. The sentence was reduced to five years' jail.

name: Mark Wilkinson
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they did not have a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. On 31 May 1999 the Commission found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Government referred the cases to the Court to seek a ruling pursuant to Article 41 on what just satisfaction, if any, should be awarded to the applicants. The applications were then allocated to the Third Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted. Sir Nicolas Bratza, the judge elected in respect of the United Kingdom, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28) The hearing was convened pursuant to the Army Act 1955. Both applicants were serving in the army and were tried by district courts-martial. Mr Wilkinson pleaded guilty to the armed forces’ disciplinary offence of absence without leave (contrary to section 38(a) of the Army act) Mr Allen pleaded guilty. to two charges of possession of controlled drugs contrary to the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, these being civilian criminal offences. The Army Board reduced the custodial element of his sentence to six months’ imprisonment. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine).

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. name: Charles Bernard O’Neill
train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 41516/10 and 75702/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The first applicant was born in 1962 and is currently detained in HMP Glenochil in Scotland. He was represented by McClure Collins Solicitors, a firm of solicitors practising in Glasgow. The second applicant, born in 1976, is currently imprisoned in HMC Edinburgh. The applicants’ complaints concerning the length of their criminal proceedings were communicated to the Government on 13 November 2012 and 17 December 2012 respectively. They were sentenced to periods of imprisonment of eight years and six years respectively following their conviction for various sexual offences. The complainer in relation to some of those offences was A.M’s son. Both applicants were detained by the police under section 14 of the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995 and removed to Queen Street Police Office in Aberdeen. On the same day the applicants were interviewed separately by police officers for over five hours. During these interviews they were directly accused of the murder of A.M. Both applicants asked police officers if they were going to be charged with the murder, but received indications to the contrary. Following the interviews, neither applicant was arrested or charged with any offence owing to insufficient evidence. The applicants were released from custody on licence on 22 May 2003 and 18 January 2002 respectively. They both travelled to Spain without notification, thereby breaching the terms of their parole licence in contravention of the Sex Offenders Act 1997. The applicants were charged with the murder of A.M. and with concealing and disposing of her body in an attempt to pervert the course of justice. They appeared on petition at Kilmarnock Sheriff Court were they were committed for further examination and remanded in custody. In late 2005 Crown Counsel had concerns regarding the sufficiency of evidence against the second applicant. On 19 December 2005 the Crown decided to take ‘no proceedings meantime’ with regard to the 2005 petition. By November 2006 both applicants had served the custodial element of their earlier criminal sentences and were released from prison. They both travelled to live in Scotland. A.M. disappeared in Spain in 2007 and returned to the UK in November 2007. The police continued to conduct periodic reviews of the decision to take "no proceedings meantime" in respect of the 2005 petition. Central Scotland Police formed ‘Operation Aspen’ to look for evidence of further sexual offending by the applicants. New evidence came to light concerning the circumstances of A.M’s disappearance and the applicants’ sexual offending. Crown Counsel concluded that there had been a material change in the prospects of securing a conviction against both applicants on the murder charges contained in the earlier 2005 petition on 9 September 2008. On 10 September 2008 the applicants were served with an indictment which contained the same charges. The applicants were convicted on numerous counts and sentenced to periods of imprisonment ranging from eight to ten years to run concurrently. They unsuccessfully sought to appeal against conviction and sentence. The applicants’ trials took place between 19 April 2010 and 13 May 2010. They were sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, with a tariff of thirty years for the first applicant and twenty-six year for the second applicant. The first applicant also argued that the murder charge against him should be dismissed for reason of delay. The High Court dismissed the minute as the arguments advanced by the second. applicant related to unreasonable delay and not to missing evidence (which was the argument raised in the original minute). The applicants appealed against conviction and sentence. were also sentenced to concurrent sentences of eight years imprisonment for attempting to pervert the course of justice. The main issue before the Supreme Court was whether the applicants could be said to have been “charged’ on 17 September 1998 or whether the appropriate “starting point” for the purposes of Article 6§1 was 5 April 2005. The court assessed the evidence in light of the relevant case-law of the domestic courts and of this Court. The applicants sought leave to appeal to the. Supreme Court against the Appeal Court’s refusal to grant leave to. appeal on the additional grounds. The applicants had been subjected to questioning on 17 September 1998 that might have affected their right to a fair trial. The court concluded that the correct “starting point” in the applicants’ proceedings was 5 April 2005 and the case was remitted to the Appeal Court. The Appeal Court dismissed the first applicant’s appeal against conviction and sentence on 27 March 2014, and the second applicant”s appeal on 19 June 2014. The case was heard at the Supreme Court in London and the appeal was dismissed on 27 May 2014 and on 19 May 2014, respectively. The appeal was adjourned until the second appeal was heard in July 2014.

The court concluded that the correct “starting point” in the applicants’ proceedings was 5 April 2005 and the case was remitted to the Appeal Court. The Appeal Court dismissed the first applicant’s appeal against conviction and sentence on 27 March 2014, and the second applicant”s appeal on 19 June 2014. name: Raja Arlewin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22302/10) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been deprived of effective access to court and that the State had failed to provide him with sufficient protection against allegations that violated his right to privacy. The application was communicated to the Government on 5 March 2012. In the show, the applicant, who was unknown to the broader public, appeared in pictures and was mentioned by name. He was singled out as the central figure of organised crime within media and advertising. The applicant brought a private prosecution against X for gross defamation, claiming damages in the amount of 250,000 Swedish kronor (SEK; approximately 27,000 euros) X disputed the claim on the grounds, inter alia, that he was not the responsible editor of the show and that he enjoyed the freedom to communicate information. The Stockholm District Court dismissed the claim in so far as it was based on the Constitutional Law. It referred to the Supreme Court judgment in an almost identical case, NJA 2002 p. 314 (see paragraphs 28-31 below), and held that Chapters 1-9 of the Constitutional law were not Article 6 of the Convention. The Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) upheld the District Court’s decision. It held that the issue for it to determine was whether the general provisions in the Constitutional Law were applicable to the programme in question. This was because the programme had first been sent by satellite link to Viasat Broadcasting UK Ltd, the British company responsible for the programme content, and thereafter uplinked to a satellite, which had in turn transmitted the programme to viewers in Sweden. As Chapters 1-9 of the Constitutional law were not applicable, X could not be held responsible for programme content under Chapter 6 of the Penal Code. The Brussels I Regulation entitled a person claiming non-contractual damages to bring actions where the harmful event occurred. The position hitherto taken by the Swedish courts ran contrary to Community law. The applicant subsequently withdrew his remaining claims before the District Court since there was no practical prospect of success in a continued procedure. He was convicted of aggravated fraud as well as tax and bookkeeping offences and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. The criminal proceedings were finalised by a Supreme Court decision to refuse leave to appeal on 4 October 2010. These proceedings, in particular their compliance with Articles 6 and 7 of the Convention, are the subject of an application lodged with the Court on 4 April 2011 (no. 32814/11)
