name: Magdalena Witek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13453/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her detention in a psychiatric hospital had been unlawful and in breach of Article 5 § 1 of the convention. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court ruled on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (former Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, now Article 29 = 1). The applicant was ordered to stay in a psychiatric hospital in October 2001 after evading justice for five years. On 19 June 2006 the Kielce Regional Court resumed the enforcement proceedings as regards the judgment of October 2001. The applicant was subsequently admitted to the Lublin Hospital on 23 September 2006. days after her arrival there. The court referred to the experts' opinion of 2000, which stressed that the applicant had behaved aggressively during her period under psychiatric observation in Morawica Hospital (in 2000) The court held that it was necessary to continue the applicant's detention in the psychiatric hospital. On 15 January 2007 the applicant filed an appeal against that decision. She stressed that over the previous five years her health had significantly improved and her relations with her mother were very good. The Kielce District Court ordered the applicant's release from hospital. The court did not agree with the expert psychiatrists opinions of 20 July 2007, 16 August 2007 and 25 September 2007 maintaining that the applicant should be kept in a psychiatric hospital. On the prosecutor's appeal, on 16 November 2007 theKielce Regional Court upheld the first-instance decision. The applicant was released from hospital on the same day. The probability of the applicant committing another similar offence was very low. Since 2002 the applicant had never behaved aggressively towards her and their relations were very good. It referred to the applicant’s mother's testimonies confirming that since 2002 theApplicant had never acted aggressively against her.

name: Jacek Dombek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 75107/01) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning alleged unlawfulness and length of the applicant’s detention on remand to the Government. The applicant, Jacek Dombek, was born in 1965 and lives in Gdańsk, Poland. He was detained in 1996 and 1997 in connection with the same criminal investigation. The applicant and 14 co-accused were indicted before the Bydgoszcz Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). The applicant’s trial started on 24 August 1999 and continued for three days. The court considered that the investigation could not be terminated earlier due to circumstances for which the authorities couldn't be held responsible, such as the complexity of the case and the seriousness of the offences. It appears that the hearing was subsequently adjourned. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed an application made by the Prosecutor General under Article 263 of the 1997 Code of Criminal Procedure (“1997 Code”) On 22 September 1999 the applicant’s lawyer submitted pleadings to the Supreme Court in which he argued that the applicant had been illegally detained. A session on prolongation of the applicant's detention had been scheduled for 1 October 1999. The Court of Appeal granted the application and prolonged the applicant.‘Of course, the applicant is guilty,’ said the judge. ‘There is a particular reason why the pre-trial detention of [the applicant] should not be lifted. From the information obtained by the Presiding Judge it appears that [ the applicant] might obstruct the proceedings.’ ‘From the information ... it appears ... that [he] might obstruction the proceedings,” the judge added. The applicant was arrested by the police in connection with criminal proceedings pending against him on 11 September 1991. On 27 September 2001 the Bydgoszcz Regional Court gave judgment. The trial court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. The applicant and the prosecutor appealed. On 17 June 2003 the Gdansk Court of Appeal allowed the appeals and quashed the impugned judgment. However, the applicant had not been released as he remained in pre-trial detention ordered in the second set of criminal proceedings (see below) The proceedings are pending before the Zielona Góra Regional Court. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to twenty-five years’ imprisonment in 2005. The applicant was released from detention in 2011. The trial court gave judgment on the applicant’s case on 28 April 2005. On 24 January 1996 the Poznań Court of Appeal quashed the impugned judgment and remitted the case to the Regional Prosecutor. On 13 March 2003 the applicant was indicted before the Zielona Góra Regional Court. The court held that the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged, the severity of the anticipated sentence and the need to secure the proper conduct of the investigation justified keeping the applicant in detention.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the administrative courts had failed to hold an oral hearing in proceedings relating to his request for occupational injury compensation. In a decision of 3 June 2008, the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint to the Government. The Court also decided to examine the merits of this complaint at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1) The applicant was born in 1930 and lives in Ingarö. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Stockholm, claiming that his injuries had been caused by his work in Sweden. In support, he submitted a medical certificate from Dr S.R., who had been working as a company doctor for more than 20 years in the food industry. The doctor, who was a specialist in orthopaedics, gave his opinion on 23 September 1997. It was based on the information in the Office’s case-file and stated essentially the following. It appeared from other medical certificates that the applicant had been healthy until his hip joint problems began in 1985-86. In 1988 his right hip and lower back had been x-rayed, which showed that the hip joint had degenerative alterations. The County Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s appeal. It did not question that his work at the slaughterhouse had caused his injuries. In support of his appeal, he submitted a medical certificate by Dr P.H., specialist in orthopaedic surgery, who had treated the applicant. Dr S.H. said that the applicant suffered from moderate arthritis in his hip joint, which had developed slowly from the age of 55 and thus was age-related, not work-related. The applicant was given three weeks in which to finalise his submissions. On 29 June 1999, the applicant renewed his request for an oral hearing but sent on the same day a fax to the court explaining that he did not request an Oral hearing. The court found that the applicant had failed to show that there was a high level of probability that his work at the slaughterhouse had caused his hip joint arthritis. The applicant made a further appeal to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) in Stockholm, maintaining his claims and adding that he wanted an oral hearing to be held so that he could prove his case. The Office disputed the applicant’s appeal and the new medical certificate, submitting that the appeal should be rejected. The court granted the applicant two weeks to finalise his submissions in the case. Subsequently, on 24 September 2001, the Administrative court of Appeal rejected the appeal. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) and requested that an oral hearing be held. He stressed that the lower courts had failed to hold a hearing, despite his express request and in violation of Article 6 of the Convention. He submitted that a hearing was necessary in order for him to describe his working conditions at the slaughterhouse and to be able to question specialists to clarify his injuries and their causes. On 10 November 2003 the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal. It gave the applicant three weeks to submit any additional comments. The case was decided on 16 July 2003 and the appeal was dismissed.

name: Taner Kılıç
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 70845/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the search carried out at the applicant’s home and office, the confiscation of videotapes during the search and a lack of legal remedies in this respect, to the Government. The Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant was represented by Mr O.K. Cengiz, a lawyer practising in İzmir. On 19 June 1999 police officers carried out a simultaneous search of all the premises mentioned in the letter of the Under-Secretary of State, including the applicant’s home and law office. The applicant filed a petition with Principal Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation, alleging an abuse of power by the Public Prosecutor and the police officers who carried out the search. He complained that, by extending the search warrant issued by the State Security Court, the public prosecutor had exceeded his authority. On 7 February 2000 the Principal Public prosecutor held that there was no need to act on the petition charging the Under Secretary of State with an Abuse of power. In May 2004 all the items confiscated during the search of 19 June 1999 were returned to the headquarters of Mazlumder. The applicant subsequently retrieved his video cassettes. In March 2003 the Public Prosecutor at the Ankara State Security Court gave a decision of non-prosecution in respect of the General Secretary of the Association. The materials seized did not reveal any criminal intention or activity, but the materials seized should be considered as evidence and that they should therefore be retained. In May 2004 the materials confiscated were returned and the applicant retrieved hisVideo cassettes, which he had been given when the search was carried out in June 1999. He filed a petition with the Public prosecutor to return the videotapes, which had been seized in the search. The application was dismissed.

name: John Hirst
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40787/98) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that there had been undue delay between the reviews by the Parole Board of his continued detention as a prisoner serving a sentence of discretionary life imprisonment. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 21 March 2000, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights. The applicant was sentenced to 15 years in prison in 1989. He was transferred to a Category B prison in 1993. In 1994, the Secretary of State decided to transfer him to Category C prison. The Parole Board decided it would not be safe to release the applicant. A psychiatric report issued about the same time stated that the applicant’s personality, described as psychopathic, had shown some capacity for change. The applicant agreed to follow and successfully completed a drugs awareness course in July 1996. In July 1996, he was released from prison on licence. He remained in prison for two years before being transferred back to Category D (open prison) He was released on licence in September 1996. The DLP did not recommend release but transfer to a Category D prison. following a long period of institutionalisation and a lack of family support. The applicant applied for leave to apply for judicial review of both decisions, alleging inter alia that the DLP had wrongly applied an ‘exceptional circumstances’ test. Leave was refused on 11 April 1997. On 21 October 1997, the applicant re-applied for leave for. judicial review. Mr Justice Potts refused leave against the. DLP’s recommendation. He found the D LP had correctly applied the statutory test concerning a risk to the public. He granted leave to applied in respect of the decision of the Secretary of State. The applicant was granted leave by the Secretary of State on 20 November 1997. Reports continued to note his progress, including the expression of genuine remorse for his offending. The DLP again considered the applicant’s case on 15 July 1998, the DLP declined to recommend release but did recommend transfer to a Category D (open) prison. “In reaching the decision that you are not yet suitable for release, the panel took into account the nature of the index offence, your violent disruptive early prison career (while recognising also the absence of any violence since 1989)”. The panel considered that you still presented too great a risk to the public to justify your release. The panel did recommend that you be transferred to open conditions. It considered that you would be unable to cope in the community, were you to be released directly or via a pre-release employment scheme. In coming to this conclusion, the panel took into account the length of time you have spent in custody, the opinion of the majority of the report writers and witnesses that the risk you present to the public could be safely managed in open conditions and the fact that the assessment and further work referred to above can be done in open Conditions. The Secretary of State rejected the DLP’s recommendation. He agreed that a full personality assessment was required of the applicant who was still seen as having a psychopathic personality. He noted that the applicant had failed to attend further courses in anger management, social skills and communications. The Court of Appeal rejected his application for leave to apply for judicial review. The applicant’s request to amend his grounds of application to add complaints about a lack of independence was refused. It was however agreed that his next review should take place in July 2000. The application was listed for hearing before the Court of appeal on 2 February 2000. It had been dormant since 21 October 1997, but had been pending since October 1996, when the DLP issued its decision. The DLP's decision of October 1996 was appealed against by the applicant. The appeal was dismissed on 3 February 2000, and the applicant was allowed to leave the prison in August 2000. He was released from the prison on 2 November 2000.

train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the grant of immunity in civil proceedings to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the case of Mr Jones amounted to a disproportionate interference with their right of access to a court under Article 6. The Redress Trust (REDRESS), Amnesty International, the International Centre for the Legal Protection of human Rights (Interights) and Justice were given leave by the President of the Chamber to intervene in the written procedure. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility of the applications at the same time. Three men claim they were tortured in Saudi Arabia. One claims he was beaten with a cane on his hands, feet, arms and legs. The other two allege they were sexually assaulted. The case was taken to the High Court, but the case was thrown out of court. It was decided the case should be heard in the Middle East Court of Appeal. The judge ruled that the case could not be heard by the UK courts as the case had been brought in the middle of a foreign country. The appeal was eventually dismissed on the grounds that the claim was a trumped-up case, and that the US courts had no authority to hear the case. The two cases were joined and on 28 October 2004 the Court of Appeal published its judgment. It unanimously dismissed Mr Jones’s appeal from the decision of the Master to refuse permission to serve Saudi Arabia outside the jurisdiction. However, it allowed the appeals in respect of the refusal of permission in each case to serve the individual defendants. The applicants appealed to the Court. of Appeal with the leave of the master. The Court of. Appeal judgment was published on October 28, 2004. It upheld the immunity of Saudi Arabia, but allowed the appeal to be heard by the. Master. The Master ruled that the applications relating to Mr. Jones should be heard separately. The appeal to the Master was dismissed by the Master. Mance LJ did not accept that the definition of torture in Article 1 of the Convention against Torture was fatal to the applicants’ claims. He noted that the House of Lords in Pinochet (No. 3) had considered that there would be no immunity from criminal prosecution in respect of an individual officer who had committed torture abroad in an official context. He did not consider it significant that Lieutenant Colonel Abdul Aziz had been described in Mr Jones’s claim as the “servant or agent” of Saudi Arabia. Nor did he accept that general differences between criminal and civil law justified a distinction in the application of immunity in the two contexts. Mance LJ considered that whether any claim in the English courts against individuals could proceed was better determined not by reference to immunity. He considered it impossible to identify any settled international principle affording the State the right to claim immunity in respect of claims directed against an official, rather than against the State, its Head of State or diplomats. He was of the view that the legislation and case-law of the United States of America (see paragraphs 112-25 below) militated strongly against any such settled principle and supported a contrary view. He noted the dicta in the separate opinion of Judges Higgins, Kooijmans and Buergenthal to the judgment of the International Court of Justice. Mance LJ concluded that giving blanket effect to a foreign State’s claim to State immunity ratione materiae in respect of a State official alleged to have committed acts of systematic torture could deprive the right of access to a court under Article 6 of real meaning. He therefore allowed the applicants’ appeals inrespect of the individual defendants and remitted them for further argument. In his concurring judgment, Lord Phillips agreed with the conclusions of Mance L J as regards both the claim against Saudi Arabia and the claims against the individual officials. In particular, he considered that the judgment in Pinochet (No. 3) (see paragraphs 44-56 below) had shown that torture could no longer fall within the scope of the official duties of a state official. Saudi Arabia appealed to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal in respect of the individual defendants. Mr Jones appealed against the. decision inrespect of his claim against Saudi Arabia itself. Lord Bingham considered that there was a ‘wealth of authority’ in the United Kingdom and elsewhere to show that a State was entitled to claim immunity for its servants or agents. In some borderline cases there could be doubt whether the. conduct of an individual had a sufficient connection with a State to entitle it to claim. immunity for his conduct. However, in his view, these were not borderline cases. The fact that conduct was unlawful or objectionable was not, of itself, a ground for refusing immunity. Lord Bingham disagreed with the applicants’ submission that torture could not be a governmental or official act. Under Article 1 of the Convention against Torture, torture had to be inflicted by or with the connivance of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity. The applicants referred to a substantial body of authority showing that the courts of the United States would not recognise acts performed by individual officials as being carried out for the purposes of immunity. Lord Bingham considered the first to be of slight legal authority, the second to be an obiter dictum and the third not to be a accurate statement of international law. It was not necessary to examine those authorities since they were only important to the extent that they expressed principles widely shared and observed among other nations. Lord Bingham said the prohibition of torture did not automatically override all other rules of international law. Article 14 of the Convention against Torture did not provide for universal civil jurisdiction. The 2004 United Nations Convention on Jurisdictional Immunities of States and Their Property (see paragraphs 75-80 below) did not provides any exception from immunity for civil claims based on acts of torture. There was no evidence that States had recognised or given effect to any international-law obligation to exercise universal jurisdiction over claims arising from alleged breaches of peremptory norms. For these reasons, Lord Bingham agreed with the Court of Appeal that the claim brought by Mr Jones against Saudi Arabia was to be dismissed. The prosecution of a servant or agent for an act of torture within article 1 of the Torture Convention is founded on an express exception from the general rule of immunity. It is, however, clear that a civil action against individual torturers based on acts of official torture does indirectly implead the state since their acts are attributable to it. Were these claims against the individual defendants to proceed and be upheld, the interests of the Kingdom would be obviously affected, even though it is not a named party. The distinction between criminal proceedings and civil proceedings was, he said, “fundamental” and one that could not be “wished away”. Lord Hoffmann said international law did not require immunity against civil suit to be accorded to officials who were alleged to have committed torture. He said: “To hold that for the purposes of state immunity [the official] was not acting in an official capacity would produce an asymmetry between the rules of liability and immunity” He also considered inappropriate the Court of Appeal’s proposed approach to the exercise of jurisdiction, on the ground that State immunity was not a self-imposed restriction but was “imposed by international law without any discrimination between one State and another” Lord Hoffmann concluded that it would be “invidious in the extreme for the judicial branch of government to have the power to decide that it will allow the investigation of allegations of torture against the officials of one foreign state but not against those of another’

train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 43748/98) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand had been unreasonably long. By a decision of 21 October 2004, the Court declared the application partly admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1) The applicant was born in 1946 and lives in Radom. He was arrested on 24 August 1994 on suspicion of extorting protection money from an escort agency. On 24 October 1994 the Gdańsk Regional Prosecutor ordered the applicant to be released on bail. On 10 November 1994 the Gdańsk Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention on remand until 21 January 1995. The court pointed out that the investigation had not yet been completed and that the group the applicant belonged to had brought improper pressure upon the witnesses to change their testimony. On 21 November 1994 an expert opinion on the state of the applicant's mental health was issued. On 17 January 1995 the GDAńsko Regional Court prolonged the appeal against the extension of the detention until 31 March 1995. On 5 April 1995 the applicant and his lawyer appealed against this decision. The appeal was dismissed on 9 March 1995 and the applicant was released on bail until 30 June 1995. On 27 June 1995 the bill of indictment was lodged with the Gdańsk Regional Court against the applicant and eleven co-accused. Appeal upheld it, referring to the seriousness of the offence in question and the complexity of the case. The court remarked that the negative effect of the continuing detention upon his family situation was not such as to call for his release. On 15 March 1996, in a separate set of criminal proceedings, the applicant was sentenced by the Elbląg Regional Court to two and a half years imprisonment and a fine. He served his sentence between 15 March1996 and 11 September 1997. The application for bail was filed in Gdańsk Regional Court in November 1996. The Regional Court requested the Supreme Court to prolong the applicant’s detention until 30 June 1997. The Supreme Court granted the Regional Court's request on 16 January 1997, pointing to the complexity of the case. The hearing scheduled for 11 June 1997 was adjourned due to the absence of some of the lawyers. On 13 August 1997 the Supreme court, relying on the grounds given above, prolonged the applicant's detention. However, the limit of the duration of the detention was set at 1 December 1997 and not at 31 December 1997 as the regional court had requested. Hearing scheduled for 1 October 1997 was adjourned because of the illness of the judge rapporteur. Gdańsk Regional Court requested the Supreme Court to prolong the applicant’s detention on remand until 30 April 1998. On 22 October 2002 the court gave a judgment by which the applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. The court decided to exclude two of the co-accused who would not appear at the hearings. The case was complex and multi-layered and the charges of a serious nature. In addition, some of the accused had contributed to the overall length of the proceedings by lodging motions with the court.

On 10 November 1994 the Gdańsk Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention on remand until 21 January 1995. The court pointed out that the investigation had not yet been completed and that the group the applicant belonged to had brought improper pressure upon the witnesses to change their testimony. On 12 April 1995 he was ordered to undergo psychiatric observation. On 9 March 1995 the prosecutor dismissed the lawyer's appeal against the decision, relying on the grounds previously invoked by the courts. The bill of indictment was lodged against the applicant and eleven co-accused on 27 June 1995. Appeal upheld it, referring to the seriousness of the offence in question and the complexity of the case. He was sentenced by the Elbląg Regional Court to two and a half years imprisonment and a fine. He served his sentence between 15 March 1996 and 11 September 1997. The application was dismissed because conditions for release referred to in Article 218 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not satisfied. Gdańsk Regional Court requested the Supreme Court to prolong the applicant’s detention until 30 June 1997. The Supreme Court granted the request on 16 January 1997, but the limit of the duration of the detention was set at 1 December 1997 and not at 31 December 1997 as the Regional Court had requested. The hearing scheduled for 11 June 1997 was adjourned due to the absence of some of the lawyers. The court did not allow the applicant's request for release. On 16 September 1997 the GdaŅk Regional Court refused to release the applicant, observing that he had failed to indicate any new relevant circumstances in the case. Hearing scheduled for 1 October 1997 was adjourned because of the illness of the judge rapporteur. The Supreme Court observed that a number of hearings had not been held due to the absence of either the co-accused or their defence counsel. On 22 October 2002 the court gave a judgment by which the applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. The case was complex and multi-layered and the charges were of a serious nature. The applicant was released under police supervision on 30 April 1998. The court decided to exclude two of the co.accused who would not appear at the hearings. It found that in view of the seriousness of the offence he was charged with, the strong probability of his guilt and the danger that he (or another member of the group) would exert additional pressure on the witnesses, the applicant's detention was warranted. An expert opinion on the state of the applicants mental health was issued on 21 November 1994. On 5 April 1995 the applicant and his lawyer appealed against this decision. The bill of indictment was lodged with the Gdańsk Regional Court against the applicant and eleven co-accused on 27 June 1995. Appeal upheld it, referring to the seriousness of the offence in question and the complexity of the case. The court refused, considering that his detention was justified by the existence of strong evidence of his guilt, the nature of the charges against him and a risk of interference with witnesses in order to influence their testimony. He was sentenced by the Elbląg Regional Court to two and a half years imprisonment and a fine. He served his sentence between 15 March 1996 and 11 September 1997. train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’s Convention”) by five Spanish nationals. The applicants submitted that they had not had a fair hearing in the judicial proceedings brought by them to halt construction of the Itoiz dam. They also complained that the Autonomous Community law in question had been enacted with a view to preventing execution of a Supreme Court judgment which had become final. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27) The case originated in an engineering project of February 1989 for the construction of a dam in Itoiz (Navarre province) which would result in the flooding of three nature reserves and a number of small villages. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applications were dismissed on 1 April 2003. The appeal was based on several allegations of unlawfulness which, in their opinion, had tainted the project. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the applicants did not have ‘victim’ status and had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. The case was referred to the Audiencia Nacional. The Audiencia Nacional partly upheld the appeal, considering in particular that, according to the law, the planned dam should have been based on the national hydrological plan, which had not been drawn up when the project was approved. The court also accepted the request for precise designation of the protection zones around the nature reserves affected by the dam. By a decision of 24 January 1996, the Audiencias granted a suspension order but directed that the necessary measures be taken to ensure the completion of work already begun. On 17 June 1996 the parliament of the Autonomous Community of Navarre (parlamento foral de Navarra) passed Autonomous community law (foral) no. 9/1996 on natural sites in Navarre. The Supreme Court definitively cancelled the dam project in so far as it concerned the 500-metre protection zones around nature reserves RN 9, 10 and 11. As a result of the judgment, the size of the planned dam, and thus of the area to be flooded, was reduced, so that the village of Itoiz, where the applicants' immovable property was located, was saved from flooding. In application of the Supreme Court's judgment, by a decision of 4 September 1997, the Audiencia Nacional declared final the interim enforcement measures ordered on 6 March 1996 concerning the prohibition on filling the reservoir and other related work. The applicant association contested the authorities' argument, claiming that the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was inapplicable in the instant case. By a decision of 21 May 1998, the Constitutional Court declared the application inadmissible on account of certain errors in its presentation which could nonetheless be corrected. In order to rectify the above-mentioned errors, the Audiencia Nacional summoned the parties on 28 May 1998 so that it could hear their submissions. Under section 37(2) of the Judicature Act, it gave notice of the questions to the Chamber of Deputies, the Senate, the government and parliament of Navarre and the Spanish government. The Audiencia Nacional forwarded to the Constitutional Court the written pleadings submitted by the applicant association during the proceedings before it. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. The Constitutional Court's judgment of 14 March 2000 held that the impugned provisions of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 were compatible with the Constitution. It observed at the outset that enforcement of the Supreme Court's judgement of 14 July 1997 had become impossible since the entry into force of the new law. The Court also ruled that, given the significance of the question raised by the Itoiz dam's construction, which could not simply be ignored, it was justifiable that the explanatory memorandum accompanying the law specifically mentioned the aim and means of environmental protection in the peripheral protection zones around the three nature reserves. The Constitutional Court examined whether the impossibility of executing the Supreme Court's judgment as a consequence of the enactment of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was justified in view of the values and assets protected by the Constitution. It found that the balance of general interests had been respected and that there was no clear lack of proportion between the conflicting interests. The Constitutional Court further noted that the system of peripheral protection zones introduced by this new law had not in itself been considered arbitrary in the Audiencia Nacional's decision. It added that the new law did not amount to ad causam legislation, being general in form and in substance, and pointed out that the impugned provisions could not be held to be contrary to Article 24 of the constitution. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. The judgment was published in the Official Gazette on 14 April 2000. It was. out that laws could be challenged before the Constitutional Court through the remedy provided for in Article 163 of the Constitution. Accordingly, the Constitutional. Court dismissed the application for an initial ruling on the legality of a law that had been passed by the Supreme Court of Justice. The decision was published on 14 April 2000, and was. in the Official Gazette on 14 April 2000. The court ruled that the law was constitutional and that it cannot be challenged in the Constitutional Court.

name: Filiz Uyan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 7496/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Ms Filiz Uyan (“the applicant”) was represented by Mrs I.G. Kireçkaya, a lawyer practising in İzmir. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. The applicant had been convicted of being a member of a terrorist organisation and sentenced to twenty-two years’ imprisonment. She was taken to a hospital by three male security officers (two gendarmes and a male prison guard) and one female prison guard in order to undergo an ultrasound scan by a gynaecologist. She refused to be examined in such conditions. The proceedings against the male prison guard were dropped on 3 December 2001. The Turkish Medical Association quashed that decision on 5 October 2002. On 23 January 2003 the İzmir Medical Association issued the doctor with a warning for professional misconduct, namely for not taking the initiative to request the male security officers to leave the consultation room or remove the applicant’s handcuffs, as required by ethical rules. The applicant objected to that decision and on 29 July 2002 the Karşıyaka Assize Court dismissed the applicant's appeal against that decision. The charges against the gendarme officers were dropped by the Buca District Governor on 28 December 2001 on the basis that the allegations were unsubstantiated.

It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The Court ruled in favour of the applicant and awarded him TRL 3,117,228,5260 in respect of pecuniary damage, plus default interest. On 24 May 2005 the Council of State upheld the judgment. On 9 September 2005 the applicant requested rectification. On 10 December 2007 the Court of State dismissed the applicant's request. The applicant was notified of this on 7 February 2008. The application was dismissed and the applicant was not notified until 8 February 2009. The case was adjourned until the end of January 2009, when the judge's decision was made final. The judge awarded the applicant $1,000,000 in damages. The award was based on a judgment made by the court on May 24, 2005. It was later reduced to $1.00, and the appeal was dismissed on December 10, 2007.

name: Kamuran Alican
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21868/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application concerns the wounding of the first applicant, who was eleven years old at the time, and the death of the second and third applicants' sons, who were fourteen and thirteen years old respectively. The applicants were represented by Mr F. Gümüş, a lawyer practising in Diyarbakır. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented in the case by their Agent. The children were grazing their sheep in the field when they found an object with an iron head which looked like a bullet. The first applicant left the other two children to find water while they were trying to hit the iron head with pieces of metal. At that moment the bullet exploded. As a result of the explosion, the first applicant suffered partial loss of the sight of one eye and the total loss of sight in the other. The criminal investigation into the incident was launched on 23 April 1994. On 6 May 1997 the military prosecutor gave a decision that there was no need to initiate criminal proceedings on the ground that there had been no fault or negligence attributable to anyone except the children. The case was brought against the Ministry of the Interior for compensation. The Ministry appealed. The Supreme Administrative Court quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on the ground that the latter had failed to determine which administrative entity had responsibility for compensating the applicant. The court was bound by the amount requested by the applicant for pecuniary damage. The Van Administrative Court, basing its decision on the doctrine of ‘social risk’, awarded the applicant's claim in full. The case was heard at the Supreme Court of Justice in Istanbul in 2001. The judge ruled in favour of the second applicant and awarded the third applicant TRL 500,000,000 for loss of income on the death of their sons. The explosion occurred in an area where rockets are launched. Yet the origin of the grenade which caused the explosion is unknown. The rocket launcher in question is frequently used by members of the PKK terrorist organisation. The grenade might have been left by terrorists who attacked the barracks. It should be concluded that the damage in the present case was not caused by the activities of military forces but rather by terrorist activities. ... The plaintiff should therefore be paid his claim in full, TRL 1,000,000,.0000 for pecuniary damage... although according to the expert reports, pec uniary damage could amount to TRL 19,237,229,0000. ... As regards non-pecuniary. damage, the plaintiff should be awarded TRL 100,000.000. In respect of Ramazan Alican, the court awarded the applicant a certain amount of compensation. The court quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on the ground that the latter had failed to determine which administrative entity, that is the Ministry of the Interior or Ministry of Defence, had responsibility for compensating the applicant. In respect of Ahmet Alican the Court awarded the second applicant TRL 366,954,3670 in respect of pecuniary damage together with legal interest running from the date of the incident, 23 April 1994. The Ministry appealed. 23 May 2002 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment.

name: Ingo Hentschel
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47274/15) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two German nationals, Mr Ingo Hentschel and Mr Matthias Stark (“the applicants”), alleged that they had been beaten and that pepper spray had been used on them by police officers. The applicants were represented by Mr M. Noli and Ms A. Luczak, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The German Government was represented by their Agents, Mr H.‑J. Behrens and Ms K. Behr, of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. After the match had ended the police cordoned off the stands of the supporters of one of the teams, including both applicants. Some of these officers started hitting the spectators with their truncheons without any prior warning as soon as they reached them. The first applicant himself was hit with a truncheon on the head, which resulted in a bleeding laceration of 3 cm behind his ear. Both applicants were able to identify their attackers as police officers, but were not able to distinguish them further, owing to their identical uniforms and the lack of identifying signs or name tags. The Government’s version of the subsequent events resulted in the arrest of one supporter and two police officers sustained minor injuries. Munich public prosecutor’s office instigated a preliminary investigation. The Government challenged the accounts of the applicants and submitted that there was no credible evidence that the applicants had deliberately been hit or harmed by police officers. The investigating division was also provided with a DVD showing excerpts of the video surveillance recorded by the riot control police at the football match. On 10 September 2008 the competent public prosecutor discontinued the investigation. He found that the investigation had produced evidence that some of the police officers had used truncheons against spectators, including women and children, in a disproportionate way and without an official order or approval. However, he concluded that the. investigation had not led to a situation where concrete acts of violence could be related to specific police. officers. The applicants appealed against the decision to discontinue the investigation. The public prosecutor reopened the investigation and ordered further enquiries. The investigating police unit was also provided with video surveillance recorded by the 23rd platoon of the 6th Dachau public-order support force battalion. After assessing all the available evidence, the public prosecutor concluded that several supporters had aggressively approached, insulted and provoked the deployed police officers and therefore a situation had existed in which the officers could have been justified in using their truncheons. The applicants had neither been able to identify a particular suspect nor to determine whether the suspected police officers had been involved. and it could not be ascertained either whether the use of force had been justified. The Munich Court of Appeal declared the applicants’ application to force further enquiries inadmissible. The applicants lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Articles 2, 19, and 103 of the German Basic Law. The court interpreted the applicants' request as an application to Force criminal proceedings (Klageerzwingungsantrag) The court held that these proceedings were only admissible if the prosecution of one or more identified accused had been requested. The applications were not supposed to identify the accused or replace investigations. Only in a case where a public prosecutor’s office had entirely refrained from investigating a crime had a court the possibility to order an investigation. The Federal Constitutional Court refused, in a reasoned decision (2 BvR 1304/12), to admit the applicants’ constitutional complaint. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. In its decision the Constitutional Court referred to the Court’s case-law concerning the procedural obligation of Article 2 of the Convention and, in particular, to the cases of McCann and Others v. the United Kingdom (27 September 1995, Series A no. 324) and Grams v Germany (dec., no. 33677/96, ECHR 1999‑VII)

The case originated in an application (no. 47274/15) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants alleged that they had been beaten and that pepper spray had been used on them by police officers who, owing to an inadequate investigation, had been neither identified nor punished. On 26 February 2016 the application was communicated to the Government of Germany. The application was brought by two German nationals, Mr Ingo Hentschel and Mr Matthias Stark, who went to a football match in Munich in December 2007. The police had predicted an increased risk of clashes between rival football supporters owing to confrontations at previous matches. A total of 227 police officers were deployed, including two squads – comprising eight to ten police officers each. Police cordoned off the stands of supporters of one of the teams, including both applicants, to prevent them from leaving the stadium and encountering supporters of the other team. The first applicant himself was hit with a truncheon on the head, which resulted in a bleeding laceration of 3 cm behind his ear. Both applicants were able to identify their attackers as police officers, but were not able to distinguish them further, owing to their identical uniforms and the lack of identifying signs or name tags. Both uniforms did not include any name tags or other signs identifying the individual officers. On the back of the helmets an identification number of the squad was displayed. Munich public prosecutor’s office instigated a preliminary investigation on 2 January 2008. The first applicant filed a criminal complaint against an unidentified police officer on 25 April 2008. Several other spectators at the match had also lodged criminal complaints against unidentified police officers. On 10 September 2008 the competent public prosecutor discontinued the investigation. He found that the investigation had produced evidence that some of the police officers had used truncheons against spectators, including women and children, in a disproportionate way and without an official order or approval. However, he concluded that the. investigation had not led to a situation where concrete acts of violence could be related to specific police. officers. The investigation was conducted by the unit of the Munich police responsible for offences perpetrated by public officials. The applicants appealed against the decision to discontinue the investigation. The public prosecutor reopened the investigation and ordered further enquiries. A further twenty-two witnesses were interviewed including fourteen platoon leaders, squad leaders and video officers of the deployed police units. The individual squad members of the three squads of the Munich riot control unit were not interviewed. The applicants had requested that they be interviewed, as the evidence had suggested that the alleged perpetrators had belonged to one of these three squads. The investigating police unit was also provided with video surveillance recorded by the 23rd platoon of the 6th Dachau public-order support force battalion. The original video tapes and possible digital copies had already been deleted and only the excerpts were still available. Munich general public prosecutor confirmed the decision of the public prosecutor’s office of 4 August 2009 to discontinue the investigation. Applicants appealed and pointed out that the members of the deployed squads had still not been questioned and that the inspected videos were fragmentary, but nonetheless contradicted certain parts of the statements made by the squad leaders. Munich Court of Appeal declared the applicants’ application to force further enquiries inadmissible on 19 September 2011. On 25 October 2011 the applicants lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Articles 2 § 2, 19 § 4 and 103 § 1 of the German Basic Law (G.C.R.) The applicants complained that the investigation had not been effective and that the Court of Appeal had not evaluated the effectiveness of the investigation. The Federal Constitutional Court refused, in a reasoned decision (2 BvR 1304/12), to admit the applicants’ constitutional complaint. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. A subsequent appeal before the Munich general public prosecutor was to no avail. The investigation against the five police officers was discontinued by the Munich public prosecutor’s office. The applicants alleged that several relevant parts of the video material, showing disproportionate police violence, had been deleted.

name: Otto Hennig
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 41444/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings against him lasted unreasonably long in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The Court declared the application admissible in a decision of 23 May 2002. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in Strasbourg, France, and the decision was published on 6 July 2012. The decision is available online at http://www.ecj.org/cases/case/41444-98.html. The applicant was suspected of tax evasion in that he had acted as a sham holder of shares in three cases concerning the years 1985–87. The Salzburg Tax Office requested the Oberwart Tax Office to transmit the applicant's tax file in order to determine the amount of evaded taxes. The Vienna Tax Office for the Audit of Large-scale Companies transferred the applicant’s file on 25 May 1994. The total amount ofevaded taxes was ATS 1,079,389. The applicant was prosecuted for tax evasion on 3 June 1994 by the Salzburger Public Prosecutor's Office. The case was settled out of court. The applicant made false statements of losses in his income tax forms between 1985 and 1987. He was charged with tax evasion of ATS 1,079,389. The applicant was convicted of tax evasion on 22 November 1995. He then filed a plea of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) and requested that the transcripts of the trial be corrected. On 25 June 1997 the Supreme Court scheduled the hearing on the plea ofnullity for 29 July 1997. On that day the Court of Appeal ruled that the applicant could not be punished for tax evasion because his letter of 14 December 1989 constituted “self-denunciation” of a tax offence. The U.S. Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's plea of nullity. This decision was pronounced orally. On 2 October 1997 the written version of the judgment, consisting of twelve pages, was served on the applicant’s counsel. The application was dismissed on 1 October 1997. The judgment was read out in court on 2 October. The applicant's counsel was served with the written judgment. The decision was read in court and signed off by the Chief Justice of the United States. The case was settled on 8 October 1997 at the Supreme Court in Washington, D.C., and the judgment was delivered on 10 October 1997 on behalf of the applicant.

The case originated in an application (no. 41444/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights on 20 March 1998. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings against him lasted unreasonably long in breach of Article 6 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Court declared the application admissible on 23 May 2002. The applicant was suspected of tax evasion in that he had acted as a sham holder of shares in three cases concerning the years 1985–87. He further asked that following a re-calculation of his income, new tax assessment orders be issued. The total amount of evaded taxes was ATS 1,079,389. The Salzburg Tax Office asked that the applicant be prosecuted for tax evasion. The Vienna Tax Office for the Audit of Large-scale Companies transferred the applicant's file on 25 May 1994. The applicant was interrogated by the Oberwart District on 8 August 1994, when interrogated by a tax court. The case was settled out of court in December 1994. The applicant was charged with tax evasion of ATS 1,079,389 in that he had made false statements of losses in his income tax forms between 1985 and 1987. On 22 November 1995 the Regional Court convicted the applicant of tax evasion, pursuant to Section 33 of the Code of Tax Offences (Finanzstrafgesetz) The applicant filed a plea of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) on 26 November 1996 and requested that the transcripts of the trial be corrected. On 25 June 1997 the Supreme Court scheduled the hearing on the applicant's plea ofnullity for 29 July 1997. Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's plea of nullity. This decision was pronounced orally. On 2 October 1997 the written version of the judgment, consisting of twelve pages, was served on the applicant. The applicant's counsel. was served with the written judgment. The application was dismissed by the Supreme Court. The appeal was dismissed. The case was dismissed and the judgment was delivered on October 2, 1997. The judge's decision was delivered orally. The Appeal was dismissed on October 3, 1997, and the appeal was concluded on October 4, 1997 with the judgment delivered by the judge. The decision was handed down on October 5, 1997 and the appeals were dismissed.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38426/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Ms Lidia Nowak (‘the applicant’), on 9 October 2003. name: Nazif Töre
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicant's right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal to the Government. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and the case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal, which ruled that the application should be allowed to stand. The decision was published on 30 April 2006. The ruling was published by the Appeal Court, which was read by the Supreme Court of Justice, on 30 May 2006. The applicant was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1998. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Malatya State Security Court without conducting a hearing since the applicant's lawyer was absent without justification. On 10 October 2002 the applicant was released from prison due to ill-health pursuant to Article 399 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The applicant was imprisoned, in total, for about six years and six months. He was released in October 2002 because of ill- health and was freed from prison in October 2003. He is now living in Russia with his wife and two children. He has been sentenced to death by lethal injection but was released on bail on October 31, 2003.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 65631/01) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that proceedings for a building permit had lasted unreasonably long, that no public hearing had been held and that the proceedings had been unfair. By a decision of 27 November 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. In particular, it declared theApplication inadmissible as regards the complaints raised by the then first applicant Mr Peter Kugler. The Court also made observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Vorarlberg Regional Government (“the Regional Government”) allowed that application on 10 October 1991 but dismissed the applicant's application for a building permit on the ground that the permit would contravene the building prohibition. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Administrative Court. On 26 February 1997 the District Administrative Authority informed the applicant of the Lech municipal authorities' submissions to the effect that the maximum building density laid down by the decree of 19 March 1992 did not allow the construction of another building on his plot of land. On 1 July 1997 the Regional Government approved the building plan. The application was dismissed on 28 October 1997. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court and requested an oral hearing. He submitted that the refusal to issue the building permit had been based on an unlawful area zoning plan and building plan. The Administrative Court dismissed the complaint. On 19 January 2005 the applicant applied for a building permit for a private house on the same plot of land. On 2 September 2005 the Lech municipal authorities granted the application. The decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 5 December 2005. The application was granted on 5 September 2005 and the application was served in December 2006. The applicant was awarded a permit to build a house in Lech on 5 August 2005.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47017/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their deportation from Norway to Pakistan would entail a violation of their rights under Article 8 of the convention. The application was communicated to the Government on 7 June 2010. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicants' father applied for family reunification in 1996 but his application was refused. An investigation by the immigration authorities revealed that for most of the period from 1992 to early 1996 the applicants and their mother had lived in Pakistan. The application relates to two men who were denied residence in Norway. The children were apprehended with a view to being deported to Pakistan. The police decided not to do so, based on their information that they had no contact with the mother or with the family in Pakistan. In September 2005 the mother was expelled to Pakistan, in compliance with the immigration authorities’ decision (see paragraph 8 above). She died in August 2007. The applicants sought to challenge the validity of the decision of 23 August 1999 and, as regards the second applicant, that of 31 May 2005. By a judgment of 13 October 2005 the Oslo City Court upheld their action. Nor did the High Court find against the applicants in October 2006. The applicants lodged a previous application (no. 565/08) under the Convention, complaining that their deportation to Pakistan would constitute a violation of Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. They also requested an interim measure to stay their deportation under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court. On 8 January 2008 the request was refused. The applicants did not pursue their application. On 6 February 2008, a Committee of three judges decided to strike it out of the Court’s list of cases. The proceedings giving rise to the present application are as follows: The Immigration Appeals Board's decisions of 31 August 2007 and 13 October 2005 regarding the second applicant. In September 2007 the applicants challenged that decision before the courts. In this connection they both requested an interlocutory injunction to stop their deportation. These requests were rejected by the City Court on 5 October 2007 and the High Court on 15 November 2007. By a judgment of 4 February 2008, the Oslo City Court quashed the Immigration Appeals Board’s decision of 31 August 2007, disagreeing with the Board's assessment that the applicants lacked special attachment to Norway. The City Court further observed that in Norway the applicants had close relatives – uncles and aunts – and had lived with these since 2001. The applicants had gone to school in Norway, had friends and acquaintances there and were mastering the Norwegian language, both oral and written. The applicants had not had contact with their father since 1996 and did not wish to have any contact with him. Their mother had died and it was uncertain whether they had other relatives in the country. They were able to speak Urdu and to understand the language in oral form but could not read or write it. The High Court found it clear that the refusal to grant residence permits constituted an interference with the applicants’ rights under paragraph 1 of Article 8 of the Convention. The State appealed to the Borgarting High Court, which overturned the City Court’s ruling by a judgment of 14 November 2008 and upheld the Immigration Appeals Board's refusal of 31 August 2007 as being lawful. The High Court found it hardly probable that the applicants had no contacts with their mother and had no knowledge of her whereabouts from 2001 until the summer of 2005. The authorities’ omission to implement “the refusal of residence” (“oppholdsnektelsen”) ought to be seen in the light of the fact that the police had been unable to get hold of their mother. There was reason to assume that during the years after 2001 the police did not in practice expect the applicants to leave the country on their own. However, after reaching the age of majority, the applicants’ choice to stay in Norway had been something for which they ought to bear the risk and responsibility. The applicants had developed a strong personal and social attachment to Norway. The High Court, nonetheless, with doubt, arrived at the conclusion that the refusal of residence had not been unlawful as being contrary to Article 8. One could therefore question whether general immigration policy considerations, which normally carried weight in cases of unlawful residence, would be sufficiently weighty to regard the refusal. of residence as being “necessary in a democratic society”. In the present case there had been no such risk as the applicants had reached the age of majority and their mother was dead. The applicants had until 2005 lived with their uncle and aunt (their mother’s brother and sister) with family in Oslo. The applicants' strong attachment to Norway had been established during unlawful residence, that they still had links to their home place in Pakistan and that they as adults had relatively good possibilities for settling in Pakistan. name: Sandro Nerva
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42295/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, in particular, that their rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and under Article 14 of the Convention had been breached given that the domestic courts of the respondent State had ruled that money which was left to them as tips by customers passed to their employer to be used as it wished. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it admissible on 11 September 2001. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). In 1979, following an inspection from the tax authorities, the applicants’ employer was required to treat tips left by cheque or credit card within the “Pay-As-You-Earn” (“PAYE”) system. Under the PAYE system an employer had to ensure that employees’ income tax and national insurance contributions were deducted from the sums paid. The applicants submitted that the staff agreement to the new system was not intended to alter the fact that the gratuities were to be paid in full to employees. The first applicant was already a staff member at the time of the introduction of the system. The remaining applicants agreed to the system when they took up employment. At the relevant time there was a legal requirement that various categories of workers, including waiting staff like the applicants, be paid a minimum sum as remuneration. The applicants sued their employer for breach of contract and challenged the employer’s right to count the tips included in cheque or credit card payments as part of their statutory minimum remunerations. On 25 May 1994 a High Court judge, Mr Justice Mance, held on a preliminary point that tips included on cheque and credit card transactions did count against the minimum sum. In his judgment, the employer obtained the legal title to a tip paid by credit card or cheque, with the result that it became the employer's property. By the time of the hearing before the Court of Appeal, the applicants had accepted that property in the tips passed to their employer. Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. Lord Justice Staughton rejected the attempts of the applicants' counsel to interpret the applicable legislation differently. He further rejected counsel’s argument that the applicants had a right to the cheque and credit card tips as money had and received for their use. Mr Justice Douglas Brown stated that the intention of the different customers could only be the subject of speculation.Lord Justice Aldous dissented. He accepted that the amount was paid to the employer and therefore it could not be said that the tip so paid never became the employer's property. However, in his opinion the intentions of the customer was the same as those of the employer. In either case, the customer had no intention of giving anything to the employer. Lord Justice Aldous said that there was no difference in principle between tips paid in cash and tips paid by cheque or credit card. In his opinion, the only difference was that in the latter cases the employer acted as agent for the customer and, when doing so, had to carry out its duties under the relevant tax legislation to ensure that tax was levied on the tips. However, the fact that tax on cheque and credit card tips was deducted under the PAYE system, instead of being paid by the waiters, did not affect the relationship between the. customer and the employee.

In 1979, following an inspection from the tax authorities, the applicants’ employer was required to treat tips left by cheque or credit card within the ‘Pay-As-You-Earn’ (‘PAYE’) system. The applicants submitted that the staff agreement to the new system was not intended to alter the fact that the gratuities were to be paid in full to employees. The applicants sued their employer for breach of contract. They challenged the employer’s right to count the tips included in cheque or credit card payments as part of their statutory minimum remuneration. The applicants’ claim covered the six-year period prior to 6 March 1989. By the time of the hearing before the Court of Appeal, the applicants had accepted that property in the cheque and credit card tips passed to their employer and no longer relied on the argument that they were to be held in trust for them. In his judgment, the employer obtained the legal title to a tip paid by credit card or cheque, with the result that it became the employer's property. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. Lord Justice Staughton observed that the relevant legislation embodied the rule that what was paid by the employer and not by any other person counted as remuneration. As to the issue of the customers’ intention when adding the tip to the cheque or credit card payment, the court considered: “This is relevant ... in deciding whether the money became the property of the employers or the waiters. But it is clear and (in this court) uncontroverted in this case that it became theProperty of the Employers. ... ” Mr Justice Douglas Brown concurred. Lord Justice Aldous observed that there was no difference in principle between tips paid in cash and tips paid by cheque or credit card. The only difference was that in the latter cases the employer acted as agent for the customer and, when doing so, had to carry out its duties under the relevant tax legislation to ensure that tax was levied on the tips. However, the fact that tax on cheque and credit card tips was deducted under the PAYE system, instead of being paid by the waiters, did not affect the relationship. The applicants applied for leave to appeal to the House of Lords. On 4 February 1997 the Appeal Committee referred the matter for an oral hearing before three Law Lords.

name: Murat Kılıç
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40498/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal due to the presence of a military judge on the bench of the Ankara State Security Court which tried and convicted him. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Court declared the application partly admissible by a decision of 8 July 2003. It retained the applicant’s complaint concerning the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the court. Ankara State Security Court found the applicant and four of his co-accused guilty of an offence under Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act. The search of their houses had uncovered the internal regulations of the party whose aim was to establish an independent Kurdish State on the territory of the Turkish State through dissemination of propaganda. The court also noted that the party was to set up by means of force an independent socialist and united State of Kurdistan within the territories of Iran, Iraq and Syria. The applicant was sentenced to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment and debarred from public service indefinitely.

name: Eliane van Glabeke
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38287/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Government submitted that the applicant had been ‘picked up’ on the public highway by a police officer who had asked for her to be admitted to hospital. The applicant disputed that account and stated that she had been arrested while cycling to the shops and taken to the police station. She had not undergone a medical examination on arrival but had been injected with unknown substances. She remained in the hospital until 8 April 2002, without being allowed to receive visits or to make or receive telephone calls. The parties have been unable to establish the date on which the letter was received. Lille State Counsel replied that he was not empowered to deal with the subject matter of the letter. On 28 March 2002 Afcap applied to the President of the Lille Tribunal de grande instance for the immediate discharge of her daughter. On 22 April 2002 State Counsel's Office decided to take no further action on that application as it was devoid of purpose. The decision was made by the Court of Appeals, who said that it was not the role of the court to decide on the case.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18851/07) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the convention. On 24 November 2009 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The application was made by a French national, Mr Arnaud Lagardère (“the applicant”), on 19 April 2007. The French Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs E. Belliard. J.-L. Lagardère was accused of misappropriation of corporate assets. A Paris court declared the prosecution against him time-barred. On 14 March 2003 the accused died. The Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation quashed and annulled the judgment of the Paris Court of Appeal concerning the civil action. The case was sent before the Versailles Court of appeal. The civil action continued when the offender’s death occurred after a decision on the criminal prosecution had been given. The judge ruled that the prosecution had lapsed, this time as a result of the accused's death. It concluded its reasoning in the following terms: “the system set in place by the Paris Criminal Court is defective.” The profit had been 94,100,000 French francs or 14,345,452.52 euros (EUR), without any real added value for the injured companies. The applicant, E.P.L., Lambda and the Principal Public Prosecutor at the Court of Appeal appealed on points of law. In support of his appeal the applicant argued that there had been a violation of Article 6 of the Convention because the criminal court had no authority to judge the matter after his father’s death. “In our modern law we no longer bring actions against the dead or the memory of the dead”, says the advocate-general at Court of Cassation. In a judgment of 25 October 2006 the Court of Cassation declared the Principal Public Prosecutor’s appeal inadmissible and rejected those lodged by the applicant and E.P.L. principle that hearings must be oral. This meant that in order for the criminal court to be able to examine the civil action alone, it would be necessary for the accused ‘at one time or another, to have had an effective opportunity to submit his arguments in full’. The Court of Appeal had ‘found Jean‑Luc Lagardère guilty’ in a case of misappropriation of corporate assets. The case was quashed and annulled on the issue of the capitalisation of the interest on the sums owed by J.-L. Lagardères’ heirs.

Judge Globe refused the applicant's request to attend the appeal against bail. He said that it would set a precedent for any defendant in custody wishing to attend an appeal in the future. Judge Globe said that he was not going to alter his view in relation to the applicant being present during the hearing. train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant maintains that when he was detained between 28 April 2003 and 1 April 2004 he was forced to testify, subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment and that the conditions of his detention were poor. On 20 December 2004 the applicant was indicted before the Katowice District Court. The bill of indictment listed several charges of fraud, forgery, perjury, robbery and kidnapping brought against thirteen accused, committed in the context of an organised criminal group. name: Gülizar Pembe
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49398/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants' plots of land in İskenderun were expropriated by the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways. A committee of experts assessed the value of these lands and the determined amounts were paid to them when the expropriation took place. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning insufficient interest payable in respect of additional compensation, the delay of the authorities in payment of the additional compensation and the length of the proceedings. The ownership of the property was transferred to the National Water Board on 23 October 1996. The court ordered the administration to pay Yüksel Bozkaya TRL 80,274,368,000 plus interest at the statutory rate. The Court of Cassation upheld the above-mentioned judgments of the İskenderun First Instance Court on 11 May, 20 May and 25 May 1998 respectively. On 8 April, 13 April, 12 May and 4 June 1999 respectively, the administration paid the applicants the amounts due together with interest. The administration has since paid out the money to the applicants, as well as the interest.
