name: Uli Lutz
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 28 January 1986. It originated in an application (no. 9912/82) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Englert and Nölkenbockhoff cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality. The Government’s memorial was lodged with the registry on 13 November 1986. The applicant informed the Registrar on the same day that he would not be filing a memorial. On 29 November, the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. There appeared before the Court: I. Maier, Ministerialdirigentin, Federal Ministry of Justice, Agent, Mr. P.-G. Pötz, Ministerlydirigent. Mr. A. Weitzel, Delegate; Mr. N. Wingerter, Rechtsanwalt; and Mr. V. Hohbach, Counsel. Uli Lutz, a German national born in 1959, lives in Heilbronn-Horkheim. In October 1980, he was riding a motor cycle and was involved in a road accident. According to the police report (Verkehrs-Ordnungswidrigkeiten-Anzeige), he had attempted to overtake a car, although the traffic situation was unclear. The result had been a collision which caused damage to both vehicles. He was fined DM 125, to which were added costs of DM 14, for ‘joint responsibility’ for the road accident due to overtaking in an unclear traffic situation. The decision was based on section 24 of the Road Traffic Act (Strassenverkehrsgesetz) and Regulations 1(2), 5 and 49. The driver of the car was likewise fined for a “regulatory offence’ (Ordnungswidrigkeit) On 24 August 1981, the District Court stayed the proceedings on the ground that they were time-barred. The applicant would have to bear his own necessary costs and expenses (notwendige Auslagen) The court informed the applicant that it intended to discontinue the proceedings and order costs against the Treasury (Staatskasse) On 9 December 1980, the Heilbronn Police Authority took a decision to impose a fine (Bussgeldbescheid) on the defendant for a breach of the Road Traffic Regulations. The defendant appealed against this decision. On 10 September 1981, the applicant challenged this decision in so far as he had been ordered to bear his own costs and expenses. The court held that Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, taken together with section 46 of the Act on ‘regulatory offences’, would be unjust to order the Treasury to bear the defendant’s necessary costs. Mr. Lutz applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) But on 2 February 1982 a bench of three of that court’s judges refused to entertain the application, holding that it had insufficient prospects of success. Mr Lutz had thus broken the basic rule in Regulation 1(2) of the Road Traffic Regulations and, in particular, had disregarded his duty under Regulation 5(3)(1) not to overtake where the traffic situation was unclear. The court held that in such circumstances it would have been unjust to award the defendant's necessary costs and expenses against the Treasury, especially as the prosecution had become time-barred during the court proceedings. The presumption of innocence precluded taking measures against a defendant that amounted in effect to a penalty. This rule was not infringed where the necessary costs and expenses of a party who had been proceeded against in respect of a ‘regulatory offence’ were not awarded against the Treasury in the event of the proceedings being discontinued. “The decision not to order the Treasury to pay the costs and. expenses of the party concerned obviously cannot be regarded as a punishment (Bestrafung) or even be equated with. such,” said the court. The decision as to costs does not make any finding that the person concerned is guilty, it derives merely from the suspicion falling on him, which had given rise to his being prosecuted.

name: Peter Roland Schwarzenberger
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 75737/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’s Convention”) on 26 July 2001. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr V. Hohbach, a lawyer practising in Heilbronn. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The judge said that the accused was aware that a human life counted for little with Schwarzenberger. ‘Because of the many heavy hammer blows on the victim’s head, the accused wanted to kill the adoptive mother of the accused, at least in order to gain the prospected loot,’ the court said. The court also said that although the accused had intended to commit the crime on his own, he was so intensely involved in the planning that his actions did not merely constitute supportive measures, but an autonomous part of the action, the more so as he pursued his own interest in the deed: to have access to the loot. The applicant was extradited to Germany on 22 April 1997. The applicant objected to the participation of judges W. and B. on the ground of possible bias (Ablehnung wegen Besorgnis der Befangenheit) He argued that the passages in the court’s judgment against D., seen from his viewpoint, were susceptible of raising doubts about the impartiality of these judges. On 12 February 1999 the main hearing was opened before a chamber of the Heilbronn Regional Court presided by judge W and including judge B.; both had already sat in the chamber which had previously tried D. The chamber found it appropriate to consider both cases in separate proceedings. Heilbronn Regional Court convicted the applicant, who had denied any involvement in the crimes, of murder and of having committed robbery followed by death. The applicant subsequently appealed on points of law, arguing that judges B. and W. should have been excluded from the trial. On 7 March 2001 the Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof) rejected the appeal as unfounded. According to the Regional Court’s findings, the applicant had killed Mrs D. in order to cover up the robbery; while D. had approved of the applicant's actions. The Regional Court based its judgment mainly on the applicant’'s own statements given both during preliminary investigations and during the main hearing. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint in which he gave a complete account of the proceedings before the lower courts. He alleged that the impugned decisions violated his right to a fair trial as guaranteed by the German Basic Law and by the Convention. According to section 24 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a judge can be challenged for fear of bias if there is a justifiable reason to doubt his impartiality. It is clear that the applicant has been exposed to a high degree of value judgments on his person and his actions. If one were to apply the ruling of the Federal Court of Justice to the present case, there would no longer be a case to challenge the impartiality of the judges. The Federal Constitutional Court, sitting as a panel of three judges, refused to accept the applicant’s complaint for adjudication on 20 June 2001. “The constitutional complaint has no prospect of success, because it is inadmissible. Its reasoning does not meet the minimum requirements found in section 23 § 1, second sentence, and section 92 of the Rules of Procedure,” the court ruled. ‘No. longer be any possibility of removing a judge for fear of bias due to the decision in a previous case ... . Such a result is unacceptable for the person concerned, as has been sufficiently demonstrated. Article 6 of the Convention has been violated for the same reasons’

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they were denied a fair hearing on account of the fact that the trial judge left the jury with the option of drawing an adverse inference from their silence during police interview. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) by a decision of 7 September 1999. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 January 2000 (Rule 59 § 2) The applicants were represented by Mr J. Wadham, a lawyer practising in London. The Government was represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. The applicants were arrested at 12.45 p.m. on 28 April 1995. In the flat were found sixteen wraps of heroin weighing between 0.07 and 0.09 g and a further quantity of heroin weighed 1.19 g. The applicants' solicitor, Mr Delbourgo, noted that the first applicant, who seemed to be in the early stages of withdrawal, was unfit to be interviewed. After a 10- to 15-minute examination, the Force Medical Examiner, Dr Youlten, stated that the applicant was fit for interview. The doctor's report notes that theFirst applicant was an opiates addict with symptoms and signs of withdrawal but that he was thinking clearly and able to answer questions. Both applicants were legally aided and represented by counsel. They were interviewed separately in the presence of their solicitor. The applicants were asked to explain their actions in apparently passing to, and being passed items from, flat 50. Both applicants gave evidence at the trial and said that the heroin found in the flat had been for their own personal use and had been purchased in bulk by the first applicant the evening before their arrest. The defence case for the applicants was that they had been unlawfully deprived of their liberty. The application to exclude the evidence was premature since the defendants had not given evidence, so that it was not clear what facts were going to be relied on in their defence. The applicants' co-accused, Mr Curtis, testified at the trial that the applicants had never given him heroin. He confirmed the applicants' account of their friendship with him and his frequent borrowing, with communication being by the balcony. When he was arrested he was told that he would not get bail which made him angry and “bloody-minded” so he decided not to help the police by answering their questions. When asked why they had made no comment to police questions during interview, both applicants stated that their solicitor's advice that they were not in a condition to do so, given their withdrawal from heroin. They stated that the polythene sheet had been planted there by the police after they had been brought to the police station. The applicants were each convicted by a majority of nine to one of being concerned in supplying heroin and possessing heroin with intent to supply. The first applicant was sentenced to a total of four years. The applicants' conviction and appeal were upheld by the Court of Appeal. The application was dismissed on appeal on November 20, 2013. The appeal was rejected on November 23, 2013 and the applicants' appeal was upheld on November 24, 2013, and the appeal was thrown out on November 25, 2013 by the court of appeal. The applications were dismissed on November 27, 2013 after the Appeal Court rejected the appeal and the applications were returned to the courts. The applicants appealed to the Court of Appeal on two primary grounds: the inclusion of the police interviews and the contents of the judge's direction. The applicants' counsel contended that the trial judge should have excluded the “no comment” interviews as they were a direct result of following their solicitor's honest advice. The Court of appeal rejected the submission that the judge had been wrong to allow the jury to draw adverse inferences from the applicants' failure to answer questions at the interview. The judge, as the fact-finding tribunal in the voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of the jury), had been correct to include the notes of interviews in evidence. The Court of Appeal did not find that this lacuna in the summing-up meant that the convictions were unsafe, having regard to the weight of the other evidence. Lord Justice Stuart-Smith explained in this connection: “We have already referred to the substantial, almost overwhelming evidence of drug supply from what was found in the [applicants'] house” All but one of the jury must have rejected the applicants' explanation of the police observations, much of which was recorded on video, the presence of the matching wraps in Curtis' flat and the elaborate security arrangements at the applicants’ own flat. The acquittal of Curtis shows that the jury regarded the evidence of the interviews as insignificant.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35494/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Jakub Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was brought by a Polish national, Mr Marian Sobczyński (‘the applicant’), on 11 July 2008. The applicant was indicted of numerous counts of tax fraud, money laundering and perjury, allegedly committed within an organised criminal gang. The first hearing took place on 23 October 2008. It appears that since then the trials have been taking place once a month or more frequently. On 6 March 2009 the Katowice Regional Court released the applicant from detention, placing him under police supervision (dozór policyjny). The applicant served two separate prison sentences imposed on him by a competent criminal court. And thus from 2 March 2007 until 31 July 2008 the applicant was serving a sentence imposed by the Wieluń District Court.

The court ordered that the applicant remain in custody until the prison sentence could be enforced. He was referred to a prison hospital for observation. The date of his admission to hospital was fixed for 1 July 2004. He appealed against the decision of 30 September 2004 on the extension of his detention. On 21 October 2004 the Częstochowa Regional Court allowed his appeal of 1 October 2004. On 6 December 2004 two appeals against the judgment of 30 September 2004 were lodged by the applicant's lawyers. On 22 June 2005 the Częstochowa Regional Court quashed the judgment and remitted the case. The proceedings are pending. On the same day he was released from detention he was sentenced to 20 years in prison. The verdict was quashed and the case was remitted on June 22, 2005. The sentence was reduced to 15 years and the sentence was suspended for two years. The case was later quashed again and the defendant was released in May, 2007. name: Lars Wassdahl
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the administrative proceedings to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The application was filed by a Swedish national, Mr Lars Wassdahl (“the applicant”), on 8 November 2003. The Swedish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr M. Falk, Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant was born in 1947 and lives in Orsa. The applicant claimed that the transactions had taken place and that his tax return should be approved. The Tax Authority decided to follow its preliminary consideration. With regard to the imposition of tax surcharges, it found that the applicant had submitted incorrect information about the purported transactions. The applicant sued the Swedish State, through the Chancellor of Justice, before the District Court (tingsrätten) in Stockholm. He sought SEK 6,850,000 (approximately EUR 736,000) in damages. He has not been successful in his appeal against the Tax Authority’s decision to disallowing the deductions or imposing tax surcharge on him. The applicant sued the Tax Authority and the administrative courts for damages. He claimed that they had not afforded him a fair procedure and that the proceedings had been of excessive length. The State contested the suit, claiming that it had not caused the applicant any injury, either by fault or neglect, for which he could claim damages. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) where the case is still pending, awaiting a decision on leave to appeal. The case is not known to have resulted in any verdicts in favor of the applicant or against the State. It is unclear how long the case would have taken to resolve.

name: Kenan Tandoğan
train_texts: The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was charged with attempting to undermine the constitutional order, an offence defined under Article 146 of the Criminal Code. The case brought against the applicant was joined with another case pending before the Istanbul State Security Court. He was also accused of homicide, armed riot against prison administration and damaging prison property. The applicant was charged with homicide in connection with the incidents in the Ümraniye Prison. On 6 July 2001 the Istanbul Assize Court held its first hearing and ordered the release of the applicant –together with twelve other accused- pending trial. Since the applicant was a minor when the crimes in question had been committed, the case should be examined by the Istanbul Juvenile Court. It accordingly declared non-jurisdiction. The case was accordingly remitted before the Court of Cassation to determine which court had jurisdiction to examine the case. According to the information in the case file based on the latest submissions by the parties the case is apparently still pending.

name: Said Mohammed Hilal
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his expulsion to Tanzania placed him at risk of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment and that he would not receive a fair trial if he were returned to Tanzania. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry [Note by the Registry]. The applicant was born in Pemba, one of the Zanzibar islands, in 1968. In November 1994 the. applicant stated that he was released from detention following pressure from CUF. leaders on the Tanzanian government. In January 1995 the police came looking for him while he was out. The applicant decided to leave his home in Tanzania, fearing for his safety. In February 1995 the applicant arrived in the UK and claimed asylum. In an interview with an interpreter the applicant said he had been tortured for three months at a police station. He was hung upside down with his feet tied together until he bled through the nose. He also said that he had no problem obtaining a passport because he had organised his passage to the UK. He had been arrested because he gave money to the CUF. A few days before he was released he was hung upside down and given electric shocks. The Secretary of State refused asylum, finding the applicant’s account implausible and noting inconsistencies in his answers. His appeal to a special adjudicator was dismissed on 8 November 1996. The applicant claimed that the Tanzanian authorities intercepted the letters he was sending home, knew that he had claimed asylum, and had summoned his parents to explain “about [their] son who [was] in a foreign country to abuse the government which [ was] in power ...” Leave to appeal to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal was refused on 10 January 1997. The applicant obtained a copy of his brother’s death certificate and a medical report which recorded that his brother died on 20 January 1995, after being brought to hospital from prison with a history of severe chest pain and general body weakness associated with a fever. He also obtained the summons from the Pemba police headquarters to his parents dated 25 November 1995. He made representations to the Secretary of State dated 30 January 1997, providing copies and requesting that his letter be considered as a fresh asylum application. By letter dated 5 February 1997 the Secretary. of State informed them that he had decided not to refer the material in question. The applicant applied for leave to apply for judicial review of the Secretary of State’s refusal to refer the new material to the special adjudicator. On 1 July 1998 the application for leave was rejected by the High Court. In its judgment it noted that the hospital records showed that his brother had died of fever. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal arguing that the secretary of state's refusal was wrong in law and “Wednesbury unreasonable” and that, in claiming that the applicant could live safely on the mainland, he was not complying with international obligations by failing to take into account the applicant's specific case or documentation. On 22 February 1999 the applicant’s wife arrived in the United Kingdom and claimed asylum shortly afterwards. She had been detained for one day in April 1995 and questioned about her husband's whereabouts. The police came to her house on 12 February 1999, wanting to know if her husband was back in Zanzibar. They were angry because he had claimed asylum and tarnished the name of the President. They threatened to arrest her instead. There was no evidence to suggest that the conclusion reached by the Secretary of State that the applicant could live without harassment on the mainland was wrong. The application was denied on 23 December 1998.

The applicant alleged that his expulsion to Tanzania placed him at risk of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment. The case has been referred to the European Court of Human rights (ECHR), which heard the case for the first time on 12 January 2013. In 1994 the man was detained at Madema police station in Zanzibar for three months. He was hung upside down with his feet tied together until he bled through the nose. In January 1995 the police came looking for him while he was out and questioned his friends. He decided to leave the country fearing for his safety. name: Mark William Grayson
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two British nationals, Mark William Grayson and John Barnham. Each applicant alleged that, in confiscation proceedings following his conviction for drugs offences, the fact that the legal burden of proof was on him to show that he did not have realisable assets equivalent to the benefit figure offended the basic principles of a fair procedure. The Court decided to examine the merits of each application at the same time as its admissibility. It also decided to join the applications (Rule 42 § 1). Judge found that the applicant had been the principal participant in the offence and must have contributed to a large extent to the purchase of the drugs. The judge was further satisfied that so large a consignment would not have represented the applicant’s first venture into drug trafficking and that he had financed the purchase with the proceeds of previous drug dealing. The largest element emerged from an analysis of 17 bank accounts which the applicant held at one time or another. The banking records demonstrated unexplained credits to the applicant's account in the two trading years ending April 1998 and April 2000 which exceeded the turnover of his business as recorded in the accounts by approximately GBP 153,000. The applicant had benefited to the amount of GBP 1,230,748.69. The judge found the applicant's realisable assets of GBP 236,000 to be less than the amount of his benefit. The judge set an additional ten years’ imprisonment to be served by the applicant if he had not paid within twelve months. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, although it reduced the default sentence of imprisonment from ten years, the statutory maximum, to eight years. Although he had been represented throughout the trial and confiscation proceedings, he was unrepresented for the appeal and put his arguments before the court in a series of letters written from prison. The court held that the additional accountancy evidence was not sufficient. Court of Appeal referred to Phillips v. the United Kingdom, no. 41087/98, ECHR 2001-VII, and observed that: “In that case the court held that the reverse onus of proof in relation to the statutory assumption at the calculation of the benefit stage is fully Convention compliant.” The Court added that although the accountancy report raised a suggestion of possible double-counting by the prosecution when it came to an analysis of realisable property, that was “irrelevant, since the judge’s order did not depend upon any calculation of realizable property’ The second applicant (Mr Barnham) was convicted of two conspiracy charges involving plans to import large consignments of cannabis into the UK. The applicant was sentenced to eleven years’ imprisonment, the judge describing him as the lead organiser in a sophisticated, established and internationally based drug trafficking business. The applicant and his wife gave evidence, to the effect that their only asset was their house in Spain, which they owned jointly. Since his conviction his wife was living with their son in England and supporting herself with a cleaning job. The defence submitted that there was no evidence capable of supporting a finding of assumed ‘hidden’ assets and such would lead to a risk of injustice. The judge ruled that the total benefit to the applicant was GBP 1,525,615. Judge found that the applicant and his wife had lied about their activities and their sources of income. He made a confiscation order equal to the amount which he had assessed as the benefit, namely GBP 1,525,615, with five years, three months’ imprisonment if the applicant had not paid within 18 months. The applicant appealed against the judge’s ruling regarding his realisable assets, asserting that Article 6 of the 1994 Act was not valid. Court of Appeal rejected this argument, holding as follows: ‘In our judgment the correct approach for the court to take when dealing with confiscation proceedings at the second stage is the same whether the benefit has been proved by evidence in addition to the statutory assumptions’ ‘The expression ‘hidden assets’ is indicative of the fact that the prosecution can have no means of knowing how and where a defendant may have dealt with or disposed of the proceeds of his criminal activities’.” ‘A defendant will know exactly how the court has determined benefit attributable to him and must prove by evidence what his realisable assets are.’ The Court of Appeal refused to certify a point of law of general public importance for appeal to the House of Lords concerning Article 6 of the Convention. , the Court of appeal refused to certified a point of law of general public interest for appeal to the House of Lords. name: Fedai Şahin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21773/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was filed by a Turkish national, Mr Fedai Şahin (“the applicant”), on 7 July 2000. The applicant was taken into custody within the context of a police operation carried out against an illegal organisation. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Criminal Code. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The case was remitted to the Istanbul Assize Court for re-trial. The court found the applicant guilty of the alleged offence and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The applicant appealed and the proceedings are currently pending before the Court of Cassation. The case was brought by the TKP/ML – TIKKO with a view to undermining the constitutional order of the State. The judge ruled that the applicant was guilty of participating in armed attacks, the killing of several individuals and robberies. The verdict was quashed on 20 March 2006 for having erred in its assessment of the facts. The application is still pending in the Court Of Cassation and the applicant has appealed the decision.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4236/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint. The complaint concerns the length of the criminal proceedings brought against the applicant and the lack of a public hearing in the determination of his compensation claim. The applicant was represented by Mrs N. Bener, a lawyer practising in Bursa. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Bursa Assize Court acquitted the applicant and two of his co-accused on 29 June 2001 after gathering the evidence mentioned in the Court of Cassation’s decision. In determining the award of pecuniary damage, the court referred to the minimum wage at the time and the applicant's loss of income during his incarceration. The court awarded the applicant 195,680,000 (TRL) (approximately EUR 116) for pec uniary damage and TRL 3,000,000.000 ( approximately EUR 1,791) for non-pecuniarydamage. The compensation proceedings were settled in December 2002. The applicant complained about the absence of an oral hearing before the Bursa Assize Court and the refusal to fix an interest rate for the compensation awarded to him. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. There is no indication that the applicant and/or his legal representative were duly notified of this hearing. In its decision the court also noted that there had been no need for an oral hear in the case. The Government stated that on 3 November 2004 the authorities paid the amount due to the applicant. The applicant was awarded an amount for costs and expenses incurred before the criminal court. However, it dismissed his request for interest running from the date of his release.

name: Janusz Wojciechowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5422/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Court's Convention. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was given notice of the application to the Government on 30 August 2007. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The first hearing was held on 17 June 2003. The applicant on several occasions challenged the presiding judge, alleging that he had infringed the rights of the defence. On 22 October 2002 and 13 May 2003 the Lublin Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s challenge. On 11 August 2004 the Court of Appeal ordered that the applicant be detained until 5 September 2004. The court found that hearings had been held regularly and that the case was particularly complex. It also held that the detention was necessary in order to prevent him and the other co-accused from interfering with the proceedings. It was sufficient to establish that evidence gathered in the case confirmed the strong suspicion of the applicant's involvement in the offences he had been charged with. The trial court held about 59 hearings. On 3 December 2004 the Lublin Regional Court delivered a judgment. It convicted the applicant of acting in an organised and armed criminal group, deriving profits from prostitution and extortion. The court sentenced him to six years’ imprisonment and a fine. name: Inga Allard
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35179/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the demolition of a house had violated her rights to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions and to respect for her home. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 22 May 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The applicant’s mother owned a number of houses. Two of the houses were used by the applicant and her two sisters. A third house situated on the property was considered too small for the applicant's needs. The applicant applied for a building permit to the Österåker Building Committee (byggnadsnämnden) The new house was built in 1988. In 1991 one of the joint owners applied for the sale of Marum 1:6 and Marum1:8 at a public auction. On 22 February 1992 the District Court decided to stay those proceedings. By a partial division on 29 June 1991, the new housewas transferred to the applicant. The applicant had appealed to the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) in 1994. She requested, inter alia, that no further action be taken on the case pending the outcome of division proceedings which she had begun in October 1990. In these proceedings, the applicant claimed that the joint ownership of the two estates should be dissolved and individual plots be assigned to the family members. Following several decisions taken by the Real Estate Formation Authority (Fastighetsbildningsmyndigheten – “the REFA”) and the courts, the case had to be referred back by the Court of Appeal to the REFA for re-examination. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, requesting an immediate stay of the demolition order. She claimed that she had not been given the opportunity to remove the house herself in accordance with the District Court’s judgment of 10 May 1990. The applicant requested a three-week respite in order to substantiate her appeal. However, at a session held on 3 June 1996, the Court. of Appeal had already examined the case and, by a decision delivered the. following day, refused the applicant leave to appeal against the District. Court's decision of 15 May 1996. Thus, no further stay of. the enforcement proceedings was granted. This could preserve the house and reduce the risk of adverse consequences for the applicant. The house in issue was therefore demolished by a construction firm. The applicant had claimed that her appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 May 1996 prevented the enforcement of the removal judgment. However, this claim was rejected by the Enforcement Office on 31 May 1996, referring to Chapter 3, section 21, of the Enforcement Code (Utsökningsbalken). The demolition of the house began on 3 June 1996 and was concluded ten days later. On 22 November 1996 the Real Estate Court gave judgment in the division proceedings. It decided that Marum 1:8 should be divided into six individual plots and one common plot. On 28 April 1997 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The applicant and her sister had claimed that other joint owners of Marum 1:6 and 1:8 should remove buildings they had erected on the estates. The District Court rejected the claims, finding that the buildings had been erected before 1991. Furthermore, considering that the claimants did not have a legitimate interest in having their cases heard, the court also decided that further litigation in this respect should not be paid for through public legal aid. With effect from the date of the judgment, the legal aid previously awarded was withdrawn. The Court of Appeal upheld the legal-aid decision. On 16 January 1998 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. No further appeal was lodged and the appellate court’s judgment acquired legal force.

The applicant had claimed that her appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 May 1996 prevented the enforcement of the removal judgment. This claim was rejected by the Enforcement Office on 31 May 1996, referring to Chapter 3, section 21, of the Enforcement Code (Utsökningsbalken). The demolition of the house began on 3 June 1996 and was concluded ten days later. On 22 November 1996 the Real Estate Court gave judgment in the division proceedings. It decided that Marum 1:8 should be divided into six individual plots and one common plot. In this respect, the Real estate Court agreed with the opinion given by the Central Office of the National Land Survey on 14 March 1996. The applicant and her sister had claimed that other joint owners of Marum 1:6 and 1:8 should remove buildings they had erected on the estates. The District Court rejected the claims, finding that the buildings had been erected before 1991. The court also decided that further litigation in this respect should not be paid for through public legal aid. With effect from the date of the judgment, the legal aid previously awarded was withdrawn. No further appeal was lodged and the appellate court’s judgment consequently acquired legal force. name: Leyla Şahin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 44774/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that a ban on wearing the Islamic headscarf in higher-education institutions violated her rights and freedoms under Articles 8, 9, 10 and 14 of the Convention. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 2 July 2002 the Chamber declared the application admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 19 November 2002. Both the applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The headscarf was worn by a student at the University of Bursa, Turkey. The student had to wear it during all lectures at the university. The headdress was banned from being worn in public places. The university issued a circular banning the headdress. The circular was issued in March 1998. The ban has been in effect since then. The woman has been banned from wearing the headwear for the next three years. She is also barred from wearing it in public in any way that is contrary to the law. The reason for the ban is not known. The school has not commented on the woman's decision to wear the headgear in public. The applicant was refused admission to three lectures and an examination because she was wearing a headscarf. She lodged an application for an order setting aside the circular of 23 February 1998. The Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the application, holding that by virtue of section 13(b) of the Higher-Education Act (Law no. 2547 – see paragraph 50 below) a university vice chancellor, as the executive organ of the university, had power to regulate students’ dress in order to maintain order. That regulatory power had to be exercised in accordance with the relevant legislation and the judgments of the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Administrative Court. The Administrative Court held that neither the regulation in issue, nor the individual measures, could be considered illegal. The applicant was suspended from Vienna University for one semester for taking part in an unauthorised assembly. She appealed the suspension, but the appeal was dismissed on 30 November 1999. On 28 June 2000 the applicant was granted an amnesty releasing her from all the disciplinary penalties and their effects. In the meantime, on 16 September 1999, the applicant had enrolled at Vienna University, where she pursued her university education. The application was dismissed after the Supreme Administrative Court ruled that it was unnecessary to examine the merits of the applicant’s appeal on points of law against the judgment of the Istanbul Administrative Court. The applicant is now studying at the University of Vienna.

Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 13 July 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. The applicants sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the Warszawa Regional Court had been excessive. They asked for an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 10,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) (approx. EUR 2,500). The court found that the 2004 Act produced legal effects as from the date of entry into force (17 September 2004), its provisions applied retroactively to all proceedings in which delays had occurred before that date and had not yet been remedied. It acknowledged that there had been a delay at the initial stage of the. proceedings but found that this situation had ceased to exist when the 2004. Act entered into force.

name: Eric Oldham
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36273/97) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant, a discretionary life prisoner who had been released on licence and recalled to prison, made two complaints under Article 5 § 4 of the Convention. He complained, firstly, that he had been denied a fair hearing before the Parole Board on 8 November 1996 and, secondly, that. he had not had his detention reviewed until just over two years later. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) On 1 July 1996 the police were called to the home of the applicant's partner, M., who is a deaf mute. She was taken to hospital where she received treatment for injuries to her face and back. The applicant's licence was revoked on the grounds that the applicant had caused M.'s injuries after drinking at least eight cans of lager. The case was referred to the Parole Board which confirmed the revocation of the licence on 12 July 1996. It was communicated to the applicant in a letter dated 15 November 1996 by the Secretary of State, who informed the applicant that his next Parole board review was set for November 1998. On 15 March 1997, the DLP decided not to extend the grant of legal aid for a further two years. The decision was made on 7 December 1998. The DLP has now extended the grant for two more years. It was the first time in more than a decade that the DPP has extended a grant for more than two years, and it is believed to be the last time they will be able to do so. The current extension of the grant is due to be completed by the end of April 2015. The full length of the new grant will be announced at a later date when it is decided whether or not it is appropriate to extend it.

The case was then adjourned for another two years until the appeal could be heard and the decision was made to extend the trial. The decision was upheld.

train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that the existence of closed-shop agreements in Denmark in their respective areas of employment had violated their right to freedom of association. The applications were allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By decisions of 20 March 2003, the applications were declared partly admissible. In a decision of 25 November 2004, a Chamber constituted within the First. Section relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, none of the parties having objected (Article 30 of the. Convention and Rule 72). A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 2005. The Court heard addresses by Mr Lego Andersen and Mr Taksøe-Jensen, as well as their replies to questions from judges. The first applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Århus, Denmark. In the spring of 1996 he did his national service. On 10 May 1996 he applied for a job as a holiday relief worker in a company, FDB Distributionen (“FDB”). In a letter of 20 May 1996, the applicant was offered the job and informed that his terms of employment would be regulated by an agreement concluded between FDB and a trade union called SID. The applicant did not want to pay the subscription to SID because he had been told that, as a holiday relief employee, he would not be given full membership of SID. On 24 June 1996, the applicant was dismissed for not satisfying the requirements for obtaining the job as he was not a member of a trade union affiliated to LO. The applicant, represented by Denmark's Free Trade Union, instituted proceedings before the High Court of Western Denmark (Vestre Landsret) against FDB, requesting that FDB be ordered to acknowledge that his dismissal was unlawful and to pay him compensation. The High Court found for FDB on 18 November 1998. On appeal, the Supreme Court (Højesteret) upheld the High Court's judgment on 8 June 1999. The Supreme Court stated as follows: “The Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act (Law no. 285 of 9 June 1982) was passed notably in order to comply with the negative right to freedom of association to the extent that such an obligation could be established according to the interpretation of Article 11 of the Convention” The second applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Haderslev, Denmark. He is a gardener by profession. He became a. gardener after he became a lawyer. He says the case-law should disregard section 2(2) of the Protection against. Dismissals due to. Association membership Act, the starting-point must be taken from the Act of 1992 incorporating the European. Convention on Human Rights. A member of SID in the mid-1980s, he resigned his membership after a few years as he felt unable to support its political affiliations. The applicant commenced the job on 17 May 1999 and rejoined SID, although he still did not agree with its political views. He was offered a job at a nursery (Gartneriet i Regnmark I/S) on condition that he became a member of the Christian Trade Union. The employer had entered into a closed-shop agreement with that trade union. He took the job and joined SID on the same day. He died on 24 July 1999.

The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that the existence of closed-shop agreements in Denmark in their respective areas of employment had violated their right to freedom of association. The applications were allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By decisions of 20 March 2003, the applications were declared partly admissible. In a decision of 25 November 2004, a Chamber of judges relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, none of the parties having objected. Third-party comments were received from the Danish Confederation of Trade Unions (Landsorganisationen – LO), which had been given leave by the President. A hearing in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 2005. The Court heard addresses by Mr Lego Andersen and Mr Taksøe-Jensen, as well as their replies to questions from judges. The first applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Århus, Denmark. He applied for a job as a holiday relief worker in a company, FDB Distributionen (“FDB”). In a letter of 20 May 1996, the applicant was offered the job from 3 June until 10 August 1996 and informed that his terms of employment would be regulated by an agreement concluded between FDB and a trade union called SID. The applicant told his employer and the shop steward that he did not want to pay the subscription to SID because he had been told that, as a holiday relief employee, he would not be given full membership. The applicant, represented by Denmark's Free Trade Union, instituted proceedings before the High Court of Western Denmark (Vestre Landsret) against FDB. He alleged that section 2(2) of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act of 9 June 1982 (Lov om beskyttelse mod afskedigelse på grund af foreningsforhold) violated Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights. On appeal, the Supreme Court (Højesteret) upheld the High Court's judgment on 8 June 1999. The starting-point must be taken from the Act of 1992 incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights. A decision abolishing or limiting the existing possibility of entering into closed-shop agreements will have far-reaching consequences for the Danish labour market. The second applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Haderslev, Denmark. He is a gardener by profession. He became a member of the Danish Labour Party in 2000. He has been in the Danish Labor Party since 2005. He was the party's candidate for the European Parliament in 2010. He was a member of SID in the mid-1980s, but resigned his membership after a few years as he felt unable to support its political affiliations. He was offered a job at a nursery (Gartneriet i Regnmark I/S) on condition that he became a member. The applicant commenced the job on 17 May 1999 and rejoined SID, although he still did not agree with its political views. He is now a member of the Christian Trade Union (Kristelig Fagforening). He is also a former member of the Norwegian Trade Union Confederation (NTU), which he left in the early 1990s.

The applications were declared partly admissible by decisions of 20 March 2003. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 2005. The Court heard addresses by Mr Lego Andersen and Mr Taksøe-Jensen, as well as their replies to questions from judges. The first applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Århus, Denmark. In the spring of 1996 he did his national service. On 10 May 1996 he applied for a job as a holiday relief worker in a company, FDB Distributionen (“FDB”). In a letter of 20 May 1996, the applicant was offered the job from 3 June until 10 August 1996 and informed that his terms of employment would be regulated by an agreement concluded between FDB and a trade union called SID. Denmark's Free Trade Union (Danmarks Frie Fagforening) was dismissed for not being a member of a trade union affiliated to LO. The High Court of Western Denmark (Vestre Landsret) ruled that FDB's dismissal was unlawful. The Court of Appeal for the High Court found for FDB, stating that the applicant was aware that membership of SID was a condition for his employment in the company. The Act in issue, and with it the applicant's dismissal, is at variance with Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, in the light of the interpretation this Article has been given by the European Court of Human Rights in its recent case-law. On appeal, the Supreme Court (Højesteret) upheld the High Court's judgment on 8 June 1999. The starting-point must be taken from the Act of 1992 incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights. A decision abolishing or limiting the existing possibility of entering into closed-shop agreements will have far-reaching consequences for the Danish labour market. The second applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Haderslev, Denmark. He is a gardener by profession. He became a judge in the case in 1999. He claimed that section 2(2), of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act of 9 June 1982 raises no doubts as to its compatibility with this judgment. A. a member of SID in the mid-1980s, but resigned his membership after a few years as he felt unable to support its political affiliations. He was offered a job at a nursery (Gartneriet i Regnmark I/S) on condition that he became a member. The employer had entered into a closed-shop agreement with that trade union. The applicant commenced the job on 17 May 1999 and rejoined SID, although he still did not agree with its political views. He died of cancer in October 2007, at the age of 68, after a long battle with liver cancer.

name: Yüksel Yiğitdoğan
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr Yüksel Yiğitdoğan, is currently serving a prison sentence in Kocaeli. He was arrested on suspicion of being a member of an illegal organisation, namely the Turkish Revolutionary Communist Union, Türkiye İhtilalci Komünistler Birliği, “the TIKB’. According to his submissions, he was subjected to ill-treatment during his time in custody. The application was communicated to the Government on 14 January 2013. The applicant was not legally represented when he made his statements to the police. On 9 August 1999 the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court filed an indictment with that court, accusing the applicant of membership of an illegal armed organisation and of involvement in activities which undermined the constitutional order of the State. The Government stated that there had been no such examination of the applicant. In the presence of a lawyer appointed by the Bar association, the applicant retracted his previous statements and maintained that he had been subjected to ill‑treatment during his time in police custody. The judge ruled that the applicant would not attend the hearing that was to be held that day as he had had no opportunity to have prior consultation. The applicant was severely beaten during his arrest in Izmir and had been subjected to electric shocks, hung by the arms, hosed with cold water and sexually assaulted during his seven-day police custody at the Istanbul Security Headquarters. He claimed that although his right arm had been broken and he had developed facial paralysis, he had not been taken to the Forensic Medicine Institute. He argued that the prison personnel and police officers concerned should be prosecuted for this. In 2004 the Istanbul State Security Courts were abolished. The case was joined to another one, in which the applicant was being tried together with some others. The court asked the public prosecutor's office to ensure the applicant’s attendance at the subsequent hearing. The case was adjourned until the end of April 2010. The judge ruled that the case should be heard again. The case was decided on the basis of the evidence given to the court by the prosecution. The prosecution claimed the case was a miscarriage of justice. The verdict was upheld by the Court of Cassation. The jury also ruled that there was no evidence of wrongdoing by the police. The decision was overturned on appeal. The appeal was denied by the judges and the matter was referred to the Supreme Court of the Republic of Turkey, which ruled the case not to be heard by the court of appeals. The court of appeal said that the decision was based on the evidence of the prosecution and not the testimony of the witnesses.

According to his submissions, he was subjected to ill-treatment during his time in police custody. On 14 January 2013 the application was communicated to the Government by the applicant’s lawyer. The Government was represented by their Agent. The application was heard on 11 February 2013. In July 1999 the Istanbul State Security Court decided to extend the applicant’s police custody by three days. On the last day of his police custody, namely on 1 August 1999 the applicant underwent another medical examination at Haseki Hospital. The report drawn up afterwards indicated a scar measuring 1 x 1 cm on his right elbow and another scratch measuring 0,5 x 1cm on his arm. The doctor recommended that the applicant undergo an orthopaedic examination. The Government stated that there had been no such examination. In August 2000 the applicant informed the Istanbul state Security Court that he would not attend the hearing that was to be held that day, as he had had no opportunity to have prior consultation. The applicant had been severely beaten during his arrest in Izmir and had been subjected to electric shocks, hung by the arms, hosed with cold water and sexually assaulted during his seven-day police custody. He claimed that although his right arm had been broken and he had developed facial paralysis, he had not been taken to the Forensic Medicine Institute. The court asked the public prosecutor’s office to ensure his attendance at the subsequent hearing. The Istanbul State Security Court gave an interlocutory decision, holding that the applicant should be brought before the court for the subsequent hearings, and that failure to do so would result in those responsible for his absence being subject to a criminal investigation. The case was transferred to the Istanbul Court of Appeal in 2007. The court ruled in 2010 that the case had not been properly investigated. The case was adjourned until the end of 2012 when it was decided to re-examine the case. The judge ruled in favor of the case and the case was returned to the court of appeal. The verdict was overturned on appeal in March 2013. The appeal was denied on the grounds that the decision was not made on behalf of the victim. The decision meant that the victim had been deprived of his right to a fair trial. The victim was also denied the right to an appeal of the decision by the court.

name: Beata Maria Nowak
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Ms A. Tomaszewska-Wójcik, a lawyer practising in Gniezno. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The case was heard by the Court on 26 August 2005. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the. same time as its admissibility. The case was settled in 1992, but the applicant appealed. The applicant was declared to have the so-called ‘third degree of invalidity’ and was granted an invalidity pension. The case was finally settled in 1998 and the applicant was fined PLN 300 for making a groundless request for the judge to withdraw from the case. She has not produced a copy of the decision given on appeal. The hearing in the case was closed on 1 July 1998. The application was dismissed on 10 September 1996. On 3 July 1998 the applicant requested the Court of Appeal to increase the interim maintenance for her house by an amount of PLN 2,000. The Court of appeal quashed the application on 17 April 1992. The applicant appealed against the decision of the Września District Court to grant a divorce in 1998. The applicant lodged a cassation appeal against the judgment of the Regional Court. On 26 July 2001 the Supreme Court held a hearing. It found, inter alia, that the District Court’s decision to proceed with the hearing on 1 July 1998 had been incorrect, but that in any event it had not prejudiced the applicant's right to defend her interests effectively in the proceedings. The Supreme Court found that the two witnesses who had been heard were immaterial for the determination of the divorce case. The judgment was served on the applicant on 11 September 2001.

name: James Malone
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8691/79) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission on 19 July 1979. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8 and 13. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Sir Vincent Evans, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. G. Wiarda, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) . Mr. Zekia and. Bernhardt, who were prevented from taking part in the consideration of the. case, were subsequently replaced by Mr. B. Walsh and E. García de Enterría, substitute judges. The Post Office Engineering Union (‘the POEU’) requested leave under Rule 37 para. 2 to submit written comments, indicating, inter alia, its “specific occupational interest’ in the case. The President of the Court directed that the oral proceedings should open on 20 February 1984 (Rule 38). The Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar by letter received on 22 December that the Delegate did not wish to file any written reply to these memorials but would be presenting his comments at the hearings. On 17 February 1984, the lawyers for the applicant filed the applicant’s memorial. On 27 October the Chamber unanimously decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. Hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 February. James Malone was charged with a number of offences relating to dishonest handling of stolen goods. His trial resulted in his being acquitted on certain counts and the jury disagreeing on the rest. He was retried on the remaining charges between April and May 1979. Following a further failure by the jury to agree, he was once more formally arraigned; the prosecution offered no evidence and he was acquitted. The Government supplied copies of extracts from a document which had been referred to in argument at the hearing. They notified the Registrar of an amendment to this document on 5 June. Mr Malone was born in 1937 and is resident in Dorking, Surrey. Malone claimed he had heard unusual noises on his telephone and alleged that the police had at times been in possession of information which they could only have obtained by telephone tapping. It was admitted by the Government that the single conversation about which evidence emerged at the applicant’s trial had been intercepted on behalf of the police pursuant to a warrant issued under the hand of the Secretary of State for the prevention and detection of crime. According to the Government, this interception was carried out in full conformity with the law and the relevant procedures. On 28 February 1979, the Vice-Chancellor, Sir Robert Megarry, dismissed the applicant's claim (Malone v. Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis (No. 2), [1979] 2 All England Law Reports 620; also reported at [ 1979] 2 Weekly Law Reports 700). The Government declined to disclose before the Commission or the Court to what extent, if at all, the applicant’s telephone calls and correspondence had been intercepted on behalf of the police authorities. It was denied that the resealing with adhesive tape or the delivery unsealed of the envelopes produced to the Commission was attributable directly or indirectly to any interception. The Government conceded that, as the applicant was at the material time suspected by the police of being concerned in the receiving of stolen property and in particular of stolen antiques, he was one of a class of persons against whom measures of interception were liable to be employed. Mr Malone believed that his telephone had been “metered” on behalf to the police by a device which automatically records all numbers dialled.

name: Kurt Nielsen
train_texts: The case originated in an application against Denmark lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that civil proceedings instituted by him had not been heard within a reasonable time. On 22 June 1999, the Court declared the application admissible. The case was heard by the Second Section of the European Court of Human rights (“the Court’s Second Chamber”) and the Court ruled that the application was admissible on the basis of admissibility and merits. The Court made its decision on 23 September 1999 and published its judgment on 25 November 1999. The application was made under former Article 25 of the Convention for the protection of human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant claimed that the defendant companies should be held liable to pay, jointly and severally, a specified amount in compensation for permanent disablement and loss of working capacity. The case was adjourned pending the outcome of the applicant’s request to the National Board of Industrial Injuries (Arbejdsskadestyrelsen, hereinafter called the NBI), to give an opinion on the degree of disablement. The applicant was hereafter examined by two medical experts at the request of the N BI. The High Court of Western Denmark (Vestre Landsret) upheld the decision on 1 October 1992. The case was heard by the City Court on 25 January 1995. By judgment of 15 February 1995 the defendant companies were held liable to pay 950,803.60 DKK plus interest to the applicant. The defendants appealed against the judgment to the High Court of Western Denmark. On 28 September 1995 the trial was fixed to commence on 1 August 1996. It was later rescheduled to commence in September 1996. The High Court upheld the judgment by judgment of 9 September 1996 and the judgment has become final. The applicant was accordingly examined again by medical experts following which the NBI submitted its opinion on 30 June 1994. The NBI said that the applicant had a degree of disablement and working capacity.

name: Gürsel Coşar
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1961 and is currently serving his prison sentence in Muğla Prison. In his statement to the police, the applicant confessed that he had been involved in the murder of a certain İ.G. When they saw that he was dead, they panicked and tried to get rid of his body. They tied heavy iron bars to his legs and placed his body on a tyre inner tube that they had taken from the boot of Y.A’s car. Then they swam far from the shore. The applicant was arrested in January 2004 for allegedly killing his friend and throwing his body into the sea. He was taken before the public prosecutor and the judge, still waiving his right to legal assistance. The judge ordered his pre-trial detention and the applicant was placed in Fethiye Prison. Other co-accused, Y.A., who had allegedly killed İ.G. according to the applicant’s statement, was arrested. The applicant took part in a reconstruction of events with the police at the scene of the incident. A doctor found two bruises 5-6 cm wide and 30 cm long on the applicant's back. The doctor noted that the bruises had been caused by a blunt object 24 to 48 hours prior to the examination. Y.A. retracted statements he had made during the preliminary investigation stage. He stated that he had been severely tortured while in police custody and had given those statements under duress. The applicant denied being involved in a money-related dispute with İ.G. He said he had never traded on the stock market on behalf of the applicant. The Fethiye Assize Court convicted the applicant and Y.A of homicide and sentenced them to life imprisonment commuted to sixteen years and eight months’ imprisonment. The sentence was commuted on 30 June 2004. The trial court heard that the applicant had tried to kill the applicant by tying an iron bar to his leg and then killing him with a tyre inner tube. The court noted that, according to the police statements from the accused, they had hit the victim on the head with an iron bar and had thrown the body and the bar into the sea. However, the court found there was no proof of the applicant’s allegations. In his appeal petition, he stated that the only evidence against him was the statement taken by the police during the investigative stage, which had been obtained under duress and should therefore not be accepted as evidence. He also pointed out that the police had not discovered a body or a murder weapon. On 18 October 2006 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of 13 July 2005. The Fethiye public prosecutor issued a decision not to prosecute anyone on the basis of the applicant’s allegations. The applicant maintained that he had been punched, kicked and beaten with wooden sticks and that his head had been hit against the walls. The public prosecutor noted that the medical reports issued at the beginning and the end of the applicants detention in police custody did not reveal any sign of ill-treatment on the applicant's body. According to the public prosecutor, the applicant had sustained the injuries after his police custody had ended. The doctor who had examined the applicant on 16 January 2004 explained that he did not remember the applicant in particular. An objection by the applicant was dismissed by the Muğla Assize Court. The public prosecutor considered that the applicant could have caused these injuries by hitting himself on the walls or his bed while in prison. In this connection, the public prosecutor relied on the statements of the doctor who had examined the applicant on 19 January 2004. On 15 December 2004 an objection by  the applicant was dismissed by  the Muğla Assize Court. The prosecutor considered that the applicant's injuries did not necessarily mean that he had been beaten, but that he could have caused them by hitting himself.

name: Tadeusz Sienkiewicz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 52468/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the proceedings in his case had not been conducted within a reasonable time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 10 September 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Poland, which quashed the judgment of the Regional Court and remitted the case for re-examination. The applicant appealed against the decision of the Szczecin Regional Court to dismiss the case. The Supreme Court quashed the Regional Court’s judgment and remitted the case for re-examination. The applicant then appealed against that judgment. The judge awarded the applicant a partial compensation. On 29 November 1999 it gave a judgment, in which it awarded the. applicant compensation. In 2000 it amended the judgment to increase the amount of the compensation. It was dismissed again on 31 May 2000. and the applicant appealed again on 2 June 2000. The appeal was dismissed on 26 June 2000 and the case was dismissed once again on 1 June 2001. The case was finally dismissed on 1 July 2001.

name: Bengt Pudas
train_texts: The case was brought before the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 13 March 1986. It originated in an application (no. 10426/83) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission on 30 March 1983 under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swedish citizen, Mr. Bengt Pudas. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 § 1 and 13 (Art. 6-1, art. 13). The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality. The applicant, Mr. Bengt Pudas, is a Swedish citizen born in 1959. He lives at Hedenäset, which is situated in the Municipality of Övertorneå and the County of Norrbotten, in the North of Sweden. On 1 February 1980, the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) of Norrabotten granted him a taxi traffic licence, and, on 20 May, a licence to carry passengers and their goods on specified interurban routes (linjetrafik). The licences were expressed in writing. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Corell for the Government, by. Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and by. Ravnsborg for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. The applicant commenced his combined taxi and interurban traffic business on 20 May 1980. Two vehicles (a Peugeot 505 and a seven-seater Citroën) were used in the business, which occupied the applicant, his father and a third driver on a part-time basis. On 2 April 1981, the County Traffic Company of Norrbotten filed an application with the County Administrative Board for a licence to provide interurban transport on routes including those covered by Mr. Pudas’ second licence. The applicant opposed the revocation of his licence. In another decision on the same day, the Board revoked the applicant’s and Mr. Wälimaa's licences for interUrban traffic, on the grounds that the plans for the future transport service offered by the County Company included a regular bus service. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Board of Transport (transportrådet), in which he alleged that the County Traffic Company’s application for a licence for the routes covered by his licence had been motivated not by any public interest in improving the transport service, but by an arrangement between the Company and Mr. Wälimaa. Only very serious reasons, such as misconduct of the licence-holder, could justify revocation. The Government dismissed the appeal on 21 October 1982. In response to a further request from the applicant, the Government declined, on 13 January 1983, to review their previous decision. The appeal was dismissed.

On 16 June 1986, the President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the five other members of the Court. The applicant, Mr. Bengt Pudas, is a Swedish citizen born in 1959. He lives at Hedenäset, which is situated in the Municipality of Övertorneå and the County of Norrbotten, in the North of Sweden. On 1 February 1980, the County Administrative Board granted him a taxi traffic licence, and, on 20 May, a licence to carry passengers and their goods on specified interurban routes (linjetrafik) The licences were expressed in writing. The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The applicant commenced his combined taxi and interurban traffic business on 20 May 1980. Two vehicles (a Peugeot 505 and a seven-seater Citroën) were used in the business, which occupied the applicant, his father and a third driver on a part-time basis. The applicant offered a service of two journeys a week at scheduled times. This service was available on request and had to be ordered one day in advance. The County Traffic Company requested that this licence be revoked, as well as a licence held since 1973 by a certain Mr. Wälimaa. In support of its application, the Company submitted that two traffic services in two different regions were to be united into one regular service. “By virtue of a subsequent order, Mr. Pudas’ licence was to cease to be valid as from the date on which the revocation of 17 August became final. The case was brought before the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 13 March 1986. It originated in an application (no. 10426/83) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission on 30 March 1983 under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swedish citizen. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 § 1 and 13 (Art. 6-1, art. 13). The applicant expressed the wish to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Corell for the Government, by Mr Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and by Mr Ravnsborg for the applicant. The applicant, Mr. Bengt Pudas, is a Swedish citizen born in 1959. On 1 February 1980, the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) of Norrbotten granted him a taxi traffic licence, and, on 20 May, a licence to carry passengers and their goods on specified interurban routes (linjetrafik) In 1981, the County Traffic Company of Norrbotten filed an application with the County Administrative Board for a licence to provide interurban transport on routes covered by Mr. Pudas’ second licence. In support of its application, the Company submitted that two traffic services in two different regions were to be united into one regular service with a single time-table. The applicant opposed the revocation of his licence. The application was rejected on the grounds that the plans for the future transport service offered by the County Company include a regular bus service which is to be created between the places in question. In another decision on the same day, the Board revoked the applicant’s and Mr. Wälimaa's licences for interurban traffic, inter alia on the following grounds. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Board of Transport (transportrådet), in which he alleged, inter alia, the following. The County Traffic Company’s application for a licence for the routes covered by his licence had been motivated not by any public interest in improving the transport service. Only very serious reasons, such as misconduct of the licence-holder, could justify revocation. When revoking his licence, the County Administrative Board had failed to take due account of his interests. The transport service on the routes concerned was not likely to be improved simply by being carried out by Mr. Wälimaa and others instead of by himself.

name: Mehmet Göç

The case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France. The suit was brought by a former employee of the İzmir 2nd Court of Taxation. On 31 July 1995 the office of the public prosecutor of Karşıyaka decided not to bring charges against the applicant for lack of evidence. On 5 September 1995 the applicant filed a complaint. under Law no. 466 with the Karşayaka Assize Court (Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi) against the Treasury requesting 200,000,000 Turkish liras. by way of compensation for his detention between “24 and 27 July 1995”.
