The case originated in an application (no. 36590/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 and 6 of the Convention. On 9 November 2000 the Chamber delivered its judgment in which it held, unanimously, that there had been a violation of Article 6. The respondent State was to pay the applicant FRF 10,000 (ten thousand French francs), in ten thousand francs, in Article 5 of Protocol No. 11. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) The case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights on 5 September 2001. A separate opinion of Judges Makarczyk and Türmen was annexed to the judgment. The Court heard addresses by Mr Dinç, Mr Özmen and Mrs Bulutlar Ulusoy, and also their replies to questions from its individual members. The case was decided on the basis of the provisions of Article 27 of the Convention and Rule 24 of the European Court of Human Rights. It was decided that all costs and expenses, together with any value-added tax that might be chargeable, to be converted into Turkish liras at the rate applicable at the date of settlement. The applicant was taken into police custody and detained at the İzmir Security Directorate. He was accused of the above offences. The applicant gave a statement in which he denied that he had been involved in the incident relating to the court's case file. Two other suspects were also detained and statements were taken from them. On 31 July 1995 the office of the public prosecutor of Karşıyaka decided not to bring charges against the applicant (takipsizlik kararı) for lack of evidence. The decision was served on the applicant on 19 August 1995. On 5 September 1995 the applicant filed a complaint. under Law no. 466 with the Karşiyaka Assize Court (Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi) against the Treasury requesting 200,000,000 Turkish. liras (TRL) by way of compensation for his detention between “24 and 27 July 1995”. The judge found that the evidence obtained was sufficient to enable him to draft his report and decided in the exercise of his discretion under section 3 of Law no. 466 that it was unnecessary to hear the applicant. The public prosecutor recommended that the applicant be granted compensation for non-pecuniary damage in an amount to be assessed by the court. The applicant requested that he be granted the sum of TRL 200,000,000 in compensation. In determining the amount of compensation the court should consider both the complainant's economic and social position as well as the intensity of his emotional suffering. The court concluded that, in determining the amount of compensation, it should have regard both to the complainant's economic and social position as well as the intensity of his emotional suffering. The applicant's lawyer and the Treasury both appealed against the award. On 17 October 1996 the Principal Public Prosecutor submitted his opinion on the merits of both parties' appeals. He advised that both appeals be rejected and that the first-instance judgment be approved, being in compliance with procedural rules and law. This opinion was not submitted to the applicant. According to information submitted by the Government, the applicant never applied to obtain the compensation awarded to him by the Karşıyaka Assize Court. having regard, inter alia, to the opinion of the Principal Public Prosecutor, upheld the judgment of 7 December 1995. The Government's information was submitted to the Supreme Court of Justice by the Turkish government. The High Court ruled that the application was legitimate and that the applicant was entitled to the compensation. The decision was upheld by the High Court and the compensation was awarded to the applicant. The case was heard in front of a jury of seven people. The jury awarded the applicant the compensation of £1,000,000.

name: Guy Couez
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the French Government on 19 September 1997. It originated in an application (no. 24271/94) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under Article 25 by a French national, Mr Guy Couez, on 8 July 1993. The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and sought leave to present his own case. The President of the Chamber refused leave and requested the applicant to appoint to represent him an advocate authorised to practise in any of the Contracting States and resident in one of them. The case of Mr Couez was heard by the Chamber of Justice in 1998. The applicant had had a heart attack during a cross-country race in 1989. He applied for extended sick-leave, but authorities refused the request. The Chamber decided to dispense with the case, having satisfied itself that the conditions for this derogation from its usual procedure had been met. The application was made under Article 50 of the Convention and the Government’s memorial was received on 1 April 1998. However, the Delegate of the Commission stated that he did not wish to submit observations on those documents. The case was decided by a vote of the Chamber, with Mr Matscher unable to take part in the further consideration. The applicant brought proceedings in the Amiens Administrative Court to challenge the Prefect’s decision of 27 December 1991 to inform him that the medical board had refused to regard sick-leave on 8 April 1990 as having been due to a work-related accident. On 5 February 1992 he also applied for a stay of execution of that decision. In the meantime, on 25 January 1992, Mr Couez had refused transfer to the administrative staff. On 3 February 1992 the Ministry of the Interior had declared him unfit for active police duties and had placed him on the ordinary sick list with retrospective effect from 8 August 1990. On 4 September 1992, in a fresh decision, he was maintained in the same position. According to the Government, the applicant submitted twenty-seven pleadings between 20 January 1992 and 28 June 1996. Mr Couez had also brought proceedings in the Amiens Administrative Court to challenge the decision of 10 July 1992 whereby he had been sent on compulsory unpaid leave of absence. He subsequently withdrew these proceedings, and on 31 May 1995 the Administrative Court delivered a judgment formally taking notice of the withdrawal. On 31 July 1995 the applicant appealed against that judgment, and the appeal was still pending in the Nancy Administrative Court of Appeal on the date of delivery of the present judgment. The proceedings to Challenge the decision requiring unpaid leave to be taken are referred to in the second part of this article.

name: Jacek Marchowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 10273/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints under Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant, Jacek Marchowski (“the applicant”), was born in 1965 and lives in Kraków, Poland. The applicant was indicted on charges of participation in a fight resulting in homicide and using false documents. Neither the applicant nor his lawyer participated in any of the sessions in connection with his applications for release. In particular, he asked to be released on bail. All those applications were dismissed, both at first instance and on appeal. The court still needed to obtain evidence from sixty-one witnesses including three anonymous witnesses. The trial began on 23 March 1998. Between 23 March and 13 July 1998 the Krakow Regional Court held thirteen hearings. The Kraków Regional Court gave judgment and sentenced the applicant to seven years’ imprisonment and extended the applicant’s detention until 31 December 1998. name: Oliver Riepan
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him, relating to charges of threatening behaviour, he did not have a public hearing as the trial was held in the prison where he was detained. By a decision of 15 June 2000 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 29 August 2000 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr W. Okresek, Head of the Constitutional Law Section at the Federal Chancellery, Agent, Mrs E. Schindler, Federal Ministry of Justice, Adviser. The applicant refused to cooperate and demanded to be returned to Stein. Prison and on 8 May 1995 to Garsten Prison, as the prison administration feared that he and a number of other inmates were devising an escape plan. On account of these incidents, criminal proceedings on charges of threatening behaviour (gefährliche Drohung) were instituted against the applicant. The Steyr Regional Court decided to hold the hearing at Garsten prison, which is situated about 5 km from Steyr. It set down 29 January 1996 as the date for the trial. The summons indicating the date and place of the hearing was served on the applicant as well as on his official defence counsel a month before the hearing. The applicant, assisted by counsel, pleaded not guilty to threatening behaviour. The court heard the four prison officers to whom the applicant had allegedly addressed threats as witnesses. The applicant filed an appeal on points of law and fact, as well as against sentence (Berufung wegen Nichtigkeit, Schuld und Strafe) He complained, in particular, as a ground of nullity, that the hearing on 29 January 1996 had not been public since it took place in the closed area of Garsten Prison. On 5 July 1996 the Linz Court of Appeal held a public hearing in the court building in the presence of the applicant and his counsel. The Court of Appeal had no doubts regarding the Regional Court's evaluation of the evidence and its establishment of the facts. The appellate court also confirmed the legal view that the applicant had, by threatening prison personnel with arson or assault, committed the offence of threatening behaviour. Finally, it found that the sentence was commensurate with the applicant's guilt. The judge had not been informed of any potential spectators at the beginning of the hearing, and the judge did not know if there would be any interested persons in the closed area where the trial was taking place. The hearing was public in the sense that any interested person would have been allowed to attend.

The case originated in an application (no. 35115/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him, relating to charges of threatening behaviour, he did not have a public hearing. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 15 June 2000 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 29 August 2000 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court Mr W. Okresek, Head of the Constitutional Law Section at the Federal Chancellery, Agent, Mrs E. Schindler, Federal Ministry of Justice, Adviser. The Steyr Regional Court (Landesgericht) decided to hold the hearing at Garsten Prison, which is situated about 5 km from Steyr. It set down 29 January 1996 as the date for the trial. The summons indicating the date and place of the hearing was served on the applicant as well as on his official defence counsel a month before the hearing. On account of these incidents, criminal proceedings on charges of threatening behaviour (gefährliche Drohung) were instituted against the applicant. The hearing list was distributed by the public prosecutor's office to the media, namely to the most important national and regional newspapers and to the national broadcasting station. The applicant filed an appeal on points of law and fact, as well as against sentence (Berufung wegen Nichtigkeit, Schuld und Strafe) He complained, in particular, as a ground of nullity, that the hearing on 29 January 1996 had not been public since it took place in the closed area of Garsten Prison. He also claimed that the room in which the hearing was held was too small to accommodate any spectators and alleged that not even the witnesses had been able to stay in the room simultaneously. Finally, he complained that the sentence was too severe. The Court of Appeal dismissed the case. The Court of Appeal stated that it had no doubts regarding the Regional Court's evaluation of the evidence and its establishment of the facts. The appellate court also confirmed the legal view that the applicant had, by threatening prison personnel with arson or assault, committed the offence of threatening behaviour. Finally, it found that the sentence was commensurate with the applicant's guilt. The trial was public in the sense that any interested person would have been allowed to attend. No such persons wishing to attend the trial had been present at the beginning of the hearing, and the judge had not been informed of any potential spectators. If the prison governor had been concerned that interested persons should not be granted access to the closed area, he would have be obliged to prohibit the conduct of the trial in that part of the prison.

name: Joe Anthony Ashendon
train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 35730/07 and 4285/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the refusal to award them their defence costs, after they had been acquitted in their respective criminal proceedings, was in violation of Article 6 § 2 of the convention. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of each application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicants and the Government each filed written observations (Rule 59 § 1). The applicants were represented by Mr G. Bromelow, a lawyer practising in London with Saunders Law Partnership LLP, assisted by Mr S. Simblet, counsel. The trial judge's summing up to the jury contained the following direction: ‘We all know this is a horrific, a disgusting episode. We all know that, and we all know – there has not been any argument about this, has there? – where moral responsibility lies. ... We are not here to dish out admonitions for immoral conduct, disgusting behaviour. We are here to judge whether a crime has been committed, whether the criminal law of the land has been broken. In order to do that you have to be objective. You have to stand back from the feelings of disgust and revulsion that come from the incident.’ The jury acquitted the applicant of the three remaining charges on 14 February 2007. When the first applicant applied for his costs (which exceeded GBP 100,000 and had been met by his family) his counsel stated: ‘This is a case in which [the first applicant] was inevitably going to be charged with a criminal offence, I do not doubt that for a moment’ The trial judge said: “With regard to a defendant’s costs you [Counsel] are right, the costs should and almost invariably would follow the event. I cannot think of another case in my 35 years’ experience in the criminal courts in which it is more apparent’ The second woman was accused of conspiring to steal money from a company. She denied the allegations, saying the tape had been taken out of context. A judge ruled that the tape could be used as evidence in the case. The case is still ongoing and the second woman is seeking compensation from the company she worked for, which has since been dissolved. The third woman has not yet been charged with any crime in relation to the incident. Three defendants, including A.R. and C.R., were convicted of the majority of the charges against them. The trial judge refused the application for a defendant’s costs order. He stated: ‘The relevant features, in my judgment, in this case are these: that [the second applicant], acting very much on the advice of her then solicitor [name omitted], exercised her right to silence when answering ‘no comment’ in her police interview. In my judgment that is a proper reason for refusing a defendant’s costs order. In no way is that decision meant to indicate that she is in any way guilty of this offence, she is not, she has rightly been acquitted by this jury.’ The jury returned a verdict of not guilty.

name: Şahin Çağdaş
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28137/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his detention for two months and twenty three-days contravened Article 5 §§ 1 and 5 of the convention. He also complained that the written opinions which the Principal Public Prosecutors submitted to the Izmir Assize Court and to the Court of Cassation on the merits of his claim and appeal had never been served on him, thus depriving him of the opportunity to put forward his counter-arguments. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52§ 1 of the Rules of Court) The applicant was accused of recruiting new members for the PKK. The charges were brought under Article 169 of the now defunct Criminal Code. The applicant was released pending trial on 3 August 2000. In November 2000 the Izmir State Security Court discontinued the prosecution against the applicant, holding that the five year statutory time-limit laid down in Articles 102§ 4 and 104§ 2 of the Criminal Code had expired. In March 2001 the applicant filed a complaint under Law no. 466 against the Treasury, requesting 10,500,000,000 Turkish liras (TRL) by way of compensation for his detention between 10 May and 3 August 1999. The applicant argued that he was not only unlawfully held in detention but was also deprived of the opportunity to be acquitted of the charges. He asked the Court of Cassation to quash the Assize Court's judgment and to award compensation. The court held that section 1 of Law no. 466 provided an exhaustive list of situations for an award of compensation and that the applicant's circumstances did not fall within any of these categories. The Principal Public Prosecutor submitted his opinion on the merits of the applicant’s appeal on 8 January 2002. He advised that the appeal be rejected and the first-instance judgment be approved, being in compliance with procedural rules and the law. On 5 February 2002 the Ninth Criminal Division of the Court Of Cassation upheld the judgment of 28 March 2001.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22695/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 6. 1 and 3 (d) were violated as he had no opportunity to examine the main. witness in the criminal proceedings against him. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was granted legal aid and was represented by Ms Słupska-Uczkiewicz, a lawyer practising in Wrocław. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. The court established the following facts. On 10 June 2000 M.H., who was at that time 17 years old, met the applicant, J.K. and another man in a bar called ‘DIK’ They told her to come to the same bar the next day at 5 p.m., which she did. On 11 June 2000 the applicant and J. K. again threatened M. H. in the bar. The applicant then led her out of the bar and together with J.k. they went to the latter’s house. They raped her in the basement of the house and threatened to kill her if she told anybody about it. M.H., who was questioned three times, described in identical terms the course of events of 10 and 11 June 2000. It is not surprising that, despite the fact that she had been close to a police station, M.H. did not try to call for help. ... [in the basement] M.h., being afraid of the accused and that [the applicant] would carry out the threats he had made, which were fully backed up by J.K. as his behaviour proves, submitted herself to all the demands of the. accused and had repeated vaginal, anal, and oral sexual intercourse. The victim could not have counted on anybody’s help in such a place and she believed that putting up any resistance would have been pointless. Victim's statements were coherent and logically linked. No injuries were established ... The test excluded the presence of semen. A lack of abrasions ... cannot prove that sexual intercourse had not taken place. The circumstances examined above allowed the court to believe that the accused, acting together and in agreement, threatening to beat M.H. up and using force by holding her arms, had raped her on 11 June 2000. The applicant’s lawyer lodged an appeal against the judgment. On 13 December 2001 the Wrocław Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) upheld the first-instance judgment and dismissed the appeal. On 14 February 2002 the applicant's lawyer lodged a cassation appeal on his behalf with the Supreme Court. M.Ł. wyższy complained that the victim has only been summoned to the hearing of 21 May 2000 once and that the summons had been sent to an address in Poland even though the trial court had known her new address in Germany. The applicant concluded that he had been deprived of the right to put questions to the witness and to confront her with other evidence, which he had repeatedly requested during the trial. On 11 March 2003 the Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal. The Supreme Court stated, in so far as relevant: “...[Article 391 § 1] does not mean that in every case when a witness is abroad an automatic application of an exception from the rule of principle of directness should apply" The victim was heard in the preparatory proceedings by a court according to the provision of Article 316 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant had been in hiding when the court heard the victim. The author of the cassation appeal ... failed to indicate what concrete, additional information he would have liked to obtain from M.H ...” said the court of appeal in a ruling on the appeal of a case against a German man accused of murdering a woman. He filed a claim for payment against his former employer on 22 May 1991. On 2 December 1991 the court gave judgment. On 9 June 1998 the applicant lodged a cassation appeal. On 16 December 1999 the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) held one hearing and gave judgment in which it dismissed the appeal. The applicant appealed to the Olsztyn District Court against a decision to dismiss him from work. The applicant lodged a claim for damages under section 16 of the 2004 Act read in conjunction with Article 417 of the Civil Code. His appeal against the judgment was dismissed by the ŁóDż Court of Appeal on 18 May 2006. The Government maintained that such an appeal was pending before the Supreme Court. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the applicant had not lodged a cassation appeal.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 18 December 1995 by the applicant, Mr Rolf Gustafson, a Swedish national. The Court's Screening Panel decided not to decline consideration and to submit it to the court on 29 March 1996. The applicant is a Swedish citizen resident in Stockholm. Since 1973 he has spent a total of eight years in prison for the commission of serious economic offences. In October 1996 he was sentenced to a one-year term of imprisonment for a serious forgery offence. The applicant claims that on two occasions, in April-June and June‑July 1991, he was the victim of kidnapping and extortion perpetrated by three persons. According to the applicant, one of the alleged perpetrators, a certain Mr L., had wanted to be paid for the part he played with him in theCommission decided to dispense with a hearing in the case. The applicant applied for compensation to the Criminal Damage Compensation Board (Brottsskadenämnden - hereinafter “the Board’) under the Criminal damage Act 1978. In his application he stated that he had sought compensation for personal injury in the amount of SEK 160,000 in the proceedings against L. The Stockholm District Court convicted L., sentenced him to six years’ imprisonment and ordered him to pay SEK 144,350 in damages to the applicant. The Court of Appeal found that the applicant, in view of his criminal background, could not be deemed a trustworthy person. It followed that the information he had provided on the events which had given rise to the kidnapping and extortion were untrue. The Board rejected the applicant’s compensation claim on 26 August 1993. The applicant requested the Board to reconsider its decision. He argued that it was clear from the judgments of the District Court and the Court of Appeal that he had been the victim of a crime. He had identified two of the three persons who were allegedly involved in the offences. The fact that the only one to be charged, L., was guilty was not a reason to doubt that he was a victim of crime. The Board upheld the decision to reject the applicant's claim for compensation. The decision was upheld on a unanimous verdict. The appeal was dismissed and the case is now closed. Inspector S. had been the principal investigator into the economic offences of which the applicant had previously been convicted. He had interrogated both the applicant and L. on a number of occasions. Inspector S. told the District Court, inter alia: “I was, probably on 4 July 1991, informed [about the alleged kidnapping of the applicant]. A colleague ... telephoned me to say that he had been informed that [the applicant] had been kidnapped ..., that the kidnapping had been staged by [L.] with the help of two ‘gorillas’, ... and that the kidnap had been combined with an extortion threat against [ the applicant] in the amount of SEK 5 million.“ On 1 June 1994 the Board rejected the applicant’s request, for the following reasons: “The submissions in this case in support of the request for reconsideration are not such as to be a reason for the Board to change its previous decision. name: Martin Brunnthaler
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 45289/99) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged in particular that the proceedings relating to his request for an industrial licence for chimney sweeping lasted unreasonably long. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 16 June 2005, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The application was allocated to the Third Section. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 3 June 1993 the Federal Minister allowed his request for transfer but dismissed his application for the industrial licence under the Trade Act (Gewerbeordnung). Referring to the submissions of the competent municipalities, he noted that there was no need for further chimney sweepers in the concerned area. On 20 July 1993 the applicant filed a complaint with the Administrative Court. He complained in particular that the Federal minister had not made sufficient investigations for his findings. On 17 April 1998 the Administrative court rejected the applicant’s complaint for non-exhaustion of administrative remedies as he had failed to file an appeal with the federal Minister for Economic Affairs. The Linz Municipal Office dismissed the applicant’s request for an industrial licence on 23 January 1997. On 21 July 1997 the Regional Governor confirmed this decision. On 30 September 1997 the Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant's complaint. The case was transferred to the Administrative Court. The Administrative Court dismissed the complaint as being unfounded on 9 September 1998. This decision was served on the applicant and his counsel on 21September 1998. The applicant filed further submissions on 13 March, 7 April, 28 April and on 15 May 1998 the applicant, in compliance with an order to remedy certain procedural effects, filed further applications. The application was dismissed again on 9 October 1998.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 67385/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had not been afforded a proper review of the lawfulness of his continued detention as a mandatory life prisoner. The Court declared the application partly admissible in May 2003. No hearing on the merits was required. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26: 1. The court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing was required (Rule 59: 3). The applicant learned that his ‘tariff’ period fixed by the trial judge on the manslaughter offence expired in June 1991. He was informed by a Home Office Memorandum of 5 June 1992 that his continued detention was based on the risk he represented. According to the applicant's submissions, his only Parole Board review took place in 1999, when, without holding an oral hearing, the Board declined to recommend release. In 1994, it concluded that his behaviour was aggressive and intimidatory and that he represented a high risk to the public. On 10 January 1997, it conclude that he remained far too great a risk to warrant transfer to open conditions.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged principally that her home and property had been destroyed during an operation by gendarmes carried out in her village in south-east Turkey. The application was declared admissible by the Commission on 23 May 1996. In its report of 6 September 1999, the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been a violation of Articles 8 and 13 of the convention. The case was referred to the Court on 23 October 1999. The judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28) and was replaced by an ad hoc judge. The facts of the case, particularly concerning events on or about 8 November 1993 when the gendarmes carried out an operation at Çitlibahçe, were disputed by the parties. The Commission, pursuant to former Article 28 § 1 (a) of the Convention, conducted an investigation with the assistance of the parties and heard witnesses in Ankara on 7 February 1997. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The Commission’s findings of fact are set out in its report of 6 September 1999 and summarised below (Section A) The applicant accepts the Commission's findings offact. PKK terrorists took away five teachers from the village of Dadaş in 1993. All, save the imam and his brother, were shot. The imam’s brother, though wounded, survived. The gendarme commander who gave evidence denied that this occurred but recalled that he had destroyed hemp crops. The Commission did not make any finding in regard to this aspect as it was not the subject-matter of any specific complaint. The Delegates found that the villagers, Remziye Çakıcı, Fevzi Okatan and Mehmet Bitgin were on the whole consistent and credible. Their evidence was found to support the testimony of the witnesses heard in this case. The Commission found in conclusion that the applicant’s property, furniture and possessions were deliberately burnt and destroyed during an operation by security forces in the village of Çitlibahçe on 8 November 1993. The Commission did not find the matters referred to by the Government as being indicative of bad faith or as materially undermining the credibility and reliability of the applicant and her witnesses. The applicant and other villagers went to Diy and other villages to give evidence to the Commission. While the Commission took note of the applicants age, its Delegates had not found any indication of mental infirmity that would cast doubt on her ability to give testimony. The Government emphasised the terrorism which was prevalent in this region from the early 1990’s and created a public danger threatening the life of the nation. The applicant had made no complaint to the public prosecutor about the alleged burning of her house and property by the gendarmes during the operation on 8 February 1993. The Government submitted a copy of the statement taken by the Diyarbakır public prosecutor from the applicant via an interpreter on 10 October 1995. This had not been provided to the Commission. The Hazro Administrative Council began an investigation and found that her claims were unsubstantiated. She acknowledged that the thumbprint on the document was hers and that she did not remember who took the statement. After the village burned down, she went to Diyarbakır. She was illiterate and ignorant and did not know anything about European human rights. She did not want to start a case in Europe in the way that he [the public prosecutor] had explained. It was for the State to look after her rights. The application which had been read out was accurate though and she had no complaints to make about the person who wrote it down. The statement recorded that she was shown the application and letter of authority and asked about them. She stated the thumbprints were hers. She said that she thought her application was going to Ankara to claim her right.

In its report of 6 September 1999, the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been a violation of Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The facts of the case, particularly concerning events on or about 8 November 1993 when the gendarmes carried out an operation at Çitlibahçe, were disputed by the parties. The Commission, pursuant to former Article 28 § 1 (a) of the Convention, conducted an investigation with the assistance of the parties and heard witnesses in Ankara on 7 February 1997. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The applicant accepts the Commission's findings of fact. The Government’s submissions concerning the facts are summarised below (Section B). PKK terrorists went to the village of Dadaş in the Hazro district and took away five teachers. All, save one of the teachers, were shot. The imam’s brother, though wounded, survived. The Commission did not make any finding in regard to this aspect as it was not the subject-matter of any specific complaint. stating that the tobacco crops were destroyed by order of the security forces. The gendarme commander who gave evidence before the Delegates denied that this occurred but recalled that he had destroyed hemp crops. The Delegates found that the villagers, Remziye Çakıcı, Fevzi Okatan and Mehmet Bitgin were on the whole consistent and credible. The Commission found in conclusion that the applicant’s property, furniture and possessions were deliberately burnt and destroyed during an operation by security forces in the village of Çitlibahçe on 8 November 1993. The Commission accepted the evidence of the applicant as regards its principal elements. It did not find the matters referred to by the Government as being indicative of bad faith or as materially undermining the credibility and reliability of the. applicant and her witnesses, which its Delegates assessed in generally positive terms. It found that the Hazro gendarmes included. Álım Dulaş and Emin Bilen in the operation since they intended to look for and take into custody Ahmet. Çakıcı, who, as a person already under suspicion of involvement in PKK activities, would be likely to have. information about the kidnap group that passed through the village. The applicant made no complaint to the public prosecutor about the alleged burning of her house and property by the gendarmes during the operation on 8 February 1993. The Government submitted a copy of the statement taken by the Diyarbakır public prosecutor from the applicant via an interpreter on 10 October 1995. This had not been provided to the Commission. She acknowledged that the thumbprint on the document was hers and that she did not remember who took the statement. As regarded the events, she could not remember the exact date but about two years before 20 or more army vehicles had been seen at her home. The applicant’s various accounts, oral and written, were inconsistent and implausible, in particular the details purportedly noted down by the Human Rights Association in her application. After the village burned down, she went to Diyarbakır. She was illiterate and ignorant and did not know anything about European human rights. She did not want to start a case in Europe in the way that he [the public prosecutor] had explained. It was for the State to look after her rights. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr Seyfettin Güneş (‘the applicant’), on 24 February 2010. The applicant was charged with being a member of Hizbullah in 2000. He was convicted and sentenced to ten years in prison in 2009. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment in 2009 and the applicant began serving his sentence in December 2009. He claims he was tortured in police custody while in custody. He has never been charged with any crime in connection with his alleged torture. The applicant has not been convicted of any offence during his time in prison. The application was brought by the public prosecutor at the Diyarbakır State Security Court. The case against the applicant and his co‑accused was joined with another case brought against a number of other people charged withBeing members of HIZbullah. In April 2010 the applicant filed a petition with the Batman public prosecutor’s office, requesting that an investigation be initiated into his ill‑treatment while in police custody in April 2000. In December 2010 a doctor from the Diyarbakır branch of the Forensic Medical Institute conducted the examination. The doctor noted that he could not see any such scar when he examined the applicant in 2010. In November 2011 the public prosecutor decided not to prosecute the officers on duty at the Batman police station at the relevant time or the three doctors who had issued the medical reports in 2000. On 19 December 2011 the applicant objected to that decision. The applicant's hip was broken while he was playing volleyball. Doctors concluded that for him to make a full recovery, he would need to have a hip replacement. A prosthetic hip was implanted after four consecutive operations carried out on unspecified dates in 2003 or 2004. On 22 October 2004 the applicant was declared unfit for military service because of the prosthesis. On 23 January 2012 the Midyat Assize Court dismissed his objection and the decision was upheld. He requested that both the police officers on duty at the relevant time and the doctors who had issued the medical reports be prosecuted. The public prosecutor noted that the statutory time-limit provided in Article 102 of the former Criminal Code (which had been in force in 2000 for prosecutions for torture) was ten years. name: Jerzy Biśta
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22807/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested by officers of the Internal Security Agency (Agencja Bezpieczeństwa Wewnętrznego) on suspicion of revealing State secrets and bribery. The court found that there was a reasonable suspicion that the applicant, while at liberty, would have had unlimited opportunities to contact other persons who were directly linked to his criminal activities. It also considered that it was necessary to keep the applicant in detention in order to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the risk that he might tamper with evidence. In the course of the investigation, the applicant’s detention was prolonged on several occasions, inter alia on 7 November and 29 December 2005 by the Szczecin District Court. In all their decisions regarding detention the authorities repeatedly relied on the original grounds given for the applicant's detention. The applicant was charged with revealing state secrets and bribery. One hundred and four persons were listed to be examined as witnesses. No other preventive measure was used to keep the applicant in custody. The application to transfer the case was filed owing to the special nature of charges brought against the applicant, including revealing State secrets and involvement in the case of high-ranking police officers. The Szczecin Regional Court decided that the applicant could be released if he put up bail of 50,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) In addition, an order was given to seize his passport and he was placed under police supervision. The applicant appealed and requested that the amount of bail be reduced. The Kraków Appeal Prosecutor appealed. It appears the applicant was eventually released on payment of the bail, at the latest on 15 December 2007. It further appears that the criminal proceedings are currently pending. The application has been referred to as ‘Censorship’ (‘ocenzurowano’)

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56827/00) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. name: Sait Uysal
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1206/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were taken into police custody on 27 June 1992 and 24 May 1992 respectively on suspicion of their membership of an illegal organisation, the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers' Party) On 12 June 1998 the applicants were released pending trial. On an unspecified date in 1998 the second applicant went abroad. The court found the applicants guilty of aiding and abetting anillegal organisation and sentenced them to three years and nine months' imprisonment, pursuant to Article 169 of the Criminal Code. On 14 October 1999 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment. Diyarbakır State Security Court found first applicant guilty of membership of a terrorist organisation and sentenced him to 12 years and 6 months' imprisonment. Court of Cassation quashed the first applicant's prison sentence. Second applicant's case was transferred to the Diyarbak Turkish Assize Court. On 14 July 2006 the court ordered an arrest warrant for the second applicant. According to the information in the case file, the trial is still pending before the DiYarbak Turkey Assize court. The second applicant was sentenced to eight years and four months in prison on 26 February 2004. The case was finally settled on 30 July 2006.

name: Erdal Kıran
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 23321/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his right of access to court was breached by the domestic court’s refusal of his legal aid request. He claimed that he had become ill during his military service as a result of the degrading treatment he had been subjected to in the army. He requested a total of 150,000 Turkish liras (TRY) (approximately 80,000 euros (EUR) at the time) in both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages. On 4 February 2009 the Supreme Military Administrative Court decided to discontinue the compensation proceedings because the applicant had not paid the necessary court fees. The applicant had to pay a total of TRY 2,384 (approximately EUR 1,300) in court fees within thirty days for the proceedings to be continued. The court ruled that the applicant should pay the fees within 30 days or the case would be adjourned. The case was settled in a settlement of approximately $1.5 million. The application was dropped in November 2008. The compensation was settled out of court in February 2009. The judge ruled in favor of the applicant and ordered the case to be dismissed.

name: Max Myer Kingsley
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that the proceedings before the Gaming Board Panel were in violation of Article 6 § 1 of the convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 14 September 1999, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. London Clubs was given certificates of consent by the Gaming Board to apply for new licences for its casinos. The Gaming Board also made cancellation applications in respect of the existing licences held by LCL. LCL agreed to surrender its existing licences if new licences were granted by the Licensing Magistrates. Objections to the issuing of new licences made by a rival casino owner were rejected. New licences were issued in October 1992, after a three day hearing before the Licenses Magistrates, and LCL’s executive directors resigned with effect from 30 April 1992, on the understanding that such resignation was involuntary and constituted dismissal by London Clubs. In November 1992 the Chairman of LCL was named along with nine others. Lady Littler, of the Gaming Board, addressed the British Casino Association. Her speech referred to London Clubs and commented: “We [the Gaming Board] satisfied ourselves that the practices we and the Police had regarded as unacceptable had ceased’ The Gaming Board alleged that the “persons” referred to were minority shareholders and no reference to the applicant was intended. The applicant did not accept this explanation, however defamation proceedings were not commenced. By a letter dated 23 April 1993, the. Gaming Board informed the applicant formally that it was “minded to revoke” the applicant’s Section 19 certificates and. that the applicant would be given the opportunity to state his. case against revocation. The Gaming Board rejected the request for an independent tribunal and a Section 19 hearing commenced on 11 April 1994 before a panel of three. The hearing was conducted in private and lasted for seven and a half days. By a letter dated 28 May 1994, the applicant was informed that the Gaming Board did not consider the applicant to be a fit and proper person to continue to hold the Board’s certificates of approval. The Board would revoke his Section 19 certificates within 21 days of receipt of the letter. The applicant sought leave to apply for judicial review of the decision. The decision was challenged on the grounds that the Panel was biased, or had the appearance of bias and that its findings were vitiated by errors of law and were irrational. The application for judicial review was dismissed on 11 January 1996 by Mr Justice Jowitt after a hearing lasting over 16 days. He delivered three separate judgments in respect of the applicant’s appeal. The first judgment dealt with the scope of the phrase “a fit and proper person” in Schedule 5 of the Gaming Act 1968. The second judgment considered the applicant's claim that he had a “legitimate expectation” that the Gaming Board would be precluded from taking account of any breaches of its guidelines. The third judgment which dealt with “Wednesbury challenges and allegations of bias runs to 165 pages.57 pages of the third judgment were devoted to the issue of bias. Jowitt J. described the test of bias under English law in the following terms (pp. 93-96 of the judgment): ‘[Counsel for the applicant] submits that the decision to revoke the applicant’s Section 19 certificates of approval should be quashed because the Panel was biased’ ‘There was no disagreement between the parties as to the approach the court should adopt when bias is alleged. It is a two stage test. The applicant has first to show from the evidence that there is an appearance of bias. Having done so, he has to go on to show that on a proper examination by the court there is demonstrated a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias’ Jowitt J. stated, further, that if, contrary to his finding, there was unconscious bias on the part of the Panel, the “doctrine of necessity” fell to be considered. He concluded that there was no unconscious bias by any of the panel members. He said: “When a body is charged by statute with the power or duty to make a decision in circumstances in which a question of bias arises, the decision will not be liable to be impugned on account of bias.” Jowitt then applied the test of bias which he had set out to the facts of the case, and concluded that, on the evidence before him, he could not say that the applicant had established a real danger of injustice having occurred. The Court of Appeal, after an oral hearing on 4 July 1996, refused an application for leave to appeal from Jowitt J.'s decision. Morritt L.J. held, on the “doctrine of necessity,” as follows: “I am prepared to assume in favour of [the applicant] that he would have an arguable case sufficient to justify leave to. appeal.” Hobhouse L. j. agreed, and the case went to the Supreme Court, where it was decided that the decision of the Panel was not irrational or unreasonable. The Court of. Appeal rejected the application, saying that the case should have been decided by an independent tribunal which did not involve an impermissible delegation. The decision for the Board was, at the end of the day, whether or not Mr Kingsley was a fit and proper person. That could not be delegated to an independent panel and if they were actuated by bias, apparent or real, then the decision would still have to be made by them. The question of bias, therefore, depends on the very limited point on whether it is arguable that Jowitt J was wrong in that respect. I am bound to say that, on that limited point, I think he was manifestly right. It seems to me that there is no arguable point, susceptible on this part of the case, which would justify giving leave to appeal.

Kingdom,. no. 30054/96 and Shanaghan v the United UK, no, 37715/97. The applicant’s son, Pearse Jordan, aged 22, was shot and killed in Belfast by an officer of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (the RUC), later identified as Sergeant A. Treacy. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Treacy and declared the application admissible on 4 April 2000. The facts of the case, in particular concerning what happened when PearseJordan was shot on 25 November 1992, are in dispute between the parties. The case was heard at the Supreme Court of Northern Ireland and the jury returned a verdict in favour of the applicant. Four civilians were walking along the road when they heard a crash behind them. They turned to see a police car pulling alongside a car and ramming it up onto the footpath. Pearse Jordan emerged from the immobilised car, and appeared shaken. He staggered across the road towards the four men followed by four police officers. An officer about 12 feet away fired a number of shots. The civilians heard no warning shout or challenge given by any of the officers. The police carried out a search of the car. The four witnesses followed the ambulance which took Pearse. Jordan to hospital where they stated that they were subjected to hostile and threatening remarks by. members of the security forces. Sergeant A thought that this was possibly the re-supply of terrorist equipment taking place. He was carrying a Smith and Wesson 59 pistol and a MP5 Heckler and Koch. Sergeant A’s car drew level with the Orion and he signalled for it to pull over. The Orion slowed falling behind and then shot past on the passenger side, accelerating down the Falls Road in the direction of the city. He told his driver to pursue him and force him off the road. The car possibly reached the speed of 60, maybe 70 miles per hour at the fastest. They were in a built up area, in traffic so it was difficult to judge. Their klaxon was going. Sergeant A said that he called out “Police. Halt.” or “Halt. Police” The driver of the Orion turned around towards him. He could not see the man’s hands which were below his waist. He feared the man was armed as he had spun round so quickly. He fired a short burst from his MP5 at the trunk of the man. The driver fell flat, toppling over. It was realised at that stage that he was seriously injured. Sergeant A quickly searched the car, while other security force personnel administered first aid to the driver. The military took over the first aid. Sergeant A said he had a clear view of the deceased from the waist up. When the deceased turned to face him, he did not make any movements towards him. His arms were down and his hands out of sight. In that short space of time, he formed the opinion that the deceased was a threat to his life. He was certain that there were no viable alternatives to discharging his own weapon. Forensic examinations of the cars involved in the incident were carried out. Interviews were conducted with the other police officers and army personnel involved. Only officer D heard shouting coming from the call sign 8 direction before the shooting. Inquest into the death of Pearse Jordan will be held on 4 January 1995. Inquest will hear evidence from all parties involved in the case. Pearse's family were not provided with any indication as to the nature of the RUC’s findings. The evidence was concluded that the evidence was insufficient to warrant the prosecution of any person. The Coroner decided to hold an inquest following the Director of Public Prosecutions’ direction of ‘no prosecution’ in respect of the fatal shooting. The inquest will be heard by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) under the direction of the Chief Constable of the Coroner. The hearing is expected to last between three and five days. Defence issued a certificate in which he identified information whose disclosure at the inquest he believed would be contrary to the public interest on grounds of national security. Defence made an application that the identities of certain military witnesses be withheld and that they should give their evidence from behind a screen. The Coroner sat for three and a half days, hearing evidence from 19 witnesses, including the applicant, 8 civilians, Soldiers V, W and X, 7 police officers and a pathologist. The applicant and his family were represented by a solicitor and counsel. The RUC were represented. The DPP decided that the evidence remained insufficient to warrant the prosecution of any person in relation to Pearse Jordan's death. The applicant's legal representatives made an application for the Coroner to discharge himself from the Inquest on the grounds that he was not conducting the inquest fairly. The Coroner refused the application. Lord Justice Carswell refused the applicant’s claims. In doing so he had regard to the inquisitorial nature of inquest proceedings. He referred to the remarks of Griffiths J in Ex parte Peach: “A coroner's inquest is an inquisitors procedure with a very limited objective indeed. The objective is limited to ascertaining the following matters: who the deceased was; how, when and where the deceased came by his death.” The applicant appealed against the decision of Lord Justice Carswell. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland on 28 June 1996. The applicant’s application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords was refused on 4 October 1996. On 16 March 1999, final judgment was given in the case of Sharon Lavery v. the Secretary of State and the Legal Aid Department, in which a challenge concerning the unavailability of legal aid for inquests was dismissed. On 2 February 2000, the applicant was informed that the Chief Constable would provide copies of the statements of the witnesses who were to appear at the inquest and copies of any statements the Coroner proposed to read out. The applicant was granted legal aid to pursue a civil action for compensation in the High Court. On 5 October 1995, the applicant served a statement of claim in the civil proceedings. On 8 October 1999, the Crown Solicitor wrote to the applicant seeking consent to a remittal of the civil action to trial. The case is currently at the discovery stage but that this cannot be concluded until the inquest is terminated. On 4 April 2000 the applicant was provided with the witness statements of persons whom the Coroner has decided should be called to give evidence at the inquest. in addition to the witnesses who gave evidence in January 1995, 12 police officers and Soldier Y.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of the Republic of Austria on 16 March and 7 April 1989 respectively. It originated in an application (no. 11761/85) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by an Austrian national, Mr Karl Obermeier, on 24 September 1985. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 ( art. 6-1) and Articles 13 and 14 (Art. 13, art. 14) of the Convention. The Court heard evidence from the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the applicant on the need for a written procedure (Rule 37) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Türk, Mrs Bernegger and Mrs Gartner for the Government and Mr Frowein for the Commission, as well as their answers to its questions. It also heard the Government’s observations on the application of this provision. It heard the response of Mr Obermeier, who was formerly employed by a private insurance company (‘the company’) as the director of their regional branch office for Upper Austria. In 1974 a dispute arose between the applicant and the company concerning various paid activities which it proposed to withdraw from him. Mr Obermeier instituted proceedings in the Vienna Labour Court (Arbeitsgericht). On 10 March 1978, the day following the first hearing, he was suspended from his duties by his employer. The company considered that it was entitled to take such a decision at any time without giving reasons. On 23 April 1981 the Linz Labour Court dismissed the applicant’s claims. On 25 November 1981 the Regional Court (Landesgericht) allowed the appeal as regards the part of the judgment concerning the revocation of the suspension. The case was therefore remitted to the Labour Court. On 21 May 1980 Mr Obermeier had been declared disabled for the purposes of the Disabled Persons (Employment) Act. On 8 May 1981, the company sought the authorisation for the applicant’s dismissal. Following a hearing, the Board gave its consent to the dismissal on 8 July 1981, finding that the relationship of trust between the parties had been irremediably undermined. The Provincial Governor (Landeshauptmann) for Upper Austria confirmed the Board's decision on 16 October 1981. The applicant then appealed to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) which dismissed his appeal on 9 March 1983. The European Commission of Human Rights declared the appeal inadmissible on 12 March 1986. The company pleaded Mr Obermeier’s lack of a legal interest (Rechtsschutzbedürfnis) in the revocation of his suspension, since in the meantime he had been dismissed. The applicant, for his part, challenged the lawfulness of his dismissal. He stressed in particular that it had been pronounced before the authorisation from the Disabled Persons Board had become final, as the case was still pending before the Administrative Court. The company sent to the applicant, on 21 December 1984, a further notification of dismissal, which was to take effect on 30 June 1985. On appeal by the applicant appealed on points of law to the Supreme Court which, on 23 October 1984, quashed the decisions of the labour courts. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) which referred the case to the Administrative Court. The latter court allowed the appeal on 21 May 1986, finding that the company had committed an error of law by dismissing Mr Obermeier before the authorisation had become final. On 1 June 1986, the Provincial Governor confirmed the Board’s decision of 14 March 1985. The applicant then asked the Board to declare, pursuant to sections 8 to 12 of the Disabled Persons (Employment) Act, that his employment contract subsisted. The Board and Provincial Governor found, on 10 February 1986 and 12 January 1987 respectively, that they lacked jurisdiction to make such a declaration. Mr Obermeier also challenged his dismissal in the labour courts. On 16 August 1982 he brought an action in the Linz Labour Court for a declaration that his dismissal was invalid. He argued that the company had not waited until the authorisation given by the Disabled Persons Board had become final in law. The court dismissed Mr Obermeier’s action on 14 August 1985 on the ground that, in the meantime, the Provincial Governor had given his retroactive consent. The parties did not appeal from this decision. The applicant filed an application on 22 July 1986 for the proceedings to be reopened (Wiederaufnahmsklage) and requested that such proceedings also deal with the second dismissal from employment. On an appeal by the company, the Linz Court of Appeal set aside this decision on 15 March 1988. The applicant claimed that he had cited at the hearing, as an additional ground for the invalidity of his dismissal, disregard of clause 33 § 9 of the collective agreement. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 29 June, holding that section 105 of the Industrial Relations Act did not apply to a disabled person. On 30 June 1988, even before a copy of the Supreme Court’s judgment had been served on him, the applicant instituted new proceedings in Linz Regional Court, sitting as a social and labour court. He sought a declaration that the second dismissal was void on the ground that the company had not obtained the prior consent of the works council. The court dismissed the action on 23 September 1988, finding that the agreement given in 1981 was also valid in relation to the 1984 dismissal. In the intervening period, Mr Obermeier had, on 22 July 1986, applied to the labour courts for the reopening of the proceedings concerning his suspension, proceedings which had been terminated by the Supreme Court on 15 July 1986. He relied on the judgment delivered by the Administrative Court on 21 May 1986 (see paragraph 25 above). On 15 October 1986 the Regional Court dismissed the application for the proceedings to be reopened, on procedural grounds. On 15 July 1987 the. Supreme Court allowed the applicant’s appeal on points of law and remitted the case to the. Linz Court of Appeal which had acquired jurisdiction by virtue of a new. Act on the social and labour courts.

name: Stanisław Marecki
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. On 23 October 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the complaint to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The courts justified their decisions prolonging the applicant’s detention on remand and their refusals to release him by the need to hear evidence from the accused and witnesses, some of whom lived abroad. The courts found on several occasions that there were no special grounds, as specified in Article 259 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that would justify lifting the detention order and imposing a less severe measure. On 23 May 2002 the Łódź Regional Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 25 years’ imprisonment. On 22 December 2003 the  Łowż Court extended his detention until 22 June 2004. The applicant lodged a claim for compensation for wrongful detention. The proceedings are still pending. The Łódż Regional Court acquitted the applicant and he was released from detention. On 6 December 2004, the Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case to the Regional Court. The case is still pending, but the applicant was acquitted in December 2004 and released from jail. The applicant has since filed a compensation claim for wrongful detainment. The court of appeal is yet to make a decision on the case. For confidential support call the Samaritans in the UK on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or click here for details.

A bill of indictment, concerning six accused and involving 140 witnesses, was filed with the Łódź Regional Court on 25 April 2000. He has been out of jail since December 2004, when he was freed from detention after serving a two-year sentence for trespassing on a public road in the city of Wrocław.

name: Saïd André Remli
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 18 January 1995. It originated in an application (no. 16839/90) against the French Republic lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a French national. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr L.-E. Pettiti, the elected judge of French nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. Saïd André Remli is currently in custody at Les Baumettes Prison in Marseilles. He and a fellow prisoner of Algerian nationality, Mr Boumédienne Merdji, knocked out a warder, who died four months later as a result of the blows he had received. The two prisoners were charged with intentional homicide for the purpose of facilitating, preparing or executing the offences of escape and attempted escape. In a judgment of 12 August 1988 the Indictment Division of the Lyons Court of Appeal committed them for trial at the Rhône Assize Court. The trial took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. The trial took place on 12, 13 and 14 April 1989. On the first day, when the sitting began, the members of the jury and two additional jurors were drawn by lot. The defendants challenged five of them, the legal maximum, and the prosecution two of them. The jury was subsequently finally empanelled and the hearing of witnesses began. On 13 April 1989, at about 1.50 p.m., as the sitting resumed, counsel for the applicant filed submissions in which they requested the court to take formal note of a remark made by one of the jurors on 12 April, before the hearing began, which had been overheard by a third person, Mrs M. On 14 April 1989 the Assize Court sentenced Mr Remli to life imprisonment and Mr Merdji to a twenty-year term. He appealed on points of law. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the lawfulness and length of the applicant’s detention. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was born in 1982 and lives in Izmir. He was arrested by police officers at the Narlıdere police station during a routine identity check on suspicion of being an army deserter (asker kaçağı). The applicant was apprehended on 22 February 2003 and held in custody between 7 and 11 March 2003. He was charged with exceeding his leave (“izin tecavüzü”) under Article 66 of the Military Criminal Code. On 14 April 2003 the Çorlu Military Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to ten months’ imprisonment. The judge deducted the period spent on the road and in custody from his prison sentence. The court noted that the applicant had failed to return to his army command at the end of his leave and that he had been apprehended on22 February 2003. It deducted the time he spent in custody and on the roads between 22 February and 7 March 2003 from his sentence.

The case originated in six applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr L. García Quinteiro, a lawyer practising in Barcelona. The Spanish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr F. Irurzun Montoro, State Counsel. In their applications, the applicants complained, among other things, that they had been dismissed by way of reprisal for belonging to a trade union and on account of its demands. They relied on Articles 10 and 11 of the convention. The applicants were delivery men employed by a company in Barcelona. They sought to secure recognition by their employer of their special “salaried worker’s status” The applicants set up the trade union Nueva Alternativa Asamblearia (NAA) to defend their interests and those of the other delivery staff who were under pressure from the company to renounce their claim to salaried status. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 December 2010 (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr Irurzun Montoro, State Counsel, Agent; (b), for the applicants Mr L. García Quinteiro, lawyer, Counsel. The applicants joined the union’s executive committee. No changes concerning the appointment of the union members or their duties have taken place since the union was formed. The union published a monthly newsletter. On the cover of the newsletter, a cartoon with speech bubbles showed a caricature of the human resources manager, G., sitting behind a desk under which a person on all fours could be seen from behind. Inside the newsletter were two articles which vehemently denounced the fact that those two individuals had testified in favour of the company P. in proceedings that the applicants had brought against their employer. The applicants challenged that decision before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 17, which, in a judgment of 8 November 2002, dismissed their claims. The cartoon was published on a noticeboard inside the company. The first article contained caricatures of A. and B., showing them gagged by a handkerchief tied behind their heads. The text underneath read as follows: “We knew who they were and how they behaved, but we didn’t know how far they were prepared to go in order to hold onto their seats and cushy jobs without doing anything” The tribunal noted that the text was a response to what had happened during proceedings brought by the applicants before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 13. The article entitled “When you’ve rented out your arse you can’T shit when you please” read as following: ‘If you belong to a works council and you have to sign agreements with your employers that will never be honoured, just to keep you quiet, and agree to changes that only benefit their cronies, and to pay cuts’ You can see the injustices meted out on your colleagues, but say nothing, for fear of drawing attention to yourself. Your lips are sealed just like your anal sphincter, because you’ve rented out your arse and you can’t shit when you please. You’re fed up with your work, pissed off, anxious, stressed and in despair. You could break everything up, tear it to pieces, crush and demolish it all. But your hands are tied by credits, IOUs and debts. You are crushed by your new SUV, your children’s after-school activities, and the twenty-five year mortgage on your semi-detached house. And you let yourself be humiliated, you swallow your pride, you shut up and you accept. The High Court of Justice of Catalonia upheld the judgment under appeal in so far as it concerned the applicants. The applicants lodged an appeal on points of law, seeking harmonisation of the relevant case-law. In a decision of 11 March 2004, the Supreme Court of Spain upheld the High Court's decision under appeal. The court referred, among other things, to the limits imposed by the principle of good faith between parties to a contract of employment and to the necessary balance that judicial decisions had to strike between a worker’s obligations under the contract and his freedom of expression. The company P. had duly shown that the applicants’ dismissal was not a measure of reprisal or punishment, but was based on a genuine, serious and sufficient cause for deciding to terminate their contracts. The applicants lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. The court found the appeal inadmissible for lack of constitutional content. The decision reads as follows: “... there is not enough evidence to show that the [appellants’] dismissal was an act of reprisal on the part of the respondent company’s ...” The court concluded that there had not been a breach of the right to freedom of expression in the context of the appellants' union activity. It added that although the Constitution does not prohibit the use of hurtful, embarrassing or vituperative expressions in every circumstance, the Court held recently in judgment no. 39/2005 of 28 February (legal ground 4), reiterating its case-law, such expressions are not forbidden.  constitutional protection afforded by Article 20 § 1 (a) of the Constitution does not, however, extend to absolutely vexatious expressions which are offensive or defamatory. The Court concludes that the appellants’ right to freedom of expression has not been infringed. “They used that right in an excessive manner by means of value judgments expressed through cartoons and comments that were offensive and humiliating for the persons concerned and impugned their honour and reputation,” the court said. The court concluded that the cartoons were not necessary for others to form an opinion about the facts of which they wished to complain, and therefore gratuitous.

train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 19462/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who was living in the neighbouring village, was suspected of having participated in the so-called “Başbağlar Massacre”. The Bakırköy Assize Court appointed one of its members as judge rapporteur (naip hakim) to investigate the case and draft a report. He stated that the applicant was heard by the judge. rapporteur on 8 June and 12 October 2000. The case was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant’s unjustified detention on remand for 384 days qualified for compensation. He did not have a regular job at the time but was unofficially working for a dairy merchant six months a year, collecting cheese from local farmers, and in return was paid TRL 100,000,0000 per month. The court concluded in line with the expert report and awarded the applicant TRL 168,114,000 for pecuniary damage. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision on the ground that the defendant had not been notified of the applicant's claim. The case was resumed before the Bakırköy Assize Court. On 18 September 2002 the judge rapporteur heard the applicant. The applicant was paid TRL 2,113,266,9740 plus TRL 1,233,300,0000 in statutory interest, applied with effect from 21 October 2002. Court refused the applicant’s claim for interest which was not covered by Law no. 466. Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the Bakırköy Assize Court, with a minor amendment regarding the costs and expenses. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court of Justice of Turkey. The appeal was dismissed on 15 January 2003 and the appeal was rejected on 16 January 2003. The case was settled out of court on 5 October 2004.
