name: Michael McGrath
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been no adequate investigation into allegations of collusion and/or involvement by security forces in his being seriously injured. By a decision of 6 March 2007 the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant was born in 1922 and lives in Granemore, County Armagh. He was shot twice in the stomach by Laurence McClure, who then placed a 10lb gelignite bomb against the door of the pub. The investigation did not close and became active again in 1978, when a Catholic priest Father Hugh Murphy was abducted by loyalist paramilitaries intending to use him as a hostage vis-à-vis the IRA. In the course of the investigation, the police arrested McCaughey, who revealed his part in the abduction of the priest and in a variety of other loyalist paramilitary incidents. The applicant was aware that charges were pending against four police officers. The Director of Public Prosecutions (‘the DPP’) entered a nolle prosequi in respect of those charges which accordingly were not proceeded with. The three officers pleaded not guilty to the charges of attempted murder. McClure had also been facing charges in relation to his involvement in the attack on Donnelly's Bar, Silverbridge, in 1975 in which three people had been killed. These charges were later dropped. McCaughey made revelations giving rise to investigations in eleven specific cases, some of which were linked in terms of the identities of those involved. Nine suspects were arrested in total, including five police officers, and all were eventually charged with offences. One of those implicated was a police officer John Weir who was named as having been involved in the murder of a shopkeeper called Strathearn in Ahoghill in April 1977. He was convicted for that murder in June 1980 and sentenced to life imprisonment. John Weir's statement made detailed allegations about security force collusion with loyalist paramilitaries in a series of incidents. He alleged inter alia that RUC Reserve Constable Laurence McClure had told him that the murder of the Reavey family members was carried out by Robert McConnell, a member of the UDR. This group used the farmhouse in Glennane owned by James Mitchell, a RUC reservist, as a base from which to carry out attacks on Catholics and nationalists. Weir also linked these attacks to the Dublin and Monaghan bombings in which 33 people were killed. The statement was obtained by the Patrick Finucane Centre, a human rights non-governmental organisation in Derry. Weir made allegations on a television programme that members of the RUC and UDR were directly involved in the attack on Donnelly's Bar. These allegations attracted considerable attention on both sides of the Irish border and became the subject of police investigation in both jurisdictions. A series of seven interviews were conducted, under cautions, between July and December 2001, of those individuals central to Weir's account who could be traced. The predominant response was denial of any involvement and claims that Weir had been untruthful. No admissions were made by any interviewee. Interviews were also conducted with less central personalities and with police officers involved in interviewing Weir in 1978. A meeting was held in Dublin last month to discuss the situation with the victims of the attack. The victims are still waiting for the outcome of an investigation into the attack, which took place in 1998. The attack is believed to have been carried out by a group of young men known as the ‘Phenomenon’. The ‘Group’ was formed by the victims’ families, who had no idea of the full extent of the damage done by the attack before the attack in 2000. The incident was described as ‘unexplained’ and ‘out of character’ by the victim’s family, who said it was a result of a ‘mishandled’ attack. There has been extensive correspondence with the families or their representatives. Application for judicial review concerning the inadequacy of the investigation. Reports of the Independent Commissions of Inquiry (Republic of Ireland) into the death of the bar owner at the time of his death. The application was successful on all counts. The bar was closed for more than two years before being re-opened. The applicant was not allowed to drink at the bar again until the bar was reopened. The case was adjourned until October 31, 2012. The judge ruled that the bar had been closed for less than two months when the application was made, and that no further action could be taken.

The case was not resolved until after the family were able to find out more about the victim's family. The victim's mother and father are waiting for the case to be settled before they can make any further comment on the case. The family will be able to make their case to the court if they are able to contact their loved ones. The victims' families are still waiting to hear back from the family members that they have been denied access to the case since it was closed in 2009. The trial of the victims is expected to last until the end of this year, but the case will not be completed until after that. name: Rolf Lundevall
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38629/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated on account of the lack of an oral hearing before the Administrative Court of Appeal in proceedings concerning social security benefits. By a decision of 4 May 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The case was brought by a Swedish national, Rolf Lundevall, who claimed that he was in need of assistance and had additional costs due to a speech impediment. The applicant. requested the Office to review its decision under chapter 20, section 10 a of the 1962 Act. He claimed that he had failed to fully state his need of assistance and. his additional costs in the original application. On 12 July 1991 the Office found that there was no basis for a review of its earlier decision. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Västmanland. On 13 November 1992 the court gave judgment in his favour. It considered that the first decision had been based on insufficient information and that the Office should therefore have reviewed that decision at the applicant’s request. The applicant made submissions in response to the Board’s appeal. On 25 February 1993 he requested the Administrative Court of Appeal to hold an oral hearing in the case. The latter request was granted by a decision of 30 December 1992. The applicant maintained that the Board had failed to adequately explain the reasons for its appeal. He requested that the court order the Board to clarify its position. The court did not do so, however, and the applicant called into question the impartiality of the proceedings. By 3 votes to 2, it quashed the County Administrative Court's judgment and confirmed the Office's decision. The case can be determined notwithstanding a failure to submit such written observations. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) of 12 July 1991. The dissenting judges considered that the applicant was entitled to the disability allowance granted to him by the County Administrative Court. Without giving any further reasons, it considered that there had been no basis for a review of the Office’s first decision. As an allowance could be given retroactively only for the two years preceding the application, he was granted an allowance as from October 1994. On 24 February 1997 the Supreme. Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal. The applicant complained about the lack of an oral hearing in the Administrative Court of Appeal.

name: Cécile Lecomte
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 80442/12) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the conditions of her detention for preventive purposes in two police stations had violated Article 3 of the convention. The Government of the French Republic, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings, indicated that they did not wish to exercise that right. The case was decided in favour of Ms Cécile Lecomte, an anti-nuclear and environmental activist, who was arrested in November 2008. The District Court found that the applicant, who had been represented by counsel throughout the proceedings before the domestic courts, and three further persons had let themselves down on a rope on a railway bridge. They had unrolled banners protesting against the castor transport. A commuter train had to be stopped because its passage would have put the protesters at risk. That detention was to last until the arrival of the “castor”0 containers in Dannenberg train station and until 10 November 2008, 0.00 p.m. at the most. The Lüneburg District Court quashed the order of 6 November 2008 for the applicant’s detention for preventive purposes and ordered her immediate release. The applicant was held in a cell in the Lüneburg Police Station from 7 p.m. onwards until 1.40pm. She was released the same day at 6.32pm. The applicant's small cell, equipped with a mattress and a chair, was lighted at least via a ventilation slot and by electric light. She went outside for a walk on the banks of the Ilmenau river with the police officers three times during that period. The places and conditions of the applicant’s detention were described as ‘disproportionate’ and ‘inhumane’ by the court. The court ruled that the applicant would commit a criminal or regulatory offence of considerable importance to the general public. The Lüneburg District Court dismissed the applicant’s action of 8 November 2008 under section 19 § 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act. The proceedings for review of the lawfulness of the applicant's detention and of the conditions thereof are set out below. The applicant was taken out for a walk on the premises of the Braunschweig Police Station, which did not dispose of a closed courtyard. She was also allowed to telephone her lawyer and her partner several times. On 9 November 2008 the applicant was allowed to stay outside on those premises from 12.22 p.m. until 12.35 p. m., without being shackled; she climbed on a tree on that occasion. The District Court found that both the order for her detention and the conditions of its execution had been unlawful. The photographs of shackled persons exposed in the detention wing of the Braunschweig Police Station may have been tasteless, but did not render the applicant’s detention unlawful as a result of intimidation. The recommendations of the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) were irrelevant here. The detention had complied with section 18 § 1 no. 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act (Polizeigewahrsamsordnung) On 8 November 2008 the applicant had been outside on the premises of the Braunschweig Police Station. She had to be shackled as, being an excellent climber, there had been a risk that she would climb on trees or buildings and abscond. The applicant had not, therefore, been “taken for a walk like an animal” on the parking. On 9 November 2008 she had not been shackled and had been allowed to climb on a tree. In that police station there were no detention cells suitable for a deprivation. The doctor who had visited the applicant in detention and persuaded the then competent District Court judge to order her release had probably been a sympathiser. The Regional Court found that the pictures of shackled persons in the corridor of the detention wing may have been tasteless. The court considered that it had been lawful for the police to leave the light switched on during the night. It noted that the applicant had climbed on a cupboard measuring 1.90 metres and had failed to descend on the police’s request. Shackling the applicant to a female police officer on 8 November 2008 had been necessary in order to prevent the applicant from being shackled. The right provided by no. 10 of the Police Custody Regulations (see paragraph 46 below) to be allowed to stay outside for 45 minutes per day had not been breached. The applicant, an excellent climber, had previously shown that she was not ready to comply with the police’s orders. The Regional Court noted that the Braunschweig Police had received some 200 telephone calls of sympathisers of the applicant, some of whom had insulted the police. It had not been unlawful in these circumstances for the police not to permit visits by persons who had presented themselves at the police station without having lodged a request for a visit. In any event, the applicant had been visited by three persons while in detention, in addition to her two visits by her doctor, C., who had prescribed her necessary medication and had brought a couple of magazines. The Federal Constitutional Court of Germany declined to consider the case on 1 December 2009. The decision was made under file no. 2 BvR 1779/10. The case will be decided by the Court of Appeal of Germany on 2 October 2010. The previous decision was the result of an appeal by the City of Düsseldorf. The appeal will be heard by the High Court of Justice on 6 October 2010, at a hearing to be held on the merits of the case. The Court will then decide whether or not to uphold the appeal. The High Court has the right to reject the appeal, which would mean that the case could not be heard. The matter will then be heard again by the Supreme Court.

A commuter train had to be stopped because its passage would have put the protesters at risk. The District Court considered that the applicant’s detention was indispensable in order to prevent the imminent commission of a regulatory offence of considerable importance to the general public. The applicant was known for expressing political protest, including protest against the transport of castor containers, by climbing actions and for being ready to breach the law in that context. The Lüneburg Regional Court, having heard the applicant in person at 2.10 p.m. on 7 November 2008, dismissed the applicant's appeal against the District Court's decision. The applicant suffered from serious rheumatism which necessitated her to move continuously and was in a poor mental condition. Her detention in Braunschweig Police Station, with little possibility to move, had already led to her joints having stiffened. Her cell was equipped with a bed, an empty desk, a chair and an open cupboard and had a barred window with frosted glass. On 9 November 2008 the applicant had been outside and had not been shackled and had been allowed to climb on a tree. The Regional Court found that the cell had been uncomfortable, but had complied with no. 15.1 of the Police Custody Regulations in the version then in force. In that police station there were no detention cells suitable for a deprivation. The conditions of the applicant’S detention, albeit onerous for the applicant, had comply with the applicable legal provisions. The judge who visited the applicant in detention and persuaded the then competent District Court judge to order her release had probably been a sympathiser. The Regional Court found that the pictures of shackled persons in the corridor of the detention wing may have been tasteless. The court considered that it had been lawful for the police to leave the light switched on during the night. By choosing not to descend her by force and by leaving the light on instead the police had respected as much as possible the applicant’s right to liberty. The right provided by no. 10 of the Police Custody Regulations (see paragraph 46 below) to be allowed to stay outside for 45 minutes per day in so far as the staffing and infrastructural situation permitted had not been breached. In any event, the applicant had been visited by three persons while in detention, in addition to her two visits by her doctor, C., who had prescribed her necessary medication and had brought a couple of magazines. The Lüneburg Regional Court ruled on 1 July 2009 that the case could not proceed. The decision was made again on 18 June 2012. The case was heard again on 21 September 2010. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the conditions of her detention for preventive purposes in two police stations had violated Article 3 of the. Convention. The application was communicated to the Government on 12 May 2014. The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights on 9 December 2012. The District Court found that the applicant, who had been represented by counsel throughout the proceedings before the domestic courts, and three further persons had let themselves down on a rope on a railway bridge. They had unrolled banners protesting against the castor transport. A commuter train had to be stopped because its passage would have put the protesters at risk. The applicant’s detention was indispensable in order to prevent the imminent commission of a regulatory offence of considerable importance to the general public, as required by section 18 § 1 no. 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act. On 9 November 2008 at 5.25 p.m. the Lüneburg District Court quashed the order of 6 November 2008 for the applicant's detention for preventive purposes. The applicant was detained in a cell in the Lüneburg Police Station from 7 p.m. onwards until 7 November 2008. She was found by a doctor of the Federal Police not to suffer from any health problems. The applicant's small cell, equipped with a mattress and a chair, was lighted at least via a ventilation slot and by electric light. She went outside for a walk on the banks of the Ilmenau river with the police officers three times during that period. The places and conditions of the applicant’s detention were described as 'disgusting' and 'repugnant' by the court. The court ruled that her continued detention was no longer proportionate. The Lüneburg District Court dismissed the applicant’s action of 8 November 2008 under section 19 § 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act (see paragraph 43 below) The proceedings for review of the lawfulness of the applicant's detention and of the conditions thereof1. The proceedings before the Lü Neuburger District Court were held on 15 July 2009. The applicant was taken out for a walk on the premises of the Braunschweig Police Station, which did not dispose of a closed courtyard. On 9 November 2008 the applicant was allowed to stay outside on those premises without being shackled. She was also allowed to telephone her lawyer and her partner several times. The District Court confirmed that the detention had complied with section 18 § 1 no. 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act. The photographs of shackled persons exposed in the detention wing of the Braunschweig Police Station may have been tasteless, but did not render the applicant’s detention unlawful as a result of intimidation. The recommendations of the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) were irrelevant here. The fact that the light had remained switched on all night was a consequence of the applicant's own behaviour. The light had therefore been necessary for her own protection. The Lüneburg Regional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 July 2009. The Regional Court confirmed that the applicant’S detention as such had complied with section 18 § 1 no. 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act. In that police station there were no detention cells suitable for a deprivation of liberty. The conditions of the. applicant's detention, albeit onerous for the applicant, had complied. with the applicable legal provisions and had not been so unacceptable as to. render the execution of her detention unlawful. The court noted that on 8 November 2008 the applicant had been outside on the premises of the Braunschweig Police Station from 2.20 p.m. until 3.02 p.M. The applicant's right to stay outside during her detention in Braunschweig had not been breached, the Regional Court found. She had climbed on a cupboard measuring 1.90 metres and had failed to descend on the police’s request. Shackling the applicant to a female police officer on 8 November 2008 had been necessary in order to prevent the applicant from being shackled. The court considered that it had been lawful for the police to leave the light switched on during the night. By choosing not to descend her by force and by leaving the light on instead the police had respected as much as possible the applicant’‘Right to liberty. of liberty lasting several days. The Regional Court noted that the Braunschweig Police had received some 200 telephone calls of sympathisers of the applicant, some of whom had insulted the police. The applicant argued, in particular, that her right to liberty and the principle of proportionality had been violated by her long illegal detention in unreasonable conditions. Her complaint was registered under file no. 2 BvR 2794/09 and the decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 6 November 2009. In any event, the applicant had been visited by three persons while in detention, in addition to two visits by her doctor, C., who had prescribed her necessary medication and had brought a couple of magazines. Her right to receive visits had not been unlawfully restricted in these circumstances. The case was heard in the German Federal Court of Justice on 21 September 2010. The court ruled in favor of the case against the German government. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court of Germany on 28 October 2009. The final decision was made on 18 June 2012. The appeal was dismissed on 24 August 2012 by the Court of Appeal of the Federal Republic of Germany. The decision was decided on the basis that the case was not the subject of a legal challenge. The Court ruled the case not to proceed with the appeal as it was not within the scope of the decision. It was also decided that the decision was not in the public interest, since the case had already been heard.

name: María Dolores Ruiz-Mateos
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court first by the Government of the Kingdom of Spain (‘the Government’) and then by the European Commission of Human Rights. The object of the application and the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent them (Rule 30) Mr Ryssdal had assumed the office of President of the Chamber and consulted the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the applicants on the organisation of the proceedings. Mr Morenilla had stated that he wished to withdraw pursuant to Rule 24 para. 2, because he had represented the Government before the Commission as Agent. On 27 November 1992 the President directed that the oral proceedings should open on 27 January 1993. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court, had replaced MrRyssdal as President, the latter being unable to take part. The Court heard addresses by the Government, the Commission and the applicants. The lawyers for the applicants and the Government’s representatives produced various documents. The expropriation of the RUMASA group gave rise to an appeal to the Constitutional Court (recurso de inconstit) The Court ruled in favour of the applicants in the case of José María Ruiz-Mateos against the Government of Spain. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Spain on 19 March 2013. The verdict was delivered by Mr Javier López de Gómez, who was the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal for Spain. Six members of the court expressed the view that the expropriation procedure followed was contrary to the Constitution. The Constitutional Court dismissed the deputies’ appeal by a judgment of 2 December 1983, adopted with the President’s casting vote. The aim of these measures was to protect the public interest because the banks had taken risks considered to be disproportionate in relation to their solvency, thereby jeopardising ‘the stability of the banking system and the interests of the depositors, employees and third parties’ The action for the restitution of the exppriated property was launched by Mr José María Ruiz-Mateos and RUMASA S.A. Court no. 18 referred to the Constitutional Court the question of the conformity of the above-mentioned articles of Law no. 7/1983 with Article 24 para. 1 of the Constitution. The Constitutional Court found the question admissible on 17 October 1984; it then gave notice of the question to the Chamber of Deputies, the Senate, the Government and the Attorney General. In the opinion of the first-instance court, the decision on the merits of the dispute depended on the validity of the provisions in issue. The applicants submitted two memorials, respectively eighty-five and thirty-seven pages long. The court held hearings on 18 June and 17 September 1984. On 27 January 1986 José María Ruiz-Mateos complained of the delay in the proceedings. The Constitutional Court joined the application (recurso de queja) to the file on 30 January, but did not pursue the matter. On 7 February he again applied to the Constitutional Court, alleging that the decision of 30 January infringed Article 24 of the Constitution. On 10 April the constitutional court dismissed the challenge on the ground that the applicant lacked locus standi. By a judgment of 19 December 1986, it held that Articles 1 and 2 of Law no. 7/1983 were compatible with Article 24. It found that legislative expropriation - even by means of a special statute concerning a specific case - was not contrary to the constitution. Two judges expressed the view, in a dissenting opinion, that the expropriation procedure used had deprived the applicants of their right of access to the courts. The applicants sought a stay of the proceedings until the European Commission and Court of Human Rights had had an opportunity to rule on their application to Strasbourg. The Audiencia provincial referred the question to the Constitutional Court on 9 July 1989. The latter court declared it admissible on 31 October 1989, then communicated it to the institutions. After a further hearing on 13 February 1989, the court refused to stay the proceedings. On 7 July 1989 it overruled the applicants’ objection to this decision. The constitutional court found the contested articles of Law no. 7/1983 to be compatible with Articles 14 and 33 para. 3 of the Constitution. The relevant Articles of the 1978 Constitution are worded as follows: Article 14 “Spaniards shall be equal before the law and may not be discriminated against in any way on account of birth, race, sex, religion, opinion or any other condition or personal or social circumstance.“ Article 24 “1. Every person has the right to obtain the effective protection of the judges and the courts in the exercise of his legitimate rights and interests”. Article 33 “ 1. Private property rights ... are recognised.” Only the rights guaranteed under Articles 14 to 29 of the Constitution may be the subject of an amparo appeal. Only the right to property secured under Article 33 is available for appeal. The judgments of the Constitutional Court shall be published in the Official State Gazette, together with any dissenting opinions. They have the force of res judicata with effect from the day following their publication, and no appeal may be brought against them. Those which declare the unconstitutionality of a law or of a rule with the Force of law shall be fully binding on all persons.Unless the judgment rules otherwise, that part of the law not affected by unconst Constitutionality shall remain in force. “ Article 36 “A question as to constitutionality referred to the Constitutional Court by a judge or court must be accompanied by a certified copy of the main file and, in so far as there are any, the observations provided for in the preceding article.” “ Article 37 “1. The Court may declare the question inadmissible, in a decision stating its reasons, after hearing only the Attorney General, when the procedural requirements are not satisfied or when the question is manifestly ill-founded.’ “ “ 2. If the question raises an issue concerning a law or another provision having the status of law adopted by an Autonomous Community, notice thereof shall also be given to its legislative and executive authorities. The Commission declared the first complaint admissible and the remainder of the application (no. 12952/87) inadmissible. The Commission expressed the opinion that there had been a violation of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) inasmuch as the applicants had not been given a fair hearing. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the three separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The decision was published by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) on 12 February 2012. The ECHR ruled in favour of the owners of the property and ruled that they had a right to challenge the public interest justification for the expropriation.

Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court, replaced Mr Ryssdal as President, the latter being unable to take part in the further consideration. The application was brought by Mr José María Ruiz-Mateos, a businessman, who held 100% of the shares in RUMASA S.A. The Government ordered the expropriation in the public interest of all the shares. The Court heard addresses by the Government, by Mr Pellonpää for the Commission and by Mr García Montes, Mr Sánchez Pardo and Mr Ruhlmann for the applicants, as well as their replies to its questions. It gave rise to an appeal to the Constitutional Court (recurso de inconstit) The decision was handed down on 9 November 2013. Law no. 7/1983 of 29 June 1983, published a day later in the Official State Gazette (Boletín Oficial del Estado), had replaced the legislative decree. Articles 1 and 2 thereof ordered the immediate expropriation and transfer of possession of the companies concerned. The aim of these measures was to protect the public interest because, in order to finance the group’s companies, its banks had taken risks considered to be disproportionate in relation to their solvency. A group of deputies contested its constitutional validity. The Constitutional Court dismissed the deputies’ appeal by a judgment of 2 December 1983. In a dissenting opinion, six members of the court expressed the view that the expropriated procedure followed was contrary to the Constitution. The first applicant requested Court no. 18 to refer to the Constitutional Court a question on the conformity of. Articles 1 and 2 of Law no. 7/1983 with Articles 14, 24 and 33 of the Constitution. The court held hearings on 18 June and 17 September 1984. The Constitutional Court found the question admissible on 17 October 1984; it then gave notice of the question to the Chamber of Deputies, the Senate, the Government and the Attorney General. In the opinion of the first-instance court, the decision on the merits of the dispute depended on the validity of the provisions in issue. The applicants submitted two memorials, respectively eighty-five and thirty-seven pages long. On 27 January 1986 José María Ruiz-Mateos complained of the delay in the proceedings. The Constitutional Court joined the application (recurso de queja) to the file on 30 January, but did not pursue the matter. On 7 February he again applied to the Constitutional Court, alleging that the decision of 30 January infringed Article 24 of the Constitution. He also maintained that he had locus standi in respect of the constitutional proceedings by virtue of his status as a party in the main proceedings. On 21 February the Constitutional court confirmed its earlier decision. It found that legislative expropriation - even by means of a special statute concerning a specific case - was not contrary to the Constitution, and that the persons concerned suffered restrictions on the judicial protection of their rights. The appeal proceedings began on 27 December 1986. On 7 July 1989 it overruled the applicants’ objection to this decision. After having received their comments, the Audiencia provincial referred the question to the Constitutional Court on 9 July 1989. The latter court declared it admissible on 31 October 1989, then communicated it to the institutions. The appeal was dismissed on 22 December 1986, but the applicants appealed to the Audiensia provincial of Madrid. The applicants sought a stay of the proceedings until the European Commission and Court of Human Rights had had an opportunity to rule on their application to Strasbourg. The court ordered an adjournment so as to allow them to submit documents in support of their first request. The relevant articles are listed in Article 37 para. 2 of Institutional Law no. 2/1979 (see paragraph 27 below). The Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies replied on 17 November that the Chamber did not intend to submit observations. Two judges expressed a dissenting opinion. The Audiencia provincial was notified of this on 25 January 1991 and set down a hearing for 22 February. The court dismissed their appeal by a judgment of 25 February. On 6 March the applicants lodged an application for the interpretation of that judgment; their application was dismissed on 11 March 1991. The Court of Appeal found the contested articles of Law. no. 7/1983 to be compatible with Articles 14 and 33 para. 3 of the Constitution. Only the rights guaranteed under Articles 14 to 29 of the Constitution may be the subject of an amparo appeal, which is not therefore available in respect of the right to property secured under Article 33. The judgments of the Constitutional Court shall be published in the Official State Gazette, together with any dissenting opinions. They have the force of res judicata with effect from the day following their publication, and no appeal may be brought against them. Those which declare the unconstitutionality of a law, and all those which do not merely recognise an individual right, shall be fully binding on all persons.Unless the judgment rules otherwise, that part of the law not affected by unconst Constitutionality shall remain in force. A question as to constitutionality referred to the Constitutional Court by a judge or court must be accompanied by a certified copy of the main file and the observations provided for in the preceding article. The Court may declare the question inadmissible, in a decision stating its reasons, after hearing only the Attorney General, when the procedural requirements are not satisfied or when the question is manifestly ill-founded. The judge shall then announce his decision, without taking any further steps, within three days. No appeal shall lie against this decision. However, the question asto constitutionality may be raised again in subsequent proceedings until the judgment has become final. The applicants complained. of their right of access to the courts to challenge the public interest justification. for the expropriation and the necessity of the immediate transfer of their property. They complained of discrimination in relation to other Spanish citizens in that the latter were subject to the ordinary law on expropriations. The Commission declared the first complaint admissible and the remainder of the application (no. 12952/87) inadmissible. In its report of 14 January 1992 (made under Article 31) (art. 31), the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been a violation of Article 6 para. 6-1. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the three separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment.

name: Jaroslaw Niedzwiecki
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 58453/00) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal of child benefits between July and December 1995 amounted to discrimination in the exercise of his right to respect for family life. By a decision of 17 June 2003 the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. In July 1995 the applicant’s daughter was born. The applicant applied to the Aschaffenburg Labour Office (Arbeitsamt) for child benefits according to Section 1 of the Federal Child Benefits Act (Bundeskindergeldgesetz, see relevant domestic law below) The Labour Office dismissed his request on 18 August 1995. The Social Court confirmed that only aliens with an unlimited residence permit or with a provisional residence permit were entitled to the payment of child benefits under Section 1 § 3 of the Child benefits Act, as in force until 31 December 1995. According to the Social Court, the legislature had only intended to grant child benefits to aliens who were likely to stay in Germany. Until December 1995 families had benefited from child benefits and tax deductions (Kinderfreibetrag) as a system of compensation (dualer Familienlastenausgleich) The applicant and his wife had paid taxes in 1995 but had not obtained child benefits. He claimed that the relevant provision of the Federal Child Benefits Act was discriminatory and racist. He alleged that the refusal of his request for child benefits infringed the principle of social justice (Sozialstaatsprinzip) The proceedings before the Tax Court are still pending. The proceedings concerning claims after 1 January 1996 have been transferred to the Nuremberg Tax Court.

The case originated in an application (no. 58453/00) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal of child benefits between July and December 1995 amounted to discrimination in the exercise of his right to respect for family life. By a decision of 17 June 2003 the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1) The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The applicant applied to the Aschaffenburg Labour Office for child benefits in July 1995. The Labour Office rejected his objection, noting that he only had a limited residence title for exceptional purposes. The applicant lodged an action with the Würzburg Social Court, claiming that he had been residing in Germany since 1987 and that he should, therefore, have the right to child benefits. The Social Court dismissed the applicant’s action regarding child benefits between July 1995 and April 1997. It confirmed that only aliens with an unlimited residence permit or with a provisional residence permit were entitled to the payment of child benefits under Section 1 § 3 of the Child Benefits Act. Until December 1995 families had benefited from child benefits and tax deductions (Kinderfreibetrag) as a system of compensation (dualer Familienlastenausgleich). The applicant and his wife had paid taxes in 1995 but had not obtained child benefits. The court considered that this taxation, not the refusal of child benefits, might have violated the Basic Law. However, it was not for the social courts to decide on that matter. The proceedings concerning claims after 1 January 1996 are still pending at the Nuremberg Tax Court (Finanzgericht). The proceedings before the Tax Court are currently pending in the Würzburg Social Court.

name: Selim Kabasakal
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that they were denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal on account of the presence of a military judge on the bench of the State Security Court which tried them. The applications were allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The Chamber decided to join the proceedings in the applications (Rule 42 § 1). By a decision of 8 March 2005 the Court declared the applications admissible. The first applicant stated that he accepted in part the accusations against him. The second applicant maintained that he was a sympathiser of the organisation and not a member. Both applicants repudiated the statements they had given to the police, claiming that they had been made under duress. The applicants maintained that, in view of the judgment of the European Court on Human Rights concerning State Security Courts, they were boycotting the court and were not going to give any statements. In a hearing held on 13 July 1999 the civilian judge who had been appointed to replace the military judge sat as a member of the trial court for the first time. On 5 October 1999 two persons filed petitions to intervene as third-parties in the proceedings. The applicants were convicted and sentenced to 12 years and 6 months in prison. The applicants appealed to the Court of Cassation against the judgment of the State Security Court. On an unspecified date, the applicants were released from prison. In their petition the applicants submitted arguments based on domestic law and, in particular, challenged the veracity of their statements to the police. Following a hearing held on 5 June 2000, the court dismissed the applicants’ appeal and upheld the first‑instance court's judgment. This decision was pronounced, in the absence of the applicants' representative, on 14 June 2000. The application was dismissed on 6 December 1999.

name: Swiadi Schatschaschwili
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr H. Meyer-Mews, a lawyer practising in Bremen. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs K. Behr, Regierungsdirektorin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The Court advised the parties on 14 January 2014 that it would continue processing the application under the name Schatschaschwili v. Germany, which was the applicant’s name as referred to in the domestic proceedings. The crimes were committed in Kassel on 14 October 2006 and in Göttingen on 3 February 2007 respectively. The applicant was given an accumulated prison sentence of nine years and six months. He was sentenced to a total of nine and a half years in prison. The court found that the applicant, acting jointly with an unidentified. accomplice and according to a previously agreed plan, entered by force into an apartment in. Kassel and robbed its occupants. The men were aware that the apartment was used for. prostitution and expected its two female occupants to keep valuables and cash in there. They had passed by the apartment in the. early evening in order to make sure that no clients were present. O. and P. were friends of L., one of the victims of the crime committed in Kassel on 14 October 2006. The two men reported to the residual members of the criminal gang that they had spotted a safe in the apartment’s kitchen. The applicant and a further accomplice, B., gained access to the apartment pretending to be potential clients. Once inside the apartment B. produced a knife that he had carried along in his jacket. Fearing for her life O. opened the safe from which B. removed EUR 300 and also handed over the contents of her wallet in the amount of EUR 250. B. left the apartment at around 8.30 p.m. taking the money. The Regional Court based its finding of facts regarding the first crime committed in Kassel on the statements made by the victims L. and I. on the occasion of their police interrogations as well as in the course of the subsequent trial. Both witnesses had identified the applicant without any hesitation as the perpetrator who had carried the gun when presented with his photo. The Regional Court found the women’s testimonies to be consistent and credible and noted that they were supported by the statements of the police officers who had attended the crime scene and had interviewed the victims. A decision of 21 February 2008 ordered that the records of the victims’ interrogations by the police and the investigating judge be read out at the trial and be admitted as evidence in the proceedings. Witnesses O. and P. had been summoned to appear before the Regional Court on 24 August 2007, the third day of the trial. They both had refused to attend the hearing relying on medical certificates dated 9 August 2007 that indicated their unstable post‑traumatic emotional and psychological condition. The Regional Court asked for the witnesses to be heard by a court in Latvia and the hearing to be transmitted by voice and image (audiovisuelle Vernehmung) But a witness hearing scheduled by the competent Latvian court for 13 February 2008 was cancelled shortly before by the presiding judge on the ground that the witnesses had demonstrated that they were still suffering from post-traumatic disorders. The Regional Court concluded that it was impossible to have the witnesses examined in the foreseeable future. A further objection against the introduction of the witnesses’ pre-trial statements by counsel of one of the co-accused was rejected by the Regional Court. The Regional Court held that notwithstanding the resulting restrictions for the defence, the trial as a whole had been fair and had complied with the requirements of Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention. The court was thus not prevented from admitting O. and P.’s pre- trial statements as evidence in the proceedings. It also held that although the applicant had not been informed about the preliminary criminal proceedings initiated against him with a view to not putting the investigations at risk, no warrant for his arrest had yet been issued. The court observed that the witnesses’ attention during the incident had been focussed on the further perpetrator carrying the knife and that the applicant himself had only stayed a short period of time in the apartment. The court had taken several items of evidence as corroborating O. and P.’s pre-trial testimonies into account when assessing their evidentiary value. The Regional Court had made considerable efforts to enable a direct examination of the accused and counsel for the defence at trial. Once the witnesses had proved to be unavailable, the court had ensured that a maximum of further witnesses who had been in contact with O.and P. in relation to the events at issue could be heard. The Regional Court noted that since neither the defence nor the court itself had had an opportunity to observe the main witnesses’ demeanour at trial or by means of an audio-visual examination. The court further emphasised that when taking into account the testimonies given by the witnesses' neighbour E. and their friend L. it had paid special attention to the fact that their statements constituted hearsay evidence. The link between the evidence obtained in the course of such separate investigations and the crime at issue could only be made after O. and P. had reported the incident of 3 February 2007 to the police. It followed from the recordings of two mobile phone conversations between one of the co-accused and the applicant. The applicant and the co-accused had denied any participation in the robbery as such or any premeditated criminal activity in this respect. Their own statements at trial had at least confirmed that one of them had visited the apartment at Göttingen on the evening before the crime. The applicant had testified that he and B. had come to the apartment with a view to making use of the women’s services as prostitutes. He further had conceded that he had followed P. when she escaped over the balcony in order to prevent her from calling the neighbours or the police since he had been afraid of getting problems in view of his criminal record and the problems he had previously had with prostitutes. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law as manifestly ill-founded in written proceedings pursuant to Article 349 (2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Prosecutor General argued that while it was true that the proceedings had been characterised by a “complete loss’ of the applicant's right to examine O. and P. name: Laleş Çeliker
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 75573/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that she had been denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was made by a Turkish national, Ms Laleş Çeliker, on 25 June 2001. Diyarbakır State Security Court held nineteen hearings and heard a number of witnesses. During these hearings, the applicant renounced her statements taken during her detention in police custody. Witnesses heard by the court stated that the applicant was an active member of the PKK and that she had been involved in armed clashes with the security forces. Taking into account her confessions before the court, the death penalty was commuted to a life sentence of imprisonment. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the first instance court. It reasoned that the decision was justified as the evidence in the case file was capable of proving the applicant's membership of an illegal organisation.

name: Elif Karakaya
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5173/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of compensation proceedings. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of this complaint at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was represented by Ms S. Kızılkaya and Mr İ.H.Altan, lawyers practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant requested compensation and legal aid. The Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected her request for legal aid on 28 June 2000. The case was referred to the Court of Jurisdictional Disputes (Uyuşmazlık mahkemesi), which held on 17 November 2003 that the matter fell within the jurisdiction of the military administrative courts. On 16 June 2004 the applicant was granted the applicant compensation with statutory interest. This judgment was delivered to the applicant on 27 July 2004. The applicant did not seek rectification. The decision was upheld by the High Court of Justice and the appeal was dismissed on 15 September 2006. The appeal was denied.

name: Maria Gollner
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that civil proceedings concerning her lasted unreasonably long. By a decision of 21 November 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided for in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal from November 2000 until December 2001. It was decided that the application was not admissible and the decision was made to dismiss the application. The time-limit for filing observations on the expert’s opinion was fixed at 28 April 1995. On 7 September 1995 the court requested the expert to supplement his opinion which he did. Following two requests by the applicant for extensions of the time- limit, she submitted her comments on the supplemented expert opinion on 10 January 1996. On 14 August 1996 the District Court gave judgment, partly dismissing the applicant's claim. Following her appeal, the St. Pölten Regional Court quashed the decision for procedural errors on 13 December 1996 and referred the case back. On 24 November 1997 the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) confirmed the decision. On 29 October 1998 the motions for provisional maintenance were partly dismissed by the District Court. On 23 November 1998 the applicant appealed against this decision. On 3 March 1999 the St. Pölten Regional Court quashed the judgment of 24 September 1998 for procedural errors and referred the case back. On 15 April 1999 the applicant therefore lodged a further appeal and requested that it be given suspensive effect to preserve the status quo before the Regional Court’s decision. A further hearing scheduled for 1 December 1999 was cancelled due to the judge's illness. Further hearings were held on 3 May 2000 and 15 June 2000. The judgment was served on 13 February 2001.

name: Karlheinz Schmidt
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 7 April 1993. It originated in an application (no. 13580/88) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The President of the Court gave the lawyer in question leave to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R R. Ryssdal. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 February 1994. The Court heard addresses by Mr Meyer-Ladewig, Mr Vögtle, Mr Weitzel and Mr Olbrich. Mr Schmidt had to pay a fire service levy (Feuerwehrabgabe) of 75 German marks (DM) for 1982. This decision was based on section 43 of the Land Fire Brigades Act, as amended on 27 November 1978. The hearing was held in Strasbourg in accordance with the decision of the President, who had also given the Government leave to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 2) The decision was contrary to the principle of equality before the law. The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal against the decision of the Constitutional Court. The case raised no issue of principle (grundlegende Bedeutung) The case was not referred back to the Constitutional Court. It would only be possible to refer the case to the Administrative Court again if it was found to be in breach of the Constitution. The appeal was dismissed on 6 October 1986. The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court of Germany on 18 August 1989. The court held that the decision was consistent with the law of the land. The Court of Appeal found that it was not a breach of law but a matter of principle. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the appeal for adjudication on the ground that it did not have sufficient prospects of success. The court had already held that there had been no violation of the principle of equal treatment. The fact that the obligation to serve in the fire brigade was limited to the male residents of a municipality still continued to be justified on account of the risks inherent in service. Some fire brigade duties were performed by women and recently fire brigades for female volunteers had even been set up. The sole decisive factor is that there remain today objective reasons (Anknüpfungspunkte) on the basis of which the legislature is entitled to treat men and women differently in this regard.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 7 April 1993. It originated in an application (no. 13580/88) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The President of the Court gave the lawyer in question leave to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality. In accordance with the decision of the President, who had also given the Government leave to use the German language, the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 February 1994. Mr Karlheinz Schmidt, a German national who was born in 1939, lives at Tettnang, in the Land of Baden-Württemberg. The relevant municipal authorities required him to pay a fire service levy (Feuerwehrabgabe) of 75 German marks (DM) for 1982. This decision was based on section 43 of the Land Fire Brigades Act, as amended on 27 November 1978. The Administrative Court rejected the appeal against the decision of the Constitutional Court. The court ruled that the obligation for men, and not women, to serve in the fire service was compatible with the Constitution. The case raised no issue of principle (grundlegende Bedeutung) The case was dismissed in 1986. The decision was upheld by the High Court of Justice. The matter was referred back to the Administrative Court for reconsideration. It was decided that the issue was not of a fundamental nature, and that there was no need to re-think the issue. The appeal was dismissed on October 6, 1986, and the case was not appealed again. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the appeal for adjudication, on the ground that it did not have sufficient prospects of success. It noted, inter alia: “... The Federal Constitutional. Court has already held, in its judgment of 17 October 1961 ..., concerning the provision which. corresponds to the present section 43 para. 2, first sentence, of the Baden-Württemberg Fire Brigades Act’’ The court said there had still been no general change in legal opinion. The fact that the obligation to serve in the fire brigade was limited to the male residents of a municipality still continued to be objectively justified on account of the risks inherent in service.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 7 April 1993, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 13580/88) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The President of the Court gave the lawyer in question leave to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 February 1994. There appeared before the Court: Mr J. Meyer-Ladewig, Ministerialdirigent, Federal Ministry of Justice, Agent, Mr R. Vögtle, Oberregierungsrat, Ministry of the Interior of the Land of Baden- Württemberg, Mrs Jungewelter, Judge at the Landgericht, and Mr Olbrich, Counsel. The Court heard addresses by the Government, Commission and applicant’s lawyer. Mr Schmidt was ordered to pay a fire service levy of 75 German marks (DM) for 1982. The decision to impose a tax on women was contrary to the principle of equality before the law. The decision was overturned by the Administrative Court in 1986. The case was not referred back to the Constitutional Court. The court ruled that the law was in line with the law at the time of the decision. It was not possible to refer the case to the courts again. The result was a ruling that women were not liable to pay the tax. The law was then changed to only apply to men. The men's right to a tax was upheld. The Court of Appeal agreed and dismissed the appeal. The matter was settled and the tax was not imposed on women. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the appeal for adjudication on the ground that it did not have sufficient prospects of success. The Land Administrative Appeals Court had found no evidence of this, the court said. Mr Schmidt applied to the Constitutional Court again in 1986 but it declined to take up the case. The court ruled that the obligation to serve in the fire brigade was limited to the male residents of a municipality still continued to be justified. Some fire brigade duties were performed by women and recently fire brigades for female volunteers had even been set up, it said. But that does not mean that there is an obligation to enact regulations differentiating between the sexes, it added.

name: Adele Ursula Price
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33394/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that her committal to prison and her treatment in detention violated Article 3 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 12 September 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible [Note by the Registry. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry]. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required, the parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The applicant alleges that she was forced to sleep in her wheelchair since the bed was hard and would have caused pain in her hips. She also alleges she was unable to use the toilet since it was higher than her wheelchair and therefore inaccessible. case had been heard during the afternoon of 20 January 1995, it was not possible to take her to prison until the next day and she spent that night in a cell in Lincoln Police Station. This cell, which contained a wooden bed and a mattress, was not specially adapted for a disabled person. Court heard that on arrival, at 7.20 p.m., the applicant told the custody officer that she suffered from kidney trouble and a recurring ear infection but that she did not require any medication. The applicant was not placed in a normal cell in New Hall, but was instead detained in the prison's health care centre. Her cell had a wider door for wheelchair access, handles for the disabled in the toilet recess and a hydraulic hospital bed. On arrival at the prison the applicant completed a medical questionnaire. She stated that she had health worries but that they were “under control – takes it as it comes’. The applicant was examined by Dr Kidd, whose notes stated: “New reception. Thalidomide victim with numerous deformities including absent arms upper/lower with dislocating L shoulder and no use in R upper limb” A “continuous medical record” on the applicant was kept during her detention. The first entry, dated 21 January 1995, stated: “I asked duty Governor, Mr Ellis, to give permission for a battery charger for Adele's wheelchair to be brought in if we could arrange it. He agreed to this and whilst here we pointed out the numerous problems staff may encounter with this inmate i.e. (1) Needs lifting in and out of bed and she says this is usually done by one person standing behind her with arms around her midriff then lifting her either onto the bed or onto her wheelchair. Because of recurrent urinary infections she should take two litres of fluid daily but usually has juice and doesn't like water, therefore will probably reduce her fluid intake.” Adele claimed that two male prison nursing officers exposed her naked from the chest down. The Government denied that these incidents occurred. The applicant made a complaint to the prison governor concerning the lack of adequate facilities, but containing no mention of the above events. Prior to her release, on 23 January 1995, the applicant was examined by Dr Kidd who found she needed catheterising due to urine retention. The medical record stated: “For release this afternoon as soon as transport arrangements can be made. ... To have bath and bladder emptied’. The remission provisions in sections 45 and 33 of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 meant that the applicant had only to serve half the sentence imposed, namely, three and a half days. The applicant claimed to have suffered health problems for ten weeks as a result of her treatment in detention, but has not provided direct medical evidence in support of this claim. She was granted legal aid, limited to obtaining evidence and seeking counsel's opinion as to merits and quantum. Counsel advised that, in the light of this case-law and the difficulties of proof which she faced, the applicant had a limited prospect of success in her claim and that, even if successful, damages were not likely to exceed 3,000 pounds sterling.

The case originated in an application (no. 33394/96) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that her committal to prison and her treatment in detention violated Article 3 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The case was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 12 September 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The applicant alleges that she was forced to sleep in her wheelchair since the bed was hard and would have caused pain in her hips. She was unable to use the toilet since it was higher than her wheelchair and therefore inaccessible. The cell contained a wooden bed and a mattress, which was not specially adapted for a disabled person. The. case had been heard during the afternoon of 20 January 1995, it was not possible to take her to prison until the next day and she spent. that night in a cell in Lincoln Police Station. The custody record states that on arrival, at 7.20 p.m., the applicant informed the custody officer that she suffered from kidney trouble and a recurring ear infection but that she did not require any medication or to see a doctor. At 8.30 a.m. she was taken to New Hall Women's Prison, Wakefield, where she was detained until the afternoon of 23 January 1995. She was not placed in a normal cell in New Hall, but was instead detained in the prison's health care centre. Her cell had a wider door for wheelchair access, handles for the disabled in the toilet recess and a hydraulic hospital bed. On arrival at the prison the applicant completed a medical questionnaire. She stated that she had health worries but that they were “under control – takes it as it comes’. The applicant was examined by Dr Kidd, whose notes stated: “New reception. Thalidomide victim with numerous deformities including absent arms upper/lower with dislocating L shoulder and no use in R upper limb. Both lower limbs are absent with small feet” A “continuous medical record” on the applicant was kept during her detention. The government submitted that on 21 January 1995 there was an incident in which Adele was left to sit on the toilet for over three hours. “Impossible to toilet during the night. Have been into Adele's cell twice. Took over 1/2 hour to toilet her then could not get her back on the bed. Given analgesia and she is getting a great deal of pain through lying on a solid mattress. Very difficult to care for her with one nurse’s help,” the Government said.“Adele should take two litres of fluid daily but usually has juice and doesn't like water, therefore will probably reduce her fluid intake. Dr Kidd will review Adele tomorrow, as he thinks there is a likelihood she will develop a UTI [urinary tract infection].” Adele was jailed for three and a half days in January 1995. Claimed she was exposed to two male prison nursing officers. The Government denied that these incidents occurred. Prior to her release, on 23 January 1995, the applicant was examined by Dr Kidd who found she needed catheterising due to urine retention. The medical record stated: “For release this afternoon as soon as transport arrangements can be made. ... To have bath and bladder emptied’. The remission provisions in sections 45 and 33 of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 meant that the applicant had only to serve half the sentence imposed, namely, three anda half days. The applicant claims to have suffered health problems for ten weeks as a result of her treatment in detention, but has not provided direct medical evidence in support of this claim. She was granted legal aid, limited to obtaining evidence and seeking counsel's opinion as to merits and quantum. Her counsel referred to the difficulties which the applicant was likely to face in proving that she had suffered the ill-treatment which she alleged, and that, even if successful, damages were not likely to exceed 3,000 pounds sterling. In the light of this advice, the applicant's legal aid certificate was discharged on 13 May 1996. ...’The applicant was collected from prison by a friend. She only asked for a bath and to be catheterised. via catheter before leaving.

name: Uğur Eşim
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 59601/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant was born in 1969 and lives in İstanbul. He was severely wounded by gunshots in a clash between the security forces and a group of terrorists in September 1990. His work capability was reduced by 33% and he was declared to be suffering from a permanent disability and discharged from the army. On 19 September 2007 he applied to the Ministry of Defence for compensation in respect of his injury. The Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected both actions as being out of time. The court held that notwithstanding the fact that the applicant had not been aware of the bullet in his head until 2007, pursuant to section 43(1) of the Supreme Military. Administrative Court Act, his compensation claims should have been lodged within five years of the incident. The decision was served on the applicant on 6 May 2009. The appeal against the decision was dismissed on 14 February 2010. The case was referred to the International Court of Justice for further proceedings. The application was dismissed by the International court of Justice on 14 January 2010 for failing to comply with the requirements of the European Court of Human Rights Act.

name: Dennis Sibson
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 21 February 1992. It originated in an application (no. 14327/88) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Dennis Sibson, a British citizen, on 17 October 1988. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 11 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 October 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mr Eadie for the Government, Mr Marxer for the Commission and Mr Bowers for the applicant. Both the Government and the applicant filed a written reply to a question put by the Court. The Registrar received further observations from the Government on the applicant’s claims under Article 50 (art. 50) and, on 20 January 1993, the applicant's comments on those observations. The applicant was employed by Courtaulds Northern Spinning Ltd (“CNS“) from November 1973 as a textile worker. The applicant was a member of the Transport and General Workers Union (‘TGWU’) from 1981 to 1984. He was based at its depot at Greengate, Lancashire, together with between forty and fifty other drivers. Mr Sibson was so dissatisfied with that decision that he resigned from TGWU by letter of 24 July and joined the United Road Transport Union instead. Some of his fellow drivers immediately ostracised him and others obstructed him in the performance of his work. After a period of “uneasy peace’, a substantial majority of the T GWU members voted in favour of (a) a closed shop agreement with CNS and (b) industrial action if he continued in employment at that depot after 25 October. CNS and TGWU contended that a closed shop agreement was in existence (which would have made any dismissal fair) The applicant declined to accept either of the alternatives then put before him - working at Greengate after rejoining TGWu or moving to Chadderton. Mr Dear refused to do that, and added that if the applicant reported to Greengate for work, he would be sent home without pay. Mr Sibson, citing his solicitor’s advice that that would constitute constructive dismissal, then said that he would resign with immediate effect. His representative in these proceedings was not legally qualified, legal aid not being available for this purpose. He lodged with the Industrial Tribunal a complaint of unfair dismissal (see paragraph 18 below) Industrial Tribunal unanimously accepted the complaint of unfair dismissal. Mr Sibson was entitled to refuse to rejoin TGWU because there was no closed shop agreement in force. The request that he move to Chadderton was not reasonable since it was not made for genuine operational reasons but solely to avoid a strike. Court of Appeal concluded that CNS had acted within its contractual rights in requiring the applicant to transfer to a nearby depot and that he could not be regarded as having been constructively dismissed. Lord Justice Slade stated, as regards this implied “mobility term’: “I cannot see how Mr Siberian could reasonably have objected to a term giving the contract this limited degree of flexibility when he entered the employment in 1973” Mr Sibson applied for legal aid to appeal to the House of Lords in 1988. Legal aid was granted for the purpose of obtaining counsel’s opinion on the merits of an appeal. On 8 August counsel advised that there were no reasonable prospects of success and that leave to appeal would not be given. Further legal aid was therefore refused on 19 August. . No question of unfair dismissal therefore arose. The appeal was dismissed on 8 August 1988. The case was heard in the High Court in March 1989. It was decided that the appeal was not likely to succeed. The judge agreed that the dismissal was not fair. The decision was quashed and the case was dismissed.

name: Abdullah Altun
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 66354/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Abdullah Altun. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the applicant's right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was a student in the Medical Faculty of the Diyarbakır Dicle University at the time of the events giving rise to the present application. The Diyarbakır State Security Court held thirty hearings and heard nineteen witnesses. The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's request for rectification of decision. He was sentenced to death under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. The applicant's behaviour during the trial was taken into account and the sentence was reduced to life in prison. The sentence was pronounced on 1 March 2000 in the presence of the applicant’s lawyer. The application was dismissed on 25 April 2000, and he was given a new sentence of life imprisonment with a minimum term of 30 years.
