name: Ahmet Kılıç
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case was heard by the Supreme Administrative Court of Turkey and the decision was delivered on 11 November 2004. The applicant was awarded his monthly salary, which was 7,630,000 Turkish Liras (TRL)0, together with the interest, for the period during which he was unemployed. On 31 May 2000 the Samsun Administrative Court followed the judgment of the Supreme Administrative Court and annulled the decision of the Municipality. The court further ordered that the applicant be reinstated in his job and that his monthly salary and related pecuniary rights be paid to him for the period during which he had been entitled to perform his duties. The Council of State rejected the appeal on 13 December 2001. This judgment was served on the applicant on 3 April 2002. The Municipality has not made any payment to the applicant. To date, the municipality has not paid the applicant any money. The applicant has been unemployed for almost a year and a half.

The case originated in an application (no. 38473/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant was represented by Mr H. Güleç, a lawyer practising in Ankara. Under Turkish law, his employment status was that of a civil servant. On 8 June 1995, relying on three appraisal reports drafted in the past two years, the Municipality terminated the applicant’s employment contract. On 31 May 2000 the Samsun Administrative Court followed the judgment of the Supreme Administrative Court and annulled the decision of the Municipality. The court further ordered that the applicant be reinstated in his job and that his monthly salary and related pecuniary rights be paid to him for the period during which he had been entitled to perform his duties. On 13 December 2001 the Council of State rejected the appeal. This judgment was served on the applicant on 3 April 2002. The Municipality has not made any payment to the applicant. To date, the municipality has not paid the applicant his salary or other compensation for his services.

name: Lars Rey
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 17350/03) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. The first two applicants, a married couple, were born in 1935 and 1944 respectively and live in Klippan. The third applicant was a limited liability company wholly owned by the first two Applicants. The applicants were represented by Mr J. Thörnhammar, a lawyer practising in Stockholm. The Swedish Government (“the Government”) was represented by Ms I. Kalmerborn, Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The bank paid the company 1.1 million SEK on 28 June 1993. The company was declared bankrupt on 7 September 1994. The applicants and a company named Boket Konsult AB (hereinafter ‘Boket’) claimed compensation from the bank in the amount of 37million SEK. The parties lodged several supplementary arguments and procedural requests and submitted documentary evidence to the court. In February 1997, the applicants and Boket asked the court to rule on the alleged breach of contract in a partial judgment. An oral preparation was held on 7 April 1998. On 29 September 1998 the court sent a summary of the cases to the parties and, by a decision of 30 September 1998, it rejected the request. Boket v. Svea is a dispute over a bank loan. The bank refused to pay 2 million SEK to Boket. The company appealed to the District Court. The District Court found in favour of the bank. The Supreme Court refused the applicants leave to appeal. The appeal court agreed with the court's reasoning and upheld its judgment. The appeals court's decision was upheld by the Supreme Court on 29 November 2002, after the applicants had been granted several respites to complete their submissions. Boket's action was struck out of the Court's list on 17 January 2000. On 5 July 2000 the court delivered another summary of the cases and gave the parties the opportunity to make comments, which they did in September 2000.

name: Kemal Evcimen
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the alleged unfairness of the proceedings against the applicant. The applicant was accused of membership of an illegal organisation, the DHKP-C (the Revolutionary People's Liberation Party- Front) The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the Proceedings before the Court. The case-file was sent to the Erzurum State Security Court in 1997. The court found that two articles published in Özgür Karadeniz on 15 November 1994 and 1 March 1995 contained separatist propaganda and incitement to hatred. It sentenced the applicant to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. On 29 May 2004 the applicant was conditionally released from prison. The cases against the applicant and his co-accused were subsequently joined before the Erzincan State Security Court. name: Jørgen Kristiansen
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings leading to his conviction he had not been afforded a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal as required by Article 6 § 1 of the convention. On 17 July 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. The High Court upheld the applicant’s conviction by a judgment of 5 by a majority of 5 to 3. The case was heard at the High Court in Oslo on 25 July 2013. The judgment was delivered by Mr Jørgen Kristiansen, who was represented by Mr K.M. Berg. In 2009, the Borgarting High Court (lagmannsrett), hearing the applicant’s appeal with a jury, convicted him on the attempted rape charge. The High Court described in detail how the applicant, after he had called Mr B (who could not come straight away), had attempted to obtain sexual contact with Ms A by force. It stated that in the beginning, when the applicant had tried to kiss and touch her, Ms A had told him that she was not interested because she was the girlfriend of Mr D and slapped the applicant. The applicant had not stopped, but had moved himself over to her seat and held her arms behind the neck support. Counsel for the defence requested that J be disqualified from taking part in the further proceedings on grounds of lack of impartiality. The High Court observed that “the jury member had formed a picture [bilde] of the victim from many years ago where she at the time had experienced her as a quiet and calm person” It pointed out that a member might be disqualified if the person in question had particular reasons for identifying himself or herself with the victim or if there were any other circumstances to the effect that he or she had a prejudging attitude because of prior knowledge. However, that was not the situation in the present case. Juror J took part in the entire trial before the High Court, including the jury’s deliberations and vote on the charge of attempted rape. The High Court had special regard to the fact that the parties to the case had requested that J recuse herself, but it found the absence of partiality so clear in this case that this could not be decisive. Neither had counsel for the defence alleged before the Supreme Court that this was a sufficient ground for disqualification. The Supreme Court, by a judgment of 26 June 2009, rejected the applicant's appeal by three votes to two.. The majority did not consider that J’’ knowledge of the victim from her. attendance at birthday parties and class outings with the victim in itself indicated an identification with the. victim or weakened in any other way the confidence in her impartiality. J’s information about Ms A had emerged after she had given evidence to the High Court for one hour. At that point, the jury, including J, had a good opportunity to form an independent and updated picture of the victim as a person. That defence counsel and the assistant advocate had requested that J withdraw could not be decisive. There were no particular circumstances capable of calling into doubt J's impartiality for the purposes of section 108 of the Administration of Courts Act, as interpreted in the light of Article 6 of the Convention. The minority considered that the case concerned a serious and stigmatising accusation against the defendant. There was a lot at stake for the victim, as she could easily perceive a verdict acquitting the defendant to mean that the jury believed she had made an unfounded and serious accusation. J’s affirmation could easily have given the impression that J expressed a positive assessment of the victim. Both counsel for the defence and the assistant advocate had demanded that J recuse herself. That J had expressed a view on how she had perceived her “at the time”, was of secondary importance. The “fear” of lack of impartiality by the applicant had been “objectively justified” (see Ferrantelli and Santangelo v. Italy, 7 August 1996, § 58, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996‑III). The court found it established, on the basis of, inter alia, the statements taken from the applicant after his arrest and the testimony given by him during the trial. He had been involved in the killing and kidnapping of a number of village guards.

The applicant, Mr Anthony Boner, is a British citizen born in 1960. He lives in Glasgow, Scotland. On 14 December 1989 three masked men, armed with a shotgun and a knife, carried out a robbery at a post office in Falkirk, Scotland, in the course of which they assaulted three post office employees. When Mrs G. was called to give evidence, the applicant’s counsel objected on the basis of her earlier presence in court. The trial judge adjourned the case and instructed prosecuting counsel to make further inquiries into the matter. On 17 April 1990 the applicant lodged an intimation of intention to appeal against conviction. Mr Boner instructed new solicitors, who asked a different counsel to advise on the prospects of an appeal and to draft a note of appeal. In his opinion dated 10 June 1990 counsel stated his view that the only possible ground of appeal related to the “admissibility of the evidence of Mrs G’ and to the question “that the trial judge erred in allowing her to be present’ Mr Boner's application to extend legal aid to appeal proceedings had been submitted in May 1990. Scottish Legal Aid Board asked the applicant to provide an opinion from counsel on the prospects of success. On 27 September 1990 the applicant’s solicitors informed the Board by telephone that counsel had finally decided that he could not support the application for legal aid or the appeal. Mr Boner presented his own case on 24 January 1991 before the High Court of Justiciary, sitting in Edinburgh and acting as an appellate court. The Crown was represented by counsel. There is no indication in the record that the court required counsel for the Crown to address it. The appeal against conviction was unanimously dismissed. The court dismissed the first two grounds of appeal relating to Mrs G. and held that these were ill-founded and that the trial judge had approached the matter properly. It did however examine other points raised by the applicant, but reached “the clear conclusion that there was no miscarriage of justice in the case’. The appeal was dismissed on all grounds except that of the applicant who did not address the court on the remaining grounds. The case was settled in 2010 and Mrs G was jailed for two and a half years in 2011. She was released in April 2013 and served two years of a five-year sentence.

On 29 September 2010 the Aachen District Court convicted him on one of the counts and sentenced him to two years and six months in jail. On 30 September 2010 both the applicant and the Public Prosecutor lodged appeals against the District Court’s judgment. The applicant and his entire family had lived on social security since 2001 and had no prospects of employment. There was, hence, an incentive for him to abscond which was not counterbalanced by his existing social ties to Germany. His only tie to Turkey, by contrast, was his parents’ holiday home. name: Richard Roy Allan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48539/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the use of covert audio and video surveillance within his cell, the prison visiting area and upon a fellow prisoner. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The case was settled in favour of the applicant. The applicant and Leroy Grant appeared in custody at the Stockport Magistrates' Court and were further remanded in custody to reappear on 23 February 1995. On 20 February 1995 Detective Chief Inspector Dunn requested permission for the cell and the visiting areas used by the applicant and Grant to be bugged with audio and video technology. In the interviews with the police which followed, the police told the applicant that he was not obliged to say anything. According to the applicant, he was interrogated. The applicant was invited to comment on the recordings made in February and March 1995. He made no comment to any question. He was interviewed by the police concerning the Kwik-Save robbery on 28 June 1995. H. had been fitted with recording devices. He was interviewed at length by the police in an attempt to ‘rattle’ or unsettle him, such that he would be more talkative and vulnerable to H. upon his return to the prison. The recording thereby obtained was adduced in evidence at the applicant's trial. The judge concluded that there was evidence on the tapes from which the jury could infer that the applicant was involved in the events of 3 February 1995, and it was not so unreliable that it could not be left to the jury to assess for themselves. No evidence, other than the alleged admissions, connected the applicant with the killing. The judge's ruling on the admissibility of the evidence was given on 26 January 1998, after a voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of a jury) and consisted of a judgment of eighteen pages. In his summing-up to the jury on 10 and 11 February 1998, the trial judge gave directions on the way in which the jury should assess the reliability of the disputed evidence. He told them that they were to judge whether the police had deliberately wound up the applicant during the interview on 28 June 1995 and how to approach the evidence put forward by H. The prosecution say the contents of the tapes of 28 June can be relied on and are consistent with what H. says [the applicant] had said to him previously. The judge also directed the jury concerning the possible drawing of inferences from the applicant's silence in police interview on 28 and 29 June and 26 July 1995. The judge refused leave to appeal against his conviction by a single judge. His renewed application was refused by the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on 18 January 1999, after a hearing at which he was represented by leading counsel. In the court's judgment of that date, Lord Justice Rose found that the trial judge gave a very careful and impeccable ruling as regards the admissibility of the tapes and evidence put forward by H. and that he had considered all the matters which he should have considered and had not considered any matter which he ought not to have considered.

Case originated in an application (no. 48539/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The case was decided in favour of the applicant and the Government on 28 August 2001. An anonymous informant told the police that the applicant had been involved in the murder of David Beesley. On 20 February 1995 Detective Chief Inspector Dunn requested permission for the cell and visiting areas used by the applicant and Leroy Grant to be bugged with audio and video technology. During this time visits to the applicant by his female friend, J.N.S, were recorded on audio and videotape in the prison visiting area between 12 and 28 March 1995. On 28 June 1995 the applicant was taken away from the prison to be interviewed by the police concerning the Kwik-Save robbery. The applicant was invited to comment on the recordings made in February and March 1995, but made no comment. H. had been fitted with recording devices. The recording thereby obtained was adduced in evidence at the applicant's trial. No evidence, other than the alleged admissions, connected the applicant with the killing of Mr Beesley. The judge concluded that there was evidence on the tapes from which the jury could infer that the applicant was involved in the events of 3 February 1995, and it was not so unreliable that it could not be left to the jury to assess for themselves. He considered that the use of an informant to talk and listen to the accused over a substantial period of time did not result in any unfairness to the applicant. The fact that H. might be considered as having much to gain in giving evidence was also a matter to be left in their assessment. The trial judge gave directions on the way in which the jury should assess the reliability of the disputed evidence. The judge's ruling on the admissibility of the evidence was given on 26 January 1998, after a voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of a jury) and consisted of a judgment of eighteen pages. H. was accordingly admitted before the jury. The defence say if you consider the whole picture you simply cannot rely upon H.; quite unsafe to do so. The prosecution say the contents of the tapes of 28 June can be relied on and are consistent with what H. says [the applicant] had said to him previously. The applicant was convicted of murder in 1998 and sentenced to life imprisonment. He lodged a notice of appeal, asserting that the judge ought to have excluded evidence of the audio- and video-recordings of his conversations with Leroy Grant and J.N.S. The judge concluded that there was evidence on the tapes from which the jury could infer that the applicants was involved in the events of 3 February 1995, and it was not so unreliable that it could not be left to the jury to assess for themselves. The judge's ruling on the admissibility of the evidence was given on 26 January 1998, after a voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of a jury) and consisted of a judgment of eighteen pages. In his summing-up to the jury on 10 and 11 February 1998, the trial judge gave directions on the way in which the jury should assess the reliability of the disputed evidence. He told them that they were to judge whether the police had deliberately wound up the applicant during the interview on 28 June 1995 and how to approach the evidence put forward by H. H. was accordingly admitted before the jury. The applicant was convicted of murder before the Crown Court at Manchester by a majority of ten to two and sentenced to life imprisonment. He was refused leave to appeal against his conviction by a single judge. His renewed application was refused by the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on 18 January 1999, after a hearing at which he was represented by leading counsel. In the court's judgment of that date, Lord Justice Rose found that the trial judge gave a very careful and impeccable ruling as regards the admissibility of the tapes and evidence put forward by H. The judge also directed the jury concerning the possible drawing of inferences from the applicant's silence in police interview on 28 and 29 June and 26 July 1995.

The Commission delegated one of its members, Mr H. Danelius, to take part in the proceedings before the Grand Chamber. The applicant and his publisher were accused of disseminating propaganda against the “indivisible unity of the State’. The public prosecutor at the Istanbul National Security Court no. 1 (“the public prosecutor’s court”) requested, inter alia, application of section 8 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) "The heart of Dersim is torn to pieces its serpentine streets explosions of dynamite the noise of excavators the soldiers’ boots" "What Scripture would accept such cruelty? … [Silently, they looked towards the village of Deşt] … and now cruelty is spreading apace our blood will mix with the blood shed. resistance and betrayal freedom and surrender side by side" "We have been the close acquaintance of the most barbaric cruelties I ask you out of love for the age in which you live how much longer will we put up with this cruelty?" "Let the festivities and celebrations begin let flames as high as the rooftops reach for the sky" Kurds 'have lived for centuries without a State, in exile, during massacres for centuries along the paths we have hauled behind us a sword but never have we been conquered by the sword' The applicant denied the charges before the National Security Court, asserting, in particular, that the passage in inverted commas (see paragraph 10 above) was a quotation which in no way reflected his own opinions. The sentence was suspended for three years and a fine of £1,000. In the National Security. Court’s view, the expression of praise apparent throughout the work amounted to separatist. propaganda that was detrimental to the unity of the Turkish nation and the territorial integrity of the. Turkish State. On an appeal by the applicant, the Court of Cassation upheld that decision on 1 December 1997. Mr Karataş was at that time still serving his sentence in Ümraniye Prison (Istanbul)

Hüseyin Karataş is a Turk of Kurdish origin and was born in 1963. He lives in Istanbul and works as a psychologist. In November 1991 he published an anthology of poems in Istanbul entitled ‘The song of a rebellion – Dersim0’ (“Dersim – Bir İsyanın Türküsü”). He requested, inter alia, application of section 8 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713 – see paragraph 18 below) and the confiscation of the copies of the work concerned (see paragraph 16 below). He relied on the following passages from the applicant’s book: “A great passion is taking shape in our holy hands – the light of ancient Kurdistan for as long as the Munzursuyu[0] is not reddened by our blood we shall not let the whelps of the Ottoman whore trample upon it after all for thousands of years we have obeyed the law freedom is the law of the clan.” “The heart of Dersim is torn to pieces its serpentine streets explosions of dynamite the noise of excavators the soldiers’ boots. On 22 February 1993 he was found guilty of the offences charged and sentenced to life in prison. The expression of praise apparent throughout the work amounted to separatist propaganda that was detrimental to the unity of the Turkish nation. On an appeal by the applicant, the Court of Cassation upheld that decision.

name: Mehmet Tanay
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18753/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that a factual error made by the Court of Cassation had infringed his right of access to court. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the applicant's application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the convention). The application was dismissed on appeal on 17 November 2007. The appeal was dismissed again on 17 December 2007. The Tunceli Court accepted the medical report and began examining the merits of the case. In an application for rectification Mrs Demirdaş argued that it was she who had been ill, not her client. The Court of Cassation held that “amending the factual error would not affect the outcome” and dismissed the rectification request. The Directorate appealed. On 13 November 2003 the Court ofCassation upheld the final ruling. The case was dismissed on 4 July 2003 and the case was settled out of court. The Director of the Forensic Medicine Institute appealed against the decision. The appeal was dismissed and the compensation was awarded on 31 May 2001.

name: Leci Gani
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 61800/08) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr Leci Gani, was born in 1975 and is currently serving a term of imprisonment in the Spanish prison of Quatre Camins in La Roca del Vallès (Barcelona) The applicant complained that he had not been given a proper and adequate opportunity, during either the investigative stage or the hearing, to challenge and question the victim, the sole witness against him in relation to all the crimes for which he had been convicted. The hearing before the Barcelona Audiencia Provincial took place on 19 April 2006. N. attended the hearing after undergoing a psychological diagnosis which established her suitability to testify in court. She had started to answer the questions posed by the public prosecutor when her statement had to be interrupted. She was said to be suffering from post‑traumatic stress symptoms that were hindering her from testifying. Those symptoms were medically confirmed after the hearing. As a consequence, she could not be cross-examined by the. public prosecutor, the private prosecutor or the applicant’s counsel. The court had already adjourned the hearing once before, following a similar reaction on the part of N. The court had previously attempted – perhaps to the point of excess – to exhaust all remedies to obtain her statement. Both the persistence in the witness’s condition during the new hearing and the failure of the therapeutic procedure, which did not lead the court to feel optimistic in the short run, justified the final decision to declare the victim's examination impracticable. The witness rightly started her statement by giving a detailed description of the evolution of her relationship with the accused, the process of rupture and how their personal relations had developed in its aftermath in the light of their common child. Her determination began to weaken when, with slightly shaking hands, she began to describe the assaults she had suffered on the second day. Barcelona Audiencia Provincial ordered that the statements which had been taken from N. during the investigation stage of the proceedings be read out. The applicant gave his alternative account of the facts. The court found that on 4 April 2004 the applicant had gone to N.’s apartment and made death threats when she had not let him in to see their son. It also found that after those three hours had elapsed, the. applicant had abducted N. He had forced her into his car after having ordered J. to take the child to an address which he would provide later by telephone. Afterwards she had been obliged to phone J. and give him the address to which he should bring the child. The applicant was sentenced as the principal offender for: (i) making very serious threats to N., to fifteen months’ imprisonment; (ii) breaking and entering into N.’s home using violence and coercion, to two and a half years’ jail. The court found that, when the applicant had been arrested at Prat de Llobregat Airport (Barcelona), he had been carrying false identification documents. He was also fined EUR 30,525 for damages. For the applicant's above-mentioned conviction the Audiencia Provincial relied mainly on the alleged victim's pre-trial statements, which had been admitted as evidence and read out at the hearing. The credibility of her testimony was enhanced by the weakness of the applicant’S statement. The court considered that the use as evidence of the victim’s pre-trial statements had not infringed the applicant's right to defend himself. The court also considered the reliability of N.’S. statement had been enhanced when confronted with the applicant’�s implausible statement. In the instant case, this crime could be considered to come under the offence of rape. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court, which on 21 February 2007 partially quashed the Audiencia Provincial's judgment. The Supreme Court reduced the penalty imposed on the applicant in respect of kidnapping to bring it into line with the prosecutor's submissions. It also lessened the classification of the offences of making threats and reducing the penalty. Supreme Court said it had repeatedly stressed that trial courts should take special care in assessing victims’ statements when they were the sole direct evidence against the accused. Law permitted that pre-trial statements could be read out in the courtroom as an alternative when a witness’s testimony could not be produced owing to circumstances beyond the parties’ control. The Supreme Court added that the delay with which N. had reported the facts to the police could be explained by her fear and by the fact that she had had a child with the applicant. In a decision served on 3 July 2008, the appeal was declared inadmissible for being devoid of any constitutional content.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that he had not been given a proper and adequate opportunity, during either the investigative stage or the hearing, to challenge and question the victim. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Albanian Government did not inform the Court of their wish to intervene in the proceedings. The case was heard by the Court on 21 October 2011. The application was decided to be decided on the merits and admissible at same time (Article 29 § 1) The hearing before the Barcelona Audiencia Provincial took place on 19 April 2006. N. attended the hearing after undergoing a psychological diagnosis which established her suitability to testify in court. She had started to answer the questions posed by the public prosecutor when her statement had to be interrupted. She was said to be suffering from post‑traumatic stress symptoms that were hindering her from testifying. Those symptoms were medically confirmed after the hearing. The court had already adjourned the hearing once before, following a similar reaction on the part of N. As a consequence, it had provided her with psychological assistance before and during the hearing to allow for her full examination, but to no avail. The court had previously attempted – perhaps to the point of excess – to exhaust all remedies to obtain her statement. It had made use of all the psychological support that the presence of officials from the victims’ service could provide to the witness, relaxation exercises during the trial, suspensions and recesses. The efforts were fruitless, however, and the witness’s resolved will to collaborate was prevented by one of the most horrific cases of psychological annihilation of a victim that this court has ever witnessed in its long professional experience. The continuation of the witness's examination would have been incompatible with Article 8 § 4 of the Protection of Victims Statute approved by a European Union Framework Decision. Barcelona Audiencia Provincial ordered that the statements which had been taken from her during the investigation stage of the proceedings be read out. The applicant gave his alternative account of the facts. The court found that on 4 April 2004 the applicant had gone to N.’s apartment and had made death threats when she had not let him in to see their son. Upon leaving the apartment, he had twice knocked a car belonging to J., a close male friend of N., causing damage to the vehicle. On 6 April 2004 at around 1 a.m., the. applicant had broken in through a window. He had punched J., who had been there with N., and then hit N. repeatedly. After those three hours had elapsed, the applicant. had abducted N. into his car after having ordered J. to take the child to an address. The applicant was sentenced as the principal offender for: (i) making very serious threats to N., to fifteen months’ imprisonment. (ii) breaking and entering into N.’s home using violence and coercion, to two and a half years’ jail. (iii) causing minor bodily injuries to J., to twelve days’ house arrest. (iv) N.'s kidnapping under threat, with the aggravating factor of family ties, to eight years' imprisonment; (v) J.'s kidnap, to three years' prison; (vi) a crime against N’S moral integrity with the. aggravating factors of family links, to 2 years' jail. He was also fined EUR 30,525 for damages. Supreme Court partially quashes the Audiencia Provincial’s judgment. The court considered that the use as evidence of the victim's pre-trial statements had not infringed the applicant's right to defend himself. The Supreme Court reduced the penalty imposed on the applicant in respect of kidnapping to bring it into line with the prosecutor's submissions. It also lessened the classification of the offence of making threats. The judge acquitted the applicant of the crime against moral integrity because, in the instant case, this crime could be considered to come under the offence. of rape. The rest of the judgment was upheld by the Supreme Court. The trial court had first tried to resolve the problem by staying the hearing. Supreme Court ruled that pre-trial statements could be read out in the courtroom as an alternative when a witness’s testimony could not be produced owing to circumstances beyond the parties’ control. The Supreme Court added that the delay with which N. had reported the facts to the police could be explained by her fear and by the fact that she had had a child with the applicant. The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. In a decision served on 3 July 2008, the appeal was declared inadmissible for being devoid of any constitutional content. The ruling was made by the Supreme Court of the Republic of Colombia.

name: Thomas Coster
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court, in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case originated in an application (no. 24876/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land in their caravans violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life. They also complained that they were subject to discrimination as gypsies. The Grand Chamber of the Court decided that the case should be decided by the Grand Chamber. The Government and the applicants each filed a memorial. Third-party comments were also received from European Roma Rights Centre. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 May 2000. The applicants are gypsies by birth. They are seeking a permanent site on which to site their caravan. They wished for their children to be brought up in a stable environment which would facilitate the continuity of their education. They faced the threat of continual eviction from the Borough of Maidstone, Kent. From 1987, the Borough was a designated area pursuant to section 12 of the Caravan Sites Act 1968 (see paragraphs 43-48 below). The applicants now have four children, Jody born in 1983. The application for a council flat in Kent was made in 1982. The applicants were refused a place on any local authorised site. They camped outside one official site for 5-6 weeks hoping to be offered a plot. No place was offered and court proceedings were brought against them by the Borough to secure their eviction from the land. In 1988, the applicants purchased land known as Summerfields in Headcorn, Kent and moved onto it, living in a caravan. They were convicted for failure to comply with the enforcement notice in July 1989. The appeal was dismissed. The Inspector accepted that the applicants were gypsies for whom conventional residence in permanent accommodation would lead to illness. The applicants made a further application for planning permission which was refused on 11 December 1989. A public enquiry was held before a Planning Inspector on 26 March 1991. The Inspector refused their appeal on 24 April 1991 and the applicants were penalised in costs on the basis that it was identical to the previous application. The applicants conceded that the only action taken since the 1989 decision by or on behalf of the family to find another site or accommodation, was a telephone call … to the [Borough], on instructions, assured the inquiry that the family would be offered short-term housing. This is the position the family have faced for a long time.” No new gypsy sites have been opened in Maidstone since 1967. The only way in which it could be made virtually invisible would be to provide physical screening which would in itself be an intrusive feature in the countryside. The provision of private sites should be encouraged, Kent County Council support the provision ofPrivate sites. There should be a flexible attitude to such planning applications. As was said in a Parliamentary answer in 1987, well-run gypsy. sites, once established, seldom give cause for serious complaints. ‘Designated’ authorities like Maidstone may still need to make extra provision in their area if the. demand for gypsy accommodation increases. The applicants made enquiries from the Borough about rehousing but no formal application was made until 21 May 1990. On 23 July 1990, the applicants were formally informed by the Borough that they were considered as intentionally homeless since they had terminated their council tenancy to move onto land not permitted for residential use. The applicants were convicted for breach of enforcement notices and ordered to pay GBP 275 each as a fine and contribute GBP 25 to the Borough’s costs. In 1991 the applicants enquired about alternative accommodation on a private site but were excluded due to the size of their family. On 24 July 1992, a fine of GBP 350 was imposed on each applicant. A third prosecution resulted in conviction and sentence was deferred to enable the applicants to move. The applicants’ names were placed on the waiting list at the end of 1992 but they removed their names from that list in January 1993. The Borough commenced its proceedings for an injunction by summons dated 22 December 1993. In May 1994 the applicants applied to the Borough for accommodation and were again offered temporary accommodation. The applicants were informed, the Government stated, of vacant plots on council and private gypsy sites in the county. One site they visited at Aylesford was infested with rats and a dangerous place for children. In February 1997, the applicants sold their land. They also sold their caravan at a substantial undervalue. They went to live temporarily in the caravan occupied by the second applicant’s brother. The applicants suffered headaches, anxiety, claustrophobia and depression requiring them to seek medical treatment. They were both prescribed medication which did not however resolve their physical sense of confinement. The applicants bought a touring caravan, which they stationed on the land of the second applicant’s brother. They took every opportunity they could to travel in the traditional style during school holidays, attending traditional gypsy fairs to continue horse trading activities. They have bought another plot of land in Yalding, Kent, with the intention of resuming their traditional life. They intend to apply for planning permission for a new caravan site on the site.

The applicants were convicted for breach of enforcement notices and ordered to pay GBP 275 each as a fine and contribute GBP 25 to the Borough’s costs. On 24 July 1992, a fine of GBP 350 was imposed on each applicant. A third prosecution resulted in conviction and sentence was deferred to enable the applicants to move. The applicants returned to their land in December 1992. They applied for Housing Association accommodation but were told that nothing would be available for six months. The Borough commenced its proceedings for an injunction by summons dated 22 December 1993. The applicants applied for judicial review to quash the injunction proceedings on the basis that the decision to pursue the injunction against them was unreasonable. In February 1997, the applicants sold their land. They also sold their caravan at a substantial undervalue. They went to live temporarily in the caravan occupied by the second applicant’s brother, which involved a family of six sharing with aFamily of five. This became intolerable. They looked for an alternative private or official site on which to station their caravan but no such site could be found. The applicants suffered headaches, anxiety, claustrophobia and depression requiring them to seek medical treatment. They were both prescribed medication which did not however resolve their physical sense of confinement. The applicants bought a touring caravan, which they stationed on the land of the second applicant’s brother. They took every opportunity they could to travel in the traditional style during school holidays, attending traditional gypsy fairs to continue horse trading activities. They have bought another plot of land in Yalding, Kent, with the intention of resuming their traditional life. They intend to apply for planning permission to return to the gypsy lifestyle. The case originated in an application (no. 24876/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by two British nationals. The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land in their caravans violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life. They further complained that they were subject to discrimination as gypsies. The panel of the Grand Chamber determined that the case should be decided by the Grand chamber. The applicants are gypsies by birth. They lived and travelled with their respective families in and around the area known as the Borough of Maidstone in Kent. From 1987, the Borough was a designated area pursuant to section 12 of the Caravan Sites Act 1968 (see paragraphs 43-48 below). The applicants wished for their children to be brought up in a stable environment which would facilitate the continuity of their education. When the second applicant became pregnant, the applicants decided to search for a permanent site on which to site their caravan. There remained few stopping places upon which they could lawfully park their caravan whilst travelling in the area and they faced the threat of continual eviction. The applicants were refused a place on any local authorised site. They camped outside one official site for 5-6 weeks hoping to be offered a plot. No place was offered and court proceedings were brought against them by the Borough to secure their eviction from the land. The Government stated that the Borough has no knowledge or record of any request by the applicants for a pitch in 1982. The appeal was dismissed. They had therefore not lost their status as gypsies as a result of their residence in. Summerfields in Headcorn, Kent and moved onto it, living in a caravan. On 11 July 1988, the second applicant made a retrospective planning application for permission to station a caravan on their site. Permission was refused. The applicants made a further application for planning permission which was refused on 11 December 1989. A public enquiry was held before a Planning Inspector on 26 March 1991. The Inspector refused their appeal on 24 April 1991 and the applicants were penalised in costs on the basis that it was identical to the previous application. The applicants conceded that the only action taken since the 1989 decision by or on behalf of the family to find another site or accommodation, was a telephone call … to the [Borough] Counsel for the borough assured the inquiry that the [applicants’] family would be offered short-term housing. This is the position they have faced for a long time. Planning judge: Mobile home would remain intrusively visible from Lenham Road and Baker lane. No new gypsy sites have been opened in Maidstone since 1967. There is nowhere within the site at which a mobile home could be positioned without causing equally serious harm. No way in which it could be made virtually invisible, …, would be to provide physical screening which would in itself be an intrusive feature in the countryside. This conflicts with generally well-respected policies aimed at protecting the landscape and at limiting residential development mainly to towns and villages. This development is in serious conflict with the Structure Plan policies aimed as protecting the character of the open countryside from development. The applicants were told that there was a waiting list for places on official sites but that since they were intentionally homeless they could not put their names on it for 2 years. In March 1992, the applicants applied to the Borough for housing on the grounds of homelessness and that contrary to the policy of refusing registration within two years after a finding of intentional homelessness the Borough agreed to re-register them as homeless on condition that they paid their arrears of rent for the council tenancy. The applicants left their land and travelled to Whitstable, Kent close to where some of the second applicant’s family had stationed their caravans. There was no sanitation or electricity and there was an infestation of rats. The applicants were offered temporary accommodation by the Borough of Aylesford. The applicants were told that nothing would be available for six months. The Government said that the applicants’ names were placed on the waiting list at the end of 1992 but they removed their names from that list in January 1993. They went to live temporarily in the caravan occupied by the second applicant’s brother, which involved a family of six sharing with aFamily of five. name: Oğuz Atakan Köseoğlu
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 73283/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 26 May 2005. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time. The case was decided by the Court on 2 March 2006. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant, and the case was dismissed. The applicant filed an action with the Izmir Administrative Court, seeking compensation for the damage he had suffered as a result of his allegedly unlawful suspension and dismissal. He also requested to be granted the rights and salaries of which he had been deprived during those periods. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's request for appeal. It opined that the reinstatement of the applicant did not give him the right to recuperate rights and earnings for the suspended and dismissal period. It reasoned that the decision of the administrative authorities. concerning his reinstatement to his previous post would not enable him to claim the rights. and earnings which were denied him during the suspension and. dismissal periods.

name: Gabriel Magee
train_texts: The case originated in three applications (nos. 26289/12, 29062/12 and 29891/12) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The first and third applicants were arrested under section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000 (“the 2000 Act”) on suspicion of involvement in the murder of a police officer on 9 March 2009. They were detained at Antrim police station on the same day. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the cases (Rule 59 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Court Judge granted warrants authorising a five-day extension of detention. In her reasoning, Judge Philpott noted that the relevant forensic evidence was central to the investigation and that the investigation was being carried out diligently and expeditiously. The second applicant was arrested under section 41 of the 2000 Act on suspicion of involvement in the murder of two soldiers at Masserene Barracks, Antrim, on 7 March 2009. On 15 March 2009 the DPP made an application to the County Court for a warrant extending the second applicant’s detention as the results of a number of forensic tests were pending. Following a hearing on 16 March 2009 a County Court judge granted both applications. The applicants sought permission to apply for judicial review of Judge Philpott’s decisions of 21 and 22 March 2009 granting further extensions to the warrants authorising their detention. The High Court of Northern Ireland heard the applications on 25 March 2009. The applicants argued that the judge had failed to address the question of whether the detention of the applicants was required while the results of forensic examinations were expected. The review of the lawfulness of the detention had to embrace an examination of the basis of the arrest, otherwise a person could be detained under the 2000 Act for up to twenty-eight days without there having been any judicial review. The judge found that the applicants’ first submission had to be read in conformity with the requirements of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. High Court of Northern Ireland found no basis for the submission that Schedule 8 was incompatible with Article 5 of the Convention. The court accepted, however, that a review of the lawfulness of the arrest need not involve a detailed analysis of the decision to arrest and should reflect the constraints that necessarily apply in many arrests for terrorist offences. The judge had not focused directly on whether the applicants had to be detained rather than released pending the outcome of the remaining forensic examinations. Although her reasons were pithily stated, they were sufficient to convey to the applicants the basis of her decision to grant the extensions. The Court found that, although there was no express power to order release in the 2000 Act as required by Article 5, such a power must be implied. High Court of Northern Ireland ruled on 24 February 2011. Case involved whether extended detention was compatible with the applicant’s rights under Article 5(1)(c), 5(2) and 5(3) of the European Convention on Human Rights (‘the Convention’) The High Court ruled that there was no authority which supported the applicants’ contention that Article 5 required that a detained person be charged well before the expiry of the twenty‑eight day period contemplated in the 2000 Act. The Court also found that there were a range of tools available to the court to preserve to the necessary extent an adversarial procedure and equality of arms. The applicants were released without charge on 25 March 2009. The first and third applicants were not subsequently charged with any offence related to the murder of the police officer. The second applicant was immediately rearrested and interviewed over the following two days. On 27 March 2009 he was charged with the murder. of the two soldiers, five attempted murders and possession of a firearm and ammunition. His application for bail was refused. The High Court refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court refused permission to appeal on the basis that the applications did not raise an arguable point of law of general public importance. On 7 November 2011 the second applicant stood trial before a judge sitting without a jury.

Court Judge granted warrants authorising a five-day extension of detention. Each of the applicants was interviewed on twelve occasions in the following five days. He was detained at Antrim Police Station on the same day. On 15 March 2009 the DPP made an application to the County Court for a warrant extending the second applicant’s detention as the results of a number of forensic tests were pending. On 21 March 2009 a judge granted both applications. On 21 March 2009 the DPP made an application to the County Court under paragraph 36 of Schedule 8 to the 2000 Act for a seven-day extension to the period specified in the warrant for further detention. The extension was sought as the results of further forensic tests which had been sent for analysis to a laboratory in Great Britain were expected to become available within the following seven days. Judge Philpott granted the application, authorising the second applicant’s continued detention until 7.20 on 28 March 2009. The applicants sought permission to apply for judicial review of Judge Philhott's decisions of 21 and 22 March 2009 granting further extensions to the warrants authorising their detention. They submitted, firstly, that the judge had been wrong to conclude that a court was precluded from investigating the lawfulness of the arrest. Ott had been wrong to disavow any review of the lawfulness of the applicants’ arrest and, as a consequence, her decision to grant extensions had to be quashed. The second applicant was immediately rearrested and interviewed over the following two days. On 7 November 2011 the second applicant stood trial before a judge sitting without a jury. On 20 January 2012 he was acquitted on all counts of the indictment. The applicants’ release from detention was confirmed on 22 March 2011. name: Mehmet Ali Yılmaz
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a ‘reasonable time’ He also claimed that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court which lacked independence and impartiality. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. In a decision of 11 January 2000, the Court retained the applicant’s complaints concerning his right of fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal. The applicant was accused of being one of the founding members and a leader of the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The court sentenced him to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in the civil service and placed him under judicial guardianship. His case was automatically referred to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) on 27 December 1995. On 23 July 1991 the applicant was conditionally released pending trial. He was convicted on account of his involvement in the killing of H.U. and bombing of the premises of a holding company and a bank.

name: Galip Yalman
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicants alleged that their case, which commenced in 1989 and terminated in 1996, was not heard within a reasonable time. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted. By a decision of 15 May 2003, the Court declared the application admissible. The Court also ruled that the Government of Turkey did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Convention institutions. The applicants requested compensation for their unjustified detention on remand. before the Sinop Assize Court against the Treasury, pursuant to Law no. 466. The applicants appealed, arguing that the amount of compensation awarded was not sufficient. On 30 May 1996 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants’ appeal and upheld the judgment of the assize court. The case is now being heard by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France. The trial is expected to last at least a few more weeks, and the verdicts are expected to be delivered by the end of the year. The appeal is not expected to take place until after the Euro 2016 elections.

name: Ferman Ayçoban
train_texts: Three Turkish nationals, Ferman Ayçoban, Aziz Yiğit, and Şirin Meygil, were detained in Elazığ Prison in Turkey. They were arrested on suspicion of being members of Hezbollah. The applicants' names were recorded on three computer hard disks. The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the applications partly inadmissible and decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility. The applications were dismissed and the case was returned to the Turkish authorities for further proceedings. The applicants gave statements to the police where they accepted the charges against them. They denied the content of their police statements alleging that they were taken under duress. On 27 December 2001 the Diyarbakır State Security Court noted that the applicants' police statements were supported by information gathered from the archive of the organisation and further evidence. It accordingly convicted the applicants of the offence as charged and sentenced them to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. The applicants appealed. The Court of Cassation, having regard, inter alia, to the opinion of the Principal Prosecutor, upheld the judgment in May 2002. The applicant's case was heard at the Supreme Court of Justice.

The police officers seized, among other things, three computer hard disks during the operation. The applicant's names were recorded on these hard disks as members of Hezbollah. On 13 January 2005 the Court joined the applications. It decided to declare the applications partly inadmissible and to communicate the complaints concerning the lack of prompt and detailed information on the nature and cause of the accusations. The applicants were accused of being members of Hezbollah. They were convicted and sentenced to 12 years and 6 months in prison. The applicants appealed but the decision was upheld in May 2002. The application was brought before the Court of Cassation in Istanbul. The court heard the transcripts of the hard disks seized during the raid in Mardin in order to place them in the custody of the court. The computer hard disks were noted to contain the names of the applicants. They deny that their names are on the disks and say they did not know how their names appeared on them. They claim that their police statements were taken under duress and that they do not know who they are.

name: Paul Matthew Coyne
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 16 September 1996. It originated in an application (no. 25942/94) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The applicant, Mr Paul Matthew Coyne, was born in 1972 and lives in Bedford. He joined the Royal Air Force (“RAF”) in 1990. In June 1992, when he was serving as a non-commissioned officer in Br., he was awarded the ‘right to a hearing’. The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza, Mr Blades and Mr Eadie. In accordance with the Court’s decision (see paragraph 5 above), a hearing limited to issues under Article 50 of the Convention took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 June 1997. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr M.R. Eaton, Deputy Legal Adviser, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. E adadie, Counsel. Mr Coyne was charged with various offences of forgery and deception. He was sentenced to nine months’ detention, dismissal from the air force and reduction to the ranks. Mr Coyne appealed his conviction and sentence on 31 January 1994, claiming that the judge advocate had erred in his summing up of the case. The decision was taken to try him by RAF court martial in Brüggen, Germany, on 26 January 1994. The charges were connected to a false application for a bank loan. The convening officer was the Air Officer Commanding no. 2 Group, RAF, Rheindahlen and as such was the senior commander of all air force personnel serving in Germany. Court of Appeal rejected the appeal on the grounds that the finding of guilt on one charge was inconsistent with the finding on the other. The decision was based on the court’s failure to consider the issue of whether the charge was ‘false’ or ‘unsubstantiated’ The appeal was accepted by the Court of Appeal on 9 March 1994. The case was heard again on 11 March 1994, and the appeal was rejected again on the same grounds. The appeal case was settled on 13 March 1994 when the court of appeal ruled that the conviction was not ‘in contravention of the law’. The conviction was upheld on the basis that the charge had been ‘inconsistent’ with another charge.

The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him. The Government expressed the view that it would not be necessary to hold oral proceedings. The Government offered to settle the case on the basis of the payment of the applicant’s reasonable legal costs and expenses. This offer was rejected by the applicant on 6 May 1997. A hearing limited to issues under Article 50 of the Convention took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 June 1997. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr M.R. Eaton, Deputy Legal Adviser, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Eadie, Counsel, for the applicant Mr G. Blades, Solicitor, and for the Commission Mr N. Bratza, Delegate. Mr Coyne was charged, pursuant to section 70 (1) of the Air Force Act 1955, with four civilian criminal offences. Charges were connected to a false application for a bank loan. Mr Coyne pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him. He was sentenced to nine months’ detention, dismissal from the air force and reduction to the ranks. On 31 January 1994 he presented a petition against conviction and sentence. He claimed that the judge advocate had erred in his summing up of the case, that he was not guilty of the first and second charges, and that the third charge was an alternative to the first. No finding was made on the fourth charge. On 8 March 1994, the Court of Appeal accepted a petition from the Defence Council to invalidate a conviction. On 11 October 1994, a court ruled that the conviction had been upheld on the grounds that the evidence was not sufficient to support the charge. The Court of appeal rejected the appeal, saying that the finding of guilt on one charge was inconsistent with the evidence on the other. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court, but the appeal was rejected on 15 October 1994. The appeal was upheld on 18 October 1994 and the conviction was quashed on the basis of the evidence that it was not enough to prove the charge was false. The judge said that the case was a miscarriage of justice and therefore the conviction should be quashed.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 54640/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. By a decision of 9 October 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. The Austrian Federal Ministry of Justice refused to grant this request. The applicant filed a complaint with the Administrative Court. The Administrative Court submitted three further requests raising the same issue. The proceedings in these cases were joined to proceedings in the applicant’s case. It argued that Article 6 of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms applied to the proceedings concerning the recognition of foreign divorce decrees as their outcome had a direct effect on the civil law relationship of the persons concerned. The recognition of foreign divorce decrees was closely linked to the question whether they could be enforced in Austria. proceedings at issue were concerned with the questions whether recognition was compatible with Austrian ordre public. name: Wim Capeau
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42914/98) against the Kingdom of Belgium lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained of a violation of Articles 5 § 1 (c), 6 § 2 and 14 of the Convention, contending that the statutory requirement to establish his innocence by adducing factual evidence was incompatible with the presumption of innocence. By a decision of 6 April 2004, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government filed observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant did not submit any observations within the time allowed. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The applicant claimed compensation for unwarranted pre-trial detention. The Minister of Justice refused the applicant's claim on the ground that he had not “established his innocence by adducing factual evidence or submitting legal argument to that effect” On 4 July 1997 the applicant contested the Minister's decision by means of an application to the Unwarranted Pre-trial Detention Appeals Board. On 1 December 1997 the Appeals Board upheld the refusal of his claim by a decision taken on the same day and served on the applicant on 29 March 1998. It noted that the grounds for presuming the guilt of the applicant, who had always denied committing the offence he stood accused of, had been held to be insufficient to justify committing him for trial.

The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. By a decision of 6 April 2004, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government filed observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant did not submit any observations within the time allowed. The case was decided in favour of the applicant, Mr Wim Capeau, and he is entitled to a compensation payment of up to 30,000 euros. The applicant claimed compensation for unwarranted pre-trial detention. The Minister of Justice refused the applicant's claim on the ground that he had not “established his innocence by adducing factual evidence or submitting legal argument to that effect” The Appeals Board upheld the refusal of his claim by a decision taken on the same day and served on the applicant on 29 March 1998. It noted that the grounds for presuming the guilt of the applicant, who had always denied committing the offence he stood accused of, had been held to be insufficient to justify committing him for trial. It observed that, although the applicant had announced his intention of submitting a pleading setting out the evidence in the file which “amply” proved his innocence, he did not do so and had not replied to the Government's submissions.

name: Allan Jacobsson
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 18 December 1987. It originated in an application (no. 10842/84) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Allan Jacobsson, a Swedish citizen, on 11 January 1984. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). The President drew by lot the names of the five other members of the Chamber on 30 January 1988, in the presence of the Registrar. The Government’s memorial and the applicant's memorial were received by the registry on 2 and 9 May 1988. On 6 March 1989 the Secretary to the Commission notified the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell for the Government and Mr Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and Mr Tullberg, Mr Petrén and Mr Magnusson for the applicant as well as their replies to its questions. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The applicant bought a property of 2,644 m², Salem 23:1, in the centre of Rönninge in the municipality of Salem, south west of Stockholm. The property was covered by an area plan (områdesplan - see paragraph 26 below), adopted in 1972, which described the property mainly as a public area containing green spaces, streets and car parking. It was also covered by a building prohibition pursuant to section 35 of the 1947 Building Act (byggnadslagen, “the 1947 Act’) issued on 26 August 1974 and lasting until 1 September 1976. The Government also claimed that the regulations for non-planned areas (utomplansbestämmelser) applied but the applicant contested this. On 1 July 1987, with the entry into force of the Plan and Building Act 1987, the existing system for prohibitions on construction was abolished and replaced by a new one. The applicant's property was supposed to be used for building blocks of flats of more than two storeys. The applicant appealed to the Board claiming that the building prohibition was not valid. The Board rejected the appeal on 25 April 1980. In April 1983 the Building Committee requested the Board to revoke, pursuant to section 168 of the 1947 Act, the right to build according to the subdivision plan of 1938. The board rejected the request on 23 March 1984, stating inter alia: “The long duration of the [building] prohibition depends to a large extent on changes in the objectives of the planning procedure as a result of the changes of municipal organisation which have occurred’. The applicant's property is situated in an area which should be used for the construction of multi-family houses in 1988. In 1983 the Municipal Council decided to issue a further building prohibition for the area in question. Challenging, inter alia, the lawfulness of the Board’s decision, the applicant appealed to the Government which, however, rejected the appeal on 15 December 1983. In the decision it was noted that the Municipality planned to carry out certain work during 1984 for the purposes of establishing the necessary plans. In a decision of 21 August 1984, the Building Committee conceded that a mistake had been made and quashed its decision of 12 June. The application was made on 10 July 1987. The validity of the subdivision plan remained unaffected. The Building Committee decided however, pursuant to the rules laid down in the new 1987 Act, to defer its decision on the request for a period of two years. This is the last step of the preparatory work in the making of a town plan. The application was denied. The building committee decided to defer the decision for two years (see paragraph 45 below) The applicant again filed a request for. a preliminary opinion regarding a building permit for his property (cf. paragraph 9 above). The request was denied and the building permit application was rejected.

Magnusson, Land Surveyor, Advisers. According to the plan the applicant’s property was supposed to be used for building blocks of flats of more than two storeys. On 15 January 1980 the Building Committee stated, in reply to a request from the applicant, that it was not prepared to grant him an exemption from the building prohibition or a permit to build a one-family house and a garage on the property. The Board rejected the appeal on 25 April 1980. The applicant again filed a request for a preliminary opinion regarding a building permit for his property. The Building Committee decided however, pursuant to the rules laid down in the new 1987 Act, to defer its decision for a period of two years. The validity of the subdivision plan (see paragraph 8 above) remained unaffected. The application was rejected by the Building Committee on 30 July 1987. The decision was made to defer the decision for two years, or until the applicant submitted another application for a permit. The applicant then applied for a new permit to build a house in the area. The request was rejected on 10 July 1987, and the application was dismissed.

name: Wolfgang Rambauske
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 45369/07) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants are the joint owners of a house in Salzburg which they had acquired in 1996. In spring 1997 they discovered that the distance between an annex to their house and the neighbouring plot of land did not correspond to the minimum distance required by the building permit. The applicants and their neighbours filed comprehensive submissions and the applicants submitted substitute plans which were then examined by a court-appointed expert. On 11 February 2009 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Until August 2000 the Appeals Commission (Bauberufungs-kommission) tried to achieve a settlement between the applicants and their neighbours. As these efforts failed, it took further evidence, asking expert A. to supplement his opinion. The parties were asked to comment by 21 February 2001. That time-limit was extended several times on the applicants’ request until 30 March 2001. The Appeals Commission held an on-site hearing on 6 July 2001. On 2 May 2003 the applicants' neighbours lodged a complaint to the Administrative Court. The Administrative Court dismissed the neighbours’ complaint as being unfounded on 27 March 2007. The judgment was served on the applicant’s counsel on 19 April 2007.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 51962/12) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The decision was published on 15 June 2014 and is available on the ECHR website. The applicants learned of this decision on 6 March 2012. Following an amendment to the law, the Diyarbakır Assize Court revised its judgment pursuant to Provisional Article 1 § 1 of the Law no. 6352 and suspended the execution of the applicants’ sentences. The applicants were found guilty as charged and sentenced to one year and eight months’ imprisonment. Their sentences were suspended on 12 October 2012, following an amendment of the law. They were sentenced to a year and a half’s imprisonment. The sentence was suspended on 8 October 2012. The application is based on the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) Section 7.2 of the Act is related to the applicants.
