name: Nurettin Peker
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42136/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been shot in the leg and then beaten up by a number of gendarmes who had been carrying out an operation in the prison where he was being detained. On 11 May 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. The applicant was dragged through a 100-metre-long human corridor formed by the gendarmes. While the prison governor and other civilian authorities were checking the inmates' identity documents, a gendarme dragged the applicant into a corner and beat him up there. He was subsequently taken to Gebze State Hospital but was brought back to the prison four days later, before his treatment was complete. The applicant was wounded by a bullet and was among those who were taken to the hospital. Seven inmates who were on hunger strike at the time and a further six who had been injured during the operation were taken. Materials used by the inmates as weapons, namely wooden sticks and iron bars, were found in the dormitories and confiscated. A doctor examined the applicant at Gebze hospital on 20 December 2000, noted a gunshot wound on his left foot and began treating it. The applicant and five other inmates who were injured in the operation were also taken to hospital. No firearms were found in the prison during the searches carried out in the immediate aftermath of the operation. During a search conducted at the prison on 29 August 2001 a pistol and seven bullets were found by the prison authorities. The inmate was indicted and over 200 of his fellow inmates were accused of obstructing law-enforcement personnel in the execution of their duties and causing criminal damage. The application was dismissed in January 2002. Two more pistols and thirty-three bullets were found in the prison on 22 January 2002. Neither officer S.Y. nor any of the gendarmes under his command had fired shots during the operation. In a letter of 27 May 2004 the Gebze prosecutor requested permission to prosecute two gendarmerie officers allegedly responsible for the applicant's injury. The Regional Administrative Court in Sakarya examined the objection lodged by the applicant against the governor's decision on 10 January 2005, and quashed the decision. It held that a judicial investigation should be carried out into the allegations against the officers. The judge ruled against the request on 13 September 2005. The two officers were later released by the prison. The case against the two officers was dismissed by the Kartal Assize Court in Istanbul in 2006. The judge ruled that the incident was not investigated in a timely manner or in an impartial fashion. The court also ruled that there was insufficient evidence that the two men had fired a gun at the victim. The victim was released from the prison in 2004. The incident is still being investigated by the Gebze Prison Authority in Gebzeg, where the incident took place. The two officers have since been released from prison by the Prison Service. The investigation into the incident is ongoing, and no arrests have been made.

name: Adam Matoń
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Kraków. He was convicted of drug trafficking, unlawful possession of firearms and membership of an organised criminal gang. There were 36 accused and 147 witnesses in the case. The proceedings are currently pending before the Katowice Regional Court. The application was decided on the admissibility and merits of the application. The Court of Appeal pointed out that the court had scheduled 58 hearings in 2001, 66 in 2002, 73 in 2003, 64 in 2004 and 85 in 2005. Several hearings had had to be postponed because defence lawyers, co-accused and witnesses were absent and assessors and judges were ill. The court found that the proceedings had been handled properly and the delays had been attributable to other persons and unexpected circumstances rather than to the court. The applicant lodged another complaint with the Katowice Court of appeal in October 2006. On 31 January 2007, the court dismissed the length complaint and said that the hearings had not amounted to an ‘excessive length’ as defined by the 2004 Act.

The application was made on 4 July 2007 by a Polish national, Mr Adam Matoń. The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Kraków. He was convicted of drug trafficking, unlawful possession of firearms and membership of an organised criminal gang. The court decided to give notice of the application to the Government and rule on the admissibility and merits of the case. The Court of Appeal pointed out that the court had scheduled 58 hearings in 2001, 66 in 2002, 73 in 2003, 64 in 2004 and 85 in 2005. However, several hearings had had to be postponed because defence lawyers, co-accused and witnesses were absent and assessors and judges were ill. The court found that the proceedings had been handled properly and the delays had been attributable to other persons and unexpected circumstances rather than to the court. A second complaint was lodged with the Katowice Court of appeal in October 2006. It was dismissed on 31 January 2007 after the court found the length complaint had not amounted to an ‘excessive length’ as defined by the 2004 Act.

name: Anthony White
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42435/02) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the right to respect for private and family life to the Government. The applicant lives in Beira, Mozambique, and brought a private prosecution against the newspapers through their legally responsible editors (ansvariga utgivare). He claimed that the editors were responsible for gross defamation, or alternatively defamation of a normal degree. He also sought compensation for mental suffering and pecuniary damage. The District Court put to the jury 66 questions relating to the articles published in Expressen. The jury answered all but six questions in the negative. As regards the remaining six questions, the jury found that certain published statements or pictures amounted to defamation of a normal degree. The court then had to make a re-assessment of liability. The contravening statements were the following: The heading on the front page stating “He is pointed out as PALME’s MURDERER” [“Han pekas ut som PALMES MÖRDARE”] together with a picture of the applicant. The text on page 6: “In addition to Long reach, Williamson and White had several companies together, some with links to the Mafia. Anthony White is one of southern Africa’s biggest poachers, tells a source. It is to a large degree his fault that the elephants in Mozambique are all but extinct. Together with Williamson, Anthony White appropriated the ivory. By a judgment of 24 February 2000, the District Court acquitted the editors in all respects and rejected the applicant's claims for damages. It found that the editors had acted in good faith and had not committed any misconduct. The editors were acquitted of all charges against them in the judgment of the district court on February 24, 2000. The appeal was dismissed on March 7, 2000, and the case was settled out of court. The Court of Appeal upheld the District Court’s judgment. A balance has to be struck between the protection against offensive statements and the demands of freedom of speech. If the information is correct it may as a rule be communicated even if it is deprecatory, if this is justifiable with reference to the public news interest. However, there is no general right always to speak the truth if the statements are offensive. In certain situations the interest of protecting someone againstoffensive statements has to yield to thePublic interest. Aftonbladet, for its part, has asserted that, in the circumstances, it was justifiable to describe Anthony White. The Court of Appeal finds that it was justifiable in the circumstances to publish Anthony White’s name and picture in Expressen and to publish information about the person Anthony White in Aftonbladet. It emerges from the information that has come to hand in the case that, within certain groups in southern Africa and Europe, it was known that Anthony White had engaged in the alleged activities. Anthony White has asserted that he is innocent of all the accusations, that the information given about him was based on pure invention, that it is unverified or given by untrustworthy persons. The information reveals that he has been much better known than he has wished to admit. The Court of Appeal takes account of the following considerations. The fact that the name and picture of the plaintiff had already been published by other news services has not relieved Expressen and Aftonbladet of the obligation to make their own assessment of the credibility of the information. It has been established that the main basis for the assertions in issue in the case was the statements made by [the former senior official of the South African security police] Dirk Coetzee. With a few exceptions, the persons contacted have not been named. Each of them separately has had high ambitions to check with reliable sources who the person Anthony White was. What has come to hand in the Case reveals that the witnesses, each one through their own work, have received concordant information. Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) refused the applicant leave to appeal. Aftonbladet must be considered to have performed the checks that were called for. The Court of Appeal finds that there was also a reasonable basis for the assertions in Aft onbladen.’’ ‘AftonBladet’ was found to have been guilty of publishing a false statement. The court also found that the assertion and the reproduction of the picture in Expressen. had not been sufficiently checked. ‘’The court of appeal found that there had been insufficient checks that had been carried out to determine whether the assertion was true.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the right to respect for private and family life to the Government. The applicant was represented by Mr E. Kalman, a lawyer practising in Stockholm. The Swedish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms I. Kalmerborn, Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The case was decided in accordance with the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The District Court put to the jury 66 questions relating to the articles published in Expressen. The jury answered all but six questions in the negative. In accordance with the applicable rules, the jury’s finding of ‘no guilt’ was final. The court then had to make a re-assessment of liability. The contravening statements or pictures were the following: The heading on the front page stating “He is pointed out as PALME’S MURDERER” [“Han pekas ut som PALMES MÖRDARE”] together with a picture of the applicant. The text on page 6: “In addition to Long reach, Williamson and White had several companies together, some with links to the Mafia. Anthony White is one of southern Africa’s biggest poachers, tells a source. It is to a large degree his fault that the elephants in Mozambique are all but extinct. Together with Williamson, Anthony White appropriated the ivory. The District Court acquitted the editors in all respects and rejected the applicant’S claims for damages. It found the editors were not responsible for the death of the elephant. The court also found that the editors had not acted in a ‘grossly negligent way’ and that they had not been negligent in their reporting of the incident. The editors’ conduct was described as ‘unacceptable’ by the court. In 2002 the Court of Appeal upheld the District Court’s judgment. Expressen claimed that, on account of the public interest, it was justifiable to name and show a photograph of Anthony White in the newspaper. Aftonbladet, for its part, has asserted that, in the circumstances,. it wasjustifiable to describe Anthony White. The information has been liable to expose him to the contempt of others and consequently, as such, constitutes defamation. The question then is whether there are grounds for excluding liability. If the information is correct it may as a rule be communicated even if it is deprecatory, if this is justifiable with reference to the public news interest. Court of Appeal agrees with the District Court’s assessment that it was obviously legitimate to write about the so-called ‘South Africa trail’ The question is whether it was justified to identify the plaintiff by name and picture in the manner employed and to publish statements to the effect that he was supposed to be guilty of large scale, serious criminality. Information in the case reveals that Anthony White has been much better known than he has wished to admit in southern Africa and among representatives of various organisations for the protection of animals and the conservation of nature. Anthony White does not therefore appear as an ordinary private person with regard to whom there is a particular interest of protection.  Expressen and Aftonbladet asserted Anthony White’s name and picture have been published in international news media and on Swedish television. In their defence, [the responsible editors] have also pointed out that, despite time constraints, they had careful checks made which gave an unequivocal picture of Anthony White. It has been established that the main basis for the assertions in issue in the case was the statements made by [the former senior official of the South African security police] Dirk Coetzee. The fact that the information had already been published by other media shows, however, that these news services might have considered that there was a reasonable basis. The Court of Appeal finds that there was also a reasonable basis for the assertions in Aftonbladet. On 29 May 2002 the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) refused the applicant leave to appeal. The Court of appeal further considers that Aft onbladnet must be considered to have performed the checks that were called for.” The Appeal concludes that the decision to publish the picture was made on the basis of a fair and reasonable basis. The Appeal's decision was published in the newspaper Expressen on 28 May 2002. The appeal was dismissed on 30 May 2002 and the case is still pending.

The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. By a judgment of 24 February 2000, the District Court acquitted the editors in all respects and rejected the applicant's claims for damages. It found that the editors had made ‘false and misleading’ statements about Anthony White. The article was published on 30 September 1996, in a run of 12 pages. A balance has to be struck between the protection against offensive statements and the demands of freedom of speech. The Court of Appeal agrees with the District Court’s assessment that it was obviously legitimate to write about the so-called ‘South Africa trail’ The question is whether it was justified to identify the plaintiff by name and picture in the manner employed and to publish statements to the effect that he was supposed to be guilty of large scale, serious criminality. The Court of Appeal takes account of the following considerations. In defence of the publications in question, [the responsible editors] have asserted, among other things, that Anthony White’s name and picture have been published in international news media and on Swedish television. The fact that the information had already been published by other media shows, however, that these news services might have considered that there was a reasonable basis for the information. Despite time constraints, they had careful checks made which gave an unequivocal picture of Anthony White. Checks have been made with several informants in different countries and in different capacities. Each of them separately has had high ambitions to find out the degree of truth of Dirk Coetzee's statements and to check with reliable sources who the person Anthony White was. With a few exceptions, the persons contacted have not been named. Aftonbladet must be considered to have performed the checks that were called for. Expressen, the Court of appeal finds that the assertions were reasonable and that they had a basis in law’

name: Jerzy Pachnik
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 53029/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr K. Drzewicki, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1) The applicant was born in 1934 and lives in Warsaw, Poland. The applicant sustained serious head injuries in a traffic accident in 1989 and was granted a disability pension. The Warsaw Regional Court awarded the applicant non-pecuniary damages and a monthly allowance to be paid by the State Treasury. The Warsaw Court of Appeal quashed the impugned judgment in respect of the monthly allowance awarded to the applicant and remitted it to the first-instance court. It upheld the remaining part of the judgment. The proceedings inrespect of the remainder of the claim are pending before the Warsaw Regional court. The applicant applied to adduce new evidence and asked the court to speed up the proceedings. The trial court held the first hearing on 20 September 2001. The court dismissed the applicant’s claims in respect. of two other co-defendants.

The Warsaw Regional Court awarded the applicant non-pecuniary damages and a monthly allowance to be paid by the State Treasury – the Regional Directorate of State Roads. It upheld the remaining part of the judgment and the proceedings are pending. The proceedings inrespect of the remainder of the claim are pending before the Warsaw Regional court. The case was settled in 2000.

name: Peter Brannigan
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 21 February 1992. It originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (nos. 14553-14554/89) both lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 19 January 1989 by Irish citizens, Mr Peter Brannigan and Mr Patrick McBride. For reasons of convenience Mr McBride will continue to be referred to in this judgment as the applicant. The Irish Government, having been informed by the Registrar of its right to intervene in the proceedings (Article 48, sub-paragraph (b), of the Convention), did not indicate any intention of so doing. The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza for the Government, by Mr Danelius for the Commission and by Mr Weatherup for the applicants. The applicants’ memorial was filed out-of-time on 31 August 1992. On 28 October 1992 the Chamber decided, pursuant to Rule 51, to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 November 1992. There appeared before the Court:. Mrs A. Glover, Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr N. Bratze, Q.C., Mr R. Weatherup, Counsel. Mr Peter Brannigan was detained for six days, 14 hours and thirty minutes. He was interrogated on forty-three occasions and denied access to books, newspapers and writing materials as well radio and television. The Government’s observations on the applicants’ Article 50 (art. 50) claims were submitted on 17 January 1993. Mr B. Repik, who had attended the hearing and taken part in the deliberations of 26 November 1992, was unable to sit in the present case after 31 December 1992, his term of office having come to an end owing to the dissolution of the Czech and Slovak Federal Republic (Articles 38 and 65 para. 3 of the Convention) ( art. 38, art. 65-3). Mr Patrick McBride was arrested at his home by police officers on 5 January 1989 at 5.05 a.m. pursuant to section 12 (1) (b) of the 1984 Act. He was then removed to Castlereagh Interrogation Centre where he was served with a copy of the “Notice to Persons in Police Custody’. He received two visits from his solicitor on 5 and 7 January 1989 and was seen by a medical practitioner on eight occasions during police custody. Mr McBride, born in 1951, was shot dead on 4 February 1992 by a policeman who had run amok and attacked Sinn Fein Headquarters in Belfast.

name: Gerhard Lang
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28648/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been discriminated against in the exercise of his rights under Articles 4 and 9 of the convention on the ground of his religion. The application was dismissed on 9 October 2000. On 17 November 2005 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the applicant’s application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof), requesting it to repeal the wording ‘recognised religious societies’ in section 24(3) of the Military Service Act. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the applicant’s complaint for lack of prospects of success. The applicant asked the Federal Ministry for Defence to take no action until the European Court of Human Rights had decided on his application. On 26 August 2003 the applicant was informed that an instruction had been issued to the Upper Austrian Military Authority not to call him up until further notice. This decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 4 July 2003.

The Court ruled in favour of the applicant and declared the rest of his complaints inadmissible. The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights (ECHRC) in Brussels on 11 January 2000. The hearing was adjourned until 2 June 2001, when the case was returned to the applicant. The applicant was accused of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court, composed of two civilian judges, two military judges and an army officer, convicted the applicant. The court acquitted the applicant of other charges. It sentenced the applicant to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in public service and placed him under judicial guardianship. In 1995 the Court of Cassation upheld the applicant’s conviction. The case was automatically referred to the Military Court ofCassation (askeri yargıtay).

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her right to remain silent and not to incriminate herself had been breached in criminal proceedings against her. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted. The Court declared the application partly admissible in a decision of 18 March 2004. The case was decided by the Court of Appeal and the verdict was handed down on 17 July 2005. The court of appeal ordered the Austrian Government to pay the applicant a fine of 50,000 euros. The applicant was fined 1,500 Austrian schillings (ATS) with two days' imprisonment in default for failing to disclose the driver of her car. She claimed that the obligation under section 103 § 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act violated the presumption of innocence and her right not to incriminate herself. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) in 1998. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant's complaint for lack of sufficient prospects of success. The amount of the penalty did not exceed ATS 10,000 and no important legal problem was at stake. The application was dismissed by the Vorarlberg Independent Administrative Panel on 26 November 1997.

Taner Apaydın had concealed signs of torture in the medical examinations conducted on several persons between 3 February and 7 October 1994 and he was, therefore, prohibited from practising as a doctor for six months. name: Kamil Tekin Sürek
train_texts: Case was referred to the Court, as established under former Article 19 of the Convention, by the European Commission of Human Rights on 17 March 1998. It originated in an application (no.24122/94) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Commission under former. Article 25 by a Turkish national, Mr Kamil Tekin Sürek, on 9 March 1994. Mr R. Bernhardt, President of the Court at the time, subsequently authorised the applicant’s lawyer to use the Turkish language in the written procedure (former Rule 27 § 3). At a later stage, Mr L. Wildhaber, President. of the new Court, authorised theApplicant's lawyer to Use the Turkish Language in the oral proceedings (Rule 36 § 5) The case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the Court. The Grand Chamber constituted for that purpose included ex officio Mr R. Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey. On 19 November 1998 Mr Wildhaber exempted Mr Türman from sitting after his withdrawal from the case. The case was heard by a Grand Chamber which included Mr A. Pastor Ridruejo, Mr G. Bonello, Mr J. Makarczyk, Mr P. Kūris, Mrs F. Tulkens, Mrs V. Strážnická, Mr V. Butkevych and Mrs H.S. Greve. It was decided that a single Grand Chamber should be constituted to hear the instant case. The case was brought by the Turkish government against the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant was a major shareholder in a Turkish limited liability company. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 3 March 1999, the case being heard simultaneously with the case of Sürek and Özdemir v. Turkey. The Court heard addresses by Mr Tezcan and Mr Kaplan. The hearing was adjourned until the end of April 1999. The decision was delivered by the President of the European Union, who was also a member of the Commission. The Commission was represented at the oral hearing by Mr D. Šváby, who had written his written pleadings. A British delegation, including Lord Avebury and MPs Leyla Zana and Orhan Doğan, was in Şırnak village. They were trying to calm down tensions in the area, but were told off by a Gendarmerie Commander. The delegation managed to persuade the people of Tepe village, which was blockaded by the security forces, that permission had been obtained for them to get the bodies of their dead. The conversation took place between Diyarbakır Security Director Ramazan Er and Gendarme Regiment Commander İsmet Yediyıldız. The applicant was charged with revealing the identity of officials mandated to fight terrorism and thus rendering them terrorist targets. The charges were brought under section 6 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act 1991. The applicant denied the charges and advanced the following arguments in his defence. The right to receive and impart information, including information concerning acts of officials, was fundamental in a democratic society. Section 6 contravened not only the Turkish Constitution but also Article 10 of the Convention. In a judgment of 2 September 1993 the National Security Court convicted the applicant under the section of the 1991 Act. The court ruled that the applicant’s conviction was ‘unjust and disproportionate’. Orhan Doğan was sentenced to pay a fine of 54,000,000 Turkish lira. He appealed, reiterating his defence before the National Security Court. He argued that the press declaration at issue had already been reported in other newspapers and magazines and that the incriminated news report had added nothing to these. On 10 December 1993 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It upheld the cogency of the National security Court's assessment of the evidence and its reasoning for rejecting the applicant's defence. The applicant’s appeal against conviction and subsequent proceedings were dismissed. He was released on bail on 14 December 1993.

name: Prem Singh
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 8 December 1994 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) The Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (“the Government’), within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 5 para. 4 ( art. 5-4) The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. Mr Prem Singh was born in 1957 and is currently resident in Wakefield, West Yorkshire. On 19 February 1973, the applicant - then aged 15 - was convicted at Leeds Crown Court of the murder of a 72-year-old woman. He had broken into her home, strangled her, cut her throat and had sexual intercourse with her at around the time of her death. Mr Singh received a mandatory sentence of detention “during Her Majesty’s pleasure’ pursuant to section 53 (1) of the Children and Young Persons Act 1933 (as amended) (see paragraph 29 below). Its effect was to render the applicant “liable to be detained in such a place and under such conditions’. Mr Singh's licence was revoked by the Secretary of State on its recommendation. He was accused of a number of alleged offences involving deception, and one of using threatening behaviour. He denied the allegations, and asked the Parole Board to review the merits of the revocation of his licence. On 19 December 1991 the Board decided against recommending Mr Singh’s release. Mr Singh received a more detailed explanation of his recall in a letter from the chief probation officer. The reason given for his recall was not the alleged offences (which were a matter for the court), but rather his failure to provide accurate information about his circumstances to his supervising probation officers. Prem Singh was jailed in 1992 after criminal charges against him were dismissed. Mr Singh asked for his case to be reconsidered and the Secretary of State referred it back to the Parole Board. On 30 July 1992 the Board again declined to recommend Mr Singh’s release. The applicant then sought judicial review of the two decisions. The Court quashed the decision of 19 December 1991 on the ground that there had been a breach of natural justice because the Board had not disclosed to Mr Singh all the reports before it. Lord Justice Evans found that Mr Singh was entitled to a fresh consideration by theParole Board under the terms of section 39 (4) of the Criminal Justice Act 1991. Prem Singh was released from prison in 1994. He was not permitted to be present at the review and had no opportunity to give oral evidence or to question those who had made allegations against him. The Board decided not to recommend release, and gave the following reasons: “The Panel accepted that Mr Singh’s representationsanswered some matters which were of concern to hisprobation officer’“ Mr Singh applied for judicial review of this decision, but he withdrew his application on or about 7 March 1994 because he had been offered an early review of his case by the Parole Board. The Secretary of State so decided in exercise of his statutory powers (see paragraph 43 below) Prem Singh was recalled to prison ‘following serious breaches of the trust placed in [him] as a life licensee’ The Secretary of State was unable to assess accurately whether he was still a threat to the public, because he had spent the three and a quarter years since his recall in a closed prison. He considered that Mr Singh’s relationship with the probation service needed to be tested in the “more challenging environment of an open prison’ On 16 March 1995 the Divisional Court quashed the Secretary of. State's decision and ordered him to reconsider it. In September 1995 Mr Singh joined a pre-release employment scheme. His provisional date for release is 18 March 1996.

He received a mandatory sentence of detention “during Her Majesty’s pleasure’ pursuant to section 53 (1) of the Children and Young Persons Act 1933 (as amended) In October 1990, having served the punitive part of his sentence (“tariff“ - see paragraph 33 below), Mr Singh was released on licence. On 11 March 1991 the applicant was arrested and interviewed at Southme me. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 27 September 1995. The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza, Mr Fitzgerald and Mr Pannick. Mr Singh was sentenced to life in 1973 for fraud and using threatening behaviour. His life licence was revoked by the Secretary of State on its recommendation on 21 March 1991. The Parole Board considered the applicant’s case on 27 August and 19 December 1991. It decided against recommending Mr Singh's immediate release. Mr Singh was granted bail on 9 December 1991 and returned to work. He was released from prison on 2 March 1993. The case was heard by the Supreme Court and Mr Singh won his freedom on 31 January 1994. He has since lived in the UK and has worked as a consultant in the IT industry. He is the father of two children, aged seven and nine. On 2 March 1992 the criminal charges against Mr Singh (see paragraph 9 above) were dismissed because the prosecution had presented the indictment out of time. Mr Singh asked for his case to be reconsidered in the light of this development, and the Secretary of State accordingly referred it back to the Parole Board. On 30 July 1992 the Board again declined to recommend Mr Singh’s release. He was not told the reasons for this decision. Prem Singh was released from prison in 1994. He had been held since the offence at the age of 15. He was not permitted to be present at the review and had no opportunity to give oral evidence or to question those who had made allegations against him. He applied for judicial review of this decision, but he withdrew his application on or about 7 March 1994 because he had been offered an early review of his case by the Parole Board. The Secretary of State so decided in exercise of his statutory powers (see paragraph 43 below) to release Mr Singh. Mr Singh entered detailed representations and the file before the Board was disclosed to him; it contained recent reports from probation officers, from a psychologist working with Mr Singh and from the Local Review Committee. He considered that Mr Singh’s relationship with the probation service needed to be tested in the “more challenging environment of an open prison’. On 16 March 1995 the Divisional Court quashed the Secretary of. State's decision and ordered him to reconsider it. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 5 para. 4 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. Prem Singh was convicted of the murder of a 72-year-old woman in 1973. He had broken into her home, strangled her, cut her throat and had sexual intercourse with her at around the time of her death. Mr Singh received a mandatory sentence of detention “during Her Majesty’s pleasure’ pursuant to section 53 (1) of the Children and Young Persons Act 1933 (as amended) (see paragraph 29 below) In October 1990, having served the punitive part of his sentence (“tariff” - see paragraph 33 below), Mr Singh was released on licence. On 11 March 1991 the applicant was arrested and interviewed at Southme. Mr Singh's life licence was revoked by the Secretary of State on its recommendation. The Parole Board considered the applicant’s case on 27 August and 19 December 1991. The Board decided against recommending Mr Singh's immediate release. Mr Singh was also charged with fraud and using threatening behaviour. He denied the accuracy of most of these allegations, and asked theParole Board to review the merits of the revocation of his licence. Under section 62 (4) of the Criminal Justice Act 1967, the Parole board was empowered at this stage to take a binding decision for Mr Singh’ s immediate release, which it did on 12 March 1991. Prem Singh was jailed for four years in 1991 for an alleged fraud. The criminal charges against him were dismissed because the prosecution had presented the indictment out of time. Mr Singh asked for his case to be reconsidered in the light of this development. The Secretary of State referred it back to the Parole Board, under the procedure set out in section 61 (1) of the Criminal Justice Act 1967. On 30 July 1992 the Board again declined to recommend Mr Singh’s release. He was not told the reasons for this decision. The applicant then sought judicial review of the two decisions. On 20 April 1993 the Divisional Court quashed the decision of 19 December 1991 on the ground that there had been a breach of natural justice. Prem Singh was convicted of an offence at the age of 15. He was sentenced to 18 months in prison. On 18 June 1993 the Parole Board considered Mr Singh’s case. The Board decided not to recommend release. Mr Singh applied for judicial review of this decision, but he withdrew his application on or about 7 March 1994 because he had been offered an early review of his case. In June 1994 the Par parole Board reconsidered Mr Singh's case in accordance with section 35 (2) of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 (see paragraph 35 below). Mr Singh entered detailed representations and the file before the Board was disclosed to him; it contained recent reports from probation officers, from a psychologist working with Mr Singh and from the Local Review Committee. All the reports which made a specific recommendation were in favour of the applicant's release as soon as possible via a pre-release hostel. Prem Singh was recalled to prison in 1990 following serious breaches of the trust placed in him as a life licensee. The Secretary of State was unable to assess accurately whether he was still a threat to the public because he had spent the three and a quarter years since his recall in a closed prison. He considered that Mr Singh’s relationship with the probation service needed to be tested in the “more challenging environment of an open prison’. Mr Singh applied for judicial review of the Secretary of. State's decision. On 16 March 1995 the Divisional Court quashed the decision and ordered him to reconsider it. In September 1995 Mr Singh joined a pre-release employment scheme. His provisional date for release is 18 March 1996.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 27225/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were members of the executive and auditors boards of the Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association (“the Association”), a non‑governmental organisation with its headquarters in Ankara. On 13 June 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the alleged breach of the applicants' right to a fair hearing to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of. the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Association was established in November 1999. In January 2001 a payment order was served on the members of the executive and auditors boards of the Association who did not pay the fine within the statutory ten-day time-limit. In April 2001 the Ankara public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against the applicants, along with seventeen other persons. On 11 September 2001, the Ankara Magistrates' Court found the applicants and the other co-accused guilty as charged and sentenced them to an increased fine of TRL 136,890,0000 per person. In their petitions, the applicants maintained that they had been deprived of the opportunity to make defence submissions and that, therefore, they did not receive a fair trial.

name: Özgür Keskin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 12305/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Özgür Keskin, was born in 1974 and lives in İzmir. He resigned from his job to perform his military service on 19 March 2007. He relied on clause 19 of the collective bargaining agreement in force at the company (“the collective agreement”) which provided for the reinstatement of employees who had quit their jobs to perform their military service. The Labour Court held that the applicant’s discharge from the military shortly after he had been enlisted fell under the provision. The first-instance court found in favour of the City Council. It held that a rejection of the applicant’s request for reinstatement could not be regarded as the termination of his employment contract. The Court of Cassation found that clause 19 of the collective agreement was not directly applicable in the case before it. No appeal was possible against this decision. The applicant could not technically ask to be reinstated. The City Council appealed against the decision and reserved its right to submit additional observations once the reasoned judgment of the first- instance court had been served on it. This decision was served on the applicant on 22 September 2008. The appeal was not communicated to the applicant.

The case originated in an application (no. 12305/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant was born in 1974 and lives in İzmir. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. The court held that the applicant’s discharge from the military shortly after he had been enlisted fell under the provision of the collective agreement, which called for the suspension of the employment contract when an employee was conscripted for reasons other than compulsory military service. The City Council appealed against the decision and reserved its right to submit additional observations once the reasoned judgment of the first-instance court had been served on it. That appeal was not communicated to the applicant. On 21 July 2008, following an examination based on the case file, the Court of Cassation quashed the first‑instance court’s judgment and found in favour of the City Council. It held that a rejection of the applicant's request for reinstatement could not be regarded as the termination of his employment contract. No appeal was possible against this decision. The City Council argued, inter alia, that the first institution ‘interpretation of the collective agreement had been erroneous’

name: Imad Al-Khawaja
train_texts: The cases originated in two application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The first applicant alleged that his trial for indecent assault had been unfair because one of the two women who made complaints against him died before the trial and her statement to the police was read to the jury. The second applicant alleged. that his. trial for wounding with intent to do grievous bodily harm had been. unfair because the statement of one witness who feared attending trial was. read to a jury. A hearing in both cases took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 January 2008. The applicant was charged on two counts of indecent assault on two female patients while they were allegedly under hypnosis. One of the complainants, S.T., committed suicide (taken to be unrelated to the assault) before the trial but had made a statement to the police. The defence accepted that if the statement was read to the jury at trial they would be in a position to rebut it through the cross-examination of other witnesses and expose inconsistencies in their evidence. The judge allowed the evidence to be admitted at trial. The jury heard evidence from a number of different witnesses and the defence were given the opportunity to cross-examine other witnesses who had produced similar evidence. The applicant was convicted by a unanimous verdict on both counts of indecent assault. He appealed against his conviction to the Court of Appeal. The appeal centred on the pre-trial ruling to admit S.T.'s statement as evidence. It was also submitted that, in his summing up, the trial judge did not give adequate directions to the jury as to the consequential disadvantage of this evidence to the applicant. On 6 September 2005 the appeal was dismissed. The court concluded that the applicant's right to a fair trial had not been infringed. With regard to the admission in evidence of the statement of the deceased complainant, the court held that it was not necessarily incompatible with Article 6. The Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords but certified that a point of law of general public importance was involved in the decision. The court also considered that the applicant had been able to attack the accuracy of the deceased complainant's statement by exploring the inconsistencies between it and the evidence given by witnesses and experts. The applicant was charged with wounding with intent and also with attempting to pervert the course of justice by telling the police that he had seen two black men stab S. When witnesses were questioned at the scene, no-one claimed to have seen the applicant stabbed S. Two days later, however, one of the witnesses, T., made a statement to police saying he saw the applicant stabbing S. In S.'s statement to the police it is clear that he did not see who stabbed him. Prosecution argued that T. was too fearful to attend trial before the jury and that he should qualify for special measures. The trial judge heard evidence from a police officer who testified that the Iranian community was close-knit and that T.'s fear was genuine. T. himself gave evidence to the judge from behind a screen. In ruling that leave should be given for the statement to be read to the jury, the trial judge stated: “I am satisfied in those circumstances upon the criminal standard of proof that this witness is genuinely in fear’. Challenge of a statement can be caused by evidence given in rebuttal; by either the defendant, if he chooses to do so, or by any other bystander – and we know that there were some – who were on the street at that time. T.'s witness statement was read to the jury in his absence. The applicant also gave evidence. On 29 April 2005, the applicant was convicted by a majority verdict, principally of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm. The appeal judges were satisfied that if they were to refuse leave, under the CJA 2003, to have T.'s statement read at trial there would be unfairness to the prosecution. The Court of Appeal acknowledged, however, that the Crown accepted that T.’s statement was “both important and probative of a major issue in the case...and had it not been admitted the prospect of a conviction would have receded and that of an acquittal advanced” Leave to appeal on conviction was refused on 24 January 2006. Court of Appeal held that the jury was informed of all matters necessary to its decision-making process. The applicant's sentence was reduced to seven years' imprisonment. The appeal was dismissed on 25 January 2006 and the applicant was sentenced to 7 years in prison. This was not a case where the witness had absented himself, whether through fear or otherwise, or had required anonymity. The reason was death, which has a finality which brings in considerations of its own. T. himself gave evidence to the judge from behind a screen. Challenge of a statement does not always come from cross-examination. Challenge can be caused by evidence given in rebuttal; by either the defendant, if he chooses to do so, or by any other bystander – and we know that there were some – who were on the street at that time. He was later sentenced to nine years' imprisonment to be served concurrently with a term of fifteen months' imprisonment for doing an act intended to pervert the course of justice. The applicant's sentence was reduced to seven years' imprisonment. Leave to appeal on conviction was refused on 24 January 2006. name: Sławomir Małasiewicz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22072/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr K. Drzewicki, of the Ministry of the Foreign Affairs. On 17 December 2002 the Fourth Section declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was declared an invalid and was granted a disability pension by the Social Security Board. No hearings were held between 24 November 1998 and 7 September 1999. At the subsequent hearings the court heard witnesses and ordered the preparation of new expert opinions. The Częstochowa Regional Court gave judgment on 30 September 2002. The court awarded the applicant PLN 85,000 in compensation but dismissed his claim for pension. Both parties appealed against this judgment. The proceedings are pending before the Court of Appeal. The judge has decided that the application should be dismissed. The hearing will be held on 7 July 2013. The case will be heard in front of the Polish Court of Appeals. It will be the first case of its kind in Poland.

The case originated in an application (no. 22072/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Sławomir Małasiewicz. In June 1995, on his way to work, the applicant bought a bottle of sparkling mineral water. While he was opening it, the bottle exploded and its metal cap hit the applicant’s left eye. The accident, despite the subsequent surgeries and medical treatment, resulted in the applicant's loss of vision. He was declared an invalid and was granted a disability pension. Between 24 November 1998 and 7 September 1999 no hearings were held. The court heard witnesses and ordered the preparation of new expert opinions. On 30 September 2002 the Częstochowa Regional Court gave judgment. The defendant was found liable for the damage sustained by the applicant. The applicant was awarded the applicant PLN 85,000 in compensation but dismissed his claim for pension. Both parties appealed against this judgment. On 4 April 2003 the applicant was exempted from the court-fees in the appeal procedure. The proceedings are pending before the Court of Appeal. The application is still pending. The case has been referred to as the ‘Patient’s case’.

The applicant was born in 1923 and lives in Penrith. His wife died on 22 December 1994. On 22 February 2001 the Inlands Revenue informed him that he was ineligible for WBA as he was not a woman.

name: Tibet Menteş
train_texts: The case involves five Turkish nationals who claim they were not paid for work they performed. The case was submitted to the European Court of Human Rights. The court was asked to rule on the validity of their claim. The decision was made to throw out the case because it was not supported by the evidence. The judge said the case was not a case of a breach of the Human Rights Act of 1998, but rather of a violation of the European Convention on Human Rights and of the Convention on the Rights of the Family. The judges then asked the parties to return the case to the ECHR for reconsideration. The ECHR denied the request, saying that it had already been ruled in favour of the workers. Workers claimed compensation for overtime hours they had worked beyond the legal working time for the previous five years of their employment. The work schedule did not take account of weekends or public holidays as the duty‑free shops remained open twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. The applicants requested further remuneration for work done on weekends and public holidays and compensation for annual leave that they had not taken. The İzmir Labour Court decided to join each applicant’s proceedings and to seek an expert report concerning the calculation of their claims for overtime, weekend and public holiday pay and remuneralation for unused annual leave. The hours worked in excess of the regular forty-five-hour working week were counted as working time. The applicants’ employer had previously been cautioned, on 25 November 1996, by the Ministry of Labour concerning its practices on working hours. On the basis of his examination of the company’s timekeeping records, the expert calculated the number of hours worked as overtime in respect of each applicant, deducting three hours of rest per each day worked. The employer did not owe anything to the applicants for weekend and public holiday work as the remuneration for those days had been in accordance with the applicable regulations. The expert also noted that the applicants could not claim any compensation for unused annual leave as they were still working at the company and such leave was only payable at the end of a contract. The applicants worked 24 hours a week and rested for 24 hours during the summer and 24 hours in the winter. The Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance judgment on 28 October 2008 and remitted the case. The employer appealed, arguing that the presumption established in the case-law of the Court of. Cassation that a person could not work more than 14 hours in. the course of a twenty-four-hour shift should be applied to the facts of the dispute. However, as determined by the well-established case- law of the Grand Chamber of. Grand. Chamber of the. Grand Chamber, the case was dismissed on the basis of the presumption that the applicants worked for 24. hours and subsequently rested for. 24 hours. An expert report calculated the applicants’ daily working time as fourteen hours. The calculation in the new report led to no overtime being found for the weeks in which the applicants had worked three days. The applicants appealed against the decision and maintained that the fact that they had worked continuously for twenty-four hours had already been confirmed by the legal records of the Ministry of Labour. On 18 March 2010 the Court of Cassation upheld the İzmir Labour Court’s decision and awarded almost ninety percent less than the previous expert report had calculated. As a result of that interpretation, some of the claimants’ claims were dismissed entirely, while the others were awarded almost 90 percent less.

The case was brought by a group of workers who claim they were denied the right to a fair share of the proceeds of their work. They also claim that they were unfairly discriminated against. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in favour of the workers. The court ruled in favor of the employees, and the case was thrown out of court. The decision was appealed to the European Union Court of Justice, who ruled that the workers were entitled to a Fair Share of the Revenue. The Supreme Court of the Europe ruled against the workers, but the appeal is still pending. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the High Court of Appeal found that the claims made by the workers had been made in good faith. Workers claimed overtime hours they had worked beyond the legal working time for the previous five years of their employment. Their work schedule did not take account of weekends or public holidays as the duty‑free shops remained open twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. The court decided to join each applicant’s proceedings and to seek an expert report concerning the calculation of their claims for overtime, weekend and public holiday pay and remuneration for unused annual leave. The hours worked in excess of the regular forty-five-hour working week were to be paid at one and a half times the regular hourly rate. The judge ruled that the workers were entitled to overtime pay, calculated on the basis of one-and-a-half times the hourly rates. The applicants’ employer had previously been cautioned, on 25 November 1996, by the Ministry of Labour concerning its practices on working hours. On the basis of his examination of the company’s timekeeping records, the expert calculated the number of hours worked as overtime in respect of each applicant, deducting three hours of rest per each day worked. The expert determined that the employer did not owe anything to the applicants for weekend and public holiday work as the remuneration for those days had been in accordance with the applicable regulations. The applicants could not claim any compensation for unused annual leave as they were still working at the company and such leave was only payable at the end of a contract. The court asked the expert to supplement his report with findings concerning the parties’ objections. The applicants worked for 24 hours and rested for 24, then 24 hours again. The employer argued that a person could not work more than 14 hours in the course of a twenty-four-hour shift. The Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance judgment on 28 October 2008 and remitted the case on the following grounds: “It can be seen from the case file that during the summer months [the applicants] worked for24 hours and subsequently rested for 48 hours”. The case was settled in May 2008 with the applicants awarded compensation for overtime as determined in the revised expert report. The defendant employer appealed, arguing that the presumption established in the case-law should be applied to the facts of the dispute. The applicants claimed they had worked for more than 14 hours a day. The Court of Cassation ruled that a person can only work for 14 hours per day. A new expert report calculated the applicants’ daily working time as 14 hours. The new report led to no overtime being found for the weeks in which the applicants had worked three days as the working time was less than the legal limit of forty-five hours. On 28 December 2009 the İzmir Labour Court rendered a final judgment in the applicants' case, based on the expert report of 21 July 2009. The applicants appealed against the decision and maintained that the fact that they had work continuously for twenty-four hours had already been confirmed by the legal records of the Ministry of Labour.

The case was brought by a group of men and women from the town of Mersin, Turkey, who claim they were denied compensation for overtime work. The case is part of the European Convention on Human Rights, signed by more than 2,000 people. The European Commission is investigating the case and will make a decision in the next few months. The Court of Appeal will decide whether the case should go to the European Court of Human Rights or the International Court of Justice. It is not known whether or not there will be any action taken against the applicants. The court will also decide if the case has any effect on the European Union’s right to freedom of speech, which is a fundamental principle. Workers claim overtime and weekend and public holiday pay should be paid to them. The court rules in favour of the workers. The case was heard at the İzmir Labour Court in December 2004. The decision was made after an expert report was submitted to the court. The applicants claim that they were not entitled to overtime pay for work beyond the legal working time for the previous five years of their employment. The Court rules that overtime pay should not be paid based on one and a half times the regular hourly rate. The application was dismissed and the case will be heard again in May 2014. It is hoped that the decision will have a deterrent effect on employers and employees. The employer did not owe anything to the applicants for weekend and public holiday work as the remuneration for those days had been in accordance with the applicable regulations. The applicants raised no objections to the expert’s conclusion on the dismissal of their claims for pay for work at the weekend and on public holidays and for unused annual leave. The defendant employer argued that the timekeeping documents could not be relied on as they were unofficial copies. It also maintained that it had been unable to pay overtime in full owing to a lack of funds from the State. It submitted that the applicants had in any event been aware of the working arrangements and had never requested a transfer. The applicants worked for 24 hours in the course of a 24-hour shift. They were awarded overtime but the Court of Cassation quashed the decision and remitted the case. An expert revised the findings as ordered and concluded that the applicants were likely to have had a minimum of three hours for rest during a twenty-four hour shift. The applicants were awarded the amounts given in the expert’s report in respect of the unpaid overtime on 26 May 2008. The first-instance judgment was quashed on 28 October 2008 and the case was remitted. In the summer months they worked for. 24 hours and subsequently rested for 24hour; and in the winter months they. worked for 20 hours and then rested for 48 hours. However, as determined by the well-established case-law of the. Grand Chamber of the Grand. Chamber of Turkey, a person could not work more than 14 hours. An expert report calculated the applicants’ daily working time as fourteen hours, in line with the Court of Cassation’s presumption of fact. The calculation in the new report led to no overtime being found for the weeks in which the applicants had worked three days as the working time was less than the legal limit of forty-five hours. The applicants appealed against the decision and maintained that the fact that they had worked continuously for twenty-four hours had already been confirmed by the legal records of the Ministry of Labour. Although they had proven that fact, the judgment had been based on the presumption that working for more than fourteen hours a day was physically impossible.
eval_texts: The case was brought by five Turkish nationals against the Government of the Republic of Turkey. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which ruled that the case was a violation of the right to a fair trial. The ECHR ruled in favour of the applicants, and the case returned to the ECHR for further proceedings. The issue was settled in the ECHR’s favour, and no further action was taken against the applicants. The court found that the applicants had not met the conditions of their case. The decision to dismiss the case meant that the Government had not fulfilled its obligation to protect the right of the people of Turkey to afair trial. Workers at the company in question had worked overtime of 139.5 hours in months which had thirty-one calendar days and 135 hours in the remaining months. Their work schedule did not take account of weekends or public holidays as the duty‑free shops remained open twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. The hours worked in excess of the regular forty-five-hour working week were to be paid at one and a half times the regular hourly rate. An expert report noted that clause 25 (c) of the collective agreement concluded between the parties provided for an entitlement to overtime pay, calculated on the basis of one-and-a-half times the hourly rates. An expert determined that the employer did not owe anything to the applicants for weekend and public holiday work as the remuneration for those days had been in accordance with the applicable regulations. The applicants raised no objections to the expert’s conclusion on the dismissal of their claims for pay for work at the weekend and on public holidays and for unused annual leave. The defendant employer maintained that it had been unable to pay overtime in full owing to a lack of funds from the State. It submitted that the applicants had in any event been aware of the working arrangements and had never requested a transfer to another unit of the General Directorate of Monopolies. Both parties appealed to the Court of Cassation. The Court quashed the first-instance judgment on 28 October 2008 and remitted the case on the following grounds: ‘It can be seen from the case file that during the summer months [the applicants] worked for 24 hours and subsequently rested for 24Hours’. The defendant employer appealed, arguing that the presumption established in the case-law that a person could not work more than 14 hours in the course of a twenty-four-hour shift should be applied to the facts of the dispute. However, as determined by the well-established case- law of the Grand Chamber of Grand Chamber, the case was dismissed. The applicants had worked continuously for twenty-four hours. Although they had proven that fact, the judgment had been based on the presumption that working for more than fourteen hours a day was physically impossible. The applicants appealed against the decision and maintained that the fact had already been confirmed by the legal records of the Ministry of Labour. On 18 March 2010 the Court of Cassation upheld the İzmir Labour Court’s decision without responding to the applicants’ objections. The application is still pending in the Supreme Court of Justice of Turkey. The appeal is being considered by a panel of judges. The case is expected to be heard on November 22, 2010.

name: Guy Laumont
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43626/98) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant complained, in particular, that he had been held in detention arbitrarily. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 31 August 2000 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible [Note by the Registry. The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry]. On 19 January 1995 the investigating judge at the Versailles tribunal de grande instance decided to have the applicant detained pending trial. He issued a warrant of commitment for armed robbery, false imprisonment, and wounding with intent and wilful violence resulting in total unfitness for work for less than eight days. The employee admitted that he had provided the applicant with information to help him commit the armed robbery in return for the sum of FRF 10,000. He also stated that he recognised the applicant while the offence was being committed despite the mask he had been wearing and that the applicant was the robber who had been carrying the sawn-off shotgun. The judge substituted for the charge of false imprisonment with voluntary release (an intermediate offence (délit) and made a partial discharge order. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Créteil public prosecutor alleging arbitrary detention but had received no reply. The Indictment Division dismissed that application for the following reason: “It is not disputed that the judgment of 27 November 1996 was delivered within the time laid down by the last paragraph of Article 214 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.” The applicant appealed on points of law, relying on grounds of appeal based, firstly, on an infringement of Article 725 and a breach of Articles 201 and 214, and Article 5 of the Convention. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on the grounds that the judge did not lay itself open to the objections raised. The applicant was charged with armed robbery, false imprisonment and other connected lesser offences. An appeal on points of law by the applicant against that judgment was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 18 December 1997. The initial warrant of commitment remained effective, in accordance with Article 181, second paragraph, of the Code, after the transfer order was issued and so remains until a decision on indictment is taken. The applicant was tried at the Versailles Assize Court, which sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment. In a judgment delivered on the same day on the civil claims the applicant was ordered to pay the civil party FRF 50,000 in damages.

The case originated in an application (no. 43626/98) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant complained, in particular, that he had been held in detention arbitrarily. He had been kept in custody even though the order extending his detention had expired. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court. The Court declared the application partly admissible on 31 August 2000. The Government, but not the applicant, filed further written observations on the merits of the case on 27 October 2000. The applicant was charged with armed robbery, false imprisonment, and wounding with intent and wilful violence resulting in total unfitness for work for less than eight days. An employee admitted that he had provided the applicant with information to help him commit the armed robbery in return for the sum of FRF 10,000. He also stated that he recognised the applicant while the offence was being committed despite the mask he had been wearing and that the applicant was the robber who had been carrying the sawn-off shotgun. The applicant was still being held in his prison in 1997 when he made a formal demand for information (sommation interpellative) about his detention. The applicant had lodged a complaint with the Créteil public prosecutor alleging arbitrary detention. The judge’s initial warrant of commitment had ceased to have any effect on 19 January 1997. The applicant appealed on points of law, relying on grounds of appeal based, firstly, on an infringement of Article 725 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, secondly, on a breach of Articles 201 and 214 of the code of criminal procedure. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on the following grounds: “It appears from the impugned judgment and the documents on the file that [the applicant] was under investigation for offences including armed robbery.” The applicant was charged with armed robbery, false imprisonment and other connected lesser offences. An appeal on points of law by the applicant against that judgment was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 18 December 1997. On 9 and 10 June 1998 the applicant was tried at the Versailles Assize Court, which sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment. In a judgment delivered on the same day on the civil claims the applicant. was ordered to pay the civil party FRF 50,000 in damages. The initial warrant of commitment remained effective, in accordance with Article 181, second paragraph, of the Code, after the transfer order was issued and so remains until a decision on indictment is taken.
