name: Helmut Bönisch
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8658/79) lodged with the Commission on 18 June 1979 by Mr. Helmut Bönisch, a German national. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. G. Wiarda, President of the Court. Their object was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 paras. 1 and 3 (d) (art. 6-3-d) of the convention. Having assumed the office of President of the Chamber, Mr. Wiarda consulted, through the Deputy Registrar, the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for Mr. Bönisch regarding the need for a written procedure. On 17 September 1984, he directed that the Agent and the. lawyer for the applicant should each have until 15 December 1984 to file a memorial and that the. Delegate should be entitled to reply in writing within two months from the date of the transmission to. him by the Registrar of whichever of the aforesaid pleadings should last be filed. Mr. Evrigenis and Mr. García de Enterría, who were prevented from taking part in the consideration of the case, were replaced by Mr. J. Cremona and Mr R. Bernhardt, substitute judges. The hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The applicant, who is a citizen of the Federal Republic of Germany born in 1936, lives in Vienna. He runs a firm that specialises in meat smoking. He bought the production plant from the firm Krizmanich GmbH, which was thereafter called Bönisch Gmbh. The maximum quantity permissible in smoked meats of a carcinogenic substance called benzopyrene 3.4 was stated to be one part per (American) billion (“ppb’) The applicant lodged three further documents on 19 February. These led to the prosecution of the applicant before the District Criminal Court. In October 1976, two samples of smoked meat from the production of the Bönisch company were drawn up for analysis by the Market Office of the City of Vienna. The samples were described as being dangerous to health and adulterated. The Institute found a benzopyrene concentration of 2.7 and 3.0 ppb respectively and an excessive water content. This opinion by the Institute amounted to the lodging of a complaint (Anzeigegutachten) It was transmitted to the prosecuting authorities with a view to the institution of criminal proceedings. The case came before the same judge of the Regional Court who in 1976 had dealt with an earlier case against the applicant (see paragraph 9 above) In 1978 Bönisch requested the hearing of a meat and sausage expert on this point. The Regional Court refused this, on the ground that black smoking was forbidden if the water content could not be limited to the required level. On 29 June 1978, the Regional Court found the applicant guilty of offences under section 56(1, nos. 1 and 2, and section 63(1), and found him guilty. and examination of witnesses and experts for the defence under the same conditions as those for the prosecution. In addition, the applicant asked for the hearing. of several experts. The expert thereafter developed his personal opinion on the issue of the benzopyrene concentration in the sausage. Mr. Bönisch appealed. He took issue with the Director of the Institute for not having adhered to the opinion of his colleagues, and submitted that the Director was biased. He also raised objections of principle against the appointment as court expert of the very person who had reported the case to the prosecuting authorities. The Vienna Court of Appeal rejected the appeal on 19 December 1978. As to the carcinogenic effects of benzopyrene, it noted that the Regional Court had based its decision on the opinions of the Medical Faculty, which, according to settled case-law, could not be contested. Apart from that, the Regional court had extensively dealt with all relevant aspects of the case before holding that the products made by the applicant were adulterated and dangerous to health. The Court of Appeal ruled out the hearing of a counter-expert since the expert opinion obtained in the first-instance proceedings was not tainted with any defects. The second proceedings found an excessive concentration of benzopyrene (6.1 ppb) and an undeclared high water-content. The case came before the same judge who again appointed the Director of the Institute as expert pursuant to section 48 of the 1975 Act. On the same day (20 September 1979), the Regional Court found the applicant guilty of offences against sections 56 and 63 of the Convention. In reply to defence counsel’s questions, he explained the method for analysing foodstuffs used by the Institute. Mr. Bönisch appealed from this decision on grounds similar to those pleaded in the first proceedings. The Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 20 May 1980. On 28 February 1984, the Federal President, exercising his power to grant a pardon, commuted the two prison sentences imposed on the applicant to fines of 30,000 and 15,000 Schillings (see paragraphs 13 and 17 above) The 1975 Act provides that the Market Office of a city shall periodically draw samples of foodstuffs and send them for analysis to the Institute. This expert must possess special professional qualifications and have a special authorisation from the Federal Ministry of Health (sections 47 and 50) Court may only call the official who carried out the analysis or formulated the opinion. The official may be the person who drew up the report which served as the complaint prompting the criminal proceedings. Only the prosecutor and the defence counsel or the accused are entitled to put questions to witnesses and experts. Witnesses, on the contrary, do not have this possibility. The provisions of the 1975 Act, as well as certain practices followed by the courts and the Institutes, have been the subject of controversy in academic writings. The court may authorise experts to examine witnesses and the accused, but not to examine the accused themselves. If any doubts persist or if the findings of these experts “are unclear, vague, contradictory“, etc, the court may call another expert. The matter was debated in Parliament prior to the passing of the Act and subsequently in 1978 when a proposed amendment to section 48 was examined. This amendment, which was not in fact adopted, provided that both the Institute’s expert and any private expert called by the accused were to be heard only as witnesses. The receipt by Institute officials of certain bonus payments also gave rise to some discussion which subsequently provoked their discontinuance. Mr. Bönisch alleged, inter alia, that the proceedings taken against him had violated two provisions of Article 6: paragraph 1, in that they had not provided a fair trial, and paragraph 3 (d) (art. 6-3-d)

Faculty, which, according to settled case-law, could not be contested. The Institute once more found an excessive concentration of benzopyrene (6.1 ppb) and an undeclared high water-content. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4317/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was indicted on several charges of fraud while acting in an organised criminal group. The court attached importance to the serious nature of the offences with which he had been charged and the likelihood of a heavy sentence being imposed on him. The applicant's detention was extended by the Wrocław-Śródmieście District Court on 22 July 2003. It was extended again on 13 October 2003 and again on 21 January 2004. On 18 February 2004 the Court dismissed the applicant’s application for release, holding that the grounds originally given for his detention were still valid. The Court also expressed an opinion that his detention could be lifted and replaced by another preventive measure. It fixed bail at 100,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) [approx. 25,500 euros]. The case was adjourned on 14 November 2003 and 12 January 2004 the court held four hearings, two of which were adjourned. Wrocław Śródmieście District Court extended the applicant’s detention until 10 April 2004. It also stated that the detention would be lifted if the applicant put up the bail. The court found that releasing the applicant on bail would be sufficient to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, taking into account the fact that it had heard evidence from him. Between 9 March 2004 and 20 March 2006 the court held thirty‑three hearings. The applicant was released on bail on 25 March 2004. The criminal proceedings are still pending. It appears that the criminal proceedings have not yet been concluded. It is possible that the applicant may still face criminal charges.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 6684/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his trial for terrorism related offences was unfair because of the way the courts in Northern Ireland had approached the question of non-disclosure of prosecution papers to the defence. He is currently detained at HMP Maghaberry, Northern Ireland. The application was given notice of the case to the Government in March 2008. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms E. Willmott. The applicant was arraigned on 8 June 2001 and pleaded not guilty to one count of possession of firearms and ammunition with intent. The defence statement was served on his behalf on 12 June 2001. On 21 September 2001, the prosecution informed the applicant that it would apply ex parte for an order preventing disclosure. In non-jury trials in Northern Ireland, such an application is made to a judge other than the trial judge. That judge is designated by the Lord Chief Justice of Northern Ireland and is referred to as the ‘disclosure judge’ (see domestic law and practice below) The applicant opposed the ex parti hearing of the prosecution's application by the disclosure judge. The disclosure judge, in an ex tempore judgment, found that it was proper to hear the application. In Rowe and Davis v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28901/95, ECHR 2000‑II, the disclosure judge allowed the prosecution's application for non-disclosure. : “... the European Court has certainly not forbidden that procedure.” He continued: “ ... I have to consider, in the light of the defence of entrapment advanced on behalf of the accused, whether the material which is the subject of the application is such that it might be of assistance to the defence or in any way undermines any part of the prosecution case’” On 18 February 2002, the judge held an ex-parte hearing. The judge ruled that the material was not prejudicial to the defence. The prosecutor should monitor the continuing non-disclosure of potentially prejudicial material, he said. The trial judge then suggested that one way of proceeding would be to appoint special counsel who would be shown the material and remain throughout the trial. The hearing took place on 1 August 2002 to allow the parties and counsel appearing for the Attorney-General to make submissions as to whether it was appropriate either for special counsel to be appointed or for the trial judge himself to consider the undisclosed material. The case was adjourned until the end of July 2002. The judge said: “On the evidence before me I do not anticipate any circumstances which would result in the material becoming of value to the defense” Trial judge said that he considered that it was in the interests of justice that he should see the statement of reasons. He stressed that he had not himself seen the material seen by the disclosure judge. Counsel for the applicant's co-accused also suggested that the trial judge recuse himself since he had seen the statements of reasons which had not been made available to the defence. The trial judge ruled that it would not be appropriate for him to recusing himself. The matter came before the disclosureJudge on 13 September 2002. In an ex tempore judgment he ruled: “There is no further safeguard that I am aware of that would be of any assistance” The disclosure judge said there were two types of material involved. The first could not assist the applicant because it was adverse to him. The second related to police procedures, was general in nature and content, and did not relate directly to the applicant. I would not regard the case as requiring the appointment of special counsel... The present reality is that I cannot foresee any circumstance in which the undisclosed material would be of assistance to the defence. But it may be that the defence may advance a proposition or raise an issue that might by remote possibility make that so, and I think if the Crown concedes that that is the position then the Crown should make the matter known to the trial judge. Britain [GC] 16 February 2000, the disclosure judge allowed the prosecution's application for non-disclosure. : “... the European Court has certainly not forbidden that procedure. ... No procedure exists to ensure that an assessment of the possible value to the defence of such material other than by the prosecutor or at his or her request is made.” He continued: “ ... I have to consider, in the light of the defence. of entrapment advanced on behalf of the accused, whether the material. which is the subject of the application is such that it might be of assistance to the. defence or in any way undermines any part of the prosecution case’. The case originated in an application (no. 6684/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 17 March 2008 the President of the Chamber to which the case had been allocated decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was arraigned on 8 June 2001 and pleaded not guilty to one count of possession of firearms and ammunition with intent. A defence statement was served on his behalf on 12 June 2001. On 21 September 2001, the prosecution informed the applicant that it would apply ex parte for an order preventing disclosure. In non-jury trials in Northern Ireland, such an application is made to a judge other than the trial judge. That judge is designated by the Lord Chief Justice of Northern Ireland and is referred to as the “disclosure judge” (see domestic law and practice below) The applicant opposed the ex parti hearing of the prosecution's application by the disclosure judge. The disclosure judge, in an ex tempore judgment, found that it was proper to hear the application. The disclosure judge allowed the prosecution's application for non-disclosure. He outlined judgments in Rowe and Davis v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28901/95, §§6 60-62, ECHR 2000‑II. The majority took the view that it was important for the trial judge to see the material personally. No procedure exists to ensure that an assessment of the possible value to the defence of such material other than by the prosecutor or at his or her discretion. “In the case [of] a non-jury trial it is obviously undesirable that prejudicial material which is not going to be part of the evidence in the case should be seen by the judge who will be tribunal of fact” The judge ruled that the material was not of value to the defence. The trial judge then suggested that special counsel be appointed to see the material. The judge decided that it was not in the public interest to disclose the material and ordered accordingly. The hearing was adjourned until 2 August 2002. This hearing took place to allow the parties and counsel appearing for the Attorney-General to make submissions as to whether it would be appropriate to have special counsel appointed or if the judge should consider the material himself. The decision was upheld. Trial judge said that he considered that it was in the interests of justice that he should see the statement of reasons. He stressed that he had not himself seen the material seen by the disclosure judge. Counsel for the applicant's co-accused also suggested that the trial judge recuse himself since he had seen the Statement of reasons which had not been made available to the defence. The trial judge ruled that it wasn't appropriate for him to recused himself. He said that seeing a document in a non-jury trial does not of necessity mean the trial is made unfair or becomes unfair. He therefore referred the matter back to the disclosureJudge. The disclosure judge said there were two types of material involved. The first could not assist the applicant because it was adverse to him. The second related to police procedures, was general in nature and content, and did not relate directly to the applicant. I would not regard the case as requiring the appointment of special counsel. I cannot foresee any circumstance in which the undisclosed material, that is the material undisclosed to the trial judge, would be of assistance to the defence. But it may be that the defence may advance a proposition or raise an issue that might by remote possibility make that so, and I think if the Crown concedes that that's the position then the Crown should make the matter known. The trial judge rejected both applications. the defence of entrapment, further disclosure was required. The trial judge found that taking the circumstantial evidence and the inferences to be drawn from it, he was satisfied of the applicant's guilt of the two offences beyond reasonable doubt. The non-disclosed material was not considered by the Court before it gave judgment. Instead, it considered the House of Lords ruling in R. v. H and C [2004] A.C. 134 (see paragraph 32 below) and reviewed this Court's judgments in Rowe and Davis and Jasper, both cited above; Fitt v the United Kingdom [GC], no. 29777/96, ECHR 2000‑II; Edwards and Lewis v. the United UK, nos. 39647/98 and 40461/98, 22 July 2003 and Dowsett v the. United Kingdom, no. 39482/98. Court of Appeal found that the applicant's defence of entrapment was well known to the trial judge, the prosecution, and the disclosure judge. No other issue had been identified that might sound on the question of disclosure. The disclosure judge had been unable to envisage any circumstances in which the non-disclosed material could assist the defence either by enhancing the case that was being made for the applicant or by undermining or weakening the prosecution case. The Court of Appeal noted that it had been the central plank of the applicant’s defence and had been thoroughly explored not only in cross-examination of the witnesses but in extensive canvassing of the various “coincidences” relied on by the applicant. After dismissing the appeal, the Court of appeal, on December 2, 2004, ruled in favor of the applicant and dismissed the appeal. The appeal against the ruling was dismissed on December 13, 2004. The court of appeal ruled that the appeal was dismissed because it was not of a general importance. The decision was appealed against by the appellant on December 15, 2004 and was dismissed by the Appeal Court on December 19.

train_texts: The case originated in five applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were members of a motor cycle club named “Screwdrivers”, which was based in Hamar and was, at the time of the events giving rise to the proceedings described below, the “Hang-Around Club” of the Hells Angels. The Chamber decided to join the proceedings in the applications. By a decision of 11 July 2006, the Court declared the applications admissible. The Government, but not the applicants, filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1). The defendants had blown up parts of the club house in 25, Konnerud Street, of another motor cycle club, named Bandidos. A Volkswagen Transporter had been placed in the latter's courtyard, loaded with explosives that were detonated. The force of the explosion had been such that metal and rubber parts had hit and killed the driver of a passing car. The building had burned down to the ground and a neighbouring property had been severely damaged, several vehicles had been totally or largely destroyed. The total damage had amounted to at least NOK 2,000,000. The applicants were indicted (count II) under Article 161(1) and (2) for the acquisition, confection or storage of explosives, or for aiding or abetting. The High Court found it correct to assess whether there were grounds for imprisonment on the basis of law enforcement considerations pursuant to Article 172. The decision included the following reasons: “The City Court has ordered detention of [the fourth applicant] on the ground of danger of evasion, see Article 171 (1) no. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the defence counsel's first supporting letter concerned imprisonment on this ground” The defence counsel has alleged that the conviction is based on the statement of a co-defendant which is contradicted by other statements and evidence. The High Court bases its judgment, as in the Borgarting High Court's ruling of 28 June 2001 in the Orderud case (appeal case 01-02109), on the fact that the qualified requirement of suspicion stated in Article 172 has usually been fulfilled. The High Court found that the law enforcement considerations which form the basis of Article 172 are so prominent here that the accused should remain in prison also after judgment. The accused's personal and family circumstances pointed out by the defence counsel cannot be given sufficient weight in the opposite direction, and continued imprisonment cannot be said to be a disproportionate measure under Article 170A. The High Court has also considered decisions included in Rt 2000, page 371, page 1664 and page 1905. Unless it is of importance for the decision. regarding whether or not the accused is to be released, especially in relation to the consideration of proportionality, where the accused. is placed during the remand period is outside the High Court's control. The applicants all appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court procedure and the sentences. The applicants argued that they had not been afforded an impartial hearing. The issue of compensation for pecuniary damage was postponed until after the appeals had been decided. The three professional judges awarded NOK 120,000 in compensation for non-pecuniarydamage to the husband of the woman killed by the explosion. The High Court dismissed the appeal against the sentence which was dismissed by a separate decision of 5 February 2003. The appeal brought by the applicants was dismissed on 21 March 2003. All five applicants were convicted by a judgment of 24 March 2003, on counts I and III. The Supreme Court unanimously rejected both appeal grounds, on procedure and sentencing, subject to certain adjustments to the number of days to be deducted on account of provisional detention. The first voting judge, Mr Justice Støle, gave inter alia the following reasons: “(13) I will first deal with the allegation that High Court judge, Judge G., was disqualified. ... (14) From the outset, I find reason to point out that our rules of procedure for criminal cases in a High Court that sits with a jury are based on a distribution of functions. The decision regarding the question of guilt is the jury's alone. (15) Following the landmark judgment by the European Court of Human Rights on 24 May 1989 in the case Hauschildt v Denmark, there is extensive Supreme Court case law on this. The question of imprisonment was decided during the investigation and without a conviction by any court. The objection on the grounds of disqualification is not aimed at the presiding judge of the High Court, but at one of the other two professional judges who took part. The question now is whether the other professional judges in a High Court that is convened with a jury are to be regarded as disqualified under section 108 of the Administration of Courts Act due to the fact that they have previously been involved in applying Article 172 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as a basis for imprisoning one or more of the accused in the same criminal case. I find that there are insufficient grounds for regarding the otherprofessional judges as being disqualified in such a situation. Juror W. went to the police at an early stage of the investigations. She believed she had seen such a car on two occasions at the Statoil petrol station on the E-18 near Lier toll station, on Saturday 30 May and on Wednesday 4 June 1997. She gave a statement regarding this to one of the detectives on Thursday 10 July 1997. W. did not give any account of her previous statement to police. She had not heard any more from the police and was not on the list of witnesses. The question was then put to the public prosecutor, and the matter was made known to the High Court when it convened on 28 February 2003. The jury was constituted with 11 members, according to Article 355 (2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court thereafter ordered that W. be allowed to sit on the jury. The High Court finds that such special circumstances exist in this case. It bases its decision on the fact that the jury member reported to the police as a witness and told the police about her observations in close connection to the day of the explosion. The question here is whether W.'s presence as a member of the jury during the first four days of the hearing may have influenced the jury's verdict. The defence counsel have alleged to the Supreme Court that the High Court has, in its reasons for regarding the other jury members as being impartial, incorrectly treated any information from W. on the same footing as information on the case that arose outside the court room. Jury members will regularly be told by the presiding judge that, when deciding on the question of guilt, they must only place emphasis on what is stated as evidence in court. There is no corresponding barrier to the jury members discussing the case among themselves – even continuously during the court hearing. I refer to the fact that W. was at no time called as a witness in the case, by either the prosecuting authority or the defendants. The prosecutor has stated to the Supreme Court that the observations she had told to the police on 10 July 1997 – including about parts of the vehicle in question's licence number – were clarified early on as being of no importance to the further investigation. (36) The jury foreperson has explained that the situation that arose after W. had withdrawn was discussed by the jury.

The applicants complained that they did not have a fair and impartial hearing before the Borgarting High Court, whose judgment of 24 March 2003 was upheld by the Supreme Court on 25 September 2003. The building had burned down to the ground and a neighbouring property had been severely damaged, several vehicles had been totally or largely destroyed. The total damage had amounted to at least NOK 2,000,000. The first voting judge, Mr Justice Støle, gave inter alia the following reasons: “(13) I will first deal with the allegation that High Court judge, Judge G., was disqualified. ... (14) From the outset, I find reason to point out that our rules of procedure for criminal cases in a High Court that sits with a jury are based on a distribution of functions.” The presiding judge in a High Court case involving a jury has a key function. The question of imprisonment was decided during the investigation and without a conviction by any court. The objection on the grounds of disqualification is not aimed at the presiding judge of the High Court, but at one of the other two professional judges who took part in the case. It appears from what I have previously quoted from the first voting judge's vote in Rt-1996-261, that the emphasis was placed on the fact that the presiding Judge in a jury case had a key role. It is for the presidingJudge to give instructions to the jury, see Article 368 (2) Judge G. of the High Court was not disqualified. She did not give any account of her previous statement to the police. She had not heard any more from the police and was not on the list of witnesses. Her statement was read out and the parties were given the opportunity to make a statement. The High Court thereafter ordered that W. be removed from the jury. (20) ... (21) I will now deal with the allegation that the jury members were disqualified. Jury member reported to the police as a witness and told the police about her observations in close connection to the day of the explosion. Her observations are of such a nature that it can be questioned whether she is impartial in this case. After this, W. withdrew from the jury and the hearing continued with the remaining 10 jury members. Defence counsel have alleged to the Supreme Court that the High Court has incorrectly treated any information from W. on the same footing as information on the case that arose outside the court room, for example in the media. The question here is whether W.'s presence as a member of the jury during the first four days of the hearing may have influenced the jury's verdict. Jury members will regularly be told by the presiding judge that, when deciding on the question of guilt, they must only place emphasis on what is stated as evidence in court. I refer to the fact that W. was at no time called as a witness in the case, by either the prosecuting authority or the defendants. (36) The jury foreperson has explained that the situation that arose after W. had withdrawn was discussed by the jury. (37)

(14) From the outset, I find reason to point out that our rules of procedure for criminal cases in a High Court that sits with a jury are based on a distribution of functions. (15) Following the landmark judgment by the European Court of Human Rights on 24 May 1989 in the case Hauschildt v Denmark (application no. 10486/83) regarding disqualification by reason of prejudice, there is extensive Supreme Court case law on this.” The question of imprisonment was decided during the investigation and without a conviction by any court. The objection on the grounds of disqualification is not aimed at the presiding judge of the High Court, but at one of the other two professional judges who took part. The question now is whether the other professional judges in a High Court that is convened with a jury are to be regarded as disqualified under section 108 of the Administration of Courts Act due to the fact that they have previously been involved in applying Article 172 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as a basis for imprisoning one or more of the accused in the same criminal case. Juror W. contacted a policeman she knew and asked if she could sit on the jury even though she had been questioned by the police on one occasion. She did not give any account of her previous statement to the police. She had not heard any more from the police and was not on the list of witnesses. The matter was made known to the High Court when it convened on 28 February 2003. The High Court thereafter ordered that W. be removed from the jury. Judge G. of the High court was not disqualified. The High Court finds that such special circumstances exist in this case. The jury member reported to the police as a witness and told the police about her observations in close connection to the day of the explosion. Her observations are of such a nature that it can be questioned whether she is impartial. After this, W. withdrew from the jury and the hearing continued with the remaining 10 jury members. The question here is whether W.'s presence as a member of the jury during the first four days of the hearing may have influenced the jury's verdict. The defence counsel have alleged to the Supreme Court that the High Court has incorrectly treated any information from W. on the same footing as information on the case that arose outside the court room. Jury members will regularly be told by the presiding judge that, when deciding on the question of guilt, they must only place emphasis on what is stated as evidence in court. There is no corresponding barrier to the jury members discussing the case among themselves – even continuously during the court hearing. I refer to the fact that W. was at no time called as a witness in the case, by either the prosecuting authority or the defendants. The prosecutor has stated to the Supreme Court that the observations she had told to the police on 10 July 1997 – including about parts of the vehicle in question's licence number – were clarified early on as being of no importance to the further investigation. (36) The jury foreperson has explained that the situation that arose after W. had withdrawn was discussed by the jury.

A Volkswagen Transporter had been placed in the latter's courtyard, loaded with explosives that were detonated. The force of the explosion had been such that metal and rubber parts had hit and killed the driver of a passing car. train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The object of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 27 August 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides, Mr Pannick and Mr Robertson. Mrs Bowman was born in 1926 and lives in London. She is the executive director of the Society for the Protection of the Unborn Child (‘SPUC’) The Court decided on 25 October 1997 that it was not necessary to hold a further hearing following the relinquishment of jurisdiction by the Chamber (Rule 38, taken together with Rule 51 § 6). Mrs Bowman is a member of the Royal Courts of Justice and the European Court of Human Rights. Major political parties have no policies with regard to abortion and embryo experimentation. Members of Parliament are allowed to vote on proposed legislation according to their consciences. SPUC arranged to have some one and a half million leaflets distributed in constituencies throughout the United Kingdom in the period before the parliamentary elections in April 1992. 25,000 copies of a leaflet which read as follows: “We are not telling you how to vote, but it is essential for you to check on Candidates’ voting intentions on abortion and on the use of the human embryo as a guinea-pig’” The leaflet was distributed by the Society for the Protection of the Unborn. Mrs Bowman was charged with an offence under subsections 75(1) and (5) of the Representation of the People Act 1983 (“the 1983 Act”), which prohibits expenditure of more than five pounds sterling (‘GBP’) by an unauthorised person during the period before an election. The judge directed her acquittal, because the summons charging her was issued before the general election in 1993. Mrs Bowman was found not guilty of the charge at Southwark Crown Court on 27 September 1993. She was sentenced to two years’ probation, and ordered to pay a fine of £1,000. The leaflet had not been issued within one year of the alleged prohibited expenditure, in accordance with the time-limit stipulated in section 176 of the 1983 Act. The proceedings were, nonetheless, reported in the press. Mrs Bowman had been convicted of an offence under similar legislation in respect of a leaflet distributed prior to the Ilford North by-election and in 1982 she had also been convicted. On both occasions she was ordered to pay a fine and the prosecution costs. In 1979, Mrs Bowman was found guilty of a similar offence. She was also found guilty in 1982 of a charge relating to the elections for the European Parliament.

name: Ivan Hooper
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that neither he nor his legal representative were given the opportunity to address the magistrates' court prior to the imposition of a binding over order. He was later committed to prison for failure to comply with its terms. By a decision of 21 October 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on their own merits. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The applicant was “bound over” in his own recognisance of 50 pounds sterling (GBP) together with a surety of GBP 250. The precise terms of the order were found by the Divisional Court (in the later judicial review proceedings) to be unclear. The applicant was committed to custody on the same day for 28 days. On 2 June 1997 the applicant was granted leave to apply for judicial review of the decision to impose the binding over order. The application was granted on 20 January 1998. The judges agreed that the order had been procedurally irregular and granted a declaration to that effect. During the course of their judgments, the judges held that there were circumstances where failing to hear a defendant or his representative prior to the order was unlawful. Mr Justice Mance quoted headnote of case of R. v. Central Criminal Court ex parte Boulding [1984] 1 QB 813. A surety required the separate approval of the court as to his suitability. The High Court accepted that the applicant's representative was effectively presented with a “fait accompli” of a nature which she had not come across before. The magistrate did not expressly invite or give opportunity for any submissions, or indeed any discussion between the applicant and his representative, about the proposed terms of the binding over order before he imposed it. The court accepted that what happens does amount to a procedural irregularity and understands the nature of the point. Mr Justice Mance stated: “What Mr Burnett [counsel for the respondent] has submitted is that it cannot be shown that it would have made any difference if the magistrate had given to the applicant [and his counsel] an opportunity to make representations” (f) had the applicant or his representative been able to make submissions about the proposed order the magistrate might have been persuaded to impose different terms. Mr Burnett did not seek to controvert that. “It seems to me certainly not beyond the bounds of possibility, that if a proper opportunity had been given to [the applicant's counsel] to consider and address the matter”

The applicant alleged that neither he nor his legal representative were given the opportunity to address the magistrates' court prior to the imposition of a binding over order. By a decision of 21 October 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case was settled on the basis that the applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merit of the case. The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal. The applicant was “bound over” in his own recognisance of 50 pounds sterling (GBP) together with a surety of GBP 250. The precise terms of the order were found by the Divisional Court (in the later judicial review proceedings) to be unclear. The applicant was granted leave to apply for judicial review of the decision to impose the binding over order. The application was granted on 20 January 1998. The Court agreed that the binding-over order had been procedurally irregular and granted a declaration to that effect. The judge said that there was a breach of natural justice or procedural irregularity in the way in which the magistrate dealt with the matter. Mr Justice Mance quoted headnote of case of R. v. Central Criminal Court ex parte Boulding [1984] 1 QB 813. A surety required the separate approval of the court as to his suitability. Magistrates needed to take particular care lest, in effect, they imposed a binding order which amounted to an automatic sentence of imprisonment without appreciating what they were doing. A defendant ought not to be put at peril of a prison sentence in default of finding a surety unless he had first been specifically invited to address the magistrates' court upon that point. The magistrate did not expressly invite or give opportunity for any submissions, or indeed any discussion, about the proposed terms of the binding over order before he imposed it. Mr Justice Mance stated that had the applicant or his representative been able to make submissions about the proposed order the magistrate might have been persuaded to impose different terms. “I do not think that the applicant should suffer from any failure, if there was any on her part, to react as another advocate, perhaps more familiar with this area of the law and practice, might have done,” said the judge. ‘The magistrate failed, in my judgment, to give the applicant ... proper time or a proper opportunity to address the terms of the proposed bind over order, particularly so far as they involved a requirement that the. applicant produce a surety in the sum of £250’

name: Ayten Ünal Tekeli
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29865/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the refusal by the domestic courts to allow her to bear only her maiden name unjustifiably interfered with her right to protection of her private life. She also alleged that she had been discriminated against in that only married men could continue to bear their own family name after they married. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 13 January 2004. Ayten Ünal Tekeli was a trainee lawyer. She took her husband’s name pursuant to Article 153 of the Turkish Civil Code. She continued putting her maiden name in front of her legal surname. She could not use both names together on official documents. An appeal by the applicant on points of law was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 6 June 1995. On 22 November 2001 the new Civil Code was enacted. Article 187 was worded identically to the former Article 153. The applicant preferred not to make use of that possibility because, in her view, the amendment in question did not satisfy her demand, which was to use her maidenname alone as her surname.

The applicant continued to see him and to have sexual relations with him. In November 1997 the applicant entered Turkey illegally. In February 1998 the applicant went to Istanbul, from where she tried to fly to Canada via France. When the applicant arrived at the airport in Paris, the French police found her to be in possession of a forged passport. Following her arrival at Istanbul Airport at 1 a.m. on 5 February 1998 she was arrested by policemen on the ground that she had entered Turkey using a forging passport. The applicant was granted refugee status by the UNHCR on the basis that she had a well-founded fear of persecution if removed to Iran. The Ankara Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s petitions on the ground that there was no need to suspend her deportation. The court found that it was not required to suspend the deportation order since no such order had yet been made. The Supreme Administrative Court is the final instance for reviewing decisions and judgments given by administrative courts. The applicant was given a residence permit pending the outcome of her application under the European Convention on Human Rights. She was accommodated at a hotel in Istanbul until she could apply for asylum. Turkey has ratified the Geneva Convention and the 1967 Protocol thereto. Foreign nationals arriving in Turkey to seek asylum must submit their asylum application to the police within five days of their arrival. Non-European asylum-seekers who receive a positive decision may then submit their cases to the UNHCR for resettlement. An asylum-seeker whose application has been refused may now appeal within fifteen days of the refusal to the competent governorship. The appeal is to be assessed by the superior of the official who took the initial decision to refuse asylum. The five-day period in which to lodge an asylum request has now been increased to ten days. In its 1999 Annual Report, Amnesty International concluded that judicial punishments amounting to more than £100,000 per person were appropriate in Iran. The 1999 Country Reports on Human Rights Practices, released on 25 February 2000 by the US Department of State, mention, with reference to Iran, that harsh punishments are carried out. Flogging was reportedly imposed for a wide range of offences, at times in conjunction with the death penalty or a custodial sentence. An Iranian woman, the co-accused of a foreign businessman, was reportedly sentenced to 100 lashes in October 1999 after she was convicted of illicit sexual relations. In November 1999 an Iranian national was acquitted after he escaped from the pit in which he had been buried to the waist in order to be stoned to death in the town of Lahijan. He had been sentenced to death for adultery.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants complained that deportation of the first, second and fourth applicants to Kosovo or Serbia would be in violation of Articles 3 and 8. The applicants are of Roma descent and lived in the village of Kosovo Polje. Following the outbreak of war in 1999, the first applicant refused to participate in the fighting and hid from the armed forces. The other applicants were subjected to threats and beatings by Serbian military. Finally, they were driven out of their home by Albanian militia. They fled by train to Suvi Do, another village in Kosovo. The applicants had felt harassed in Kosovo because of their being Roma, but they had not been subjected to any persecution, allegedly due to their isolation. They applied for asylum and permanent residence permits on arrival. On 13 March 2008 the Migration Board (Migrationsverket) rejected their applications. The Board found that neither the general situation in Kosovo nor that in Serbia was such that it in itself constituted grounds for granting asylum. It also found that the applicants were not to be considered as refugees or as in need of any other specific protection. In regard to the applicants’ Roma ethnicity, the Board noted that the first applicant’s mother was Serb, that none of the family members spoke Romani or had any contact with other Roma. Family moved to children’s home in July 2008, when authorities decided that the parents did not have the ability to take care of their children under the existing circumstances. The applicants also submitted several medical certificates regarding the first, second and third applicants. According to the certificates, there was a risk that they might commit suicide if they were to be expelled from Sweden. The third applicant would soon be 18 years old. The Board noted that treatment for depression was offered both in Kosovo and Serbia. It further noted that the applicant's health had not improved after he had received treatment in Sweden and that his condition would probably only improve if he were in a more secure and stable environment. Migration Court of Appeal (Migrationsöverdomstolen) ruled that the applicants had been subjected to persecution in Kosovo due to their ethnicity and that this had caused their health problems. Two lay judges delivered a dissenting opinion finding that the third applicant’s health constituted a sufficient reason to grant him a residence permit. The court found that the medical certificates showed that he suffered from severe mental illness, that he was unlikely to get better in the foreseeable future and that the necessary treatment presupposed he was in a safe, secure and stable environment. The judge found that he had no right to remain in Sweden and should therefore be expelled together with the other applicants. The applicants lodged a new request for residence permits on the basis that there were impediments to the enforcement of their deportation order. They submitted new medical certificates and argued that their conditions had worsened. The Migration Board rejected the request as it found that the applicants had invoked no new circumstances of importance. The applicants requested the Court to indicate to the Swedish Government under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court a suspension of the first, second and fourth applicants’ deportation to Kosovo or Serbia. The court ruled that all of the applicants should be granted permanent residence permits. The family’s situation had to be taken as a whole. Although the third applicant had reached the age of majority, they could no longer be granted permits on account of family ties to him. On 16 June 2011, the applicants submitted new medical certificates issued by Ann-Marie Nyberg and dated June 2011. According to these, the first applicant had been feeling slightly better since the family had moved from the children’s home to an apartment in Trollhättan in December 2010. However, he still suffered from feelings of futility and despair. The second applicant had recently been feeling worse again due to her fear of a possible deportation. The third applicant had gradually been feeling better since he had been granted a residence permit. The fourth applicant had, due to his young age, was spared the traumatic experiences in Kosovo but a disruption of the family could be expected to cause him a severe trauma.

name: Stanisław Kumenda
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2369/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been unlawfully detained in a regular detention centre pending his transfer to a psychiatric hospital. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J.Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The application was given priority, in accordance with Rule 41 of the Rules of Court. The court relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offence with which he was charged and the need to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings. The applicant's detention was extended by the Wodzisław Śląski District Court on 14 May 2008. The court considered that there was a high probability that the applicant had committed the offence with which he was charged. On 18 August 2008 the court again extended the applicant's Detention. On 22 April 2009 the Court ordered the applicant to be placed in Rybnik Psychiatric Hospital. The hospital replied that owing to a strain on resources and a temporary lack of available beds it would not be possible to admit the applicant before 29 June 2009. The applicant was transferred to Rybnk Psychiatric Hospital on June 29 2009.

name: Zbigniew Radaj
train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 29537/95 and 35453/97) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applications were allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) On 14 October 1999 the Court decided to join the applications. By a decision of 21 March 2002 the Court declared the applications partly admissible. The Court ruled that the applications were admissible under Article 27 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The Polish Government was represented by their Agent, Mr Krzysztof Drzewicki of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He reiterated his complaint on 31 July 1996 in a letter to the President of the Regional Court. In reply, on 15 October 1996, he was told that Article 8 of the Convention did not prohibit censorship of correspondence of persons detained on remand. The correspondence sent to the European Commission of Human Rights fell within the scope of this provision. It was further stated that the text of the convention did not contain provisions relating to the inviolability of the correspondence to and from the European commission of Human rights. The case was eventually settled in 1997, with the judge being released on bail. The trial is still ongoing, and the judge has yet to be sentenced.

The Court ruled that the applications were admissible on the grounds of the applicant's right to a fair hearing. The decision was made by the Court’s Fourth Section. The European Commission of Human Rights said correspondence sent to it fell within the scope of Article 8 of the Convention. The President of the Regional Court said Article 8 did not prohibit censorship of correspondence of persons detained on remand. It was also permitted under Section 33 § 2 of the Rules of Detention on Remand. He reiterated his complaint on 31 July 1996 in a letter to the President of The Regional Court. In reply, on 15 October 1996, the President told him that the text of the convention did not contain provisions relating to the inviolability of the correspondence to and from the European Commission. The correspondence was also said to fall within this provision.

name: William Goodwin

The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) The President granted leave to Article 19 and Interights, two London based non-governmental human rights organisations, to submit observations on national law in the area in question in the present case. Their comments were filed on 10 March 1995. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 April 1995. Following deliberations on 27 April 1995 the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of a Grand Chamber (Rule 51 para. 1). The Grand Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr Ryssdal, President of the Court, Mr R. Bernhardt, Vice-President, and the other members of the Chamber which had relinquished jurisdiction. Mr William Goodwin, a British national, is a journalist and lives in London. On 2 November 1989 the applicant was telephoned by a person who, according to the applicant, had previously supplied him with information on the activities of various companies. The source gave him information about Tetra Ltd (“Tetra“), to the effect that the company was in the process of raising a £5 million loan and had financial problems. The information derived from a draft of Tetra’s confidential corporate plan. On 1 November 1989 there had been eight numbered copies of the most recent draft of the plan. Five had been in the possession of senior Tetra employees, one with its accountants and one with a bank. The accountants’ file had last been seen at about 3 p.m. on 1 November in a room they had been using at Tetra's premises. Tetra applied for an injunction restraining publishers of The Engineer from publishing any information derived from the corporate plan. Tetra stated that if the plan were to be made public it could result in a complete loss of confidence in the company on the part of its actual and potential creditors, its customers and in particular its suppliers. If the company went into liquidation, there would be approximately four hundred redundancies. The High Court made a further order to the effect that the. applicant represented all persons who had received the plan or information derived. from it without authority. The motion was then adjourned for the applicant to bring this order to. the attention of his source. Judge says there is strong prima facie evidence that the company has suffered aserious wrong by the theft of its confidential file. Court of Appeal rejected application by the applicant for a stay of execution of the High Court’s order, but substituted an order requiring the applicant either to disclose his notes to Tetra or to deliver them to the Court of appeal in a sealed envelope with accompanying affidavit. The applicant did not comply with this order. The judge concluded: ‘In the circumstance of this case,in which a remedy against the source is urgently needed, Ithink that disclosure is necessary in the interests ofjustice.’ Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 12 December 1989. Lord Donaldson held: “The existence of someone with access to highly confidentialinformation belonging to the plaintiffs who was prepared tobreak his obligations of confidentiality in this way was apermanent threat to the Plaintiffs’ interests.” The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal at a later date. The case was referred to the House of Lords by Mr Justice Hoffmann on 22 November 1989. Mr Hoffmann ruled that disclosure of Mr Goodwin’s notes was not “necessary in the interests of justice’ within the meaning of section 10 of the 1981 Act. A. a particular case in which disclosure is necessary in thegeneral interests of the administration of justice. A. a case where the public interest in maintaining the confidentiality of journalistic sourcesexists, but the facts of this particular case add absolutelynothing to it. No `iniquity’ has been shown. No shareholders have been kept in the dark. No publichas no legitimate interest in the business of the plaintiffs. This is in reality apiece of wholly unjustified intrusion into privacy. I am left in no doubt that, notwithstanding thegeneral need to protect journalistic sources, this is a casein which the balance comes down in favour of disclosure. Iwould dismiss the companies’ appeals. The House of Lords upheld the Court of Appeal’s decision on 4 April 1990, applying the principle expounded by Lord Reid in Norwich Pharmacal Co. v. Customs and Excise Commissioners [1974] Appeal Cases 133. Justice McCowan stated that the applicant must have been “amazingly naïve’ if it had not occurred to him that the source had been at the very least guilty of breach of confidence. Lord Bridge, in the first of the five separate speeches given in the applicant's case, underlined that in applying section 10 it was necessary to carry out a balancing exercise between the need to protect sources and the “interests of justice’ 'In the interests of justice' is not the technical sense in which section 10 is used. It is about protecting people from serious wrongs. The judge's task will always be to weigh in the scales the importance of enabling the ends ofjustice to be attained in the circumstances of the particular case. In this balancing exercise it is only if the judge is satisfied that disclosure in theinterests of justice is of such preponderating importance asto override the statutory privilege against disclosure that the threshold of necessity will be reached. Many factors will be relevant on both sides of the scale. It would be foolish to attempt to give a comprehensive guidance as to how the balancing exercise should be. The importance of protecting asource from disclosure in pursuance of the policy underlyingthe statute will also vary within a spectrum. One importantfactor will be the nature of the information obtained fromthe source. The greater the legitimate interest in theinformation which the source has given to the publisher orintended publisher, the greater the importance ofprotecting the source. If it appears that the information was obtainedillegally, this will diminish the importance. of protecting the source unless, of course, this factor is counterbalancedby a clear public interest in publication. be carriedout. I draw attention to theseconsiderations by way of illustration only and I emphasiseonce again that they are in no way intended to be read as acode ... The applicant was served with a motion seeking his committal for contempt of court. On 24 November, at a hearing in the High Court, counsel for the applicant had conceded that he had been in contempt but the motion was adjourned pending the appeal. Following the House of Lord’s dismissal of the appeal, the High court, on 10 April 1990, fined the applicant £5,000 for contempt. The applicant was also fined £3,000 by the Court of Appeal. The High Court found that the applicant should have “recognised that [the information] was both confidential and damaging’. The judge also ruled that the information was ‘of preponderating importance’ for the interests of justice.

I am loath in a judgment given in open court to give adetailed explanation of why this is a case in which, if thefull facts were known, there would, Ithink, be a significant lessening in public confidence in theadministration of justice generally’ Lord Goodwin: 'I am left in no doubt that, notwithstanding thegeneral need to protect journalistic sources, this is a case in which the balance comes down in favour of disclosure. No shareholders have been kept in the dark. Indeed the publichas no legitimate interest in the business of the plaintiffs. This is in reality apiece of wholly unjustified intrusion into privacy.’ The Court of Appeal granted the applicant leave to appeal to the House of Lords. Lord Diplock said in Secretary of State for Defence v. Guardian Newspapers Ltd [1985] Appeal Cases 339,350: `The exceptions include no reference to “the public interest“generally’ The judge’s task will always be toweigh in the scales the importance of enabling the ends ofjustice to be attained in the circumstances of the particular case. In this balancing exercise it isonly if the judge is satisfied that disclosure in theinterests of justice is of such preponderating importance asto override the statutory privilege against disclosure that the threshold of necessity will be reached. Whether the necessity of disclosure in this sense is established is certainly a question of fact rather than anissue calling for the exercise of the judge's discretion. The importance of protecting asource from disclosure in pursuance of the policy underlyingthe statute will also vary within a spectrum. The greater the legitimate interest in theinformation which the source has given to the publisher orintended publisher, the greater will be the importance ofprotecting the source. If it appears that the information was obtainedillegally, this will diminish the importance. of protecting the source unless, of course, this factor is counterbalancedby a clear public interest in publication of the information. be carriedout. I draw attention to theseconsiderations by way of illustration only and I emphasiseonce again that they are in no way intended to be read as acode ... The court also ruled that the source's complicity in the breach of confidentiality was ‘gross’ and that ‘the test of necessity for disclosure is satisfied’ The judge added that “the interest served by the publication of the information. is much diminished by the source’’

name: Nouredine Meftah
train_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants complained in particular that the procedure in the Court of Cassation was unfair and contravened Article 6 of the Convention. The Court delivered its judgments on 27 February 2001 in Mr Adoud's and Mr Bosoni's case and on 26 April 2001 in the case of Mr Meftah. The court held unanimously that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’). The judgment was delivered by Mr L. The Court heard addresses by Mr Rio, Mr Abraham and Mr Cotte, and also their replies to questions put by some of the judges. The case of Mr Bosoni was heard in the Court of Cassation. Mr Adoud was found guilty of driving at 143 k.p.h. in a 90 k.m. speed-limit zone. The most recent case is the case of Mr Adoud, who was convicted of exceeding the speed limit by at least 40 k.P.h, and banned from driving for 21 days.

name: Rémi Bertuzzi
train_texts: A French national, Mr Rémi Bertuzzi (‘the applicant’), on 10 February 1997. The applicant alleged that he had been unable to obtain legal representation under the legal-aid scheme to bring proceedings against a lawyer. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. It was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the merits of the case. The Court declared the application partly admissible on 16 April 2002. The case was taken to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. The applicant requested a fourth lawyer in late October or early November 1995. The last of the four lawyers withdrew from the case. The applicant wrote to the Minister of Justice on 14 June 1996. All he received in reply was a letter which arrived on 21 June 1996 informing him that his request had been transferred to the Director of the Civil Affairs Department. In March 1997 the applicant received a reply from the president of the bar council informing him. that the grant of legal aid dated 1 June 1995 had lapsed. Consequently, he was advised to make a fresh application if he wished to pursue his claim against Mr T. The application was rejected.

train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his pre-trial detention had exceeded a “reasonable time’ within the meaning of Article 5 § 3. The Prosecutor requested that thirty-four witnesses be heard by the trial court and the testimonies of a further one hundred and four witnesses be read out at the trial. The first hearing was scheduled on 28 December 2000. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The application was made by a Polish national named Adam Kauczor (“the applicant”) Between 2001 and 2003 the court held a hearing every two or three months. The first hearing scheduled on 5 July 2003 was adjourned due to the absence of a key witness and one of the lay judges. In 2006 the court scheduled twenty-three hearings, of which eleven did not take place. It appears that between January and October 2007 the court schedule nine hearings. The applicant’s trial commenced de novo on 21 May 2003 because the judge rapporteur had retired. On 16 September 2005 the President of the Criminal Section (przewodniczący wydziału) ordered that hearings be scheduled more often than once a month. The applicant was detained from March 2005 to December 2007. The case is currently pending before the Katowice Regional Court as the court of first instance. The applicant lodged a complaint about unreasonable length of proceedings under the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The application was dismissed on 25 October 2006. On an unspecified date that decision was upheld by the Katwice Court of Appeal. The court held that there had been no inactivity or undue delay in the proceedings. The judge decided to lift the preventive measure and to release the applicant on 11 December 2007, but the case is still pending. It was observed that until April 2003 the court had been dealing with the case speedily and there had been no periods of inactivity. It was acknowledged that the proceedings had been obstructed when the case had had to be opened de novo and a new judge rapporteur had been assigned. The applicant himself had contributed to the delay because of his multiple requests for new evidence to be admitted, according to the court. The court emphasised that from end of 2003 until the end of 2006 over fifty hearings had been scheduled. The fact that some of them were cancelled was attributable to objective factors such as the absence of a lay judge, illness of a presiding judge or absence of the applicant’s lawyer.

The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) The parties did not file observations on the merits. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the. merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The. Chamber decided that there was no need to hear the case as the application was not admissible. The applicant was required to attend an interview at Woodbourne Police Station on 26 June 1998. The purpose of the interview was to compel the applicant to disclose his defence. On 25 February 1999, the applicant was convicted of this offence in the Magistrates' Court and fined the sum of GBP 200. In July 2002, the Belfast County Court allowed the applicant's appeal against conviction, finding that the prosecution had not proved the absence of a reasonable excuse. The judge noted that the Northern Ireland Court of Appeal had dealt with a similar case (Clinton v. Bradley [2000] NI 196) which related to the same legislation and the same investigation. The applicant had not been interviewed by the police, or charged with any offence. The judge took the view that once he had been questioned and charged, the applicant had a right not to answer questions that would have tended to incriminate him. The only outstanding matter was whether the applicant should have attended the interview and then refused toanswer questions, or, as he did, refuse to attend the interview once he failed to receive the assurances he had asked for. Lord Justice Carswell, giving judgment, considered, in the light of R. v. Hertfordshire County Council, ex parte Green Environmental Industries Ltd ([2000] AC 326), that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention is directed towards the fairness of the trial itself. The appeal was upheld, and the applicant's conviction confirmed. He was asked by the office of the Director of Public Prosecutions to state a case for the Court of Appeal. But he died before having prepared the stated case. The case was to have been heard by the Supreme Court, but the case was not heard before he died. He died before he could make the case for it, which would have been the first in a decade. He was buried in a private funeral on the Isle of Wight on Friday, November 17, 2013. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation. It originated in an application (no. 11368/85) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swiss national and a Turkish national on 10 January 1985. Both sought a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings. The President of the Court gave Mr. Schönenberger leave to appear on his own behalf, while Mr. Durmaz designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Jacot-Guillarmod and Mr. Levi for the Government, Mr. Trechsel for the Commission and Mr Schönenberger, Ms. Hug and Mr Garbade for the applicants. At the hearing, the Commission, the Government and the applicants lodged with the registry various documents, either at the President’s request or on their own initiative. The first applicant, Edmund Schöonenberger, who is a Swiss citizen born in 1942, practises as a Rechtsanwalt. Mehmet Durmaz, a Turkish national born in 1950, lives at Onex, in Switzerland. He is a taxi-driver. in Zürich. He was arrested in connection with suspected offences under federal legislation relating to the misuse of drugs. His wife, who had been informed of the arrest on 16 February, spoke on the telephone to the Pfäffikon district prosecutor on 20 and 24 February. She asked him whether her husband had a lawyer. He replied that he had not but added that he would take care of it. In a second letter, which reached him on 28 February, she expressed the hope that the ‘lawyer’ - whose name she did not mention - “would look after [him]’ The district prosecutor probably received the letter and enclosure for Mr. Durmaz on Monday 27 February, but kept them from him without telling him that he had received them. The prosecutor’s office returned to Mr. Schönenberger the said documents together with the copy of the covering letter. On the same day, he asked Mr.Durmaz to choose a lawyer. The presiding judge of the Pfäffikon District Court duly appointed Mr. Garbade on 1 March. In an order made on 1 May, the prosecutor's office decided not to communicate to the suspect the letter. It did so on the following ground (translation from the German): “As long as Edmund Schöonenberger is not the suspect’d authorised legal representative, the general provisions of the Prisons Ordinance apply to him” Mr. Durmaz was freed on 23 March 1984. On 29 May 1985 the Zürich district prosecutor ordered that he had no case to answer as it could not be excluded beyond all possible doubt that someone else had been mistaken for him. In respect of his detention on remand, the prosecutor awarded him 3,000 Swiss francs (CHF) which was increased to 3,565 CHF on 30 October 1985. The appeals against the Pfäffikon district prosecutor’s order of 1 March 1984 were dismissed by the presiding judge of the Pfäffkon District Court on 11 April 1984. The Federal Court allowed the appeal in part on 20 June 1984. The Federal Court held that a suspect is under no obligation to make any statements. A person who has been charged with a criminal offence is at all times entitled to ask for a lawyer and to receive a form for giving authority to act. The measure was a disproportionate restriction on freedom of correspondence and on the rights of the defence. The Department of Justice’s decision. was contrary to the Constitution: since these documents did not relate to pending criminal proceedings, section 53(3) could not be relied on in respect of them. The Federal Court awarded the applicants costs of 500 CHF and ruled that the measure was not disproportionate. The applicants applied to the Commission on 10 January 1985 (application no. 11368/85) They claimed that the Pfäffikon district prosecutor’s stopping of the letter from Mr. Schönenberger to Mr. Durmaz had violated their right to respect for their correspondence (Article 8 of the Convention) (art. 8) and their freedom of expression (Article 10) The general principle laid down in the disputed ordinance cannot be criticised as being unconstitutional, at least not if regard is had to the fact that correspondence with the supervising authorities and defence lawyers is not subject to any marked degree of control. Commission declared the application admissible on 4 March 1986. In its report of 12 December 1986, the Commission expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a breach of Article 8 (art. 8) and that no separate issue arose under Article 10. The full text of the Commission’s opinion is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The Government confirmed the submissions contained in their written pleadings. In them they invited the Court ‘to conclude that in the present case the non-forwarding of the letter in issue addressed by the first applicant to the second applicant, who was detained on remand and did not know the sender’

train_texts: Two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Turkish nationals. The cases originated in two applications (nos. 27080/08 and 40982/08) against the Republic of Turkey. The applicants were born in 1973 and 1965, respectively, and live in Samsun and Ankara. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. The President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplications at the same time as their admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was acquitted of the offences with which he was charged in June 2002. On 22 March 2004 the Court of Cassation upheld the applicant's acquittal. On 26 April 2005 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment of the Ankara Administrative Court. The final decision was served on the applicant on 4 March 2008. The written opinions of the public prosecutor and of the judge rapporteur concerning his appeal request were not communicated to the applicant. The application was dismissed on 23 January 2008 and the appeal was dismissed again on 23 February 2008. It is not known if the applicant will be able to return to his job as a civil servant in Turkey.
