name: Samuel Betteridge
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention, in violation of Article 5 of the convention. At the time of the lodging of his application he was detained at HM Prison Whatton, Nottingham. He was originally sentenced to life imprisonment with a tariff (i.e. minimum term to be served before eligibility for release arose) of five years. Upon appeal, this was reduced to a sentence of imprisonment for public protection (“IPP” – see paragraphs 22-23 below) The case was decided on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant’s tariff expired on 18 December 2008, by which time no Parole Board review had taken place. The applicant challenged, by way of judicial review proceedings, the delay in fixing a Parole board hearing. The hearing was eventually rescheduled for September 2009. The panel was unable to provide a panel for the hearing and it did not take place in May as planned. They were not satisfied that sufficient evidence exists that your risk of sexual and/or violent offending has yet reduced to a level such that that risk can be safely managed out of closed conditions. They feared that there had been an underestimate of risk and an insufficient attention to the sadistic elements of the offences in other assessments. The High Court handed down its judgment in the judicial review proceedings on 23 June 2009. The judge outlined the background to the applicant’s claim, as follows: “4. a breach, having regard in particular to the fact that the pre-tariff advisory opinion of the Parole Board had effectively made it clear there was no chance of release upon expiry of the tariff (see paragraph 7 above)” The judge then considered the terms of theParole Board recommendation of September 2008 and considered that it followed ‘inevitably’ from it that the panel, if asked, would not conceivably have directed the applicant's release. The judge said that Article 5(4) requires a speedy hearing to determine the lawfulness of the detention. He concluded that the September 2008 advisory opinion in the applicant’s case could not address the question whether the post-tariff detention was lawful. However, any breach would not require payment of damages, because it was plain that in any case the Parole Board would not have ordered the applicant's release, he said. The judge said steps were being taken to seek further manpower to enable the Paroles Board to meet its obligations under Article 5 (4) of the European Convention on Human Rights. He said the Secretary of State and the Par parole board are working together, aware of the problems. Judge says it would be inappropriate for an individual to ‘jump the queue’ for judicial review. The applicant had originally sought a mandatory order requiring that his case be heard in September. The judge agreed with the decision not to pursue the claim for such an order. But he recorded that there was a breach, but it is a breach that will not provide, for this particular claimant, any great advantage. He decided: “In all the circumstances I do not think that it is necessary for me to make any formal declaration in the circumstances of this case. However, there is no question but that steps are now being taken by the Board in conjunction with the Ministry to ensure there is a speedy hearing.” The judge noted that the measures put in place to alleviate the problem will not have immediate effect. The delays continue and the backlog has not improved, and indeed that latter point is made clear by evidence produced by the Secretary of State and by the Parole Board. The authorities will now appreciate the need to get on top of this problem and to ensure that the hearings that are required are provided, and that the requirements of Article 5(4) are met. train_texts: The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 14 April 2008. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Jakub Wołąsiewicz, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike the application out of its list of cases, in accordance with Article 37 § 1 of the convention. The application was dismissed and the case was adjourned until a later date. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal from December 2008 to February 2009. The decision was made on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant sought a ruling that the length of the proceedings before the Otwock District Court had been excessive and an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 10,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) On 6 May 2005 the Warsaw Regional Court dismissed the applicant's complaint. It held that the proceedings had been conducted with due diligence and within a reasonable time. It limited its examination of the length‑of‑proceedings issue to the period after the entry into force of the 2004 Act. It stressed that the Act could not be applied to the protracted length of court proceedings occurring before that date. The Regional Court found that there were no delays for which the District Court could be held responsible.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35141/06) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged a breach of Article 8 in relation to the contact restrictions following the taking into public care of her three children. On 20 January 2009 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) On 1 February 2011 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and the above application was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section. On 3 May 2005 the applicant contacted BUP in a state of despair and, in response, a social emergency unit (social beredskap) went to the applicant’s home, accompanied by police and a chief physician from the adult psychiatric clinic. The authorities found the interior of the home completely destitute; there was hardly any furniture and there was no electricity or running water. On the following day, the applicant was committed to compulsory psychiatric care in accordance with the Act on Compulsory Psychiatric Care (Lagen om psykiatrisk tvångsvård, 1991:1128). The applicant claimed that she was not ill but agreed to the placement of the children in the temporary family home. A week later she was released from psychiatric care and returned to her home. The Social Council applied to the County Administrative Court for a permanent care order in respect of all three children. The council maintained that the applicant had shown a serious lack of ability to care for her children. In its view, the children’s behaviour showed that their development had already been harmed. Since the applicant did not agree to voluntary care, it was necessary to take the children into public care on a permanent basis. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) in Sundsvall. On 9 January 2006 the Administrative court of Appeal upheld the lower court's judgment in full. The children were placed in three different family homes, all within approximately 50 km of Skellefteå, as one family was not able to provide the care and support that each child needed. The applicant, through her legal counsel, requested the Social Council to allow her more time with her children as she felt that the children were being deprived of contact with her. The Social Council decided to restrict the applicant’s contact rights to all three children. This meant that each parent should meet with the children once every three months in a neutral environment where the family home parents and the social worker responsible for the file should be present. The decision was based on an investigation carried out by the Social Council, in consultation with BUP, into the children’s situation. The Social Council concluded in its investigation report that the children had a right to contact with their mother but that their best interests required that the contact be limited. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court and requested that she be granted contact rights to her children much more often than only twice a year. She could see no reason for such restricted contact and found it to be contrary to the best interests of the children as they would forget their mother. They had lived with her until May 2005 and they had had a close and warm relationship. The children should also see and get to know their father but this should not limit her contact with them. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Administrative Court of Appeal. She wanted to see her children at least once a month in order to ensure that they would not forget her. She felt that the family home parents had a negative attitude towards her and that this influenced the children. The Social Council contested the appeal. It submitted that the children were currently in the process of developing and learning things that they had not had the opportunity to learn before. It noted that the last meeting between the applicant and her children, on 23 January 2007, had passed without incident, partly because eight adults had been present to ensure the children’s well-being. The Social Council found that despite the applicant’s visits having been planned and very structured, the children had still had negative reactions before and after each meeting. The applicant appealed to the Administrative Court of Appeal, maintaining that she wanted contact rights with her children during one weekend per month, without the presence of others. The court found that with the support of the Social Council and the family homes during the meetings, these could be increased to four times per year for the applicant. In its view, this would provide the children with a good contact with their mother while not jeopardising their continued development. It noted that the limited contact had been in place for roughly two years and had contributed to the children developing positively. In February 2009 the applicant voluntarily underwent a neuropsychological examination during two days at Stavanger University Hospital, upon request by the Social Council. The council wanted to know if the applicant suffered from a disorder or mental illness and, if so, what support she would need. The examination concluded that the applicant fulfilled the criteria for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) that was mainly inattentive in nature. It recommended supplementary examinations and made a number of proposals for supportive measures, including establishing fixed structures and routines in her daily life. It concluded that it would not be in the best interest of the children to increase the applicant’s contact rights further than decided by the lower court. S. before, during and after the meetings. In 2005 the applicant contacted BUP in a state of despair and, in response, a social emergency unit (social beredskap) went to the applicant’s home, accompanied by police and a chief physician from the adult psychiatric clinic. The case originated in an application (no. 36144/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, Mr Meydin Athan, was born in 1974 and lives in Diyarbakır. In the course of a military operation, several terrorists were killed by the security forces in Bingöl. On 28 March 2006 a large group of people assembled at their funeral and protested. About 1,500 to 2,000 people resisted the police, attacking them with stones and blocking the traffic by burning tyres. The applicant was sentenced to six years and three months in prison in 2007. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court on 30 May 2011. In 2008 the public prosecutor issued a decision not to prosecute the applicant on the ground that the complainant’s statement had not been taken by the police. In the meantime, on the basis of the medical reports, the applicant filed a complaint with the Diyarbakır Public Prosecutor alleging ill-treatment by police officers. He also alleged that the doctor who had not found any new traces of ill- treatment was guilty of professional misconduct. The Siverek Assize Court rejected an appeal lodged by the applicant in 2009.

The case originated in an application (no. 36144/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1974 and lives in Diyarbakır. On 28 March 2006 a large group of people assembled at their funeral and protested against the security forces. In the course of the events about 1,500 to 2,000 people resisted the police, attacking them with stones, blocking the traffic by burning tyres and damaging nearby shops and public buildings. Many demonstrators were arrested by the police. According to the documents in the case file, the applicant was among those who were arrested on the night of 30 March 2006. No new signs of physical violence were found on the applicant. On 2 May 2006 the Diyarbakır Public Prosecutor issued an indictment charging the applicant with involvement in the activities of an illegal organisation. The applicant, along with ten other persons, was questioned by the investigating judge. He stated that the injuries had not occurred during the incidents but had been inflicted by police officers while he had been in police custody. The judge remanded the applicant in custody. In May 2007 he was convicted under Article 314 of the Criminal Code and sentenced to six years and three months’ imprisonment. On 30 May 2011 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 of the convention on account of the reasoning relied on by the Norwegian courts in refusing his compensation claim with respect to damage sustained in criminal proceedings in which he had been acquitted. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 September 2002. The Court heard addresses by Mr Krokeide (counsel for Mr O, who pleaded the common issues relevant to both his case and that of Mr Hammern), Mr Wiig and Mr Elgesem. The applicant spent three periods in pre-trial detention – respectively 7, 7 and 32 days – a total of 46 days. On the same date the charges against the six other accused persons were also reduced. The Court found the applicant not guilty of all the charges, but found him guilty of one of the charges. The court found that the allegations against the applicant were founded on the basis of false information. The jury also found that there was no evidence that the applicant had sexually abused any of the children. The applicant's trial took place before the Frostating High Court (lagmannsrett), sitting with three judges and a jury, over a period of 43 days, between 15 November 1993 and 31 January 1994. They later claimed compensation under Articles 444 to 446 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (straffeprosessloven). The local sheriff obtained a settlement of NOK 200,000 in compensation for non-pecuniary damage; the five others obtained a court order requiring the State to pay NOK200,000 to each of them. The applicant's wife obtained, in addition, NOK 140,000 for pecuniaries damage. The Appeals Selection Committee rejected the appeal. He requested the Supreme Court to quash the High Court's decision. 's decision contained assumptions of criminal liability and that, consequently, it violated Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The Compensation case must be determined on an independent basis and the rules on evidence applying in such compensation cases do not differ from those which apply to ordinary compensation claims. The Supreme Court concluded that the rules in Article 444 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not, as such, contrary to Article 6§ 2. The Appeals Selection. Committee further recalled that in the above case the Supreme. Court considered the relationship between the conditions for compensation under Article 444. and the case-law of the European Court of Human Rights, in particular the Sekanina v. Austria judgment of 25 August 1993 (Series A no. 266-A). The Appeals Selection Committee says the High Court was aware of the rules in Article 6 § 2 of the Convention, the European Court's Sekanina judgment and the 1994 decision of the Supreme Court. The Committee says it would base itself on this view in its assessment of the present case. The High Court clearly specifies that Mr Hammern is not liable under the criminal law, according to the Committee. The question is whether he is able to show that he did not carry out the acts which were referred to in the indictment, the Committee says. It adds that the decision must be formulated in the light of the conditions for compensation as mentioned above. Mr Hammern was found guilty of sexually abusing 10 children. The children themselves gave statements to their parents, during the judicial examinations and to a psychologist, about abuse by Mr Hammern. The Court has been able to apprise itself of how the children during the examinations changed their behaviour when presented with questions of sexual abuse. The High Court does not find any reason to go further into the discussion about the possibility of paedophilia. It is not only the so-called real paedophiles who commit abuse against children. Nor can a diagnosis which excludes paedophila be deemed accurate, or notional paedophili be defined precisely. The Appeals Selection Committee finds that the High Court' s reasoning does not go further than is necessary to carry out a careful examination of the compensation claim. The Committee once more emphasises that a refusal to award compensation under Article 444 does not imply that the previous acquittal is being undermined.” In the light of the foregoing, the appeal must be rejected,” the committee says. The appeal is expected to be heard at a date to be decided in the next few weeks. The case was brought by former British Airways executive David Hicks, who was sentenced to eight years in prison for fraud. Hicks was released on bail and is currently serving a five-year prison sentence. He is due to be sentenced in September.

It was possible to perpetrate such abuse without it being revealed either from a technical or practical point of view. It is not only the so-called real paedophiles who commit abuse against children. Nor can a diagnosis which excludes paedophilia be deemed accurate. The High Court does not find any reason to go further into the discussion about the possibility of paedophileilia. The children markedly changed their behaviour, inter alia, in the form of bedwetting, refusing or expressing fear about going to the kindergarten. The Appeals Selection Committee said that the High Court' s reasoning does not go further than is necessary to carry out a careful examination of the compensation claim. The Committee once more emphasises that a refusal to award compensation under Article 444 does not imply that the previous acquittal is being undermined.” In the light of the foregoing, the appeal must be rejected,” the committee said. The appeal was rejected by the Supreme Court of England and Wales, which ruled on the case earlier this month. The High Court said the decision was based on the rules of evidence applying in such cases. It said that this did not infringe on the presumption of innocence laid down in the Convention.

name: Mehdi Zana
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his conviction constituted an unjustified interference with his right to freedom of expression. He claimed that he was denied a fair hearing on account of the presence of a military judge on the bench of the Istanbul State Security Court. The complaint was declared inadmissible and the applicant retained his complaint under Article 6 of the Convention for examination on the merits. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was settled in favour of the applicant by a decision of 19 September 2000. The application was filed by a Turkish national, Mr Mehdi Zana. The applicant was charged with disseminating separatist propaganda against the indivisibility of the State on account of his speech. He was sentenced to 2 years’ imprisonment and a fine of 100,000,000 Turkish Liras (TRL) The applicant appealed against his conviction. On 16 February 1996 the court confirmed the applicant’s conviction, but reduced the sentence imposed on the applicant. The applicant learned of this decision in July 1995 while he was in prison. It finally sentenced the applicant to 1 year’‘We have taken an oath not to withdraw, even if only a single warrior remains... Kurdistan is seen on the horizon...’ On 12 January 1998 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's appeal, upholding the State Security Court’s reasoning and its assessment of the evidence. The applicant appealed against the ruling. The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court of Appeal on 12 January 1999. The appeal was dismissed on 15 January 1998. The case was settled in the Supreme court of Appeal in March 1998. As a result of the decision, the applicant was not allowed to appeal against the decision of the High Court of Appeals, which was upheld on 19 January 1998 and the appeal was thrown out on 25 January 1998, and the case was quashed.

The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his conviction constituted an unjustified interference with his right to freedom of expression. The case was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. A decision of 19 September 2000 declared the applicant’s complaint under Articles 9 and 10 of the Convention inadmissible and retained his complaint under Article 6 § 1 for examination on the merits. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merit of the case was required. The Court ruled in favour of the Government and the application was dismissed. The decision was published in full in the European Human Rights Convention (ECHR) edition of 2000. The applicant was charged with disseminating separatist propaganda against the indivisibility of the State on account of his speech. The court held that the following phrases in the applicant’s speech contravened section 8 of the 1991 Act: “... We know how to die for our cause and we do even die...” The Istanbul State Security Court considered that the incriminated speech, taken as a whole, amounted to propaganda, including violence. The applicant appealed against his conviction. On 16 February 1996 the court confirmed the applicant's conviction, but reduced the sentence imposed on the applicant. It finally sentenced the applicant to 1 year's imprisonment and a fine of 100,000,000 Turkish Liras. On 12 January 1998 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's appeal, upholding the State Security Court’s reasoning and its assessment of the evidence. The applicant. appealed. The appeal was dismissed on 11 January 1998. The case continues to be heard by the Supreme Court of the Republic of Croatia. The application was dismissed after the judge ruled that there was insufficient evidence to support it. The court dismissed the appeal on 13 January 1998 and the appeal was thrown out on 14 January 1998, with the decision to be appealed again on 15 January 1998 by the applicant. The judge ruled in favor of the applicant on 15 February 1998, and the case was dismissed.

name: Velimir Janosevic
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated as the Tax Authority's decisions on taxes and tax surcharges had been enforced prior to a court determination of the dispute. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 September 2000. The Court heard addresses by Mr Thörnhammar and Ms Kalmerborn. By a decision of 26 September2000, following the hearing, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Tax Authority increased the applicant's liability to income tax by 286,859 Swedish kronor (SEK) The additional taxes levied on the applicant, including interest and surcharges, totalled SEK 1,020,300, of which SEK 161,261 were surcharges. As he risked being declared bankrupt before his tax liability had been determined by the courts, he also requested a stay of execution in respect of the amounts assessed. The amounts relating to value-added tax and employer's contributions were payable on 5 January 1996 and those relating to incometax on 10 April 1996. The Tax Authority considers that the prerequisites laid down in section 49, subsection 1(2) or (3), of the Tax Collection Act [Uppbördslagen, 1953:272] have been fulfilled. Tax Authority: 'The applicant's ability to pay is open to serious doubt' County Administrative Court: 'Only a banker's guarantee will be accepted as security' Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) refused leave to appeal against appellate court's decisions. Both claims rested on the contention that it would be unreasonable and amount to a violation of Article 6 of the Convention for enforcement proceedings to be instituted against the applicant without a court having first determined whether he had any liability to pay the amounts involved. The applicant, who did not furnish security, lodged a notice of appeal. In May 1997 the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten), in Stockholm refused him leave to Appeal against the County Administrative. Court's judgments. In November 1998, the Supreme Administrative court refused to hear his appeal. Tax liability as of 22 March 1996 amounted to SEK 653,144, including penalties for late payment (dröjsmålsavgifter) that had accrued since the final date on which payment could have been made. That amount included SEK 89,323, plus 6% in penalties for early payment, in tax surcharges. The only property owned by the applicant was some vehicles, but of insufficient value to cover the debt. The applicant's appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 18 June 1996. Leave to appeal against the appellate court's decision was refused by the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) on 18 September 1996. The whole debt became statute-barred on 31 December 2001, at the end of the fifth year following the day it became due. On 30 October 1997 the applicant was sentenced by the District Court to ten months' imprisonment for tax fraud (skattebedrägeri) and a bookkeeping offence (bokföringsbrott) The judgment was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 16 November 1998. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 4 March 1999. Further proceedings concerning the taxes and tax surcharges concerning the applicant were automatically referred to the County Administrative Court for determination. By a letter of 5 September 2001 the applicant requested an oral hearing at which it was proposed that certain witnesses would give evidence. Later, asked by the County. Administrative Court to clarify his request, the applicant stated that an Oral hearing was not required on the issue of the assessment of the tax. surcharges. The County Administrative Court upheld the Tax Authority's decisions of 22 and 27 December 1995 and rejected the applicant's request for an oral hearing. Administrative Court informed the applicant that it did not find a hearing necessary and ordered him to make his final observations in the case in writing. The applicant has appealed to the Administrative Court of Appeal, where the dispute is at present pending. The Court considered that there had been sufficient reasons to impose the surcharges in question and that no legal basis for remitting them had been shown. It dismissed the applicant’s argument that the allegedly excessive length of the proceedings constituted by itself a reason to remit the tax surcharges.

name: Ewa Glesmann
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by a lawyer practising in Berlin. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. Both parents declared their consent to the child’s temporary placement in a foster family. This measure was originally planned for a short period of time during which a court-appointed expert was to prepare his opinion on custody rights. The Government contested the applicant's submissions, which are contested by the Government. The District Court ordered the preparation of an expert opinion on the questions of parental authority and access rights. On 9 February 1998 the expert E. submitted her expert opinion. She considered that the child S. suffered from a serious emotional disorder which had been caused by family tensions and that S. should be offered psychotherapy in order to overcome her traumata. On 29 October 1998, during the hearing on the parents' divorce, both parents’ counsels unanimously declared that they presently did not lodge any motions regarding parental authority. On 10 February 1999 the applicant filed a motion with the Pankow-Weissensee District Court with the aim to be granted regular access rights to her daughter. She declared that she did not wish to have the child’s placement with the foster family terminated. On 9 September 1999 the District Court ordered the parents to pay the costs of the child's care. On 29 June 2000 the court ordered that the child be returned to his mother. On 3 August 2000 the child was returned to her mother. The child was taken to hospital. On 5 September 2000 the boy was released from hospital. The boy was taken back to his parents. On 2 October 2000 the parents were ordered to pay back the full cost of the care for the child. The children were returned to their mother on 9 September 2000. The court ruled that the parents must pay back all the money they had spent on the child’s care. The case was settled out of court. S. was sent to live with her mother in a foster home. She has been in the home for four years. In 2001 she asked to be returned to the care of her mother. The mother and father agreed to let the child stay with them. But the decision was later overturned and the child was sent back to the foster care home. The child is now being cared for by her mother, who is in the same foster home as the child. The case is being heard by the court again, but no decision has yet been made. It is unclear if the child will ever return to the home where she was raised as a child. On 5 March 2002 the applicant requested that a court decision be given immediately. On 9 February 2002 the child’s curator informed the court that she would need another six weeks to prepare her submissions. On 28 June 2002 the court requested the Youth Office to report on the child's present life circumstances and on the discontinuation of therapy. On 6 January 2003 the District Court proposed that the parents should abstain from making use of access rights for one year and that contact should be carefully re-established afterwards. The applicant rejected this proposal and submitted that recent visiting contacts between herself and her daughter had developed in a more positive way. On 24 April 2003 the Pankow-Weissensee District Court, following a hearing attended by the applicant, ruled that the child should remain with the foster family. District Court was unable to accept the child’s wishes and her present life circumstances within the foster family. It would be potentially harmful for the child's well-being to remove her from there. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Berlin Court of Appeal (Kammergericht) She emphasised the measures taken by the District Court were disproportionate and that the placement was devised as a temporary measure. On 12 January 2004 the Court of appeal held a hearing in the presence of S., her curator ad litem, her parents, two representatives of the Youth Office and the foster parents, withdrew parental authority from the parents and transferred it to the Youth office. Furthermore, visiting contacts between the child and her parents were suspended for one year. Court of Appeal quashed the District Court’s decision, transferred sole parental authority to the child's father and granted the applicant visiting rights once per month for five and a half hours each. The Court of Appeal conceded that the alienation between the applicant and her daughter had to a substantial degree been caused by the period of time which had elapsed since her placement in the foster family. The proceedings could and should have been conducted in a considerably more stringent way. However, the decision had to be taken in accordance with the child�s welfare, which was not defined by earlier shortcomings of the proceedings. The child was free to visit her mother at any other time if she wished. The applicant was ordered to contribute to the costs incurred by the accommodation of her daughter in the foster family from 25 June 1997 until 31 December 1998. She lodged a complaint against the Court of Appeal’s decision, in which she alleged that the impugned decision was disproportionate and violated her right to the enjoyment of her family life under Article 6 of the Basic Law. The Federal Constitutional Court, sitting as a panel of three judges, refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint for adjudication without giving any further reasons. The case was settled out of court in July 2005. The appeal was dismissed by the Berlin-Brandenburg Administrative Court in September 2005.

Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by a lawyer practising in Berlin. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. Both parents declared their consent to the child’s temporary placement in a foster family in 1997. This measure was originally planned for a short period of time during which a court-appointed expert was to prepare his opinion on custody rights. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The child suffered from a serious emotional disorder caused by family tensions. The decision on custody and access rights should be suspended until the child had stabilised. Both parents’ counsels unanimously declared that they presently did not lodge any motions regarding parental authority. The divorce was decreed on that same day. The applicant filed a motion with the Pankow-Weissensee District Court with the aim to be granted regular access rights to her daughter. It was proposed to instigate contacts between the child and her parents under psychotherapeutic or pedagogical guidance. In the course of the discussion the Child and Youth Psychiatric Service convinced the expert that S. was not in need of psychotherapy. On 9 September 1999 the District Court ordered that the child be returned to his parents. The child’s relationship with his parents was broken when he was not returned. On 24 October 1999 the child was returned to the parents. On 9 February 2000 the court ruled that the father should pay part of the costs of the child's care. On 6 March 2000 the father was ordered to pay the rest of the cost. On 22 September 2000 the judge ruled that he should pay the full cost of the care for the child. On 3 April 2000 the Court ruled that no further action should be taken against the father. On 23 October 2000, the Court agreed that the boy could return to his mother. The case was settled out of court and the child returned home. S. was placed in the care of her father and step-mother in January 2001. Her mother asked the court to allow the child to stay with her. In July 2001 the child was moved back to her parents' care. She was told that she would be allowed to visit her mother once a month. In September 2001 she was allowed to see her mother for the first time since her birth. She then returned to her step-father and stepmother. The child was placed with a foster family until she was old enough to leave the home. The foster family was then allowed to return to the home to live with her mother and stepfather. The child’s curator reported that S. wished to live with the foster family and was seriously opposed to contacts with her parents. She had discontinued psychotherapy on 5 March 2002 as a continuation of her efforts would be harmful for the child. Under the present circumstances, the parents had to cope with the fact that it was in the child's best interest to remain with the Foster. However, it was essential for both the parents and the child that visiting contact were not discontinued completely. The applicant rejected this proposal and submitted that recent visiting contacts between herself and her daughter had developed in a more positive way. On 24 April 2003 the Pankow-Weissensee District Court, following a hearing attended by the judge, ruled that contact should be carefully re-established afterwards. The child’s placement in the foster family had been devised as a temporary measure and considered the measures taken by the District Court to be disproportionate. The child's curator ad litem lodged an appeal with the Berlin Court of Appeal (Kammergericht) The District Court considered that the applicant was unable to accept that a parent-child relationship had developed between the child and her foster parents. It would be potentially harmful for the child's well-being to remove her from there, as requested by the applicant. It followed that parental authority had to be withdrawn from both parents and transferred to the Youth Office. Furthermore, visiting contacts between the girl and her parents were suspended for one year. The Court of Appeal quashed the District Court’s decision. It transferred sole parental authority to the child's father and granted the applicant visiting rights once per month for five and a half hours each. The child found a sense of security and stability in the foster family, where she had been living for six and aHalf years. The decision had to be taken in accordance with the child’'s welfare, which was not defined by earlier shortcomings of the proceedings. The court noted that the prerequisites of section 1666 of the Civil Code had not been met. It also stated that the child was free to visit her mother at any other time if she wanted. The applicant was ordered to contribute to the costs incurred by the accommodation of her daughter in the foster family from 25 June 1997 until 31 December 1998. On 1 March 2004 the applicant lodged a complaint against the Court of Appeal’s decision. She alleged that the impugned decision was disproportionate and violated her right to the enjoyment of her family life under Article 6 of the Basic Law. On 12 October 2004 the Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint for adjudication. On 19 September 2005 the Berlin-Brandenburg Administrative court of Appeal refused to grant the applicant leave to appeal. If the applicant wishes to appeal, she can do so.

The case originated in an application (no. 25706/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr T. Kochanowski, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The German Government (the Government) were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. On 19 June 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The Polish Government, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings (Article 36 § 1 and Rule 44), did not indicate that they wished to exercise that right. The applicant was not informed about the foster parents’ place of residence for almost two years and was thus prevented from exercising access rights. On 9 February 1998 the expert E. submitted her expert opinion. She considered that the child S. suffered from a serious emotional disorder which had been caused by family tensions and that S. should be offered psychotherapy in order to overcome her traumata. The decision on custody and access rights should be suspended until the child had stabilised. The applicant consented to the child’s remaining with the foster family for the duration of the necessary psychotherapy, which she estimated at one year. On 29 October 1998, during the hearing on the parents' divorce, both parents” counsels declared that they presently did not lodge any motions regarding parental authority. The child was taken from her parents in August 1999. The child was supposed to be returned to her parents by the end of the month. But the child was not returned to the parents until October 2000. The parents were ordered to pay for the child's care until the child is old enough to return to the care of her parents. The father was then told he had to pay the rest of the costs himself. The boy's mother was told she would not have to pay again until after the child had left the care home. The family agreed to let the father pay the remaining costs of the child’s care. The mother and the child were reunited on October 30, 2000. The child was to be returned to her parents after a month. The child’s father and mother were unhappy with the arrangement. The court ruled that the child should stay with her parents for at least another month. After this, the child was allowed to go back to the foster family. The mother and father were allowed to return to the child for a month at a time. They were then allowed to leave the child at the care of the foster parents. The parents were not allowed to see the child again until after the month was up. The decision to return the child to her family was made by the court on 15 January 2001. On 5 March 2002 the applicant requested that a court decision be given immediately. On 9 February 2002 the child’s curator informed the court that she would need another six weeks to prepare her submissions. On 28 June 2002 the court requested the Youth Office to report on the child's present life circumstances and on the discontinuation of therapy. On 6 January 2003 the Pankow-Weissensee District Court proposed that the parents should abstain from making use of access rights for one year and that contact should be carefully re-established afterwards. The applicant rejected this proposal and submitted that recent visiting contacts between herself and her daughter had developed in a more positive way. The District Court considered that the applicant was unable to accept the child’s wishes and her present life circumstances within the foster family. It followed that parental authority had to be withdrawn from both parents and transferred to the Youth Office. On 8 August 2003 the applicant lodged an appeal with the Berlin Court of Appeal (Kammergericht) and considered the measures taken by the District Court to be disproportionate. On 12 January 2004 the Court of appeal held a hearing in the presence of S., her curator ad litem, her parents, her curator and two representatives of the Youth office and the foster parents. The applicant withdrew parental authority from the parents, transferred it to the youth office and suspended visiting contacts between the child and her parents. The Court of Appeal quashed the District Court’s decision, transferred sole parental authority to the child's father and granted the applicant visiting rights once per month for five and a half hours each. All parties heard in the proceedings had confirmed that the child found a sense of security and stability in the foster family, where she had been living for six and ahalf years. The child had consistently expressed the wish to live with the fosterFamily as a full family member. The Court of appeal conceded that the alienation between the applicant and her daughter had to a substantial degree been caused by the period of time which had elapsed since her placement. The applicant was ordered to contribute to the costs incurred by the accommodation of her daughter in the foster family from 25 June 1997 until 31 December 1998. She lodged a complaint against the Court of Appeal’s decision, in which she gave a full account of the proceedings before the civil courts and alleged that the impugned decision was disproportionate and violated her right to the enjoyment of her family life under Article 6 of the Basic Law. On 12 October 2004 the Federal Constitutional Court, sitting as a panel of three judges, refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint for adjudication. If the applicant wishes to appeal, she can do so.

name: Gisèle Augusto
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 71665/01) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was lodged by a French national, Ms Gisèle Augusto (“the applicant”), on 31 August 2000. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Lyon-Caen, a lawyer practising in Paris. The French Government were represented by their Agent, Mr R. Abraham, then by his successor, Ms E. Belliard, Director of Legal Affairs. The applicant lodged a notice of appeal on points of law on 27 May 1998. In further pleadings her lawyer filed with the Court of Cassation on 23 October 1998, she invoked, inter alia, a violation of ‘the requirements of the rights of the defence’ and of “equality of arms in a fair trial within the meaning of Article 6” of the Convention. The accredited doctor of the national tribunal for claims relating to disability and level of insurance coverage for accidents at work observes the following: ‘On 1 June 1996 the subject was in a fit state to carry on working without seriously jeopardising her health and did not suffer from a permanent incapacity to work of at least 50%’ The Employment and Welfare Division of the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal in the following terms: “... on the one hand, the accredited doctor instructed, under the terms of Article R. 143‑28 of the Social Security Code then in force, to carry out a preliminary review of the case.” “Without laying itself open to the objection raised in the ground of appeal, the national disability tribunal, in the light of the findings of its accredited doctor and having analysed the different evidence adduced, considered, as it was within its exclusive jurisdiction to do, that Ms Augusto's disability rate was less than 50%.” For these reasons, the appeal ... is dismissed.

The case originated in an application (no. 71665/01) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1936 and lives in Vouziers. By a decision of 17 May 1996 the occupational counselling and redeployment board (“the COTOREP”) gave the applicant a 50 to 79% disability rating and issued her with a card certifying that she found it difficult to remain in a standing position. On 18 November 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant lodged a notice of appeal on points of law on 27 May 1998. In further pleadings her lawyer filed with the Court of Cassation on 23 October 1998, she invoked, inter alia, a violation of ‘the requirements of the rights of the defence’ and of “ equality of arms in a fair trial within the meaning of Article 6” of the Convention. The accredited doctor of the national tribunal for claims relating to disability and level of insurance coverage for accidents at work observes the following: ‘On 1 June 1996 the subject was in a fit state to carry on working without seriously jeopardising her health and, considering her physical and mental fitness for work, did not suffer from a permanent incapacity to work' The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's appeal in the following terms. Ms Augusto’s disability rate – the COTOREP evaluation of which was not binding on it – was less than 50% and that the applicant was therefore not entitled to a retirement pension on the ground of incapacity to work. For these reasons, the appeal ... is dismissed.’ The appeal was dismissed by the Employment and Welfare Division of the Court ofCassation on 2 March 2000. The appeal is dismissed on the grounds that the tribunal had acted within its exclusive jurisdiction to do so. The Appeal is dismissed and the appeal is decided.

name: Adnan Levent Çamlar
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28226/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr Adnan Levent Çamlar (“the applicant”), was arrested in London on suspicion of trafficking of illegal drugs in 1997. The Crown Court acquitted the applicant of all charges and ordered his release in 1998. On 24 June 2013 the complaints under Article 6. 1 and 3(d) of the. Convention concerning the independence and impartiality of the İzmir State Security. Court and the applicant’s inability to examine or have examined witnesses were communicated to the. Government. The application was declared inadmissible. The applicant was accused of being involved in the trafficking of illegal drugs in Turkey. His case was heard by the İzmir State Security Court. He was acquitted by the Crown Court in December 1998. In March 2003 the applicant submitted his written defence to the court and requested his acquittal. The applicant was released pending trial in October 2003. The application was dropped in November 2004. The case has been referred to as Turkey’s ‘drug scandal’ by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR). The case against the applicant was dropped on November 14, 2009. It was reopened on November 30, 2009, and the case is still ongoing. The court has not ruled on whether the applicant should be acquitted or convicted. The applicant was convicted of smuggling illegal drugs in March 2003. He appealed the conviction, claiming the evidence was insufficient to prove his involvement. The Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance court's judgment in 2006. In July 2008 the applicant was sentenced to twenty years and ten months in prison and a fine. The applicant appealed again in 2009 and the higher court upheld the judgment. The case was decided on the basis of the same principles as that of the British court, but with a minor procedural correction. It was decided that the offence at issue concerned the exportation of illegal drugs and accordingly the case differed from that concluded in the United Kingdom.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 4 August 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Cangı, a lawyer practising in İzmir. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. On 24 June 2013 the complaints under Article 6. 1 and 3(d) were communicated to the Government and the. remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The application was filed by a Turkish national, Mr Adnan Levent Çamlar, who was born in 1965 and lives in London. The applicant was charged with the trafficking of illegal drugs in Turkey. The case was adjourned until after the applicant’s acquittal in 2003. The applicant denied his involvement in the alleged offence. He requested to have certain witnesses, including his counsel in the United Kingdom, heard. The court rejected that request, finding that the statements of the witnesses called by the applicant would not contribute to the case in view of the information already available concerning the proceedings in the U.K. The judge sitting on the İzmir State Security Court hearing the case was replaced by a civilian judge on 15 July 1999. On 20 September 1999 the applicant went back to Turkey; he was placed in detention on remand the following day. The applicant was found guilty of exporting illegal drugs in March 2003. He appealed against his conviction on the basis of evidence which according to a British court was insufficient to prove his involvement in the alleged acts. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the İzmir State Security Court on 4 March 2004. In June 2005, the applicant requested the reassessment of his case and the application of the more favourable clauses in the new Code. On 3 July 2008 the applicant was sentenced to twenty years and ten months of imprisonment and a fine. The higher court upheld the judge's decision with a minor procedural correction. The high court dismissed the applicant’s remaining grounds for appeal.

name: Norman Scarth
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 4 December 1998. It originated in an application (no. 33745/96) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under former Article 25. The applicant requested permission to present his own case. The Government conceded that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention in the circumstances of the case. On 1 June 1999 the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case and the Government agreed to waive the right to the presence of an ad hoc judge. The case was heard by the Grand Chamber on 14 January 1999. The case was referred for hearing by way of arbitration under Order 19, rule 7, of the County Court Rules. Mr Scarth made an application for the main hearing to be in public and for evidence to be given on oath. This application was heard on 3 January 1995 and refused. The reasons for the refusal were not recorded formally, but in a note of 21 July 1997 prepared in the context of the Convention proceedings, District Judge Elliott made the following comments: “At this stage I can only say that it is likely that I took the view that the [applicant's] reasons as set out in his application were not in my view good Reasons for the private nature of arbitration proceedings to be dispensed with” Mr Scarth applied to appeal against the decision, alleging a lack of public hearing, misconduct by the judge and an overall unfairness of the proceedings. Mr Scarth was heard in open court and leave was refused on 9 November 1995. Lord Justice Morritt noted that the ‘European Convention on Human Rights is not part of our law in the way the European Community law is’. He further found that the judge could not be said to have been guilty of any misconduct. He refused the application on 9 May 1995 and made a costs order against Mr. Scarth. These costs were subsequently assessed at GBP 1,032.76. Under the Civil Procedure Rules, which came into force on 26 April 1999, hearings, including those in small claims cases, are to be held in public. There is a discretion for the court to hold a hearing in private where: (a) publicity would defeat the object of the hearing; (b) it involves matters relating to national security; (c) it involved confidential information (including information relating to personal financial matters) and publicity would damage that confidentiality. (d) a private hearing is necessary to protect the interests of any child or person suffering from mental incapacity; (e) it is a hearing of an application made without notice and it would be unjust to the respondent for there to be a public hearing.

name: Ali Erdem

name: Havva Kaba
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1236/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were born in 1978, 2001 and 1997 respectively and live in Istanbul. The first applicant is the wife and the second and third applicants are the children of Mr Yusuf Kaba, who was an officer in the Turkish Navy and died of cancer in 2003. According to the applicants, Mr Kaba's exposure to asbestos at Hasköy Dock had caused his cancer. They were also concerned about allegedly inadequate treatment he received at the GATA military hospital. In January 2004 the applicants again requested legal aid to pay the court fees. The Military Supreme Administrative Court refused to grant the applicants legal aid, once again without giving reasons. The court also decided to discontinue the compensation proceedings because the applicants had not paid the necessary court Fees. This decision was served on the applicants on 4 June 2004. The applicants' lawyer referred to the relevant statements of means provided by the domestic authorities. He further stated that while lodging the case he had submitted the relevant medical records concerning Mr Yusuf Kaba, a report on the asbestos levels at Hasköy Dock and an expert report, and that this evidence should be sufficient to prove that they had a well-founded case.

name: Janusz Niećko
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3500/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was charged, inter alia, with acting in and leading an organised armed criminal group, ordering murder, extortion and supplying drugs. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Court’s decision to rule in favour of the applicant was based on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences with which he had been charged. The trial court held about 59 hearings. On 3 December 2004 the Lublin Regional Court delivered a judgment. It convicted the applicant of most of the charges and acquitted him of one charge (ordering murder). It sentenced him to seven years' imprisonment and a fine. He remained in detention pending appeal. On 4 October 2005 the Court of Appeal upheld the Regional Court's judgment for the most part. It remitted the case only in respect of the one charge of which the applicant had been acquitted. The applicant filed a number of applications for release on health grounds. However, the courts refused all those applications. He also unsuccessfully appealed against decisions prolonging his detention on remand.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the administrative courts had failed to hold an oral hearing in proceedings relating to his request for life annuity. The Swedish Government were represented by their Agent, Ms G. Isaksson, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 2 February 2011. The applicant’s legal counsel appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Södermanland, claiming that the applicant had a right to a life annuity since his illnesses had been work-related. At times he had had up to three different jobs, each one of which had been hectic and thereby created a difficult and very stressful situation. He produced a medical opinion by Dr. C-G.E., dated 5 February 2003, which stated that known risk factors for arteriosclerosis and heart attack were, among other factors, diabetes, smoking and high blood pressure. The case originated in an application (no. 35605/97) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The Chamber decided, by six votes to one, that the finding of a violation constituted sufficient just satisfaction for the non-pecuniary damage sustained by the applicant. Third-party comments were received from Liberty, a non-governmental organisation based in London. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 7 November 2001 (Rule 59 § 2) The Court heard addresses by Lord Goldsmith and Mr Greenwood, and also their replies to questions from individual members. The composition of the Grand Chamber was determined according to the provisions of Article 27 §§ 2 and 3 of the convention and Rule 24. The applicant and the other executive directors of London Clubs Limited (“LCL”) resigned with effect from 30 April 1992. London Clubs would apply for new licences via reconstituted operating companies. If successful, LCL would surrender its existing licences, avoiding the necessity for the applications for cancellation or renewal to be heard. The Gaming Board issued LCL with certificates of consent, which LCL was statutorily obliged to obtain from the Gaming Board as a prerequisite to making an application to the Licensing Magistrates. Objections to the issuing of new licences were made by a rival casino owner, but these objections were rejected. New licences were granted in October 1992, after a three day hearing before the Lic licensing magistrates. Lady Littler's speech at the British Casino Association luncheon referred to London Clubs in 1992. LCL's legal advisers entered into correspondence with Gaming Board's solicitors, on the basis that the speech was defamatory. The Gaming Board was considering whether the applicant was a fit and proper person to hold the Board's certificate of approval. The applicant did not accept this explanation, but did not institute defamation proceedings. The Gaming Board informed the applicant formally that it was “minded to revoke” the applicant's section 19 certificates and that the applicant would be given the opportunity to state his case against revocation either in writing or orally at an interview before the Gaming Board (“a section 19 hearing”). The applicant's principal objection was based on the fact that the. Gaming Board had already publicly expressed the view (at the hearing before the Licensing Magistrates) that. the. applicant was not a fit to remain an executive director of London Clubs. The first judgment dealt with the applicant's appeal. The decision was challenged on the grounds that the Panel was biased, or had the appearance of bias, and that its findings were vitiated by errors of law and were irrational. The application was dismissed after the first judgment was delivered. Mr Justice Jowitt described the test of bias under English law in the following terms (pp. 93-96 of the judgment): “[Counsel for the applicant] submits that the decision to revoke the applicant's section 19 certificates of approval should be quashed because the Panel was biased. The grounds on which leave to move for judicial review were granted asserted firstly that the Board could not and did not approach its decision with objectivity and impartiality. Secondly, it was asserted that whether or not there was actual bias the applicant reasonably believed there was. Third, the judge said he was not concerned to review findings of fact, as for an appeal, but rather to assess whether the findings of the Panel disclosed illegality, irrationality or procedural impropriety. The court must reach its own factual conclusion is this: is there a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias? By “real” is meant not without substance. A real danger clearly involves more than a minimal risk, less than a probability. A decision-maker may have unfairly regarded with disfavour one party's case either consciously or unconsciously. The court is not concerned strictly with the appearance of bias but rather with establishing the possibility that there was actual although unconscious bias. The applicants expressly disavow any suggestion of actual bias. Where, as here, the applicants explicitly disavowed any suggestion, the court must necessarily be asking itself whether there is areal danger that the decision-makers was unconsciously biased. It is not necessary for the court to reach a conclusion on the facts. Mr Justice Jowitt stated further that if, contrary to his finding, there was unconscious bias on the part of the Panel, the “doctrine of necessity” fell to be considered. He said: “When a body is charged by statute with the power or duty, which cannot be delegated, to make a decision a question of bias arises.” The decision will not be liable to be impugned on account of bias provided that: (i) if only some of those. charged with thePower or Duty to decide are potentially affected by bias such of them as can lawfully withdraw from the decision-making do so. The applicant had failed to establish that the Panel's decision was irrational or unreasonable or to make out any sufficient ground for judicial review. Lord Justice Morritt (with whom Lord Justice Hobhouse agreed) held that there was a real risk that the decision of the tribunal had been actuated by bias even though they were not in fact biased against him. The decision for the Board was, at the end of the day, whether or not Mr Kingsley was a fit and proper person. "It seems to me that there is no arguable point, susceptible on this part of the case, which would justify giving leave to appeal," he said. "There would be no meaningful independent panel and the decision would stand because the decision has to be made by the Board and could not be delegated to the independent tribunal," he added. "The decision would be that there was no need to appeal and that the board had the right to make the decision, and that this was the only way to resolve the matter" "There was no reason to think there was a need for an independent panel," the judge said. 'There would have been no reason at all to think that the Board would not have made the right decision to appeal the decision'

name: Michael Becker
train_texts: The case originated in an application against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, in particular, that in the proceedings for the withdrawing of his driving licence he did not have a hearing before the Administrative Court. Two different sets of proceedings were initiated against the applicant. On 28 September 2009 the application was communicated to the Government. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Europe, Integration and Foreign Affairs. The case was decided on 22 April 2008. The applicant appealed and argued that the DAA should have obtained the report of a technical expert on the functioning of the breathlyser. On 19 December 2005 the Lower Austria Regional Governor (Landeshauptmann) dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Administrative Court and requested an oral hearing. The Regional Governor concluded that refusing to undergo a breathalyser test was as serious as driving under the influence of alcohol because it prevented the authorities from verifying whether a person was actually drunk. The additional measure imposed on the applicant was therefore justified in order to improve his attitude. In such circumstances a request for obtaining a report by a technical Expert amounted to an inadmissible request for evidence (Erkundungsbeweis). The DAA issued a penal order (Straferkenntnis) and imposed a fine for refusal to take the breathalyser test. The applicant appealed. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s request for a hearing as it found that an oral hearing was not likely to contribute to the clarification of the case. The fine imposed by the DAA had expired ipso iure. The Lower Austria Independent Administrative Panel found that, since no decision had been taken within the prescribed time limit of 15 months after the lodging of the appeal, the fine had expired. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the applicant, and the fine was paid.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented by Ms A. Stock, Mr M. Muller, Mr Tim Otty and Mr K. Yıldız of the Kurdish Human Rights Project (London) The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicants’ right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicants were taken into police custody on 5 February 1997 and the first applicant on 6 February 1997. They were accused of disseminating propaganda in support of an armed, illegal organisation, namely the Hezbollah. The Ankara State Security Court found the applicants guilty as charged, sentenced them to three years and nine months’ imprisonment and debarred them from public service for three years. On 21 September 1998 the Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the Ankara State security Court. The applicants have since been released from prison. The cases were brought to light by the Turkish public prosecutor’s office on 13 February 1997, and by the investigating judge attached to the Ankara state security court on 13 March 1997.

name: Paul Quinn
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36887/97) against Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that section 52 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 constituted a violation of the rights guaranteed by Articles 6, 10 and 13 of the Convention. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) and the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The judge elected in respect of Ireland withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28) and was appointed by the Government to sit in his place. Police were escorting a post office van carrying significant sums of money on its way to Adare village, Co. Limerick. When the two vehicles arrived at the post office in Adare, the police car was rammed from behind by a stolen vehicle and immediately surrounded by five heavily armed and masked individuals dressed in paramilitary style uniforms. One of the five opened fire at point blank range on the police officers and one of those officers died instantly and the other was seriously wounded. The police suspected a local unit of the Irish Republican Army (an unlawful paramilitary organisation known as the IRA) and the IRA later claimed responsibility for the murder. It was also suspected by the police that, on the night prior to the attack, the stolen vehicle together with all firearms and ammunition used in the attempted robbery had been stored in a safe house in Patrickswell. Many of the questions put to the applicant related to the attack in Adare and to his alleged membership of the IRA. On several occasions during those interviews he was also requested to account for his movements during certain periods of time on 6 and 7 June 1996. In being so requested, he was informed by the questioning police officers that a failure to provide this information would constitute an offence under section 52 of the 1939 Act for which the potential penalty was six months’ imprisonment. The applicant was also informed, on certain occasions only, that the initial caution given to him did not apply. On 17 January 1997 he was charged on three counts of refusing to give an account of his movements. He was convicted on the second charge (a section 52 request made on 21 July 1996) and was sentenced to six months' imprisonment.

name: Karin Andersson
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29878/09) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been denied effective access to court in relation to decisions taken on the construction of a railway, in violation of their rights under Articles 6 and 8. The application was communicated to the Government on 21 May 2012. The case was decided in favor of the applicants on 6 June 2013. The decision was handed down on 9 June 2014 and the case is now being heard by the European Court of Human rights. The proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. The Government stated, inter alia, that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment. The property owners claimed that the decision contradicted Swedish law as well as applicable European Union law, including the Habitats Directive. On 12 June 2003 the Government, after having heard the application and allowed the construction of the railway in the proposed “corridor” under the condition that the NRA adopt a railway plan before 1 July 2009 and also a specific plan for the realisation of the necessary environmental compensation measures. The NRA applied to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. The Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005, considering itself bound by the Government’s decision of 12 June 2003 on the permissibility of the railway project, the court decided to grant all the permits requested by the NRA. On 15 June 2006 the Environmental Court of Appeal (Miljööverdomstolen) in Stockholm quashed the judgments and referred the cases back to the latter instance. 12 applicants appealed to the Government against the railway plan. Supreme Court refused leave to appeal and the Environmental Court of Appeal’s judgment became final. All applicants except Mr Osterman appealed against the part which concerned the permit to construct the bridges. Supreme Administrative Court, after having held a hearing in the case, rejected the petition, finding that the railroad plan was in line with the EU Habitats Directive. Proceedings on adoption of railway plan were held in June 2005 in Gothenburg and were presented to the public on 21 June 2005. The court considered itself bound by the Government's decision as to the permissibility of the railway project and limited its examination to the environmental compensation measures. The Government had not been obliged to review its decision of 12 June 2003 on the permissibility of the railway project and the designation of the ‘corridor’ in which the railway could be located. These issues could not be examined in the third stage of the decision process. The court, in the instant case, should have examined all the objections presented by the appellants, including the claim that there were better alternative locations for the railway. According to the dissenting judge, a full judicial review had also been foreseen by the court in its earlier decision. One judge dissented, considering that the Supreme Administrative Court’s judgment contravened its decision on 1 December 2004. It appears that at least ten of the applicants have received some form of compensation as a consequence of the railway construction. In one case, the change to noise-reducing windows was partly paid by the NRA. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values. It is not clear whether the other applicants requested compensation. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in favour of the building of a rail link between London and the North of England. The High Court ruled in favor of the construction of a railway link between the North and the South of England between 2008 and 2012.
