The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been denied effective access to court in relation to decisions taken on the construction of a railway, in violation of their rights under Articles 6 and 8. The application was communicated to the Government on 21 May 2012. The case was heard by a three-judge panel on 2 September 2013. The jury decided in favour of the applicants, and the case was adjourned until the next hearing on 6 October 2013. The proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. The Government stated, inter alia, that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment. The property owners claimed that the decision contradicted Swedish law as well as applicable European Union law, including the Habitats Directive. A number of individual property owners, including three of the applicants in the present case, petitioned the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) for a judicial review of the case and requested that the Government’s decision be quashed. The Court of Appeal ruled against the Government's decision. NRA applied to County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. They also applied to Environmental Court (miljödomstolen) in Umeå for permits to build two bridges. Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the petitions for a judicial review because it was not possible to determine who should be considered an interested party at that stage of the railway planning. Environmental Court of Appeal quashed the Environmental Court’s judgments and referred the cases back to the latter instance. The appellate court found that the decision had not contained a detailed examination of measures necessary to compensate for environmental harm caused by the railway project. In 2005 the NRA adopted a railway plan for the area in question. Twelve applicants – all but Ms Holmström, Mr Härestål and Mr Höjer – appealed to the Government against the railway plan. They essentially complained of the specific stretch of the railway, invoking, inter alia, nuisance such as noise and vibrations affecting the enjoyment of their property. The Supreme Administrative Court, after having held a hearing in the case, rejected the petition, finding that the railroad plan was in line with the EU Habitats Directive. On 9 May 2008 the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) refused leave to appeal and the Environmental Court of Appeal’s judgment became final. The court considered that the question of permissibility of a railway project was within the power of the Government. The Government’s decision was binding for the subsequent proceedings in that courts and other decision-making bodies could not examine issues that had been determined by that decision. In the third stage of the decision process – the adoption of the railway plan – it was for the authorities and courts to decide only on the precise location. One judge dissented, considering that the Supreme Administrative Court's judgment contravened its decision of 1 December 2004. According to the dissenting judge, a full judicial review had also been foreseen by the court in its earlier decision. At least ten of the applicants (including seven with houses or land situated outside the “corridor’) have received some form of compensation. In one case, the change to noise-reducing windows was partly paid by the NRA. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values. It is not clear whether the other applicants requested compensation. The case was heard at the High Court in Dublin on Wednesday. The hearing was adjourned until October 26, when the case will be heard again at the Court of Appeal in Dublin.

name: Simeon Szypusz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8400/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had not had a fair trial as there were insufficient guarantees to exclude legitimate doubt regarding the independence and impartiality of the tribunal which tried him on criminal charges. The Crown case was that D.G. had been summoned to the scene by the applicant and another co-accused, M.H., using a mobile telephone belonging to M.h. The claimant, Simeon Szypusz, is currently detained in HMP Lowdham Grange, Nottingham. Crown case was that six relevant calls were made from M.H.'s mobile telephone to D.G. or one of his associates. An important part of the Crown case involved video recordings from closed circuit television (CCTV) cameras near the scene. A compilation of the CCTV footage was shown a number of times during the trial. It was played on specialist digital equipment, which was more sophisticated than an ordinary video recorder. The machine was operated by a detective constable, Officer M, who had been specially instructed how to use it. Officer M was a member of the investigating team of police officers which had conducted the inquiry into the applicant's case. He was, formally speaking, a witness in the case. The judge told the jury that should they wish to view the recordings again, they only had to ask. The jury subsequently retired. On the second day of their deliberations, they indicated their wish to start reviewing the video evidence in the afternoon. Counsel were advised of the jury's request and the court convened with junior counsel for the applicant among those attending. The only issue that arises as a result of the CCTV request is who exactly is present in court when they view the material. It is a matter that we have discussed between counsel, and of course, subject to your Lordship's view, I think the general view is that if they are able to watch it on their own, it would be much more constructive. The judge instructed the jury to return and directed them as follows: “We are going to leave [Officer M] in this court with you, and he will play any part of the video that you have seen, and will play it as you think fit. Remember that there is more than one camera that operates – that sometimes you are viewing camera no. 1, and I think at other times camera No. 2. name: İbrahim Güler
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1942/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, Mr İbrahim Güler, is a Turkish national who was born in 1973 and is currently serving a prison service in Diyarbakır. The applicant was represented by Ms A. Pamukçu Yördem, a lawyer. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. The application was communicated to the Government on 29 September 2010. The applicant was charged with attempting to undermine the constitutional order of the State. State Security Courts were abolished on 16 June 2004 by Law no. 5190. The case was accordingly transferred to the Diyarbakır Assize Court. On 31 March 2005 the first-instance court convicted the applicant as charged. On 11 December 2006 the Court of Cassation quashed the conviction. On 9 November 2007 he was again convicted as charged and sentenced to life imprisonment. On 21 January 2009 the court upheld the conviction and sentenced him to life in prison. The applicant denies all the accusations against him. He was released from prison in November 2013.

name: Anthony M. Tyrer

The purpose of the Commission’s request is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 3 (art. 3) of the Convention. EVANS, Legal Advisers’ Branch, Home Office. Anthony Tyrer was sentenced to three strokes of the birch in 1972. He appealed against the sentence to the High Court of Justice of the Isle of Man. The appeal was heard and dismissed on the afternoon of 28 April 1972; the court considered that an unprovoked assault occasioning actual bodily harm was always very serious and that there were no reasons for interfering with the sentence. The applicant was made to take down his trousers and underpants and bend over a table; he was held by two policemen whilst a third administered the punishment. The birching raised, but did not cut, the applicant’s skin and he was sore for about a week and a half afterwards. The applicant was sentenced pursuant to section 56 (1) of the Petty Sessions and Summary Jurisdiction Act 1927 (as amended by section 8 of the Summary Juridiction Act 1960) The expressions “child“ and “young person’ mean, respectively, an individual of or over the age of 10 and under 14 and an individuals of or under 14. The sentence was governed by the following provisions: “(a) the instrument used shall, in the case of a child, be a cane, and in any other case shall be a birch rod; (b) the court in its sentence shall specify the number of strokes to be inflicted; and (c) the whipping shall be inflicted privately as soon as practicable after sentence. The whipping shall be inflicted on the posterior over the child’s ordinary cloth trousers. A medical practitioner shall be present during a birching and may at his discretion order the stopping of the punishment at any time. A report of the facts shall be forwarded immediately to His Excellency. The Isle of Man is not a part of the United Kingdom but a dependency of the Crown with its own government, legislature and courts and its own administrative, fiscal and legal systems. The Crown is ultimately responsible for the good government of the Island and acts in this respect through the Privy Council on the recommendation of Ministers of the UK Government. Judicial corporal punishment of adults and juveniles was abolished in England, Wales and Scotland in 1948 and in Northern Ireland in 1968. The punishment remained in existence in the Isle of Man. The name and address of a juvenile sentenced in the Isle of Man, whether to corporal punishment or otherwise, are not published. The average number of crimes of violence to the person per annum was: between 1966 and 1968 - 35; between 1969 and 1971 - 52; between 1972 and 1974 - 59; and between 1975 and 1977 - 56. In the three years 1975 to 1977, only one young male was convicted of a crime of violence. At the 1976 census, the Island’s population stood at 60,496. The applicant also claimed damages as well as repeal of the legislation concerned. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40072/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was filed by an Austrian national, Helmut Kucera, on 5 August 1997. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complains that he had not been able to attend the oral hearing on his appeal against sentence before the Vienna Court of Appeal. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible on 20 March 2001. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section on 1 November 2001. On 5 September 1993 he raped E.P., had beaten and strangled her, had forced her to swallow drugs, had burned her skin with cigarettes and had cut her vagina with a knife causing a deep laceration as well as opening the abdominal cavity. On 12 April 1994 the Court of Assizes convicted the applicant of both offences of aggravated rape and sentenced him to 14 years’ imprisonment. In assessing the penalty, the court considered as mitigating circumstances the applicant’s partial confession and that he had acted under the influence of alcohol and drugs. As aggravating circumstances it considered the applicant's criminal record, the fact he had committed two rapes and his extreme brutality when committing the offences. The applicant did not request to attend the hearings before the Supreme Court or the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) The Supreme Court, sitting in private, rejected as inadmissible the applicant’s plea of nullity on 8 October 1996. On 4 December 1996, the Vienna court fixed the hearing date for the applicant's appeal against the sentence for 18 December 1996. The applicant received a notification which stated that he, being detained, could only appear through his counsel and would not be brought to the court as the conditions of Section 296 § 3 [Section 294 § 5] of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozeßordnung) were not fulfilled.

The application was filed by an Austrian national, Helmut Kucera (“the applicant”), on 5 August 1997. The applicant was born in 1957 and is presently detained at the Krems Stein prison. The Vienna Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against the applicant charging him with two counts of rape under aggravated circumstances, i.e. having caused serious injuries. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant raped E.P., beat and strangled her, forced her to swallow drugs, burned her skin with cigarettes and cut her vagina with a knife. He was sentenced to 14 years’ imprisonment. In assessing the penalty, the court considered as mitigating circumstances the applicant’s partial confession and that he had acted under the influence of alcohol and drugs. As aggravating circumstances, it considered the applicant's criminal record, the fact he had committed two rapes and his extreme brutality when committing the offences. In his appeal against sentence the applicant submitted that the Court of Assizes had failed to give sufficient weight to the requested witnesses from Poland. The applicant did not request to attend the hearings before the Supreme Court or the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) The Supreme Court, sitting in private, rejected as inadmissible the applicant’s plea of nullity. The applicant received a notification which stated that he, being detained, could only appear through his counsel and would not be brought to the court as the conditions of Section 296 § 3 [Section 294 § 5] of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozeßordnung) were not fulfilled. On 18 December 1996, after having held a hearing in the absence of the applicant but in the presence of his defence counsel, dismissed the appeal against the sentence.

name: Asim Sahin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30943/96) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the German court decisions dismissing his request for a right of access to his child, born out of wedlock, amounted to a breach of his right to respect for his family life. He relied on Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention. On 11 October 2001 the Chamber delivered its judgment in which it held, by five votes to two, that there had been a violation of Article 8 of the convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the ECHR. The Government argued that the Chamber should not have found violations of Article 8 and 14 of the Convention. The Grand Chamber decided that there had been a violation of Article 14. It also held, by five votes to two, that the respondent State was to pay the applicant 50,000 (fifty thousand German marks) in respect of non-pecuniary damage. The separate opinion of Mr Pellonpää joined by Mrs Vajić was annexed to the judgment. The applicant is the father of G., born out of wedlock on 29 June 1988. He acknowledged paternity of the unborn child and undertook to pay maintenance. Father applied to the Wiesbaden District Court for a decision granting him a right of access to his daughter. The court, referring to Article 1711 of the Civil Code, observed that the mother, as the person having custody, determined the father's right to the child. The Court found as follows: “The Court is convinced that the petitioner's wish for [G.] to visit him is motivated by attachment to his child and genuine affection for her. It nonetheless takes the view that personal contact with her father is not in the child's best interests, since her mother dislikes her father so deeply and opposes all contact so fiercely” The applicant appealed to the Wiesbaden Regional Court. The Regional Court ordered a psychological expert opinion on the question whether contact with the applicant was in G.'s interests. On 17 December 1992 the applicant requested the Regional Court to progress with the proceedings. He also applied for a provisional order granting him a right of access to G. during one afternoon every week and prohibiting her mother from obstructing such contact. The expert reached the conclusion that a right. of access without prior conversations to overcome the conflicts between the. parents was not in the child's interests. The judge found that G. had repressed the memories of her father and that hearing the. child in court would place a strain on her. The father of a child born out of wedlock was denied access to his child. The father and the child's mother entered into an agreement to have parental therapy. The Wiesbaden Regional Court dismissed the father's appeal in August 1993. After the Federal Constitutional Court's decisions of 1971 and 1981, the constitutionality of Article 1711 can no longer be seriously doubted, he says. He argues that the legal conditions for granting access to the father are different from those for parents who do not have custody. The main reason for the weaker legal position of the father is his different social position, he writes. He says the father should be able to satisfy himself as to the child’s welfare and development. Court is bound by Article 1711. Under that provision, the guardianship court decides to grant a father access to a child born out of wedlock if this is beneficial for the child's welfare. It is in fact important for children not simply to have a fantasy picture of their fathers, but to be able to form a personal, realistic picture. If the father were granted access to [G.] in present circumstances, she would have to shuttle between hostile camps, which should not be asked of her. If – as in this case – there is a danger that differences between parents may affect a child, then special circumstances are needed. The Regional Court finally considered that exceptionally it had not been required to hear the child, since questioning her about her relationship with her father would have placed a psychological strain on her. In finding that therapy had not enabled the parents to put their former conflicts behind them, the Court did not have to decide who was to blame for this ... The decisive factor is always the child's point of view. of all this, the report finds that she does not suffer as a result of the present situation. The Court can rely fully on the report, which has no apparent defects and is not invalidated by the fact that the father sees the situation differently.”

The case originated in an application (no. 30943/96) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) by a German national of Turkish origin. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the German court decisions dismissing his request for a right of access to his child, born out of wedlock, amounted to a breach of his right to respect for his family life. He relied on Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention. On 11 October 2001 the Chamber delivered its judgment in which it held, by five votes to two, that there had been a violation of Article 8 of the convention. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the ECHR in 2002. The Grand Chamber ruled that there had been a violation of Article 14 of the Convention taken in conjunction with Article 8. It also ruled that the respondent State was to pay the applicant 50,000 (fifty thousand German marks) in respect of non-pecuniary damage. The Government argued that the Chamber should not have found violations of Article 8 and 14. The case was eventually decided in favour of the father of the child born out of wedlock on 29 June 1988. The applicant, born in 1950, was a Turkish national at the time of the events complained of. He subsequently obtained German nationality. The applicant applied to the Wiesbaden District Court for a decision granting him a right of access to his daughter. The court found as follows: “The Court is convinced that the petitioner's wish for [G.] to visit him is motivated by attachment to his child and genuine affection for her. It nonetheless takes the view that personal contact with her father is not in the child's best interests, since her mother dislikes her father so deeply and opposes all contact so fiercely.” The court observed that the mother, as the person having custody, determined the father's right to access to the child and that the guardianship court could only grant the father a right to see his daughter if it was in her best interests. The applicant appealed to the Wiesbaden Regional Court in 1992. The Regional Court ordered a psychological expert opinion on the question whether contact with the applicant was in G.'s interests. The expert reached the conclusion that a right of access without prior conversations to overcome the conflicts between the parents was not in the child's interests. On 17 December 1992 the applicant requested the Regional Court to progress with the proceedings. He also applied for a provisional order granting him a right. of access to G. during one afternoon every week and prohibiting her mother. from obstructing such contact. The judge in the case ruled that there was no urgency and that the applicant could be expected to await the outcome of the main proceedings. The applicant and the child's mother entered into an agreement. Under terms of this agreement, the applicant declared that he would refrain from instituting any court proceedings. The proceedings were suspended until the termination of this therapy. On 25 August 1993 the Wiesbaden Regional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal. After the Federal Constitutional Court's decisions of 1971 and 1981, the constitutionality of Article 1711 can no longer be seriously doubted. For considerations of legal policy, the guardianship court may decide that the father is entitled to access if this is in the child’s best interests. The law leaves it up to the person having custody, as a rule the mother, to determine whether, and to what extent, the father should be able to spend time with his child. The court decides to grant a father access to a child born out of wedlock if this is beneficial for the child's welfare. In the meantime, the courts are bound by Article 1711. This interpretation justifies the assumption that fathers should generally be granted access to their children. It is in fact important for children not simply to have a fantasy picture of their fathers, but to be able to form a personal, realistic picture of them. The Regional Court is convinced that the father in this case is motivated by attachment to [G.] and genuine affection for her. However, the court is not necessarily obliged to grant him access if there are serious tensions between the parents. The Regional Court finally considered that exceptionally it had not been required to hear the child, since questioning her about her relationship with her father would have placed a psychological strain on her. The decisive factor is always the child's point of view. of all this, the report finds that she does not suffer as a result of the present situation. The Court can rely fully on the report, which has no apparent defects and is not invalidated by the fact that the father sees the situation differently.” On 1 December 1998 the Federal Constitutional Court, sitting as a panel of three judges, refused to entertain the applicant's constitutional complaint.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40518/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) by a Turkish national. The applicant alleged under Article 5 of the Convention that he was not brought promptly before a judge. He further alleged that he had been denied a fair hearing on account of the presence of a military judge on the bench of the Diyarbakır State Security Court which tried and convicted him. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 10 April 2003, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant was arrested in September 1997 and handed over to the Siirt Police Headquarters. The applicant gave a detailed account of his involvement within the PKK and of the activities he had carried out on behalf of that organisation. He maintained that his police statements were correct and that he had nothing to add to them. On 2 October 1997 the public prosecutor filed an indictment with the Diyarbakır State Security Court against the applicant and requested the court to sentence him pursuant to Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act. In the proceedings the applicant mainly repeated the statements he had made to the police. He also claimed that the money found in his possession had been given to him by the PKK to obtain a false passport in 1992. The prosecutor accused the applicant of carrying out activities aimed at breaking up the unity of the State. The applicant’s appeal against the judgment was rejected by the Court of Cassation on 22 May 2001. The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. The application was dismissed after the applicant was found not guilty by reason of his good conduct during the trial. It was rejected after the appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Justice on 2 November 2000. The trial court found the applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to the death penalty under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. The conviction was overturned after the court took into account the applicant's good Conduct during the Trial.

By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court declared the application against Turkey to be a success. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. No representations from the applicant were made to the MCTC about his arrest status. It was considered that he was likely to suborn witnesses and that it was “undesirable in the interests of discipline that he should be at large or consort with his comrades” No reasons were noted as to why the applicant had been detained except in the last form (dated 7 February 2000) which recorded the same reasons as in the above-noted 8-day reports. The applicant's representative applied for a writ of habeas corpus to the High Court. A return date was fixed for 3 March 2000. The application was served on the CO of the MCTC on 19 February 2000. On 22 February 2000 the applicant was released from close arrest and he was posted to the 47th Regiment Royal Artillery. He was released on 2 March 2000, the same CO swore an affidavit setting out the reasons for the applicant's release. The applicant and his two co-defendants were tried by Army General Court Martial on a joint charge of rape between 14 May and 25 May 2001. All three defendants were acquitted. The judge ruled that the applicant should be posted with immediate effect to a different unit in a different country namely the UK, and issued with specific orders preventing him from being able to influence the witnesses. He wrote: 'I decided that the interests of justice could be met by releasing the Applicant into open arrest even though the allegation against him was that he had committed rape and indecent assault...and despite the fact that there was evidence that he, with others, concocted a story and interfered with a witness'

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 473/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike out the application, in accordance with Article 37. The applicant was a serving police officer in Gdynia. In November 1992 he was charged with numerous counts of fraud. In January 2005 the court severed the charges against him and four other accused. Gdynia District Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to one year and six months’ imprisonment and a fine of 800 Polish zlotys (PLN) The applicant appealed. On 11 December 2006 his appeal was dismissed by the Gdańsk Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). The Regional Court found that there were no delays for which the District Court could be held responsible. Pointing to the complexity of the case and the voluminous documentation gathered in the proceedings the Regional Court held that the proceedings had been conducted with due diligence and within a reasonable time. The application was dismissed on 13 November 2006.

name: Anne-Marie Christensen
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 247/07) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained about the length of civil proceedings and lack of an effective remedy under Articles 6 and 13 of the convention. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs Nina Holst-Christensen of the Ministry of Justice. The case was heard by the Court on 13 December 2006. The Court ruled that the application was admissible on the admissibility and the merits of the case. The decision was published on 17 December 2007. The applicant instituted civil proceedings against the medical consultant who performed the two cystoscopic examinations in May 1992. alleging malpractice. During the proceedings before the High Court, which ended on 13 November 2002, the applicant changed counsel at least five times. A significant amount of time was spent on the drafting and discussion of various questions to be submitted to the Medico‑Legal Council (Retslægerådet) for an expert opinion. The Medico-Legal Council issued its opinion on 22 December 1997. The case was accordingly adjourned five times and, at a hearing on 11 December 1998, the High court fixed a time limit for 20 January 1999 for the applicant to finish her draft questions. The case was first heard in January 2000. The applicant. requested leave to appeal against the order. The proceedings were thus adjourned until 5 May 2000, when her request was refused by the Leave to Appeal Board (Procesbevillingsnævnet) Beforehand, however, on 16 March 2000 the High Court re-submitted the matter, including the original questions, to the Medico-Legal Council. On 4 July 2000 the applicant requested that the Patients’ Injury Appeals Board’s decision of 20 January 2000 be joined to the proceedings. Her request was granted and the patients’ injury Appeals Board submitted its writ of defense on 3 October 2000. The High Court held a hearing on 3 April 2002. The trial was held on 9 and 11 November 2002. By judgment of 13 November 2002 the High Court found against the applicant. She was ordered to pay the opponent parties’ costs amounting to a total of 100,000 Danish kroner (DKK), equal to approximately 13,500 Euros (EUR). The applicant was also ordered to submit her draft questions to the Medico‑Legal Council. The application was dismissed on 8 January 2003. The Supreme Court approved nine of the applicant’s seventeen draft questions on 14 January 2004. The applicant requested an adjournment of the proceedings, inter alia, because she wanted to request that further witnesses be heard. In 2004 the applicant was granted free legal aid in the Supreme Court proceedings by the Directorate of Civil Law (Civilretsdirektoratet) Her request for a re‑scheduling of the trial was refused on 5 April 2005. On 13 June 2005 the applicant’s ninth counsel stated that he was unable to appear for the hearing. The following day the applicant's counsel resigned from the case. The Supreme Court had to cancel the trial planned for 20 June 2005 and adjourn the case on 15 June 2005. The appeal trial should take place on 6 June 2006. The case was adjourned on 13 September 2005 and the appeal hearing took place on 23 August 2005. The trial was held as scheduled on 6 June 2006, and by judgment of 15 June 2006 the Supreme Court upheld the High Court’s judgment. Since the applicant had been granted legal aid in the proceedings, the Treasury was ordered to pay the opponent parties’ costs, altogether in the amount of DKK 200,000, equal to approximately EUR 26,900. The applicant’S lawyer's fee was also to be paid by the Treasury in so far as it was not covered by private legal insurance. The same applied to the fee for one of the applicant's previous lawyers before the Supreme court, which had been set at DKK 60,000.

name: H. Rydz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13167/02) lodged on 1 March 2002 with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the length of his detention was excessive and that the criminal proceedings in his case exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of the treaty. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The decision was based on a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged, the severity of the sentence he faced and the need to secure the proper conduct of the investigation. In October 1999 the public prosecutor ordered expert opinions on the kind of injuries the victims had suffered. The opinions were submitted on 6 and 15 October 1999. The applicant was charged with seven offences: participation in an organised criminal gang, gang rape (including statutory rape) and with threatening the victims and persuading them not to inform the police about the crimes. The preparatory proceedings, during which the prosecutor examined a total of 66 witnesses and obtained over 150 other items of evidence, were closed on 3 December 1999. On the same date the publicProsecutor lodged a bill of indictment comprising 59 charges and five victims. In 2000 the first-instance court held 11 hearings during which evidence of the witnesses and defendants was heard. The case involved thirteen defendants and sixty-six witnesses. The hearing scheduled for 30 January 2001 was adjourned in order to have one of the victims heard with the assistance of a psychologist. It was proved that two of the defendants had exerted improper pressure on witnesses and thus caused them to alter significantly their versions of the events. The court requested the police to determine the whereabouts of nine witnesses. Fines were imposed on eleven absent witnesses. Several witnesses had changed their testimonies and the reading out of their earlier statements had been justified. Almost thirty witnesses remained to be heard at that stage of the proceedings. The applicant served a one-year prison sentence imposed in separate proceedings. On 7 November 2001 the Wrocław Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until 15 February 2002. The court noted that, since June 2000, the first-instance court had held seven hearings and examined ten witnesses. The absence of other witnesses was the major reason for the prolongation of the proceedings. The appellate court also pointed to the fact that the examination of the witnesses had been very time-consuming owing to the complexity of the case and the mental state of the victims. From 10 April 2002 until 9 December 2002 the applicant was serving a prison sentence imposed on him in separate proceedings. For more information on this case visit the website: http://www.wrocławscourt of appeal.org/. Opole Regional Court found the applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to nine years' imprisonment. All the accused appealed. Wrocław Court of Appeal upheld the judgment with respect to the applicant. Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's cassation appeal on 11 March 2005. On 29 April 2005 the Court of appeal dismissed the complaint as ill-founded. The court admitted that the proceedings had lasted a considerable period of time but stated that this fact alone could not lead to the conclusion that the applicant’s right to a trial within a reasonable time had been violated. The applicant lodged a new complaint about the undue length of the proceedings on 24 February 2005.

The case originated in an application (no. 13167/02) lodged on 1 March 2002 with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the length of his detention was excessive and that the criminal proceedings in his case exceeded a “reasonable time’ The applicant was arrested on suspicion of having committed multiple gang rape (including statutory rape), of inducing the victims to take intoxicants and of persuading the victims not to inform the police about those crimes. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was charged with seven offences: participation in an organised criminal gang, gang rape (including statutory rape) committed with extreme cruelty and in conjunction with deprivation of liberty. The court found that the grounds for detention on remand were still valid and owing to the fact that the crimes had been committed in co-operation with other persons, there remained a high risk that the applicant might interfere with the course of justice and exert pressure on witnesses and victims. Seven other hearings scheduled in 2000 were cancelled or adjourned for reasons not attributable to the court, in particular the absence of the suspects' ability to understand the meaning of their acts. The case involved thirteen defendants and sixty-six witnesses. The hearing scheduled for 30 January 2001 was adjourned in order to have one of the victims heard with the assistance of a psychologist. It was proved that two of the defendants had exerted improper pressure on witnesses and thus caused them to alter their versions of the events. Several witnesses had changed their testimonies and the reading out of their earlier statements had been justified. Almost thirty witnesses remained to be heard at that stage of the proceedings and there was a need to summon further witnesses. Fines were imposed on eleven absent witnesses. From 11 April 2001 until 10 April 2002 the applicant served a one-year prison sentence imposed in separate proceedings. On 28 June 2001 the Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until 15 November 2001. The Wrocław Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until 15 February 2002. The court noted that, since June 2000, the first-instance court had held seven hearings and examined ten witnesses. The absence of other witnesses was the major reason for the prolongation of the proceedings, but the trial court had taken proper measures to speed up the trial. The appellate court also pointed to the fact that the examination of the witnesses had been very time-consuming owing to the complexity of the case and the mental state of the victims. From 10 April 2002 until 9 December 2002 the applicant was serving a prison sentence imposed on him in separate proceedings. The applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to nine years' imprisonment and a four-year period of deprivation of his civic rights. The court dismissed the defendant's request to summon other absent witnesses, having found that their examination would not add anything to the case. The Wrocław Court of Appeal rejected the applicant's complaint of 25 January 2005 about the excessive length of the proceedings before the Opole Regional Court, finding that it had been lodged after the termination of proceedings. The case originated in an application (no. 13167/02) lodged on 1 March 2002 with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the length of his detention was excessive. The President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the applicant's application at the same time as its admissibility. The decision was based on a reasonable suspicion, confirmed by testimonies of the victims and of other suspects, that the applicant had committed the offences. The case was opened in October 1999. The applicant was charged with participation in an organised criminal gang, gang rape (including statutory rape) committed with extreme cruelty and in conjunction with deprivation of liberty. He was also charged with threatening the victims and persuading them not to inform the police about the crimes. The court found that the grounds for detention on remand were still valid and that there remained a high risk that the applicant might interfere with the course of justice and exert pressure on witnesses and victims. The case was closed on 3 December 1999, and the investigation was prolonged until 31 December 1999. In 2000 the first-instance court held 11 hearings during which the evidence of the witnesses and defendants was heard. At the hearing of 24 May 2000 the court prolonged the applicant's detention until 15 November 2000. The court remanded in custody one of the defendants who had failed to appear at a hearing and lifted the detention of another. In 2001 nineteen hearings were held and three had to be adjourned or cancelled because of the illness of a judge, the absence of a witness or the fact that the case file was with the Court of Appeal which was deciding on the prolongation of the detention. Fines were imposed on eleven absent witnesses. Several witnesses had changed their testimonies and the reading out of their earlier statements had been justified. Almost thirty witnesses remained to be heard at that stage of the proceedings. Wrocław Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until 15 February 2002. The court noted that, since June 2000, the first-instance court had held seven hearings and examined ten witnesses. The absence of other witnesses was the major reason for the prolongation of the proceedings; however, the trial court had taken proper measures to speed up the trial. The parties had also requested additional witnesses to be heard. and to cross-examine them. The applicant was serving a prison sentence imposed on him in separate proceedings from 10 April 2002 until 9 December 2002. Up to 31 July 2002 nine hearings had been held during which the court took evidence from further witnesses and an expert. One witness was examined at his place. The applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to nine years' imprisonment and a four-year period of deprivation of his civic rights. All the accused appealed. Wrocław Court of Appeal rejected the applicant's complaint of 25 January 2005 about the excessive length of the proceedings before the Opole Regional Court. The applicant lodged a new complaint about the undue length of. the proceedings, referring to his application pending before the Court, on 24 February 2005. On 29 April 2005 the Court of. Appeal dismissed the complaint as ill-founded. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal on 11 March 2005. The court examined solely the part of the. proceedings conducted before theOpole Regional court. It admitted that the proceedings had lasted a considerable. period of time but stated that this fact alone could not lead to the conclusion that the. applicant's right to a trial was violated.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56811/00) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Davood Amrollahi, an Iranian national, complained under Article 8 that, as a result of his expulsion from Denmark, he will be separated from his wife and children. The Court decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings not to expel the applicant. By a decision of 28 June 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. In 1992 he was granted a residence and work permit in Denmark. In 1997 he was found guilty of drug trafficking and sentenced to three years' imprisonment. He was released in 1998 and has since worked as a carer for elderly people. He has three children, two of whom have been born to him and the other two to his ex-wife. He is still living in Denmark and has worked at a local retirement home. He also has a son and a daughter from a previous relationship who he has not had any contact with since he left the army in 1987. He now lives with his wife and children in the city of Copenhagen, Denmark, and has a new job. On 17 December 1998 the applicant had served two-thirds of his sentence and was due to be released on parole. Since he did not consent to the deportation and refused to leave the country voluntarily, he was detained as from that date in accordance with the Aliens Act. The applicant appealed against this decision to the Refugee Board (Flygtningenævnet), which on 16 April 1999 requested the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to provide more information on the situation in Iran. On 3 March 2000 the High Court of Western Denmark quashed the above decision and dismissed the applicant's request for reconsideration of the expulsion order. By judgment of 14 February 2000 the City Court revoked the decision to expel the applicant. The applicant was released from his detention on 11 May 2000. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision of 3 March 2000. On 7 September 2000 the Supreme Court agreed that a request for a review of an expulsion order pursuant to section 50 of the Aliens Act could only be examined once by the courts. The case was settled at the London Court of Human Rights on 4 March 2000, and the application was dismissed on 9 April 2000, with the judge ruling that the applicant was not entitled to a review. The appeal was rejected on 4 May 2000 and the case was dismissed. The applicant was later granted a stay of deportation and released from prison on 6 July 2000.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13378/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was allocated to a Chamber within the Fourth Section of the Court. On 12 December 2006 the Chamber unanimously declared the application admissible and delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been no violation of Article 14. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber on 23 May 2007, pursuant to a request by the applicants dated 8 March 2007. In addition, third-party comments were received from the Belgian and Irish Governments on 28 May 2007. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 12 September 2007 (Rule 59 § 3) The applicants are unmarried sisters, born on 26 May 1918 and 2 December 1925 respectively. name: Yetgin Adırbelli
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20775/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were members of the People’s Democratic Party (DEHAP) in Şırnak. They were arrested ‘in connection with the armed attack and in accordance with a decision of the İdil Magistrates’ Court’. The court granted the request and authorised the security forces to conduct one search during the daytime at the applicants’ homes with a view to obtaining evidence. On 14 September 2007 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. During the house search, the security forces seized music compact discs from the houses of Beşir Gasyak and Resul Kervanoğlu. Amongst those discs found in the former’s house, certain allegedly contained separatist propaganda. During their detention in police custody, the applicants had a meeting with their representative, Mr Elçi, upon their request. The applicants all maintained that they had been in their homes at the time of the incident and had had no involvement in the armed attack. Yetgin Adırbelli, Gülek Adılbelli and Mehmet Goran did not request a lawyer. The applicants were charged with aiding and abetting the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers’ Party), an illegal organisation. Yetgin Adırbelli had been arrested on suspicion of being in possession of a firearm and there had been an investigation in respect of Metin Goran as he had been suspected of forgery. The prosecutor decided to release them and referred Beşir Gasyak to the single judge of the İdil Magistrates’ Court. On 12 March 2003 the public prosecutor at the Diyarbakır State Security Court issued a decision not to prosecute, on the ground that there was insufficient evidence to initiate criminal proceedings.

name: Wolfgang Adam Wenner
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the refusal to grant him drug substitution treatment during his imprisonment, including a refusal to have the necessity of such treatment examined by an external medical expert, breached Article 3 of the convention. On 17 June 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. The application was brought by a German national, Mr Wolfgang Adam Wenner (‘the applicant’), who has been addicted to heroin since 1973. The Government were represented by one of their Agents, Mr H.‑J. Behrens, of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. The applicant was transferred back to Kaisheim Prison on 30 April 2010. The prison doctors gave him various painkillers for chronic pain resulting from his polyneuropathy, on a daily basis. During his detention, the pain in his feet, neck and spine became such that, at least during certain periods, he spent most of his time in bed. The applicant was examined by an external doctor for internal medicine, H., on the prison authorities’ request in October 2010. H. did not consider any changes in the treatment of the applicant’s HIV and hepatitis C infections necessary. He explained that from a medical point of view, drug substitution treatment had to be provided to the applicant. He subsequently confirmed that the applicant should be examined by a doctor specialised in drug addiction therapy to that end. The applicant claimed that drug substitution treatment was the only adequate treatment for his medical condition. He also claimed that he was in need of Interferon therapy in order to treat his hepatitis C infection. Substitution also helped to protect other prisoners from infection when using the same needles as he did for the consumption of drugs. He stood hardly any chance of leading a totally drug‑free life on release from prison. His rehabilitation could therefore better be furthered by providing him drug substitution therapy. The decision of the prison authorities to refuse the applicant treatment with Diamorphin, Polamidon or another heroin substitute for his heroin addiction was not justified. The applicant was severely addicted to drugs and had not received drug substitution treatment prior to his current detention in Kaisheim Prison. The prison authorities argued that substitution treatment was neither necessary from a medical point of view nor a suitable measure for the applicant’s rehabilitation. After three years in detention, he no longer suffered from physical withdrawal symptoms. His condition with regard to his HIV and hepatitis C infections was stable and did not require any therapy. As suggested by the prison doctor, the applicant should use the opportunity to wean himself off opioids, such as heroin and its substitutes, while in prison, as it was very difficult to obtain drugs there. The applicant appealed against the decision of the prison authorities to the Augsburg Regional Court. He argued that the authorities of Kaisheim Prison, where no substitution treatment had ever been provided, had omitted to examine the medical necessity of drug substitution therapy. He also argued that under the applicable administrative rules for substitution treatment in prison in the Land of Baden-Württemberg, he would be provided with drug substitution treatment. On 9 August 2012 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal as ill‑founded. On 10 September 2012 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. The proceedings before the Munich Court of appeal continued until April 2012. The applicant was denied drug substitution therapy, the only suitable therapy to treat his chronic pain. He complained that his right to respect for his physical integrity under the Basic Law had been breached. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant’s constitutional complaint without giving reasons (file no. 2 BvR 2263/12). On 3 December 2014 the applicant was released. When examined by a doctor on 5 December 2014 he tested positive for methadone and cocaine. The doctor confirmed that the applicant would receive drug substitution treatment from 8 December 2014 onwards. train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 12 July 1993. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality. The applicant was convicted of the murder of a woman whom he had violently assaulted in 1964. In June 1981 he killed a 75 year-old woman who was placing flowers on a family grave in a London cemetery. He cut her throat with a knife. In December 1981 he pleaded not guilty to murder, but guilty to manslaughter on the ground of diminished responsibility. In January 1982 a discretionary sentence of life imprisonment was imposed (see paragraph 12 below) The applicant claims that he was informed in 1983 by prison officers at H.M. Prison Wormwood Scrubs that he. was subject to the regime for discretionary life sentences. The court revoked his life licence under section 62 (7) of the Criminal Justice Act 1967. The applicant was considered for parole by the Parole Board in January 1989. The Board recommended that his case be referred again to the local review committee in 1994. Since then he has been transferred to Gartree Prison where he is held as a “Category A’ (high security) prisoner. He should have been told in February, but owing to an oversight he was not informed until last month. He was informed that the “tariff’ in respect of his conviction in 1964 had now been served and that his continued detention was based on the risk he represented. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35070/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that she had been denied a fair hearing on account of the presence of a military judge on the bench of the Istanbul State Security Court. She also complained that the Court of Cassation had based its decision on witness statements taken at the police station, which the witnesses subsequently repudiated as having been made under duress. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) By a decision of 20 May 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant was charged with aiding and abetting members of an illegal armed organisation. The Istanbul State Security Court acquitted her of the charges for lack of evidence. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first court. On 18 December 1995 the applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to three years and nine months' imprisonment and debarred her from holding public office for three years. The applicant appealed. On 9 July 1996 the Court ofCassation dismissed the applicant's request for a hearing holding that the request had been introduced out of time. The case was referred once again to the Istanbul state Security Court. The application was dismissed on 9 July 1998 on the grounds that the application had been brought too late.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29296/95) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that his detention in police custody lasted seven days without being brought before a judge or other officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. On 30 May 2000 the Chamber retained the applicant's complaints under Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and this case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the PKK. He was sentenced to three years' imprisonment in accordance with Article 168 § 2 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The applicant was released pending trial in 1996 and released from prison in 1998. He is currently living in the United States. The application was brought before the İstanbul State Security Court on 12 June 1995. On 23 August 1995 the Chief Public Prosecutor filed an indictment with the  Court charging the applicant with membership of the PKK and the applicant was charged with membership. The charges were brought under Article 168 Sections 2 and 5 of the Turkish Criminal Code and Law no. 3713.

name: John Bryan
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 9 September 1994 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 19178/91) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a British citizen. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 May 1995. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Liddy, Mr Owen and Mr Pannick as well as replies to its questions. The applicant appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment under section 174 (2) (a), (b), (g) and (h) of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990. An inspector was appointed to conduct an inquiry and determine the appeal. Mr Bryan was a Principal Housing and Planning Inspector, a civil servant and a member of the salaried staff of the Department of the Environment. The inspector rejected the appeal under grounds (a), (b), and (g), but allowed it under ground (h) to the extent that the compliance period should be extended from three to six months. He held, inter alia, as follows: “The appeal on ground (b) ... (12) What I need to decide in respect of this ground of appeal is whether, as a matter of fact and degree, the buildings could, from their appearance and layout, be considered to have been designed for the purposes of agriculture. (13) In my opinion, as originally constructed,. the buildings would have led any reasonable person to have concluded that he or she was looking at the start of a small new detached housing estate. The appeal on ground (a) fails. (16) The appeal buildings lie in part of the green belt ... They also lie within the Higher Whitley Conservation Area. They did not look as if they had been designed for the purposes of agriculture. (19) These objections amount to sound and clear-cut reasons why planning permission should be withheld. (20) You said that demolition of the buildings and the removal of the materials was an excessive requirement. I do not agree. The decision turns on the following main issues. Whether, if the development is inappropriate to the greenbelt, there are any special circumstances to justify the granting of planning permission. The High Court dismissed the appeal on 8 March 1991. The judge, Mr Lionel Read, QC, found inter alia as follows: “A principal argument on behalf of the applicant at the inquiry under [ground] (b) was that the erection of the two buildings was permitted development under the General Development Order’. The appeal on ground (h) (21) ... Mr Bryan wanted more time in order to erect a replacement or replacements before demolition. I will increase the period to 6 months ... (22) I have taken account of all the other matters raised, including the possibility of your client putting up a large steel-clad building under permitted development rights, but find they do not affect my decision.“ The inspector extended the applicant’s time for complying with the enforcement notice under ground (h) The question whether the alterations proposed to a building were, as he evidently thought, a ‘matter of cosmetics’ and would not meet the main objections was entirely a matter of planning judgment for him. It is to be remembered that, in order to stay within his General Development Order rights, the applicant must erect replacement buildings which, by their appearance and layout, could be considered as designed for the purposes of agriculture. If they are, their effect on the green belt, the countryside and the conservation area is irrelevant to the exercise of that right. In the result, I find no error of law and I dismiss the application.

The case was referred to the Court on 9 September 1994 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 19178/91) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a British citizen. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 (art-6-1) of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 May 1995. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Liddy, Mr Owen and Mr Pannick as well as replies to its questions. The applicant appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment under section 174 (2) (a), (b), (g) and (h) TCPA (see paragraph 19 below). In accordance with the relevant legislation, an inspector was appointed to conduct an inquiry and determine the appeal. The hearing was heard by the Court in Strasbourg in May 1995 after a preparatory meeting had been held beforehand. The application was brought by Mr John Bryan, a farmer and a contractor. Inspector rejected the appeal under grounds (a), (b), and (g) but allowed it under ground (h) to the extent that the compliance period should be extended from three to six months. He held, inter alia, as follows: “The appeal on ground (b) ... (12) What I need to decide in respect of this ground of appeal is whether, as a matter of fact and degree, the buildings could, from their appearance and layout, be considered to have been designed for the purposes of agriculture. The size, layout, and original external appearance of the buildings and their detailing did little to change that view.” The two appeal buildings look like part of a small estate of detached houses. The use of domestic-style eaves and gable barge boarding. The residential look of the ‘porch’ to No. 1 building. And the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food’s view about the uneconomic layout of both buildings as originally built all add to the impression that these buildings were not designed for agricultural purposes. I shall also consider the effect of the development on the countryside surrounding the village. I do not agree that demolition of the buildings and the removal of the materials was an excessive requirement. The appeal on ground (a) fails. The High Court dismissed the applicant's appeal against the inspector's decision under section 289 TCPA (see paragraph 24 below). The appeal was dismissed by the High Court on 8 March 1991, the judge, Mr Lionel Read, QC, finding inter alia as follows: “A principal argument on behalf of the applicant at the inquiry under [ground] (b) was that the erection of the two buildings was permitted development under the General Development Order’. The appeal on ground (h) (21) ... Mr Bryan wanted more time in order to erect a replacement or replacements before demolition. I see no need to insist on a period which would make undue difficulty for him. I will increase the period to 6 months. The applicant wanted more time to erect a replacement or replacements. Whether the existence of these General Development Order rights provided sufficient reason for the inspector to grant planning permission for the buildings in fact erected was a matter for judgment - the inspector’s judgment. Whether another decision-maker would have reached the same conclusion as did this inspector is not to the point. Nor is the view of this court, which does not sit on appeal from the judgment of inspectors, relevant. In the result, I find no error of law and I dismiss the application.“At the hearing held before the European Commission of Human Rights on 14 October 1993, the applicant's representatives stated that, although they had not represented the applicant before the High Court, they surmised that the challenge to the inspector's ground (b) reasoning had been raised in the Notice of Motion. The Court of Appeal, on 11 June 1991, also refused leave to appeal.

The application was brought by Mr Bryan, a farmer and a contractor from Warrington, Cheshire. The inspector was appointed by the Secretary of State after approval of the Lord Chancellor. In his decision letter of 1 October 1990 the inspector rejected the appeal under grounds (a), (b), and (g) but allowed it under ground (h) to the extent that the compliance period should be extended from three to six months. He held, inter alia, as follows: “The appeal on ground (b) ... (12) What I need to decide in respect of this ground of appeal is whether, as a matter of fact and degree, the buildings could, from their appearance and layout, be considered to have been designed for the purposes of agriculture" The appeal on ground (a) fails. The appeal onGround (g) (20) You said that demolition of the buildings and the removal of the materials was an excessive requirement. I do not agree. Harm to the purpose of the green belt has been caused. The appearance and character of the conservation area has not been preserved. These objections amount to sound and clear-cut reasons why planning permission should be withheld. It does not affect my decision to deny planning permission for the appeal buildings. The two appeal buildings look like part of a small estate of detached houses with access roads and suitable garden areas. The third building, not subject of this appeal, exacerbates this impression. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court on 8 March 1991, the judge, Mr Lionel Read, QC, finding inter alia as follows: “A principal argument on behalf of the applicant at the inquiry under [ground] (b) was that the erection of the two buildings was permitted development under the General Development Order ... ... The applicant does not challenge the inspector’s decision under ground (b). Nevertheless paragraphs 14 and 15 of the decision letter, where he is still dealing with that ground, are relevant to the court's consideration of his decision on grounds (a) and (g) ... In my judgment ... it cannot be said that the inspector failed to take into account the fact that the applicant might, within his General. Development Order rights, erect buildings of a broadly similar nature.“ The applicant wanted more time to erect a replacement or replacements. The inspector extended the applicant’s time for complying with the enforcement notice under ground (h). Whether the existence of these General Development Order rights provided sufficient reason for the inspector to grant planning permission for the buildings in fact erected, whether or not conditioned as suggested by the applicant, was a matter for judgment - the inspector's judgment. Whether another decision-maker would have reached the same conclusion as did this inspector is not to the point. Nor is the view of this court, which does not sit on appeal from the judgment of inspectors, relevant. In the result, I find no error of law and I dismiss the application.

The applicant appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment under section 174 (2) (a), (b), (g) and (h) TCPA (see paragraph 19 below). In accordance with the relevant legislation, an inspector was appointed to conduct an inquiry and determine the appeal. The inspector was a Principal Housing and Planning Inspector, a civil servant and a member of the salaried staff of the Department of the Environment. The buildings would have led any reasonable person to have concluded that he or she was looking at the start of a small new detached housing estate. Numerous features of the buildings were more suited to houses than barns. The original openings in building No. 1 were said to be doorways for a veal calf unit. But this building did not incorporate internal drainage considered necessary for such stock. Other features in both buildings include the extensive use of Georgian-style windows and other windows made for domestic use. I understand that Mr Bryan’s contacts allowed him to buy these windows cheaply. But whatever their source, they contribute to an impression that the buildings look more like houses than Barns. The appeal on ground (a) fails. The appeal onGround (b) also fails. Both appeal buildings look like part of a small estate of detached houses with access roads and suitable garden areas. The use of domestic-style eaves and gable barge boarding. The residential look of the ‘porch’ to No. 1 building. And the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food’s view about the uneconomic layout of both buildings as originally built all add to the impression that these buildings were not designed for agricultural purposes. (17) ... (18) The appeal buildings have neither enhanced nor preserved the appearance of this part of the conservation area. (19) These objections amount to sound and clear-cut reasons why planning permission should be withheld. The High Court dismissed the applicant's appeal against the inspector's decision. The judge said that the inspector failed to take into account the fact that the applicant might, within his General Development Order rights, erect buildings of a broadly similar nature. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court on 8 March 1991, the judge, Mr Lionel Read, QC, finding inter alia as follows: “A principal argument on behalf of the applicant at the inquiry under [ground] (b) was that the erection of the two buildings was permitted development under the General development Order’. The applicant appealed against this decision under section 289 TCPA (see paragraph 24 below). Inspector extended applicant’s time for complying with the enforcement notice under ground (h) Because the applicant had those rights and wanted more time to erect a replacement or replacements, the inspector extended his time. Whether the existence of these General Development Order rights provided sufficient reason for the inspector to grant planning permission for the buildings in fact erected was a matter for judgment - the inspector's judgment. Whether another decision-maker would have reached the same conclusion as did this inspector is not to the point. Nor is the view of this court, which does not sit on appeal from the judgment of inspectors, relevant. In the result, I find no error of law and I dismiss the application.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43452/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was an anaesthesiologist working at the Kars State Hospital when criminal proceedings were instigated against him for alleged involvement in the activities of an illegal organisation. He was accused together with other suspects of hanging posters and banners in various places in Ankara on behalf of that organisation. On the basis of the evidence contained in the case file, the Ankara State Security Court convicted the applicant under Article 7 § 1 of Law no. 3713 and sentenced him to two years and six months' imprisonment. On 28 February 2002, the Supreme Disciplinary Commission of the Ministry of Health decided to dismiss the applicant from the civil service. The applicant's objection to this decision was dismissed by the administrative court who noted, inter alia, that, according to the disciplinary investigation, the applicant had taken fifteen days leave from 2 June 2000 in pursuit of his illegal activities. The court also noted that the applicant's conviction had become final. This decision was subsequently upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court on 27 December 2005. According to an attestation dated 10 September 2007 the applicant is currently employed at Atasam hospital in Samsun. However, he did not submit any court decisions.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 52363/11) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant is the former head of the Basque separatist organisation Iparretarrak. After his detention in 1988, he was convicted several times: on 4 March 1991 he was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment for criminal association with a view to preparing a terrorist offence. In 2007 the Sentence enforcement division of the Paris Court of Appeal released him on licence from 14 February 2007 to 14 February 2014. The Government pointed out that the applicant was the first person sentenced to life imprisonment for offences linked to terrorism ever to be released on licence. The applicant took part in a peaceful demonstration outside Agen Prison in support of Basque detainees being held there. The media reported on that demonstration. The Paris Sentence Enforcement Court delivered a judgment on 14 May 2008 imposing additional special obligations on the applicant. On 18 February 2010 the Public Prosecutor’s Office requested that the sentence enforcement judge of the Regional Court of Paris add both the aforementioned obligations. The latter judgment was quashed by judgment of the Criminal Chamber of the Court of Cassation on 10 June 2009, on the grounds that the court did not have jurisdiction to modify the obligations for release on licence, for which matter the sentenceenforcement judge held jurisdiction. Philippe Bidart was convicted of promoting Basque separatism and supporting detainees convicted of or charged with terrorist acts. He was also prohibited from discussing that offence in public. The Paris Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 31 August 2010. The Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on points of law lodged by the applicant, on the grounds that the judgment had properly applied Article 132-45 [16] of the Penal Code, in compliance with the legal texts and conventions relevant to the applicant’s appeal (including Article 10 of the Convention) ... The right of the applicant association to freedom of artistic expression outweighed Mr Meischberger's personal interests. The limits of artistic freedom were exceeded when the image of a person was substantially deformed by wholly imaginary elements without it being evident. The court further added that there appeared to be no danger of recurrence (Wiederholungsgefahr) The painting in the present case was not intended to be a parable or even an exaggerated criticism conveying a basic message. It therefore did not fall within the scope of Article 10 of the Convention. It constituted a debasement of Mr Meischberger's public standing (Entwürdigung öffentlichen Ansehens) The applicant association could not justify the exhibition of the painting under the artistic freedom protected by Article 17a of the Basic Law (Staatsgrundsgesetz) The Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) rejected an appeal by the applicant association as it did not concern a legal question of considerable interest.
