name: Johann Widmann
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42032/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of the administrative proceedings exceeded the reasonable time requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. By a decision of 6 June 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Court ruled that the application was admissible on the basis of the merits. The applicant appealed to the Agricultural Authority of first instance (Landesregierung als Agrarbehörde erster Instanz - “the Agricultural Authority’) to grant him the necessary quantity of timber for the maintenance of existing and the edification of new alpine cabins. The Agricultural Authority held a hearing and on 20 June 1989 a forestry expert delivered his opinion. On 2 February 1990 the Salzburg Regional Land Reform Board dismissed the appeal and ordered the Federal Forestry Administration to provide the applicant with a smaller quantity of Timber within four weeks. The applicant appealed against this decision, claiming that a fixed annual supply of timber should be granted irrespective of the need for the cabins to be maintained. The legal instrument of 1868 only conferred a right to obtain timber for the maintenance of cabins. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the complaint for lack of sufficient prospects of success and remitted the case to the Administrative Court. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's complaint on 11 December 1997. It confirmed that the applicant was entitled to obtain a variable quantity of timber dependent on the need to maintain his alp's cabins, but not a fixed annual quantity. The decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 28 January 1998.

name: Hermance Merger
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68864/01) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two French nationals, Ms Hermance Merger and Ms Clémentine Cros (“the applicants”), alleged a violation of Article 8 and Article 14. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Court declared the application admissible in March 2004. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59): the case was heard by the Chamber that would consider the case. The first man's will stated that his wife's share of the estate would be split between him and her four children. When the first man died in 1986, his children asked the court to take back the money. The court agreed and the first couple were awarded a large sum of money. They also received the rights to a portion of their father's estate. However, they were not entitled to the money as it had been given to them as part of a gift to their father. The first daughter, the second wife, was left the remainder of her father's fortune. She was awarded the money for the first time in a will signed in 1986. The first applicant was an illegitimate child who had been conceived when her father was bound by marriage to a person other than her mother. Under the terms of the deed of division, she was required to pay an equalising balance to the other heirs in the French franc equivalent of 236,187 euros (EUR) The second applicant sold her home to pay that balance on behalf of her daughter, who had no property of her own. In a judgment of 3 May 2000, the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants' appeal. Following that judgment, the equalising Balance was duly paid to theother heirs. The first applicant completed her studies in December 1993.

Wiarda, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) of the Rules of Court). Hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. Ermacora for the Commission and by Mr Proksch for the applicant. The Chamber decided under Rule 50 of the Rules of Court to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. On 27 March, the Court decided on 27 March that the proceedings should continue without resumption. The applicant, who is a United States citizen, lives in Munich in the Federal Republic of Germany. Wishing to build a holiday residence in Hopfgarten, a village in the Austrian Tyrol, she approached, with the assistance of municipal officials, the owners of a plot of land. Sale negotiations began in 1971 and apparently led, in 1973, to an initial contract. The contract could not take effect unless it were approved by the local Real Property Transactions Authority (Grundverkehrsbehörde) The 1970/1973 Act applies to agricultural and forestry land and also to any land over which rights are acquired by, in particular, a natural person who does not possess Austrian nationality (section 1(1) and (2) There were, in fact, already 110 foreign landowners in Hopfgarten. It could be seen from a series of decisions of the Regional Authority that this municipality was one of those where the danger of foreign domination was imminent. The contract in question was therefore contrary to social and economic interests within the meaning of the above-mentioned Act. The applicant received a copy of the appeal but did not file any observations in reply. According to the minutes of the hearing, the rapporteur presented the facts and read out the expert opinions and observations received during the course of the investigation. The applicant stated that she had signed the initial contract (Erstvertrag), which could not then be found, on 13 March 1973. Regional Authority was indeed a “tribunal“ within the meaning of Article 6 (art. 6) of. the Convention. It gave decisions which the executive could neither annul nor vary. Government stated that during the last ten years or so the Regional Authority had not approved any acquisition of real property in Hopfgarten by a foreigner. Its membership varies according to the subject-matter of the contract to be examined. In the case of agricultural or forestry land - whether the buyer be Austrian or foreign - its voting members are: “(a) a person experienced inReal Property transaction matters, who shall act as chairman; (b) a member of the judiciary (Richterstand); (c) a legally qualified civil servant with training in realProperty transaction matters.” The Constitutional Court held, the Act did not fix the duration of the members’ term of office, conferred on the said Government the power of appointing the members. Only Austrian citizens who have reached the age of 25 years and are in full possession of their legal rights shall be eligible for appointment as members or substitute members. The details of the Real Property Transactions Authorities’ procedure (such as the convening of sittings, summoning of substitute members, conduct of voting, keeping of minutes and signing of decisions) shall be laid down by the Tyrolean legislature. Re-appointment is possible. Members and substitute members shall hold office for three years. The executive may neither annul nor vary their decisions. Members of the Real Property Transactions Authorities receive for their work remuneration and a travel allowance. The parties are entitled to consult the case-file (section 17) and must be given an opportunity of presenting their arguments (section 37) The competent authority may decide to hold a hearing (section 39(2), which will not take place in public. In certain circumstances which may give reason to doubt his impartiality, the civil servant concerned must arrange to be replaced (section 7). The parties have the right to be heard (rechtliches Gehör) and, inter alia, to adduce their arguments and evidence. In her application of 19 September 1979 to the Commission (no. 8790/79), Mrs. Sramek alleged that she had not received a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. In its report of 8 December 1982, the Commission expressed the opinion, by eleven votes to one, that there had been a violation of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the separate opinion contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment. The Commission declared the application admissible on 4 March 1982. Austria asked the Court “to hold that in the present case the provisions of paragraph 1 of Article 6 (art. 6-1) of the Convention ... were not violated’. The facts underlying the dispute do not indicate any breach by the Republic of Austria of its obligations under the Convention’, it said. The Court ruled in favour of Austria in the 1984 case, and ruled against the Netherlands in the 1986 case. The case has been described as ‘a landmark in the history of international law’ and ‘one of the most significant legal developments of the 20th century’ by the European Court of Human Rights.

name: Ekrem Ütebay
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40555/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr Ekrem Ütebay (‘the applicant’), on 1 October 2004. On 6 November 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The applicant was born in 1973 and lived in İstanbul. He died on 14 June 2005. For practical reasons, he will continue to be called ‘the Applicant’ in this judgment, although his family is now to be regarded as such. The case against the applicant continued before the Istanbul State Security Court. The case was still pending before the domestic courts when the applicant died on 14 June 2005. On 5 April 2004 the applicant was released pending trial. The applicant's defence submissions were not submitted to the court when his case was separated from the file. The court rejected the applicant's requests for release, taking into account the nature of the alleged offence and the state of the evidence. The judge sitting on the bench was replaced by a civilian judge on 18 June 1999. The Criminal Code of Turkey was amended on 16 June 1999 to include a charge of attempted murder. The charge was changed to attempted murder on 17 June 1999, and the charge was added to the Criminal Code. The application was dismissed by the court on 19 June 1999 and the case was dismissed on 24 June 2000.

name: Dennis Stafford
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that his detention after recall on life licence had ceased to be justified by the original sentence. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 29 May 2001 it was declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section, composed of the following judges: Mr J.-P. Costa, President, Mr W. Fuhrmann, Mr P. Kūris, Mrs F. Tulkens, Mr K. Jungwiert and Sir Nicolas Bratza. On 4 September 2001 the Chamber relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber. The applicant was convicted of murder in 1967. He was released on licence in April 1979. His licence required him to cooperate with his probation officer. In September 1980 his licence was revoked and thereafter he was continuously “unlawfully at large’ In April 1989 the applicant was arrested in the United Kingdom, having returned from South Africa in possession of a false passport. In July 1993 he was arrested and remanded in custody on counterfeiting charges. On 19 July 1994 he was convicted on two counts of conspiracy to forge travellers' cheques and passports and sentenced to six years' imprisonment. The Secretary of State accepted the Parole Board's recommendation, revoking the licence under section 39(1) of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 (‘the 1991 Act’). The applicant was released in March 1991. In 1996 the Parole Board conducted a formal review of the applicant's case and recommended his release on life licence. In 1997 the Secretary of State rejected the Board's recommendation in the following terms. The applicant was granted leave to seek judicial review of his decisions to reject the board's recommendation for immediate release. On 1 July 1997, but for the revocation of his life licence, the applicant would have been released from prison on the expiry of the sentence for fraud, pursuant to provisions whereby prisoners serving determinate sentences of more than more than 10 years are eligible for release. The Panel took the view after lengthy consideration that nothing further would be gained by a period in open conditions. The successful return to the community would be best facilitated by returning to his family directly. The Secretary of State acknowledged in the proceedings that there was not a significant risk that the applicant would commit further violent offences. But he asserted that he could lawfully detain a post-tariff mandatory life prisoner solely because there was a risk that he might commit further non-violent imprisonable offences. Four years were released after serving two-thirds of their sentence (section 33 of the 1991 Act). The applicant is now serving the equivalent of a determinate sentence of about five years, albeit in open conditions. This term has not been imposed on him by way of punishment, because he has already served the punitive terms which his previous, very serious, offences have been thought to merit. It is not submitted that the term imposed bears any relation to the gravity of any future imprisonable offence. The applicant was moved to open conditions on 16 December 1997. The Secretary of State decided that the applicant should spend only six months in open conditions before his next review. The House of Lords dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Court of Appeal's decision. On 22 December 1998 the applicant was released on licence by the Secretary of state. In his speech, with which the rest of the judges agreed, Lord Steyn held that section 35(2) of the 1991 Act conferred a wide administrative discretion on the secretary of state to decide upon the release on licence of mandatory life prisoners. He expressly repeated Lord Bingham's concern that the imposition of a substantial term of imprisonment by exercise of administrative discretion was hard to reconcile with ordinary concepts of the rule of law.

The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his detention after recall on life licence had ceased to be justified by the original sentence. On 29 May 2001 it was declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 August 2001. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry. The case was heard at the High Court in London on 20 February 2002. The applicant was convicted of murder in 1967 and released on licence in 1979. He left the UK in breach of his licence and went to live in South Africa. In September 1980 his licence was revoked and thereafter he was continuously ‘unlawfully at large’ In April 1989 the applicant was arrested in the United Kingdom, having returned from South Africa in possession of a false passport. In July 1993 he was arrested and remanded in custody on counterfeiting charges. On 19 July 1994 he was convicted on two counts of conspiracy to forge travellers' cheques and passports and sentenced to six years' imprisonment. The Court heard addresses by Mr Fitzgerald and Mr Pannick. In 1996 the Parole Board conducted a formal review of the applicant's case and recommended his release on life licence. In 1997 the Secretary of State rejected the Board's recommendation. The applicant was granted leave to seek judicial review of his decision. The appeal was unsuccessful and he was released from prison on 1 July 1997, but for the revocation of his life licence, the applicant would have been released on the expiry of his sentence for fraud, pursuant to provisions. for prisoners serving determinate sentences of more than more than 10 years. The application was made to the Court of Appeal for the Human Rights Act, which has been struck down by the European Court of Justice. Four-year mandatory life prisoners were released after serving two-thirds of their sentence (section 33 of the 1991 Act). The applicant is now serving the equivalent of a determinate sentence of about five years, albeit in open conditions. The Secretary of State acknowledged in the proceedings that there was not a significant risk that the applicant would commit further violent offences, but asserted that he could lawfully detain a post-tariff mandatory life prisoner solely because there was a risk that he might commit further non-violent imprisonable offences. The imposition of what is in effect a substantial term of imprisonment by the exercise of executive discretion, without trial, lies uneasily with ordinary concepts of the rule of law. The House of Lords dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Court of Appeal's decision. Lord Steyn held that section 35(2) of the 1991 Act conferred a wide administrative discretion on the Secretary of State to decide upon the release on licence of mandatory life prisoners. He said there was no fundamental common-law principle of retributive proportionality which restrained him from detaining a mandatory life prisoner by reference to a risk that he may in future commit a serious but non-violent offence. He expressly repeated Lord Bingham's concern that the imposition of a substantial term of imprisonment by exercise of administrative discretion was hard to reconcile with ordinary concepts of the rule of law.

The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 29 May 2001 it was declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section, composed of the following judges: Mr J.-P. Costa, President, Mr W. Fuhrmann, Mr P. Kūris, Mrs F. Tulkens, Mr K. Jungwiert and Sir Nicolas Bratza. The applicant was convicted of murder in 1967. He was released on licence in April 1979. name: Necdet Bulut
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 77092/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Ms G. Altay, Mr Ü. Kuş and Mr H. Karakuş, lawyers practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 3 July 2003 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The Court informed the parties that in accordance with Article 29 §§ 1 and 3 it would decide on both the admissibility and merits of the Application. The applicant had a fracture of the fibula in his lower leg. A cap gun (a toy gun that creates a loud sound akin to a gunshot and a puff of smoke when the trigger is pulled) had been found in the applicant's possession. Forensic experts at the Istanbul Criminal Police Laboratory examined samples taken from the hands and palms of the applicant and the other suspects. They found no traces of gunpowder. The applicant claimed that he had started to run out of fear after he had heard gunshots nearby and that the police officers had beaten him when they caught him. The Istanbul State Security Court heard evidence from the suspects arrested at the same time as the applicant. The Kartal public prosecutor instigated an investigation into the incident. On 23 March 2001 he decided not to prosecute the eight police officers who took part in the incident on the ground that there was no evidence supporting the suspects' allegations that they had been ill-treated during arrest. The applicant's objection to this decision was dismissed by the Kadıköy Assize Court on 17 May 2001. The suspect's claim that he was injured as a result of the clash between the police officers and the suspects after the latter had responded to the officers' order to surrender by opening fire from the tent was dismissed. Some of the accused referred to hearing gunshots from a wedding nearby.

name: Fatma Tunç

name: Ali Başpınar
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court made the following decision. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way). The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court convicted the applicant of membership and of his illegal activities within the latter. It sentenced the applicant to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in the civil service and placed him under judicial guardianship. On 27 December 1995 the Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that the first instance court wrongly assessed the evidence before it. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the latter court.

The case originated in an application (no. 29280/95) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court ruled that the application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints (Rule 43 § 2). The Court ruled in favour of the applicant in this case. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. He was sentenced to life imprisonment, permanently debarred from employment in the civil service and placed under judicial guardianship. His case was automatically referred to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay). It quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that the first instance court wrongly assessed the evidence before it. It referred the case to the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi). The criminal proceedings are still pending.

name: Alfred Worm
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 4 July 1996 and by the Government of the Republic of Austria (‘the Government’) on 11 September 1996. It originated in an application (no. 22714/93) against Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by an Austrian national, Mr Alfred Worm, on 28 July 1993. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31). Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 April 1997. Court heard addresses by Mr Geus, Mr Masser and Mr Cede and also replies to its questions. The applicant, Mr Alfred Worm, is a journalist. Mr Androsch had been convicted by the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) of having made false statements as a witness on two occasions in 1989. The court found that he had wrongly stated that certain amounts of money had been put at his disposal by a Mr S., whereas in fact they had been transferred from anonymous bank accounts operated by his wife and himself. Hannes Androsch was convicted of having evaded taxes between 1973 and 1981. He was sentenced to a fine of 1.8 million Austrian schillings (ATS) The atmosphere during the trial was glacial. ‘Above all, there were to be no mistakes during the proceedings. The case was to be handled with common prudence, properly and to the best of our knowledge and belief – but not with kid gloves!’ – Mr Heinz Tschernutter, tax investigator and witness. On the day before the trial [the Austrian newspaper] Die Presse dropped the bombshell that was meant to shake all Austria. Lawyer Herbert Schachter was quoted as saying: ‘I’m sure that Dr Androsh will present his case in an impressive manner.’ Judge Zeilinger knows the file inside out, as was clear from each of his questions. The public prosecutor, Matousek, is able to find his way around in the dark generated by the ‘international legal adviser's’ murky financial deals. Anyone venturing into the maze of Androsch's accounts containing undeclared money is amazed by the structure's simplicity. It is not only wholly lacking in sophistication but is almost astoundingly crude. Crude not because Androsh lacked intelligence but rather because it was based on the cast-iron foundation of the misplaced loyalty of officials. While he was Finance Minister, until January 1981, he could rely on the zealous but unlawful obedience of a number of powerful officials. It has been known since 1980 that Androsch evaded taxes. Tax officials Walter Handerek, Heinz Tschernutter and Gerhard Berner were treated by defending counsel Herbert Schachter as though they were the accused rather than Androsh. The legal proceedings which were adjourned on Friday furnished further proof that for years the accused escaped prosecution thanks to the zealous obedience of officials. It is both symptomatic and revealing that ‘seven inspections’ had been carried out and on each occasion had found in his favour, and that it was very unfair that just the eighth inspection should shatter the ideal world of his illusory innocence. Androsch's defence in court was disgraceful. He either took refuge in lapses of memory or blamed his ‘adoptive father’ No new submissions were made in court – either as regards accounts containing undeclared money or as regards the funding for his villas. He paid less and less attention to the judge's questions and treated the public prosecutor with increasingly provocative contempt. He turned to look more and more often at the public in the gallery, seeking approval, and his gestures increasingly reminded one of the self-satisfied, powerful Vice-Chancellor and Finance Minister accustomed to talking politics. The judge forced himself to be polite even when he was clearly irritated by the defendant's bored self-assurance. Judge Zeilinger had prepared for this trial keenly and diligently. By citing facts he kept forcing Androsch into corners from which he could only escape by taking refuge in memory lapses. The defendant sensed weakness and made full use of his own – supposed – strength. He forged a link with the public while severing the one with the court. There comes a point in every trial after which the court expects some sign of understanding. It hopes for a trace of humility that may be appraised as a mitigating circumstance. But he has shown no humility to date, not even for a second. It is now for him to display greatness. The judicial system has uncovered serious matters. The article, unlike court reports of the scandal press, analysed the conduct of the presiding judge, the public prosecutor, defence counsel and in particular the accused, Mr Androsch. It appeared from the article that the applicant assumed that the investigations carried out by the tax authorities were correct. He subjected the statements made by the accused at the trial to a critical psychological analysis. However, his way of writing and the wording used were not capable of influencing these proceedings. Even to a lay judge,. the applicant's person and his activities as a journalist in the. Androschi case were well known. The Vienna Court of Appeal, sitting as a court of three professional judges on an appeal by the public. prosecutor, held a hearing in the presence of the applicant and his counsel. The court held that the offence defined in section 23 of the Media Act must be classified as a potentially endangering offence. The Court of Appeal also contested the Regional Court's assumption that everybody, including the lay judges, knew the applicant's long-standing commitment in the Androsch case and would therefore not be influenced by his article. It observed that ‘the objective element of the offence is constituted not only by unfavourable comment on evidence but also by favourable comment’. The full text of the judgment was served on the applicant on 25 March 1993 and the publishing firm was made jointly and severally liable for payment of the fine. The court found that the applicant's expertise and involvement in the subject matter rather reinforced the impression that he had written the article with the intention of influencing the outcome of the proceedings. From the beginning he had been convinced that Mr Androsch had committed tax evasion. In the article in issue he had not only criticised Mr Androshch's statement but had also anticipated the outcome. The judgment ended as follows: ‘Even the quotation of the answer given by Mr Heinz Tschernutter placed at the top of the article – ‘Above all, there were to be no mistakes during the proceedings’ – gives the average reader the impression the court was being advised and urged to follow the same approach.’

Judge Zeilinger knows the file inside out, as was clear from each of his questions. Anyone venturing into the maze of Androsch's accounts containing undeclared money is amazed by the structure's simplicity. It is not only wholly lacking in sophistication but is almost astoundingly crude. The alleged tax evasion was perhaps ‘long-term’ but by no means ‘ingenious and sophisticated’ The opposite was true: anyone venturing in the maze. It has been known since 1980 that Androsch evaded taxes. The tax officials Walter Handerek, Heinz Tschernutter and Gerhard Berner, who reopened the file between 1985 and 1988, were treated by defending counsel Herbert Schachter as though they were the accused rather than AndrosCh. He has in the meantime become so completely immersed in the role of the innocent victim that he cannot subjectively conceive of ever having been the guilty party. Androsch's defence in court was disgraceful; after so many years one would at least have expected properly constructed arguments. Each time Judge Zeilinger asked him a specific question he either took refuge in lapses of memory or blamed his ‘adoptive father’ He even trotted out the late Sir Arthur Stein, the explorer of the Silk Road, from whom he claims to have received a legacy. The court kept trying very gently to bring the defendant back down to earth from his long-winded waffling. And each time he replied ‘I can't say. After all, I do have other things to do’ Androsch succumbed to his own charm. Defence counsel interrupted the judge. He talked and talked, a volubility that the Kronen Zeitung mistook for ‘brilliant rhetoric’. In reality the defendant was distancing himself as much as possible from his own responsibility. Judge Zeilinger had prepared for this trial keenly and diligently. By citing facts he kept forcing Androsch into corners from which he could only escape by taking refuge in memory lapses. The article, unlike court reports of the scandal press, analysed the conduct of the presiding judge, the public prosecutor, defence counsel and in particular the accused, Mr Androsch, almost as a psychologist would have done. It appeared from the article that the applicant assumed that the investigations carried out by the tax authorities were correct. He subjected the statements made by the accused at the trial to a critical psychological analysis. However, his way of writing and the wording used were not capable of influencing these proceedings. The court found that it was clear for every reader, who was vaguely familiar with the issue, that. the applicant, who had been working for Profil for many years, had intensively dealt with the so-called ‘Causa AndrosCh’ and had frequently reported on it. The court held that the offence defined in section 23 of the Media Act must be classified as a potentially endangering offence. The Court of Appeal also contested the Regional Court's assumption that everybody, including the lay judges, knew the applicant's long-standing commitment in the Androsch case and would therefore not be influenced by his article. The full text of the judgment was served on the applicant on 25 March 1993. The court convicted the applicant of having exercised prohibited influence on criminal proceedings and imposed on him forty day-fines of ATS 1,200 each, that is ATS 48,000. The publishing firm was made jointly and severally liable for payment of the fine. The court found that the applicant's expertise and involvement in the subject matter rather reinforced the impression that he had written the article with the intention of influencing the outcome of the proceedings. He had researched into the case since 1978 and had written more than a hundred articles about it. From the beginning he had been convinced that Mr Androsch had committed tax evasion. In the article in issue he had not only criticised Mr Andosch's statement but had also anticipated the outcome. It was in no way certain that the lay judges regularly read Profil. On the contrary, in spectacular proceedings like the ones in issue, it happened frequently that lay judges would follow the reports in papers they did not usually read.

But he now has a few weeks to consider whether it is consonant with the principles of a State based on the rule of law for a Finance Minister and his family to have at their disposal accounts containing millions in undeclared funds. It is now for him to display greatness.‘In many major trials the sinner has been given a fair chance to the very end' The article, unlike court reports of the scandal press, analysed the conduct of the presiding judge, the public prosecutor, defence counsel and in particular the accused, Mr Androsch, almost as a psychologist would have done. It appeared from the article that the applicant assumed that the investigations carried out by the tax authorities were correct. He subjected the statements made by the accused at the trial to a critical psychological analysis. However, his way of writing and the wording used were not capable of influencing these proceedings. Even to a lay judge,. the applicant's person and his activities as a journalist in the AndrosCh case were well known. Thus he would not expect the applicant to give a neutral account. The court held that the offence defined in section 23 of the Media Act must be classified as a potentially endangering offence. The Court of Appeal also contested the Regional Court's assumption that everybody, including the lay judges, knew the applicant's long-standing commitment in the Androsch case and would therefore not be influenced by his article. The full text of the judgment was served on the applicant on 25 March 1993. The court convicted the applicant of having exercised prohibited influence on criminal proceedings and imposed on him forty day-fines of ATS 1,200 each, that is ATS 48,000. The publishing firm was made jointly and severally liable for payment of the fine. It was inferred from the article that the accused wished to usurp the position of the judges dealing with the case. There was no doubt that, at least with regard to the lay judges, the reading of the incriminated article was capable of influencing the outcome of the criminal proceedings. The court further found that the applicant's expertise and involvement in the subject matter rather reinforced the impression that he had written the article with the intention to influence the outcome. The judgment ended as follows: ‘Even the quotation of the answer given by Mr Heinz Tschernutter placed at the top of the article – ‘Above all, there were to be no mistakes during the proceedings’ – gives the average reader the impression the court was being advised and urged to follow the same approach’.

name: Oya Ataman
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 74552/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a lawyer and member of the administrative board of the Istanbul Human Rights Association, organised a demonstration in Sultanahmet Square in Istanbul, in the form of a march followed by a statement to the press. The police asked the group to disperse and to end the gathering, and informed them via a loudspeaker that the demonstration, for which advance notice had not been submitted, was unlawful. The demonstrators refused to obey and attempted to continue marching towards the police, who dispersed the group using a kind of tear gas known as “pepper spray” The police arrested thirty-nine demonstrators, including the applicant, and took them to a police station. After an identity check, and in view of her profession, the applicant was released. The application was made in June 2000 for the case to be set aside. The applicant applied to the Beyoğlu Assize Court seeking to have that decision set aside on the ground that no offence had been committed. The court upheld the decision that there was no case to answer on 25 September 2000. The application was rejected. The case was referred to the Turkish Supreme Court of Justice, which decided that it was not a case of unlawful arrest. The judge ruled that the applicant had not been unlawfully prevented from making the public statement scheduled for the end of the demonstration. The appeal was rejected on 30 June 2000, and the case was dismissed.

The applicant appealed again on 25 December 2000 and again the appeals were dismissed. The application was rejected on 25 November 2000 and on 25 March 2000 the appeal was upheld. The judge ruled that the applicant was not guilty.

name: Antun Petrovic
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 5 December 1996. It originated in an application (no. 20458/92) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by an Austrian national, Mr Antun Petrovic, on 3 August 1992. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 14 taken together with Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31) Antun Petrovic claimed a parental leave allowance (Karenzurlaubsgeld) in 1989. His claim was turned down by the local employment office on the ground that only mothers could claim such an allowance when a child was born. He appealed against that decision to the Vienna Regional Employment Office (Landesarbeitsamt) On 18 August 1989 he lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 October 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Marxer, Mr Laimer and Mr Okresek. The Constitutional Court declined to accept the complaint for adjudication on the ground that it did not have sufficient prospects of success. The court held that section 26(1) did not infringe the applicant’s constitutional rights and was not contrary to Article 8 or Article 12 of the Convention. It added that even if regard was had to recent statutory amendments (section 26 of the Unemployment Benefit Act had been amended by a federal law of 12 December 1989 – see paragraph 15 below) the applicant's complaint was unfounded, seeing that the legislature had a certain amount of time in which to adapt new rules to changes in society (Anpassung gesetzlicher Vorschriften an geänderte Verhältnisse).

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the monitoring of her telephone calls, e-mail correspondence and Internet usage under Articles 8 and 13. The Court declared the application partly admissible in March 2006. The Government stated that the monitoring consisted of analysis of the College telephone bills showing telephone numbers called, the dates and times of the calls, and their length and cost. The case was decided on 7 March 2006 and the verdict published on 11 March 2007. The decision has been appealed by the applicant and the Government. The appeal has been dismissed by the Court and the decision published on 9 March 2009. The Government accepted that this monitoring took the form of analysing the websites visited, the times and dates of the visits to the websites and their duration. The applicant did not comment on the manner in which her Internet usage was monitored but submitted that it took place over a much longer period of time than the Government had admitted. The Government submitted that the monitoring of telephone usage took place for a few months up to about 22 November 1999. She stated that on at least one occasion the DP became aware of the name of an individual with whom she had exchanged incoming and outgoing telephone calls. By an e-mail of 24 November 1999, the CP advised the applicant that the information technology department of the College was investigating only her e-mails. There was no policy in force at the College at the material time regarding the monitoring of telephone, e-mail or Internet usage by employees. The applicant was informed by other members of staff that between 1996 and late 1999 several of her activities had been monitored by the DP or those acting on his behalf. She further believed that the DP became aware of a legally privileged fax that was sent by herself to her solicitors. Her personal movements, both at work and when on annual or sick leave, were the subject of surveillance. The Court heard that the applicant provided the Court with statements from other staff alleging inappropriate and intrusive monitoring of their movements.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 9 September 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 15890/89) against Denmark lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Danish national, Mr Jens Olaf Jersild, on 25 July 1989. The object of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The hearing was to take place on 20 April 1994. The case was brought by a New York based human rights organisation, Human Rights Watch. The application was made by the applicant's lawyers and the Government. The hearing was adjourned until the next hearing on 15 April. It was to be heard by a Grand Chamber rather than a Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights. The decision was taken by the President of the Chamber, Mr Ryssdal, acting through the Registrar. The applicant’s lawyers were represented by Mr A. Philip. The Court was to hear the case for a period of three months. The outcome of the hearing was expected to be decided by the end of the third week of April. The Greenjackets case was heard at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 April 1994. Mr Jens Olaf Jersild, a Danish national, is a journalist and lives in Copenhagen. He was employed by Danmarks Radio (Danish Broadcasting Corporation), which broadcasts not only radio but also television programmes. In 1985 the newspaper Information published an article describing the racist attitudes of members of a group of young people, calling themselves “the GreenJackets’. In the light of this article, the editors of the Sunday News Magazine decided to produce a documentary on the Greenjacket group. Subsequently the applicant contacted representatives of the group, inviting three of them together with Mr Per Axholt, a social worker employed at the local youth centre, to take part in a television interview. During the interview, which was conducted by the applicant, the three Green Jackets said they were not racist. Interview lasted between five and six hours, of which between two and two and a half hours were video-recorded. Danmarks Radio paid the interviewees fees in accordance with its usual practice. applicant subsequently edited and cut the film of the interview down to a few minutes. The transcript of the Greenjackets item reads as follows: ‘It’s good being a racist. We believe Denmark is for the Danes.’ ‘I just ran into a petrol station with a ... gun and made them give me some money. Then I ran out again. That's all. I don’t wish to discuss that’. There are 20-25 young people from STUDSEN in the same group. They meet not far away from the public housing area near some old houses which are to be torn down. The group meet here to reaffirm among other things their racism, their hatred of immigrants and their support for the Ku Klux Klan. A nigger is not a human being, it’s an ape. People should be allowed to keep slaves, I think so anyway. There are many blacks, for example in the USA, who have important jobs. Of course, there is always someone who wants to show off, as if they are better than the white man, but in the long run, it's thewhite man who is better. Henrik is one of the strongest supporters of the Klan. He hates the foreign workers, 'Perkere' [a very derogatory word in Danish for immigrant workers]. They come up here, man, and sponge on our society. They get everything paid, and things like that, that can’t be right. Half of the prison population in ‘Vestre’ are in there because of drugs, half of those in Vestre prison anyway, they are the people who are serving animal. animal, that goes for all the other foreign workers as well, Turks, Yugoslavs and whatever they are called. They are the first on the housing list, they get better flats than us. Per Axholt, known as ‘Pax’ [(P)], is employed in the youth centre in Studsgårdsgade. He has worked there for several years, but many give up a lot sooner because of the tough environment. He feels that the reasons why the young people are persecuting the immigrants is that they are themselves powerless and disappointed. What do you think they would say that they want, if you asked them? (P) Just what you and I want. Some control over their lives, work which may be considered decent and which they like, a reasonable economic situation, a reasonably functioning family, a wife or a husband and some children. Germain 'Perkere' has been involved in crime since he was 14. He says he has had a criminal career since the age of 15 onwards. Says he has committed his first crime when he was just 14-years-old. Says the threat of imprisonment does not deter him from doing illegal activities. Says people don't fear jail because there are no bad consequences if they do it. Perkere says people are doing it because they have nothing better to do. "There has been pinching of videos, where the ‘Perkeres’ have been our customers, so they have money. If people want to be out here and have a nice time" Youths said they would like to move back to Studsgårdsgade where they grew up. They said they were released from prison the next day after causing trouble at the pub. The Bishop of Ålborg complained to the Minister of Justice. The Public Prosecutor instituted criminal proceedings in the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret) against the three youths interviewed by the applicant. They were charged with a violation of Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code (straffeloven) (see paragraph 19 below) for having made the statements cited below. “Just take a picture of a gorilla, man, and then look at a nigger, it’s. it s a gorilla.’ “ “... the Northern States wanted that the niggers should be free human beings, man. They are not human being, they are animals.” “ ... I just wouldn’t accept it, if she was mugging old women and stealing their handbags’ ‘A nigger is not a human being, it’s an animal, that goes for all the other foreign workers as well, Turks, Yugoslavs and whatever they are called.’ “It’�s drugs they are selling, man, half of the prison population in ‘Vestre’ are in there because of drugs ... they are the people who are serving time for dealing drugs ...“ “What we don’t like is when they walk around in those Zimbabwe-clothes and then speak this hula-hula language in the street ...’ The applicant was convicted of aiding and abetting the Greenjackets, as was the programme controller. The applicant and Mr Jensen appealed against the City Court’s judgment to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret) The applicant explained that, although he had suspected that the GreenJackets’ statements were punishable, he had refrained from omitting these from the programme, considering it a breach of Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code. The High Court ruled that the applicant had taken the initiative of making the television programme and that he had been well aware in advance that discriminatory statements of a racist nature were likely to be made. High Court dismissed appeal by five votes to one. Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in a judgment of 13 February 1989. The majority held: “The defendants have caused the publication of the racist statements made by a narrow circle of persons and thereby made those persons liable to punishment’. The dissenting member was of the view that, although the statements by the Greenjackets constituted offences under Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code, the applicant and Mr Jensen had not transgressed the bounds of the freedom of speech to be enjoyed by television and other media. Although it concerned a relatively small group of people holding extreme views, the programme had a fair degree of news and information value. The majority had attached importance to the fact that they had caused the racist statements to be made public. The applicant’s item had not been a direct report on a meeting. He had himself contacted the three youths and caused them to make assertions such as those previously made in Information. The statements would hardly have been punishable under Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code had they not been made to a wide circle (“videre kreds“) of people. Their news or information value was not such as to justify their dissemination and therefore did not warrant acquitting the defendants. I therefore vote in favour of the defendants’ acquittal. The minority, on the other hand, considered that the right to information overrode the interests protected by Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code. train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 32849/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of his detention on remand had been unreasonable. Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the unreasonable length of the applicant's pre-trial detention to the Government. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case was decided by the Court on 13 September 2005. The ruling was unanimous. The applicant and 15 co-accused were indicted before the Bielsko-Biała Regional Court on 22 November 2002. On 27 November 2002 the pre-trial detention of the applicant and 14 other persons was further extended. The first hearing was held on 13 November 2003. In total, the trial court held 36 hearings. The applicant's request of 5 May 2003 to lift his pre- Trial detention was dismissed on 9 June 2003. The Court of Appeal granted the application on 6 August 2003. On 17 December 2003 the Court ruled that it was still necessary to extend the detention on remand with respect to all the accused. The Bielsko-Biała Regional Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to 8 years' imprisonment. The applicant appealed against this decision, but it was dismissed on 21 July 2004. On 26 January 2006 the Katowice Court of Appeal upheld the judgment. It appears that the applicant did not lodge a cassation appeal. The judgment is final and the applicant is currently on remand in a Polish prison in Poland. The case is described as one of the most complex in the history of the country's legal system. The judge said that the case was complex because of the number of co-accused and the advanced stage of the proceedings.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 23883/06) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants alleged that their eviction from their flat following their refusal to remove a satellite dish resulted in violations of Articles 8 and 10 of the convention. The applicants were represented by Mr U. Isaksson, a lawyer practising in Stockholm, and by Ms S. Wikström, lawyers of the Stockholm Tenants' Association. The Swedish Government was represented by their Agent, Mr C.-H Ehrenkrona, Ministry for Foreign Affairs. Landlord initiated proceedings against applicants and other tenants who had installed satellite dishes in the same house. Landlord claimed that the applicants' satellite installation violated the express ban in Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. The applicants, as well as the other tenants summoned, contested the landlord's claims before the Rent Review Board. They stated that, by mounting satellite dishes for the reception of television programmes, some of which were broadcast in their mother tongues, they were exercising their freedom to receive information, as protected by the Swedish Constitution, Article 10 of the Convention and EC law. The new installation was, they claimed, in conformity with the rules. Landlord appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) The court held an oral hearing at which, inter alia, Mr Tornefelt gave evidence. It also made an inspection of the applicants' satellite installation. By a final decision of 20 December 2005, the court found that the applicants had disregarded their obligations as tenants, under the tenancy agreement and Chapter 12, section 25 of the Land Code, to such a degree that the agreement should not be extended. The only inconvenience for the landlord was the aesthetic aspect. The applicants' interest in being able to watch television programmes that were not accessible by other available means weighed more heavily. Landlord had made a reasonable distinction between acceptable and unacceptable satellite installations. Court found that the applicants' dish was virtually always positioned outside the kitchen window and thus constituted a permanent installation. Landlord offered the applicants the option of staying in their flat if they agreed to remove the satellite dish. They did not agree to do this, however, and instead moved on 1 June 2006. They have stated that, largely because of the scarcity of flats for rent in the Stockholm area but also due to there being a court eviction order against them, they were forced to move to Västerås, approximately 110 km west of Stockholm. Although their satellite installation did not pose any real safety threat, their interests could not be allowed to override the weighty and reasonable interest of the landlord.

The Rent Review Board gave a decision on 21 October 2004 finding in their favour. The landlord appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt). The court held an oral hearing at which, inter alia, Mr Tornefelt gave evidence. It also made an inspection of the applicants' satellite installation. By a final decision of 20 December 2005, the court found that the applicants had disregarded their obligations as tenants, under the tenancy agreement and Chapter 12, section 25 of the Land Code, to such a degree that the agreement should not be extended. The only inconvenience for the landlord was the aesthetic aspect. The applicants' interest in being able to watch television programmes not accessible by other available means weighed more heavily. Landlord had made a reasonable distinction between acceptable and unacceptable satellite installations. Court found that the applicants' dish was virtually always positioned outside the kitchen window and thus constituted a permanent installation. Landlord offered the applicants the option of staying in their flat if they agreed to remove the satellite dish. They did not agree to do this, however, and instead moved on 1 June 2006. The applicants' three children had had to change nursery and school and leave friends. They have stated that, largely because of the scarcity of flats for rent in the Stockholm area but also due to there being a court eviction order against them, they were forced to move to Västerås.

name: Geoffrey Robins
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 16 September 1996. It originated in an application (no. 22410/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and sought leave to present their own case. The President of the Chamber, Mr R. Bernhardt, declined to grant the requested leave and the applicants subsequently designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30 § 1). The Chamber was constituted on 17 September 1996 by ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality. The case involved a dispute between neighbours over sewerage. Mr and Mrs Robins won their case, but were not in receipt of legal aid. They requested a hearing to determine costs issues. The Chamber decided to dispense with a hearing in the case, having satisfied itself that the conditions for this derogation from its usual procedure had been met. The Government, applicants and Commission were invited to submit written comments on the matters raised in the memorials. The Registrar subsequently received letters from the Government’s Agent and the applicants’ solicitors on the subject, inter alia, of the claimants’ claims under Article 50 of the Convention. The applicants applied for legal aid in 1991. The court received a report from the LAB outlining events from the time the applicants first applied. This report was sent to the parties on 14 January 1992, when they were informed that the matter could be re-listed for hearing. A fresh Department of Social Security assessment of the applicants’ means was required in view of the fact that they had separated. The DSS later explained, in a letter filed with the court on 10 November 1992, that a delay of nine months had been caused because of a misapprehension in this respect. The restored hearing was held on 12–13 November 1992 before Judge Darwall-Smith. The applicants were requested to lodge the relevant documents by 2 May 1994. Extensions of this time-limit were granted on 25 April, 24 May, 16 June, 6 July and again on 27 July 1994 at the request of the applicants. It later transpired that Judge Clarke’s notes had been either lost or did not exist. On 6 October 1994, the applicants’ request that transcripts of the judgment of Judge Darwall-Smith be produced at public expense. Another extension of the time- limit for the submission of documents was granted on 16 February 1995. The application was listed for hearing on 29 March 1995. After the hearing on 19 June 1995, the Court of Appeal confirmed Judge Dar wall Smith's judgment of 13 November 1992 and dismissed the appeal.

name: Joseph Keegan
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 7 April 1993. It originated in an application (no. 16969/90) against Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 1 May 1990 by an Irish citizen, Mr Joseph Keegan. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 8 and/or 14. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr B. Walsh, the elected judge of Irish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 November 1993. The Registrar consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the procedure (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38) The Court heard addresses by Sir Basil Hall, Ms Browne and Mr Gleeson as well as replies to questions put by several of its members. The proceedings before the Circuit Court were heard before the European Court of Human Rights and were recorded. The application was brought by a man who claimed he was the father of a child adopted by his ex-girlfriend. The father applied to be appointed guardian under section 6A, sub-section 1, of the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964, which would have enabled him to challenge the proposed adoption. Pursuant to the Adoption Act 1952, an adoption order cannot be made, inter alia, without the consent of the child’s mother and the child's guardian. While a married man is a guardian of his children, an unmarried man is not unless so appointed by the court (see paragraphs 25 and 26 below). On 29 May 1989 the Circuit Court appointed the applicant guardian and awarded him custody. Mr Justice Barron of the High Court stated: “I am of the opinion that in considering the applications both for custody and guardianship I must have regard to circumstances as they presently exist’ Chief Justice Finlay stated that the High Court had incorrectly construed section 6A of the 1964 Act. He considered that the Act only gave the natural father a right to apply to be guardian. It did not equate his position with that of a married father. The first and paramount consideration in the exercise of the court’s discretion was the welfare of the child, and the blood link between child and father as merely one of the many relevant factors which may be viewed by the court as relevant to that question. The extent and character of the rights which accrue arising from the relationship of a father to a child to whose mother he is not married must vary very greatly, depending on the circumstances of each individual case. The High Court heard, inter alia, the evidence of a consultant child psychiatrist who considered that the child would suffer short-term trauma if moved to the applicant’s custody. The matter was then referred back to the High Court for the case to be decided in light of this interpretation. Mr Justice Barron recalled that the applicant wished bona fide to have custody of his daughter and that he felt the existence of an emotional bond. He had also noted that if the child remained with the adopters she would obtain the benefit of a higher standard of living and would be likely to remain at school longer. In his view “to do otherwise would be to favour the affluent as against the less well-off which does not accord with the constitutional obligation to hold all citizens as human persons equal before the law’ The father's desire to be involved in the guardianship of and to enjoy the society of his child is not a factor which I am to take into account. In these circumstances, the welfare of the infant requires her to remain in her present custody. Accordingly the application for relief must be refused.“An adoption order was subsequently made in respect of the child’s welfare,” the judge said. “The quality of welfare likely to be. achieved with the prospective adopters would not be to an important extent better than that likely to. be achieved by custody with the father. enumerated.” The judge added, “In my view these differences and the danger to her psychological health are of such an importance that I cannot hold that the quality of. welfare would be better’

The judge heard the evidence of the applicant and the Government. The father applied to be appointed guardian under section 6A, sub-section 1, of the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964. He also applied for custody of the child. Pursuant to the Adoption Act 1952, an adoption order cannot be made, inter alia, without the consent of the mother and the child’s guardian. The High Court found in July 1989 that the applicant was a fit person to beappointed guardian and that there were no circumstances involving the child which required that the father's rights be denied. He had also noted that if the child remained with the adopters she would obtain the benefit of a higher standard of living and would be likely to remain at school longer. An adoption order was subsequently made in respect of the child. The application for relief must be refused. The welfare of the infant requires her to remain in her present custody. In these circumstances, the baby's welfare is of such importance that the adoption order must be rejected. The father's wish and desire to be involved in the guardianship of and to enjoy the society of his child is not a factor which I am to take into account. The Adoption Act 1952 says an adoption order cannot be made, inter alia, without the consent of the mother and the guardian. Chief Justice Finlay ruled that the High Court had incorrectly construed section 6A of the 1964 Act. He considered that the Act only gave the natural father a right to apply to be guardian. The first and paramount consideration in the exercise of the court’s discretion was the welfare of the child. “... although there may be rights of interest or concern arising from the blood link between the father and the child, no constitutional right to guardianship in the father of theChild exists,” he said. He concluded that: ‘... regard should not be had to the objective of satisfying the wishes and desires of the father to be involved in the guardianship of’ The High Court resumed its examination of the case in early 1990. It heard, inter alia, the evidence of a consultant child psychiatrist who considered that the child would suffer short-term trauma if moved to the applicant’s custody. The matter was then referred back to the High Court for the case to be decided in light of this interpretation. He had also noted that if the child remained with the adopters she would obtain the benefit of a higher standard of living and would be likely to remain at school longer. But he considered that differences springing solely from socio-economic causes should not be taken into account where one of the claimants is a natural parent. An adoption order was subsequently made in respect of the child. In these circumstances, the welfare of the infant requires her to remain in her present custody. Accordingly the application for relief must be refused.“The father’s wish and desire to be involved in the guardianship of and to enjoy the society of his child is not a factor which I am to take into account.” “I cannot hold that the quality of welfare likely to be. achieved with the prospective adopters would not be to an important extent better than that likely to. be achieved by custody with the father.’ “ “

name: Vincent Kelly
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30054/96) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants, next-of-kin of nine men killed during a security force operation at Loughgall on 8 May 1987, alleged that their relatives had been kill unjustifiably. They invoked Articles 2, 6, 14 and 13 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of Jordan v. the United UK ( no. 24746/94) and McKerr v the United. Kingdom (No. 28883/95) The application was brought by the. Human Rights Commission on 23 March 2000, which. had been given leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure (Article 36. § 2 of the Convention and Rule 61. § 3). A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building on 4 April 2000. The applicants accepted that the summaries below are an accurate reflection of the written. statements made by the official personnel involved, without making. any admission as to the credibility, consistency and veracity of these statements. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Korff. The RUC station, which operated on a part-time basis only, was opened as normal at 9 a.m. on 8 May 1987. Three armed men who said they were from the IRA entered the house of the Mackle family in Aghinlig Upper, Dungannon. At about 6.30 p.m., a vehicle pulled up outside and a fourth man arrived. It appears that a bomb containing 300 to 400 pounds of explosives was prepared in the yard of the house and placed in the bucket of the digger. The owner, Mr McGrath, waited four hours and reported the incident to Coalisland RUC at approximately 6.50 p.M. The incident at Loughgall took place on Sunday, August 7. The soldiers reported a number of sightings of the blue Hiace van passing in front of the RUC station in both directions. Reports that the van had been hijacked, and that a digger was acting suspiciously in the area, were also received. Given this information and the knowledge that diggers had been used in previous terrorist attacks, the soldiers were on full alert when, between 7.15 and 7.30 p.m., the blue van came from the LoughGall direction and parked outside the station on the far side of the road facing Armagh. A man, dressed in blue overalls and wearing a balaclava, emerged from the rear of the van and began to walk into the roadway. Soldiers A, B, D and E moved towards the front of the RUC station and continued to fire at the men near the van. Constables B and C were led outside by Constable A and Soldier C, who administered first aid to them. Soldier F also left the station by the rear and did not take any part in the shooting. Soldiers K and R observed what they thought was a gunman lying in the grass behind the police station. He failed to stand up when challenged to do so, and both soldiers fired several rounds at what turned out to be a large lump of wood. Soldier V saw something in his hand which he regarded as an immediate threat and fired two bursts from his rifle until the man fell. The bodies were wearing blue boiler suits except where specified otherwise. The first body (Patrick Kelly) was found lying on his back still moving. Soldier X checking the body found that the man was holding a cigarette lighter. There were two significantly bullet damaged vehicles, a blue Toyota Hiace van (with approximately 125 bullet holes in the bodywork) and a white Citroen car with approximately 34 bullet holes. In the vicinity of the junction of Clovenden Road/Ballygasey Road there were bullet damaged Vauxhall Cavalier and Ford estate cars. The scene can be described as follows: Red Sierra 15 metres from position 6, blue Escort about 70 metres from the scene which was empty and white Sierra, with three female occupants. Post mortem examination revealed at least a dozen wounds to the torso and head. There were four loaded rifles and one shotgun found in the van. The pathologist observed at least twenty separate missile wounds (i.e. bullet and fragment) and found that discharge abrasion on an entry wound on the front of the neck indicated that when the gun was discharged the muzzle was within several feet of the body, probably while it was lying on the ground. The sixth body (Eugene Kelly), which had massive head damage and multiple injuries elsewhere, was seated in the driver seat. There was a revolver lying between the driver’s seat and his door. The seventh body was not wearing a boiler suit and there was a cigarette lighter close to the right hand. The body of Antony Hughes was found in the driver's seat of a white Citroen car. The body was not wearing a boiler suit. The post mortem examination showed twenty-nine wounds (bullet and shrapnel) The firearms used by Soldiers A to X were delivered the following day to the Northern Ireland Forensic Science Laboratory for examination. In total, 678 spent cartridge cases were recovered, 78 of which were from IRA weapons. The DPP concluded that the evidence did not warrant the prosecution of any person involved in the shootings. The inquest was adjourned on 6 September 1990, pending the determination of the Devine case, before the Court of Appeal (and subsequently the House of Lords) The inquest into the deaths of the men in the present case was opened on 30 May 1995 in public before a Coroner and a jury of 10 members. The RUC and Ministry of Defence were represented. On the first day of the inquest, counsel representing the families of six out of the nine deceased sought for the statements of prospective witnesses to be made available to them. This request was refused. On 31 May 1995 the families withdrew from the hearing to seek a remedy by way of judicial review. This step was taken because it was felt “utterly impossible for the applicants’ interests to be fairly or adequately represented”. All nine men died from serious and multiple gun shot wounds. Family of Declan Arthurs sought judicial review of the Coroner’s decisions not to allow the legal representatives to see witness statements before they gave evidence. The judge placed considerable emphasis on the character of an inquest as a fact finding exercise and not a method of apportioning guilt. None of the soldiers appeared but their statements were lodged. Mr Justice McCollum in the High Court refused to quash the coroner's decisions or the jury verdict. No further steps were taken to pursue the proceedings by the family of Kevin Antony McKearney. The family of Antony Hughes settled proceedings for 100,000 pounds sterling.

The case originated in an application (no. 30054/96) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants were next-of-kin of nine men killed during a security force operation at Loughgall on 8 May 1987.
