train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5989/03) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that civil proceedings initiated by her had not been determined within a reasonable time. The Court declared the application admissible in September 2005. The case was assigned to the newly constituted Fifth Section of the Court on 1 April 2006. The judge said that the case could not be decided on the merits. The court ruled in favour of the applicant and the Government filed observations on the merit of their case. The decision was handed down at the end of February 2006. The applicant claimed compensation for her medical costs, loss of working capacity and disablement. She accused the County of Frederiksborg (Frederiksborg Amt) of being responsible for the hospital. The applicant was awarded anticipatory pension at some time during 1994. The City Court of Hillerød set the case down for trial in 1995. The case was re-submitted to the Medico‑Legal Council on 17 June 1994 with further questions. The Medico-Legal Council submitted their opinion to the National Board of Health on 10 October 1994. On 5 March 1993 the applicant's complaint was sent for preliminary examination. The National Patients' Complaints Board found against the applicant in February 1994. The City Court asked the parties what was upholding the case on 16 May 1995. The parties did not reply within three weeks. The applicant's pleading no. 1 was filed on 9 April 1996, following which the court ordered that the applicant's counsel file a pleading within fourteen days. The City Court agreed to draft questions to the Medico-Legal Council, when the material was available. In October 1996 the parties informed the City Court of their intentions anew to put questions before the medico-legal council. Thus, the parties requested an adjournment of the proceedings. The case was adjourned until the end of May 1996. It was decided that the case would go to trial in June 1996. The case was brought before a dental specialist and the National Board of Industrial Injuries. The case was adjourned until after the European Court of Justice ruled. The City Court ordered the counsel to file a pleading by 21 October 1998. The final claim amounted to 908,996 Danish kroner (DKK) The case has been referred to as the 'Danish Case' by the World Health Organisation (WHO) The hearing was re-scheduled for 21 August 1998 and the claim was submitted a few days later. The hearing also discussed whether to hold a separate hearing of parts of the case and adjourn other parts while awaiting a preliminary ruling from the EU. The applicant's amended claim amounted to DKK 908,583 in compensation. She waived her request for having part of the case heard separately in order to await the ruling of the European Court of Justice. The City Court found that a basis of liability existed, and that compensation could be granted for the pain, but not for the applicant's reduced ability to open her mouth. The trial was held on 22 and 23 February 1999 and the case was set down for judgment. The National Board of Industrial Injuries issued their opinion on 13 January 2000. She resumed work on 4 July 2000 on a part-time basis, although still reduced compared to normal. The case was heard in the City Court in August 2000. The applicant was granted compensation in the amount of DKK 676,900. The defendant was ordered to pay the applicant's costs and expenses. The County of Frederiksborg appealed against the judgment to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret). The parties entered a friendly settlement in November 2002. The High Court ordered that each party should pay their own costs. According to Danish law it is not a requirement for instituting civil court proceedings that administrative appeal proceedings have been exhausted beforehand, unless specifically provided. A Supreme Court judgment printed in the Weekly Law Review (Ugeskrift for Retsvæsen), 2005, page 2390, concerned a patient who died due to cancer. Surviving spouse claims compensation for pain and suffering, loss of working capacity, and loss of dependency. to medical malpractice. Without pursuing the case before any administrative bodies, the surviving spouse brought an action directly before the City Court, claiming compensation for compensation for injury, suffering, and for permanent injury. The case is still ongoing and is expected to be heard again in early 2018. The hearing will be held at the City and County Court in London on Tuesday. name: Jean-Marie Colombani
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 51279/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Two French nationals, Mr Jean-Marie Colombani and Mr Eric Incyan, and the company Le Monde (‘the applicants’) alleged a violation of their freedom of expression. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The Government, but not the applicants, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The European Commission requested the Observatoire géopolitique des drogues to prepare a report on drug production and trafficking in Morocco. The Commission asked the Observatory for a revised version of the report, with the names of the drug traffickers deleted. The report contained twelve chapters with the following titles. It related how, over a period of ten years, there had been a tenfold increase in the area of land that had historically been used for cannabis production in the region of Er Rif. Current levels of production made “the sharif kingdom a serious contender for the title of the world’s leading exporter of cannabis”. The article in Le Monde was relatively short (it ran to some thirty or so lines in two columns), but gave details of the confidential report. Le Monde published a report commissioned by the European Union in 1994. The King of Morocco asked for criminal proceedings to be instituted against Le Monde. Mr Colombani, the editor-in-chief, and Mr Incyan, the author of the article, were summoned to appear in the Paris Criminal Court on charges of insulting a foreign head of State. The court found that the journalist had merely quoted extracts from what was undisputedly a reliable report, without distorting or misinterpreting it or making groundless attacks. In a judgment of 6 March 1997, the Paris Court of Appeal, while recognising that ‘in just a few years Morocco has become the world’s leading cannabis exporter, accepted that he had acted in good faith and was acquitted’ The Court of Appeal noted that the journalist had not shown that he had ‘contacted any Moroccan dignitaries, officials, public authorities or services for an explanation for the failure to match words with deeds’ The applicants were found guilty of insulting a foreign head of State and sentenced to fines of 5,000 French francs (FRF) each. They were ordered to pay King Hassan II, who had successfully applied to be joined as a civil party to the proceedings, FRF 1 in damages and FRF 10,000 pursuant to Article 475-1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court of appeal also ordered Le Monde to make additional reparation in the form of a report publishing details of the convictions. Court of Appeal found that the charge of duplicity had been repeated twice and that the insistence on drawing the reader’s attention to the King in person, in an article that portrayed Morocco as the world's leading hashish exporter, was tainted with malicious intent. Court of Appeal had found that ‘pernicious statements had been made to dramatic effect solely in order to preserve the country’S image’ ‘‘The charge that pernicious. statements were made to Dramatic effect solely to preserve [Moroccan] image was a false charge,’’ said the court of appeal.

name: Christina Riepl
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37040/02) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two Austrian nationals, Franz and Christina Riepl (‘the applicants’), were represented by Mr H. Blum, a lawyer practising in Linz. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) was represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Departement at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The application for a double garage in Freistadt, Germany, was dismissed in 2002. The Municipal Council quashed the building permit of 16 August 1994 and remitted the case back to the Mayor of Freistsadt. The applicant agreed to pay the fees incurred by the applicants’ representation in the proceedings so far, on the condition that they amended their request for a building permit in accordance with the newly established building scheme (Bebauungsplan) The application was granted on 28 March 2002 after the applicants submitted the corrected plans for the double garage with a parking area. The application has since been approved.

They applied for a building permit for an adjoining building with a garage on their property. name: Bogusław Kijowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33829/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the domestic authorities had failed to take effective steps to enforce his right to respect for his family life in respect of his two sons. The application was given priority by the President of the Fourth Section, who gave notice of the application to the Government. The Government submitted that the child's psychological problems had been caused by the trauma of being kidnapped by his father. The case was decided on the merits of the case at the same time as its admissibility. In August 2003 the applicant's wife informed the prosecutor that her son had been kidnapped by the applicant. In May 2004 the parties and A were examined by experts from the RODK (Regional Family Consultation Centre) Their opinion was that A should live with his mother, although the applicant should enjoy extensive contact rights. The Government submitted that the applicant had been hindering her contact with A; the applicant denied this. In November 2004 the court changed its decision of 19 November 2003 and made a residence order for A. The applicant was granted contact rights and was ordered to return the child to his wife. On 8 March 2007 the applicant was arrested. A was kept by the applicant in spite of the final judgment of 30 June 2006 and the previous order of 22 November 2004. The applicant and his mother were found guilty of keeping A with them, in breach of domestic decisions. On 4 December 2009 the Krakow Regional Court quashed that judgment. It appears that the proceedings are pending before the trial court. A ran away from his mother's house in March 2008 and went to his father's house, located 100 kilometres away. The child stated that he preferred to live with his father and that his mother had been threatening him and had forbidden him to call his father. On 1 April 2008 A joined his father in Kraków. The child apparently felt that he had been treated differently from his brother B and that his mother had threatened that he would be taken to a children's home. The court did not consider that there was enough evidence to issue an interim order changing the earlier decision of A's place of residence before the case was ready for a decision on the merits. An appeal by the applicant against this decision was dismissed on 20 July 2009. On 15 February 2010 the Kraków District Court allowed the applicant's request of 8 April 2008, granted him full parental responsibility and ordered A's return to his mother's care. The RODK ruled that the best interests of A required that the residence order be changed to allow A to live with the applicant. The case involved a Polish father and his two children. The court banned all contact between the applicant and his younger son. The father appealed against the decision, but the appeal was dismissed. A further appeal against the latter decision was dismissed on 20 July 2010 by the Tarnów Regional Court. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court of Poland, which will decide whether or not to uphold the decision of the Dąbrowa Tarnowska District Court to ban all contact with the applicant's younger son, B. The decision is expected to be made within two months. The applicant is the father of a seven-year-old boy called A.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a Polish national, Mr Bogusław Kijowski. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the domestic authorities had failed to take effective steps to enforce his right to respect for his family life in respect of his two sons, as guaranteed by Article 8 of the Agreement. The application was granted legal aid, and the applicant was represented by Mr Z. Cichoń, a lawyer practising in Krakow. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In August 2003 the applicant's wife informed the prosecutor that her son had been kidnapped by the applicant. In May 2004 the parties and A were examined by experts from the RODK (Regional Family Consultation Centre) Their opinion was that A should live with his mother, although the applicant should enjoy extensive contact rights. The Government submitted that the applicant had been hindering her contact with A; the applicant denied this. On 22 November 2004 the court changed its decision of 19 November 2003 and made a residence order for A with the applicant’s wife. The applicant was granted contact rights and was ordered to return the child to his wife. Subsequently, the applicant attempted to visit B; but his wife apparently hindered his contact with his younger son. The child ran away from his mother's house in March 2008 and went to his father's house 100 kilometres away. The applicant took him to the police station and A was returned to his mother. On 1 April 2008 A ran away again and joined his father in Kraków. They have been living together since then. The child stated that he preferred to live with his father and that his mother had been threatening him and had forbidden him to call his father. The court dismissed the applicant's request for an interim order changing the child's place of residence (o zabezpieczenie wniosku) On 4 December 2009 the Krakow Regional Court quashed that judgment. The child had been living with the applicant from August 2003 to March 2007 and since April 2008. The court did not consider that there was enough evidence to issue an interim order changing the earlier decision of A's place of residence before the case was ready for a decision on the merits. On 15 February 2010 the Kraków District Court allowed the applicant's request of 8 April 2008, granted him full parental responsibility and ordered A's return to his mother's home. The opinion was finally submitted to the court on 16 December 2009. The experts took into account the feelings and choices made by A and the family situation characterised by a prolonged conflict between his parents. The court considered that A's negative attitude towards his mother, which manifested itself during the period when he was under her care in 2007, had been caused by the lengthy period of total deprivation of any contact between them. The court concluded that the best interests of the child required all contact between him and the applicant to cease. The applicant appealed against this decision, but on 11 June 2010 the Dabrowa Tarnowska District Court rejected the appeal for failure to lodge it in accordance with formal requirements, namely by lodging it out of time. A further appeal against the latter decision was dismissed on 20 July 2010 by the Tarnów Regional Court.

The Government submitted that the applicant had been hindering her contact with A; the applicant denied this. On 22 November 2004 the court changed its decision of 19 November 2003 and made a residence order for A. The applicant was granted contact rights and was ordered to return the child to his wife. However, the applicant failed to comply with this decision and refused to return A. On 8 March 2007 the applicant was arrested. The child ran away from his mother's house in March 2008 and went to his father's house, located 100 kilometres away. The applicant took him to the police station and A was returned to his mother. On 1 April 2008 A ran away again and joined his father in Kraków. The child stated that he preferred to live with his father and that his mother had been threatening him and had forbidden him to call his father. The court dismissed the applicant's request for an interim order changing the child's place of residence (o zabezpieczenie wniosku) on 14 April 2008. On 4 December 2009 the Krakow Regional Court quashed that judgment. The court established that A had had de facto residence with the applicant between August 2003 and March 2007 and since April 2008. The court did not consider that there was enough evidence to issue an interim order changing the earlier decision of A's place of residence before the case was ready for a decision on the merits. An appeal by the applicant against this decision was dismissed on 20 July 2009. On 15 February 2010 the Kraków District Court allowed the applicant's request of 8 April 2008, granted him full parental responsibility and ordered A's return to his mother. The opinion was finally submitted to the court on 16 December 2009. According to the experts the best interests of A required that the residence order be changed. The court considered that A's negative attitude towards his mother, which manifested itself during the period when he was under her care in 2007, had been caused by the lengthy period of total deprivation of any contact between them. The court concluded that the best interests of the child required all contact between him and the applicant to cease. The applicant appealed against this decision, but on 11 June 2010 the Dabrowa Tarnowska District Court rejected the appeal for failure to lodge it in accordance with formal requirements, namely by lodging it out of time. A further appeal against the latter decision was dismissed on 20 July 2010 by the Tarnów Regional Court.
eval_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 33829/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the domestic authorities had failed to take effective steps to enforce his right to respect for his family life in respect of his two sons. The Government submitted that the child's psychological problems had been caused by the trauma of being kidnapped by his father. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1). The President also gave priority to the application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. In August 2003 the applicant's wife informed the prosecutor that her son had been kidnapped by the applicant. The Government submitted that the applicant had been hindering her contact with A; the applicant denied this. In May 2004 the parties and A were examined by experts from the RODK (Regional Family Consultation Centre) Their opinion was that A should live with his mother, although the applicant should enjoy extensive contact rights. In November 2004 the court changed its decision of 19 November 2003 and made a residence order for A. The applicant was granted contact rights and was ordered to return the child to his wife. In December 2004 the Brzesko District Court dismissed his action contesting his paternity of B. Subsequently, the applicant attempted to visit B but his wife apparently hindered his contact with his younger son. The child ran away from his mother's house and went to his father's house, 100 kilometres away. The applicant took him to the police station and A was returned to his mother. On 1 April 2008 A ran away again and joined his father in Kraków. The child stated that he preferred to live with his father and that his mother had been threatening him and had forbidden him to call his father. The court dismissed the applicant's request for an interim order changing the child's place of residence (o zabezpieczenie wniosku) on 14 April 2008. On 4 December 2009 the Krakow Regional Court quashed that judgment. The court established that A had had de facto residence with the applicant between August 2003 and March 2007 and since April 2008. The child obviously had a stronger attachment to his father. The court did not consider that there was enough evidence to issue an interim order changing the earlier decision of A's place of residence before the case was ready for a decision on the merits. An appeal by the applicant against this decision was dismissed on 20 July 2009. On 15 February 2010 the Kraków District Court allowed the applicant's request of 8 April 2008, granted him full parental responsibility and ordered A's return to his mother. The opinion was finally submitted to the court on 16 December 2009. The court considered that A's negative attitude towards his mother, which manifested itself during the period when he was under her care in 2007, had been caused by the lengthy period of total deprivation of any contact between them. The court concluded that the best interests of the child required all contact between him and the applicant to cease. The applicant appealed against this decision, but on 11 June 2010 the Dabrowa Tarnowska District Court rejected the appeal for failure to lodge it in accordance with formal requirements. A further appeal against the latter decision was dismissed on 20 July 2010 by the Tarnów Regional Court. The judge found that the applicant had never wanted his second child, contested his paternity of him and had seen B only twice: once after B's birth in 2003.

name: Lech Majewski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 52690/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Mr Lech Majewski alleged that upon his arrival in the Białystok Remand Centre, on 14 December 1989, he had been beaten and insulted by the prison guards. The applicant claimed that in consequence of the excessive use of force against him he had sustained a spinal injury and suffered permanent disability. On 24 August 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant lodged a civil action for compensation against the State Treasury- Szczecin Remand Centre in 1991. He claimed PLN 2,500 in compensation for an accident which had occurred in 1983, during his detention. The applicant complained that the medical treatment he had received at the material time had been inadequate. The State Treasury appealed the judgment, which was quashed and dismissed the applicant’s action. The application was returned to the Białystok Regional Court, which decided that it was competent to deal with the case. The case was adjourned until 2001, when the applicant appealed the decision again. The applicant lodged a complaint alleging that his right to have his case examined within a reasonable time had been breached. He had lodged a civil action on 28 January 1991 and despite the fact that he had not contributed to their length, the proceedings were still pending before the District Court. The applicant relied on the 2004 Act on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within areasonable time. The court examined only the course of the proceedings after the remittal of the case by the appellate court on 13 November 2002 and found no delays. As result, the court found that during this period the District court had not violated the applicant’s right tohave his case heard. be obtained. The case was heard in the Szczecin Regional Court between 24 May 1991 and 14 May 2002. The case was transferred to the District Court during the period between that time and the present. The judge ruled that the Regional Court was not entitled to examine the course of the proceedings in the case. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the case had not been heard in a reasonable time. The court said that the civil proceedings in this case are pending before the Sz czecin District Court. The appeal was denied and the case was dismissed by the judge on the basis that it had been heard over a period of more than a year.

The case originated in an application (no. 52690/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant claimed that upon his arrival in the Białystok Remand Centre, on 14 December 1989, he had been beaten and insulted by the prison guards and had subsequently not received proper medical care. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent Mr. J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant filed a civil action for compensation against the State Treasury- Szczecin Remand Centre. He claimed PLN 2,500 in compensation for an accident which had occurred in 1983, during his detention. The applicant’s court-appointed lawyer refused to lodge a cassation appeal against this judgment on his behalf as he apparently found no legal grounds for it. The application was settled by the Białystok Regional Court, which awarded him compensation but dismissed the rest of his claims for compensation. The case was adjourned until 2001, when the applicant was released from prison. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal in 1998. The applicant lodged a complaint alleging that his right to have his case examined within a reasonable time had been breached. He submitted that he had lodged a civil action on 28 January 1991 and despite the fact he had not contributed to their length, the proceedings were still pending before the District Court. According to the 2004 Act the Regional Court – being the court above the one conducting the impugned proceedings - was competent to examine the complaint. The court examined only the course of the proceedings after the remittal of the case by the appellate court on 13 November 2002 and found no delays on the part of the District court. As result, the court found that during this period the applicant’s right to be heard had not been violated. The case was heard at the Szczecin Regional Court between 24 May 1991 and 14 May 2002. The case was transferred to the Regional Court during that period. The applicant complained that the proceedings before the District Court exceeded a reasonable time. The Regional Court was not entitled to examine the course of the proceedings in this case before it. It appears that the civil proceedings are pending before the Sz czecin District Court. The application has now been thrown out of court by the High Court of Poland. The High Court has ruled that the case should not have been heard by the Regional court in the first place. The appeal is expected to be heard again in May 2015.

name: Duncan Lustig-Prean
train_texts: The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy on the sole ground that they are homosexual constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Commission decided to adjourn the applications pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) pursuant to Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome by the English High Court on the question of the applicability of the Council Directive on the Implementation of the Principle of Equal Treatment for Men and Women. The application for legal aid was made under Protocol No. 11, which came into force on 1 November 1998. On 13 July 1998 the High Court delivered its judgment withdrawing its reference of the above question given the decision of the ECJ in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins (13 July 1998). On 4 May 1999 the President of the Chamber decided to grant Mr Lustig-Prean legal aid. The hearing in this case took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 May 1999. The Court heard addresses by D. Pannick QC, Mr J. Bowers QC, and Ms H. Larter, Solicitors. The first applicant joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. He became a midshipman in the executive branch of the navy in 1983. His evaluation of November 1989 noted that he was an officer with “great potential” In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. In early June 1994 he was informed that the RN Special Investigations Branch (“the service police”) had been given his name anonymously in connection with an allegation of homosexuality and was investigating the matter. The applicant was interviewed on 13 June 1994 by personnel from the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately twenty minutes. The applicant’s commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000) His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. Mr Beckett (the second applicant) joined the Royal Navy, enlisting for twenty-two years’ service. In 1991 he became a substantive weapons engineering mechanic. In 1994 the Admiralty Board informed the applicant that it had decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995.  applicant was interviewed by the service police in May 1993. He admitted his homosexuality to the chaplain and was cautioned in the same terms as the first applicant. He was told he would not be questioned on the above admissions prior to a search of his locker. During the search, slides (of himself, his partner and some of his service friends) and personal postcards were seized. The applicant was then questioned about his first and current homosexual relationship which began in December 1992. Details were sought as to how and what he did when he realised he was homosexual and, in this respect, he was asked what sort of feelings he had for a man. He later clarified that he first had “niggling doubts” about his sexual orientation approximately two and a half years previously. The service police report completed after the applicant’s interview included several internal documents where it was noted that the applicant, in openly declaring his homosexuality and his relationship with a civilian, had effectively disposed “of any immediate potential security concern” For that reason, it was considered in the report that “no cause was identified for conducting a security interview with Beckett” That report also accepted that a case for fraudulent entry into the armed forces would be inappropriate given the date when the applicant had discovered his homosexuality. The applicant completed his duties and remained in communal sleeping accommodation with no reported difficulties. The applicants’ judicial review proceedings (R.C. v. Ministry of Defence, ex parte Smith and Others 2 Weeky Law Reports 305) were successful. Lord Justice Simon Brown gave the main judgment of the court. He found that in none of the cases before him was it suggested that the applicants’ sexual orientation had in any way affected their ability to carry out their work or had any ill-effect on discipline. He considered that the balance of argument clearly lay with the applicants. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise” Simon Brown LJ said the courts owe a duty to remain within their constitutional bounds and not trespass beyond them. He emphasised that, even where the most fundamental human rights were being restricted, “the threshold of unreasonableness is not lowered’ He found that the Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and that the domestic courts could not rule on Convention matters. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals in the armed forces. A brief analysis of the Convention’s case-law led the judge to comment that he strongly suspected that, as far as the United Kingdom’�s obligations were concerned, the days of the policy were numbered. In August 1995 a consultation paper was circulated by the Ministry of Defence to “management’ levels in the armed forces relating to the policy against homosexuals in those forces. The applicants in the judicial review proceedings had argued that the MoD’s position was “bereft of factual evidence’. On 3 November 1995 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment. He considered that the court may not interfere with the exercise of an administrative discretion on substantive grounds save where the court is satisfied that the decision is unreasonable in the sense that it is beyond the range of responses open to a reasonable decision- maker. The case concerned innate qualities of a very personal kind, that the decisions of which the applicants complained had had a profound effect on their careers and prospects. The greater the policy content of the decision and the more remote the subject matter of a decision from ordinary judicial experience, the more hesitant the court had to be in holding a decision to be irrational. The Master of the Rolls concluded that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed in this case. Henry LJ of the Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls. He questioned the utility of a debate as to the likely fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights. He also found that the Equal Treatment Directive did not apply to complaints in relation to sexual orientation. Thorpe LJ agreed with both preceding judgments and, in particular, with the views expressed on the rationality test to be applied and on its application in the particular case. It was important to highlight this point since Parliament had not given the domestic courts primary jurisdiction over human rights issues contained in the Convention. In December 1995 Mr Lustig-Prean issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination contrary to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. Those proceedings were adjourned pending the above-described application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords. In December 1997 Mr Beckett also issued proceedings claiming sexual discrimination Contrary to the 1975 Act. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the withdrawal of those proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed by the Industrial tribunal. The applicants’ Industrial Tribunal proceedings can be found at: http://www.justgiving.com/case/LustigPrean-Beckett-Sexually-Discriminatory-Discrimination.

The case originated in two applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy on the sole ground that they are homosexual constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention. The applications were joined to two similar applications (nos. 33985/96 and 33986/96, Smith v. the United UK and Grady v the United Kingdom). The Government, represented by Mr M. Eaton and, subsequently, by Mr C. Whomersley, both Agents, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, submitted their observations on 17 October 1997, to which the applicants replied on 20 November and 8 December 1997, respectively. After Protocol No. 11 entered into force on 1 November 1998. the Commission granted Mr Beckett legal aid. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 May 1999. The Court heard addresses by Mr Pannick and Mr Eadie. The Circumstances of the case can be found at: http://www.courts.org.uk/cases/Beckett-Lustig-Prean- v. European Commission of Human Rights (ECJ v. Beckett) (Case No. 1 of 1998) (For. more details, see: http: //www.champions.org/Human-Rights-Case-No.1 of 1998/Becket-L Lustig- prean-v.ECJ. In June 1994 the applicant was informed that the Royal Navy Special Investigations Branch (“the service police”) had been given his name anonymously in connection with an allegation of homosexuality. The applicant was interviewed on 13 June 1994 by personnel from the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately twenty minutes. He then confirmed that he was homosexual, acknowledging that he had been a practising homosexual since his teenage years. He was then asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject), what type of sexual relations he hadhad with a particular person, when and where this had occurred and about his current relationship. The second applicant joined the Royal Navy in 1989. In 1991 he became a substantive weapons engineering mechanic. On 16 December 1994 the Admiralty Board informed the applicant that it had decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. The applicant’s commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000). His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal. It was indicated a number of times that the purpose of the second interview was to avoid further investigations.  applicant's report dated 27 November 1992 noted that he displayed potential in a number of areas essential to good leadership. In May 1993 the applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter (he wished to collect his Aids test results) and consequently he spoke with the chaplain, to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. The applicant was then called for interview by the service police. He was cautioned in the same terms as the first applicant and told that he would not be questioned on the above admissions prior to a search of his locker. His consent to the search was requested and given. During the search, slides (of himself, his partner and some of his service friends) and personal postcards were seized. The service police report completed after the applicant’s interview included several internal documents where it was noted that the applicant, in openly declaring his homosexuality and his relationship with a civilian, had effectively disposed “of any immediate potential security concern” For that reason, it was considered in the report that “no cause was identified for conducting a security interview with Beckett”. That report also accepted that a case for fraudulent entry into the armed forces would be inappropriate given the date when the applicant had discovered his homosexuality. The applicant was also asked about gay bars he frequented, whether he had ever joined contact magazines and whether he agreed that his secret life could be used as a basis to blackmail him. Four soldiers were discharged on the sole ground of sexual orientation. All were devastated by their discharge. High Court dismissed the application for judicial review, Lord Justice Simon Brown giving the main judgment of the court. He considered that the balance of argument clearly lay with the applicants. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise.” He concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles, adapted to a human rights context, should be applied. Simon Brown LJ also found that the Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. He pointed out that, although he might have considered the Minister wrong, “…[the courts] owe a duty ... to remain within their constitutional bounds and not trespass beyond them” It followed that the applications had to be rejected “ albeit with hesitation and regret”. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals into the armed services. A brief analysis of the Convention’s case-law led the judge to comment that he strongly suspected that, as far as the United Kingdom’S obligations were concerned, the days of the policy were numbered. In August 1995 a consultation paper was circulated by the Ministry of Defence to ‘management’ levels in the armed forces. It was indicated that the case was likely to progress to the European courts. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal on 3 November 1995. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment. He considered that the court’s approach to the issue of “irrationality” was an accurate distillation of the relevant jurisprudence on the subject. The more substantial the interference with human rights, the more the court will require by way of justification before it is satisfied that the decision is reasonable. The Master of the Rolls noted that the case concerned innate qualities of a very personal kind, that the decisions of which the applicants complained had had a profound effect on their careers and prospects and that the applicants’ rights as human beings were very much in issue. He considered that the greater the policy content of the decision and the more remote the subject matter of a decision from ordinary judicial experience, the more hesitant the court had to be in holding a decision to be irrational. However, he concluded that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed in this case. Henry LJ of the Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls and, in particular, with the latter’s approach to the irrationality test. He questioned the utility of a debate as to the likely fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights. He also found that the Equal Treatment Directive did not apply to complaints in relation to sexual orientation. Thorpe LJ agreed with both preceding judgments and with the views expressed on the rationality test to be applied and on its application in the particular case. It was important to highlight that Parliament had not given the domestic courts primary jurisdiction over human rights issues contained in the Convention. In December 1995 Mr Lustig-Prean issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination contrary to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. On 19 March 1996 the Appeals Committee of the House of Lords refused leave to appeal to the Lords. Mr Beckett requested the withdrawal of his Industrial Tribunal proceedings and those proceedings were dismissed on 25 April 1996. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the withdrawing of those proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed by the Industrial tribunal. The applicants’ industrial tribunal proceedings were also dismissed on 27 April 1998.

All four of the applicants had exemplary service records, some with reports written in glowing terms. In none of the cases before him was it suggested that the applicants’ sexual orientation had in any way affected their ability to carry out their work or had any ill-effect on discipline. All were devastated by their discharge. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. It was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer. Simon Brown LJ found that the Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted same-sex marriage. A brief analysis of the Convention’s case-law led the judge to comment that he strongly suspected that, as far as the United Kingdom’S obligations were concerned, the days of the policy were numbered. It followed that the applications had to be rejected “albeit with hesitation and regret”. The court would not, for example, be inclined to overlook some minor flaw in the decision-making process. In August 1995 a consultation paper was circulated by the Ministry of Defence to ‘management’ levels in the armed forces. It was indicated that the case was likely to progress to the European courts. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment (with which the two other judges of the Court. of Appeal agreed). He considered that the court’s approach to the issue of ‘irrationality’ was an accurate distillation of the relevant jurisprudence on the subject. The more substantial the interference with human rights, the more the court will require by way of justification before it is satisfied that the decision is reasonable. The Master of the Rolls noted that the case concerned innate qualities of a very personal kind, that the decisions of which the applicants complained had had a profound effect on their careers and prospects and that the applicants’ rights as human beings were very much in issue. He concluded that the policy could not be considered ‘irrational’ at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed in this case. While the court must properly defer to the expertise of responsible decision-makers, it must not shrink from its fundamental duty to ‘do right to all manner of people’ …” Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls. He accepted that the Equal Treatment Directive did not apply to complaints in relation to sexual orientation. But he questioned the utility of a debate as to the likely fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights. The Court of Appeal did not entertain “hypothetical questions’ as to whether the policy answered a ‘pressing social need’ and, in particular, was proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued. He also found that Parliament had not given the domestic courts primary jurisdiction over human rights issues contained in the Convention. The applicants’ challenge to the arguments in support of the policy was ‘completely persuasive’ The policy was, in his view, ‘ripe for review and for consideration of its replacement by a strict conduct code’ Mr Lustig-Prean issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination contrary to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. Those proceedings were adjourned pending the above-described application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords. Mr Beckett requested the withdrawal of his Industrial Tribunal proceedings and those proceedings were dismissed on 25 April 1996. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the withdraw of those proceedings which were dismissed in August 1998.
eval_texts: The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy on the sole ground that they are homosexual constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. On 17 January 1998 the Commission decided to adjourn the applications pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) pursuant to Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome by the English High Court on the question of the applicability of the Council Directive on the Implementation of the Principle of Equal Treatment for Men and Women. The High Court delivered its judgment withdrawing its reference of the above question given the decision of the ECJ in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins (13 July 1998) The Commission granted Mr Beckett legal aid. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 May 1999. Mr Lustig-Prean was granted legal aid on 4 May 1999 by the President of the Chamber. The Court heard addresses by Mr Pannick and Mr Eadie. The Circumstances of the case were heard by the Court on 17 May 1999, and the case was quashed on 2 June 1999. In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. He had been involved in a steady relationship with a civilian partner. In early June 1994 he was informed that the Royal Navy Special Investigations Branch (“the service police”) had been given his name anonymously in connection with an allegation of homosexuality. The applicant was interviewed on 13 June 1994 by personnel from the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately twenty minutes. He then confirmed that he was homosexual, acknowledging that he had been a practising homosexual since his teenage years. He was then asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject) and about his current relationship. An anonymous letter claimed that the applicant had had a relationship with a serviceman. The applicant's commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000) His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. Mr Beckett (the second applicant) joined the Royal Navy, enlisting for twenty-two years’ service. In 1991 he became a substantive weapons engineering mechanic. In 1994 the Admiralty Board informed the applicant that it had decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy.  applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter (he wished to collect his Aids test results) He spoke with the chaplain, to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. On 10 May 1993 the applicant was asked by his lieutenant-commander to repeat what he had told the Chaplain. He again admitted his homosexuality to that officer and was then called for interview by the service police. He was cautioned in the same terms as the first applicant and told that he would not be questioned on the above admissions prior to a search of his locker. His consent to the search was requested and given. During the search, slides (of himself, his partner and some of his service friends) and personal postcards were seized. The applicant was discharged on 28 July 1993 on the basis of his homosexuality. The applicant complained about the decision to discharge him to the Admiralty Board. The applicants’ judicial review proceedings (R.C. v. Ministry of Defence, ex parte Smith and Others 2 Weeky Law Reports 305) were dismissed in December 1994. On 7 June 1995 the applicants obtained leave to apply for judicial review of the decisions to discharge them from the armed forces. The claimants argued that the policy of the MoD against homosexuals in the armed force was ‘irrational’ and that it was in breach of the Convention and the Equal Treatment Directive. Four men were discharged on the sole ground of sexual orientation. The High Court dismissed the application for judicial review. Lord Justice Simon Brown gave the main judgment of the court. He considered that the balance of argument clearly lay with the applicants. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise.” The court had to be scrupulous to ensure that no recognised ground of challenge was in truth available to an applicant before rejecting the application. Simon Brown LJ also found that the Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals into the armed services. A brief analysis of the Convention’s case-law led the judge to comment that he strongly suspected that, as far as the United Kingdom's obligations were concerned, the days of the policy were numbered. It followed that the applications had to be rejected “albeit with hesitation and regret”. He pointed out that, although he might have considered the Minister wrong, “…[the courts] owe a duty ... to remain within their constitutional bounds’ In August 1995 a consultation paper was circulated by the Ministry of Defence to “management’s levels in the armed forces relating to the policy against homosexuals in those forces. On 3 November 1995 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment (with which the two other judges of the Court. of Appeal agreed). The more substantial the interference with human rights, the more the court will require by way of justification before it is satisfied that the decision is reasonable in the sense outlined above” He went on to quote from, inter alia, the. Master of the Rolls ruled that the decision could not be considered ‘irrational’ at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces. He concluded that the threshold of irrationality was ‘a high one’ and that it had not been crossed in this case. While the court must properly defer to the expertise of responsible decision-makers, it must not shrink from its fundamental duty to ‘do right to all manner of people’ …”. The court has the constitutional role and duty of ensuring that the rights of citizens are not abused by the unlawful exercise of executive power. “It is, inevitably, common ground that the United Kingdom’s obligation, binding in international law, to respect and ensure compliance with [Article 8 of the Convention] is not’ The Court of Appeal did not entertain “hypothetical questions’ about the fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights with which the primary adjudicating role on the Convention lay. In Henry LJ’s view, the only relevance of the Convention was as ‘background to the complaint of irrationality’, which point had been already made by the Master of the Rolls. Parliament had not given the domestic courts primary jurisdiction over human rights issues contained in the Convention. The evidence and submissions before the Court. of Appeal related to that court’S secondary jurisdiction and not to its primary jurisdiction. Mr Lustig-Prean and Mr Beckett applied for leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The Appeals Committee refused their appeal on 19 March 1996. The applicants’ Industrial Tribunal proceedings were dismissed by the Industrial Tribunal on 25 April 1996. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the withdrawal of those proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed. The case was referred to the European Court of Justice (ECJ) for consideration in relation to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. The ECJ ruled in favour of the applicants in December 1998. The Court of Appeal ruled in March 1999 that the sexual discrimination Act 1975 had not been breached and that the application was dismissed.

name: Peter Maxwell
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 12 July 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 3 August 1993 by. the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (“the Government’), within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision. as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) (Art. 6-3-c) The applicant, Mr Peter Maxwell, is a British citizen born in 1944. On 14 or 15 February 1990 two masked men broke into a private house, situated in Stevenston, Scotland. They assaulted the occupant causing him severe injury and permanent disfigurement. On 19 February 1990 Mr Maxwell was arrested together with another man. They were indicted on a charge of assault. Both held in custody until trial started on 28 May 1990. On 29 May 1990 the jury found the applicant guilty of the charge. The judge sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. Legal aid had been made available to the applicant for the preparation of his defence and for his representation by counsel at the trial. The applicant lodged with the court a note of appeal setting out grounds which he formulated himself. The grounds of appeal can be summarised as follows: (a) the applicant had not been able to substantiate his contention that a crucial witness was giving false evidence against him because to do so would have involved revealing to the jury a previous conviction. (b) a number of witnesses had not be called by the Crown or by the Defence; (c) crucial evidence had been entirely fabricated; (d) the verdict of the jury was not supported by the evidence; (e) his legal advisers had disregarded instructions which he had given them and had not defended him in accordance with his instructions. Mr Maxwell appealed against the refusal of legal aid. His solicitors advised him that he should abandon his appeal but he chose not to accept their advice. The applicant decided to proceed with his appeal personally. On 21 March 1991, the applicant addressed the High Court of Justiciary on his grounds of appeal. Presiding over the three-judge bench was the Lord Justice Clerk, one of the two most senior judges in Scotland. The Crown was represented by counsel but there is no indication that he intervened at the hearing. On the same date the court dismissed the appeal. The judgment gave full consideration to each of the grounds. of appeal, but was satisfied that they had no substance and that there had been no miscarriage of justice.

The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides and Lord Rodger as well as replies to its questions. The applicant was allowed legal aid for the preparation of his defence and for his representation by counsel at the trial. The applicants case was decided by the Court of Human Rights, with Mr Maxwell's verdict read out by the Chief Justice of the European Court of Justice. The decision of the Court was read out in its entirety by Mr Justice R.J. R. Martin. The opinion of the court was that Mr Maxwell’s conviction on the charge of assault was not justified by the circumstances. The applicant lodged with the court a note of appeal setting out grounds which he formulated himself. The grounds of appeal can be summarised as follows: (a) the applicant had not been able to substantiate his contention that a crucial witness was giving false evidence against him because to do so would have involved revealing to the jury a previous conviction; (b) a number of witnesses had not be called by the Crown or by the Defence; (c) crucial evidence had been entirely fabricated; (d) the verdict of the jury was not supported by the evidence; (e) his legal advisers had disregarded instructions which he had given them and had not defended him in accordance with his instructions. On 25 January 1991, the Board informed Mr Maxwell that his application had been refused. His solicitors advised him that he should abandon his appeal but he chose not to accept their advice. Following the refusal of legal aid, the solicitors declined to continue to act for the applicant. The applicant decided to proceed with his appeal personally. The Crown was represented by counsel but there is no indication that he intervened at the hearing. On the same date the court dismissed the appeal. In his judgment the Lord Justice Clerk noted that detailed grounds of appeal had been put forward and that the applicant had addressed the court at some length upon those grounds. He was satisfied that they had no substance and that there had been no miscarriage of justice.

name: Kemal Turhan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4397/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant requested 5,500 Turkish liras (TRY) as compensation from the court and reserved his right to increase this claim in due course. He was represented by Mr A.F. Demirkan, a lawyer practising in Bursa. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 12 June 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. On 23 March and 13 November 2009 the administration paid TRY 8,920 and 53,081 respectively. According to the information provided by the applicant, there has been no outstanding debt in the execution files. The payment was made on the basis that the debt had already been settled. The debt was paid in full on the 23rd and 13th of November 2009. The amount was paid on the 21st and 22nd of the same month. The total amount of the payment was paid was TRY 7,920,000 (Troy per person) and TRY 53,000,000 ($7,940,000) respectively.

name: Louise O’Keeffe
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35810/09) against Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant mainly complained under Article 3 that the system of primary education had failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1973. She also relied on Article 8 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, both alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Chamber, unanimously, struck out the complaints regarding the length of the domestic proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy in that regard, given the friendly settlement reached between the parties on those issues. It also declared admissible the remaining complaints. The applicant attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was owned, through trustees, by the Catholic Bishop of the Diocese of Cork and Ross. The manager (S.), acting on behalf of the bishop, was the local parish priest. The latter being elderly and infirm, a local priest (Ó.) was the de facto manager. The term “manager” used below refers both to Ó. and to the management function he performed. The applicant and the Government each filed further observations (Rule 59 § 1) on the merits. The Irish Human Rights Commission and the European Centre for Law and Justice had been given leave by the President of the Chamber to intervene. In 1971 a parent of a child complained to the manager that L.H. had sexually abused her child. That complaint was not reported to the police, to the Department or to any other State authority. In September 1973 other parents brought to the applicant’s parents’ attention similar allegations. Those allegations were not reported at that time. In 1996 she was contacted by the police who were investigating a complaint made in 1995 by a former pupil of Dunderrow National School against L. H. The applicant made a statement to thePolice in January 1997 and was referred for counselling. L.h. was charged with 386 criminal offences of sexual abuse involving some twenty-one former pupils of the school. In 1998 he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was sentenced to imprisonment. His licence to teach was withdrawn by the Minister for Education under Rule 108 of the National School Rules 1965 (“the 1965 Rules’) An initial award (44,814.14 euros (EUR) was made by a single judge. The applicant appealed to a CICT panel. She claimed that the CICT gave her the option of continuing her appeal (at the risk of finding that her CICT application would be rejected as out of time) or of accepting the initial offer. The award was made on an ex gratia basis. Since the State is never a party to CICT proceedings, it became aware of this award later before the High Court (see directly below) The High Court awarded damages payable by L.H. in the sum of EUR 305,104. The first payment was received in November 2007 so that she has been paid in the region of EUR 31,000 to date. She registered a judgment mortgage against that part of the family home owned by L.-H. The applicant took enforcement proceedings. L. claimed he had insufficient means and she obtained an instalment order of EUR 400 per month. The State Defendants applied for a direction to strike out the case. The High Court hearing against the State Defendants began on 2 March 2004. On 5 March 2004, the High Court judge, in response to the applicant’s complaint regarding the absence of a State system for adverting to and addressing sexual abuse in national schools, asked Counsel for the applicant as follows: “What evidence do I have, or what should I have deduce[d] from the evidence that has been given?” The High Court accepted the State Defendants’ application on 9 March 2004. On 20 January 2006 the High Court delivered judgment. It found that the action was not statute barred. It also concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the sexual assaults perpetrated by L.H. given the relationship between the State and the denominational management of national schools. In May 2006 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court. Her Notice of Appeal challenged the finding on vicarious liability. By a majority judgment of 19 December 2008 (Hardiman J and Fennelly J, with whom Chief Justice Murray and Mr Justice. Mr Justice Fennel) the appeal was dismissed. Dissenting churches and the Catholic Church wished to ensure that children of their denominations be educated in schools controlled by the denomination and not by the State or the established (Anglican) Church. Those churches were “remarkably successful’ in achieving this aim. State funding was accorded on a proportionate basis to all denominational schools, but the population was at the time overwhelmingly Catholic so that the majority of national schools had Catholic patrons and managers. The Catholic Church had responded that there could be no interference whatever with the “inherited tradition of managerial rights of schooling”. It had to be Catholic schools under Catholic management, Catholic teachers, Catholic children. The Constitution reflected a largely State-funded, but entirely clerically administered, system of education. Most were under the control of Catholic patrons and managers. Hardiman J referred to the ‘urgent desire’ of the denominations to maintain their role in primary education. The provision of education was belatedly and at least partially placed on a statutory basis by the Education Act 1998. Prior to that Act the system had been administered by the 1965 Rules as well as by other ministerial letters, circulars and notes. No complaint, on the evidence, was directed to the Minister or to any State body. The matter was handled, so to speak, ‘in house’ at the election of the complainants. Hardiman J observed that the sexual abuse of a pupil was the negation of what L.H. was employed to do. But he also found that in 1973 it “was an unusual act, little discussed, and certainly not regarded as an ordinary foreseeable risk of attending at a school” He considered it ‘notable’ that she did not sue the patron, the diocese of which he was bishop, his successors or his estate, the trustees of the property of the Diocese of Cork and Ross (owners of the school), the manager or his Estate or successors. In particular, even applying the wider form of vicarious liability invoked, the Minister’s absence of direct control over L.C.H., long since ceded to the manager and the Patron, prevented a finding against the Minister. Hardiman J concluded by pointing out that nothing in the judgment could be interpreted as suggesting liability on the part of the Church. The Court was confronted for the first time with questions relating to the liability of institutions including the State for sexual abuse of schoolchildren in a national school by a teacher. Cases of sexual abuse had preoccupied the criminal courts and the Supreme Court for many years and it was surprising that the court was confronted with the issue of liability for the abuse of children in a school by an employee of the Catholic Church. It was quite impossible to do so because those authorities had not been heard by the Supreme court since the applicant had not sued them. Fennelly J also described in some detail the history and consequent circumstances of the case. Legal status of national schools, which system had survived independence in 1922 and the enactment of the Constitution in 1937. Fennelly J accepted the expert’s evidence that it was not a State system but rather a “State-supported system’ He noted the clear division of power between the State (funding and fixing the curriculum) and the manager (day-to-day running of the school including hiring and firing teachers) He concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the acts of L.H. or for the failure of the manager to report the 1971 complaint to the State. Geoghegan J dissented. The applicant was legally represented throughout the civil proceedings, although she did not have legal aid. If an allegation of sexual assault by a teacher on a national-school pupil was considered well-founded by an inquiry set up by the Department, it could lead to the withdrawal of recognition or to a police investigation. If the police found the complaint justified, the teacher’s licence to teach could be withdrawn. The Supreme Court vacated the High Court order for costs against the applicant since it was not disputed that hers was an important and complex test case. It determined that each party had to bear its own costs related to the action against the State Defendants.

The applicant mainly complained under Article 3 that the system of primary education had failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1973.
