The Chamber, unanimously, struck out the complaints regarding the length of the domestic proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy in that regard, given the friendly settlement reached between the parties on those issues. It also declared admissible the remaining complaints. The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in Cork, Ireland. He attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was owned, through trustees, by the Catholic Bishop of the Diocese of Cork and Ross. The manager (S), acting on behalf of the bishop, was the local parish priest. The latter being elderly and infirm, a local priest (Ó.) was the de facto manager. The term “manager” used below refers both to Ó. and to the management function he performed. The applicant and the Government each filed further observations on the merits. The case was heard in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 6 March 2013. The applicant was subjected to approximately twenty sexual assaults by L.H. during music lessons in his classroom in 1973. The applicant suppressed the sexual abuse. She had significant psychological difficulties but did not associate those with the abuse. In 1996 she was contacted by the police who were investigating a complaint made in 1995 by a former pupil of Dunderrow National School against L.h. L. H. was charged with 386 criminal offences of sexual abuse involving some twenty-one former pupils of the school during a three-year period. He was acquitted of most of the charges but was convicted of two counts of indecent assault on a child. L.H. pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was sentenced to imprisonment. His licence to teach was withdrawn by the Minister for Education. An initial award (44,814.14 euros (EUR) was made by a single judge. The applicant appealed to a CICT panel. She claimed that the CICT gave her the option of continuing her appeal (at the risk of finding that her CICT application would be rejected as out of time) or of accepting the initial offer. The award was made on an ex gratia basis. Since the State is never a party to CICT proceedings, it became aware of this award later before the High Court (see directly below) The High Court assessed and awarded damages payable by L.H. in the sum of EUR 305,104, comprising EUR 200,000 in general damages. The first payment was received in November 2007 so that she has been paid in the region of EUR 31,000 to date. She registered a judgment mortgage against that part of the family home owned by L.-H. L. claimed he had insufficient means and she obtained an instalment order of EUR 400 per month. The State Defendants applied for a direction to strike out the case when the High Court hearing against the State Defendants began on 2 March 2004. The High Court judge, in response to the applicant’s complaint regarding the absence of a State system for adverting to and addressing sexual abuse in national schools, asked Counsel for the applicant as follows. The High Court accepted the State Defendants’ application. The trial finished on 12 March 2004. On 20 January 2006 the High Court delivered judgment. It found that the action was not statute barred. It also concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the sexual assaults perpetrated by L.H. given the relationship between the State and the denominational management of national schools. In May 2006 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court. Her Notice of Appeal challenged the finding on vicarious liability. By a majority judgment of 19 December 2008 (Hardiman J and Fennelly J, with whom Chief Justice Murray and Mr Justice. Mr Justice Fennell) the appeal was dismissed. Dissenting churches and the Catholic Church wished to ensure that children of their denominations be educated in schools controlled by the denomination. Those churches were ‘remarkably successful’ in achieving this aim. From the very beginning of the Irish system of national education, State authorities paid for the system but did not administer it. The latter function was left to the local denominational manager. State funding was accorded on a proportionate basis to all denominational schools. The population was at the time overwhelmingly Catholic so that the majority of national schools had Catholic patrons and managers. The Catholic Church had responded that there could be no interference whatever with the ‘inherited tradition of managerial rights of schooling’ Hardiman J noted that, in recent times and after more than a century and a half, the provision of education was belatedly and at least partially placed on a statutory basis by the Education Act 1998. Prior to that Act the system had been administered by the 1965 Rules as well as by other ministerial letters, circulars and notes. Hardiman J referred to the “urgent desire” of the denominations to maintain their role in primary education. As a result there were approximately 3,000 national schools in Ireland: most were under the control of Catholic patrons and managers, a few were under control of other denominations and even fewer were controlled by non-denominational groups. Hardiman J found that the sexual abuse of a pupil was the negation of what L.H. was employed to do. In 1973 it “was an unusual act, little discussed, and certainly not regarded as an ordinary foreseeable risk of attending at a school’. He concluded that, having regard to the relevant test for vicarious liability and to the above-described arrangements for the control and management of national schools, the State Defendants were not liable to the applicant for the wrongs committed against her. In particular, even applying the wider form of Vicarious liability invoked, the Minister’s absence of direct control over L.h., long since ceded to the manager and the patron, prevented a finding against the Minister. The relationship of L. h. and the State – a “triangular one with the Church” – was entirely sui generis and a product of Ireland’S unique history. Hardiman J: The Minister can hardly be responsible for a failure to ‘cease’ a course of action of whose existence he was quite unaware. Kenny J: In my view the Constitution specifically envisages, not indeed a delegation but a ceding of the actual running of schools to the interests represented by the patron and the manager. Fennelly J: It was surprising that that court was confronted for the first time with questions relating to the liability of institutions including the State for sexual abuse of schoolchildren in a national school by a teacher. No liability on the part of the Church could be interpreted because those authorities had not been heard by the Supreme Court. Legal status of national schools, which system had survived independence in 1922 and the enactment of the Constitution in 1937. He accepted the expert’s evidence that it was not a State system but rather a “State-supported system’ He noted the clear division of power between the State (funding and fixing the curriculum) and the manager (day-to-day running of the school including hiring and firing teachers) Fennelly J concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the acts of L.H. or for the failure of the manager to report the 1971 complaint to the State. Geoghegan J dissented. The applicant was legally represented throughout the civil proceedings, although she did not have legal aid. Geoghegan J relied, notably, on the role of school inspectors. If an allegation of sexual assault by a teacher on a national-school pupil was considered well-founded by an inquiry set up by the Department, it could lead to the withdrawal of recognition or to a police investigation. By a judgment of 9 May 2009 the Supreme Court vacated the High Court order for costs against the applicant since it was not disputed that hers was an important and complex test case. It determined that each party had to bear its own costs related to the action against the State Defendants.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28895/95) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged in particular that civil proceedings instituted by him in 1987 had been unfair and lasted unreasonably long. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 12 October 1999 the Chamber declared the remainder of the application admissible. The applicant made a claim against the defendant in 3 Cg 216/88 in 1988. The judge dealing with the applicant’s case was replaced by a new judge on 1 November 1988. On 23 June 1988 the District Court invited the defendant to comment on the applicant's submissions. A second hearing took place on 1 December 1989. The court adjourned the case pending the outcome of further parallel proceedings against the same defendant. The final decision in the latter proceedings entered into force on 4 November 1993. On 15 November 1993 the applicant requested the resumption of the previous proceedings. He also increased the amount claimed to AS 24,339.80 and submitted documentation. The applicant’s appeal against the part of the judgment against him was dismissed by the Salzburg Regional Court on 20 January 1999. The applicant was awarded his costs. against him as to AS 9,182. The latter judgment was received by the applicant�s representative on 4 February 1999. He was also awarded the right to appeal against part of it. The appeal was dismissed and the applicant was given the costs of the suit. The application was dismissed on 21 January 1999 and the costs were awarded on 22 January 1999, when the case was still before the court. The case was settled in favour of the applicant on 23 January 1999 with the costs paid by the defendant.

In 1998 the Salzburg Regional Court allowed the applicant's appeal in part, and remitted the case to the District Court which, on 20 July 1998, gave judgment in his favour. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11032/04) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Administrative Court failed to hold an oral hearing, which was in breach of Article 6. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Mr F. Trauttmannsdorff, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant filed an objection (Vorstellung) with the Lower Austria Regional Government on 13 September 2000. He requested it to hear representatives of the District Farmer's Association (DFA, Bezirksbauernkammer) and the Austrian beekeeper association (ABA, Österreichischer Imkerbund) The Regional Government quashed the municipality's decision on 10 January 2001 and referred the case back to the municipal council. The applicant lodged further grounds in support of his appeal on 19 March, 4 and 24 April 2001. He also submitted a statement by the Tulln Administrative District Authority and a document he referred to as a business plan. The applicant's complaint was dismissed by the Lower Austria Regional Government on 22 July 2002. The applicant lodged a further complaint with the Administrative Court on 22 August 2002 and repeated his request for an oral hearing. The Administrative Court found that, despite its request for a detailed business plan, the applicant had failed to provide one. It found that the alleged need for a shed for the so-called agricultural enterprise had not been made out. Accordingly, the application was dismissed on 16 September 2003 and the applicant did not have to apply for a new shed. The case was dismissed as inadmissible for non-exhaustion of administrative remedies as the applicant failed to file an objection against the decision.

The municipal council also rejected the applicant's appeal on 29 January 2002. It held that the planned construction would conflict with the zoning plan and that the building would not resemble a shed for agricultural use. name: Vernon John Davies
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged, in particular, a breach of his right under Article 6 § 1 to a fair hearing within a reasonable time. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it partly inadmissible on 26 September 2000. On 15 April 2002 the Government submitted observations in connection with the applicant's claims under Article 41 of the treaty. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The case was adjourned until May 1994. The Court of Appeal ruled that it was not in the public interest to continue. The case was eventually dismissed on May 6, 1995. The verdict was made public on May 8, 1995, but the appeal was not heard until May 24, 1996. The appeal was denied on May 26, 1997, and the case was dismissed on June 13, 1998. The trial was reopened on June 19, 1998, and it was decided that the case should be thrown out of court. The decision was made on June 26, 1998 and the trial was completed on July 2, 1999. The matter was heard at the High Court of Justice, which ruled that the trial could continue without delay. The judge's decision was upheld on July 13, 2000. Blackspur proceedings against the applicant were discontinued on 12 January 1998, after a “Carecraft” agreement (see paragraph 23 below) was reached between the applicant and the Secretary of State in other proceedings under the CDDA. As part of the settlement, the applicant agreed to pay the secretary of state's costs of GBP 94,000. The court observed that the delay by the Secretary. of State had not affected the timing of the hearing or prejudiced the applicant, and that, once the. proceedings had commenced, “the respondents' main concern was to delay the proceedings until after the conclusion of. the criminal trial, not to hurry them on”.

The case originated in an application (no. 42007/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The Court of Appeal ruled that the case was not in the public interest. The case was eventually thrown out of the Supreme Court in August 1995. The appeal was eventually dismissed in May 1998. The court's decision to dismiss the case led to a review of the case by the Court of Appeals. The Supreme Court ruled in June 1998 that the appeal was not a success and that the matter should be dismissed. The matter was referred to the High Court, which made the decision on appeal. The High Court ruled on the appeal's appeal, and the decision was overturned. The trial was the first of its kind in the UK. The Blackspur proceedings against the applicant were discontinued on 12 January 1998, after a “Carecraft” agreement (see paragraph 23 below) was reached between the applicant and the Secretary of State in other proceedings under the CDDA. As part of the settlement, the applicant agreed to pay the secretary of state's costs of GBP 94,000. The applicant was also granted an extension of time until 9 February 1998. The case was decided in favour of the applicant, and the case was settled out of court in the shape of a ‘carecraft’ agreement. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) The applicant was born in 1979. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32869/96) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. name: Martha Nölkenbockhoff
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 28 January 1986. It originated in an application (no. 10300/83) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mrs. Martha Nölkenbockhoff, on 7 February 1983. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 2. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Lutz and Englert cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The applicant’s memorial - drafted in German - was lodged with the registry on 1 July 1986. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government, by. Mr. Weitzel for the Commission and by Mr. Bergemann for the applicant, as well as their replies to its. questions. The Commission, the Government and the applicant filed a number of documents and written comments. between 9 February and 22 May 1987, the Commission,. the applicant and the Government filed documents and. written comments either at the Court's request or of their own motion. Martha Nölkenbockhoff is the widow of a German businessman. He was a senior manager in Stumm AG, whose trading activities centred on iron, steel and fuel, including motor fuel. The company was declared insolvent in 1974 and he was arrested under a warrant issued by the Essen District Court. Other senior managers in the company were also arrested. The trial hearings began on 29 October 1976 before the 6th Criminal Chamber (6. Grosse Strafkammer) and lasted until 11 July 1980. The applicant’s husband was defended by two counsel, one of whom was assigned by the court. The Regional Court delivered its judgment, which ran to 579 pages. Mr. NöLkenbocksh was found guilty inter alia on several charges of breach of trust (Untreue), criminal bankruptcy and fraud. Mr. Nölkenbockhoff entered an appeal on points of law on the same day that judgment was given. In determining the sentences, the Regional Court took into account as extenuating circumstances the length of the proceedings and, in respect of the applicant’s husband, his detention on remand for some three years. The Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof) had not given a decision by the time he died on 13 November, so that the proceedings came to an end without any decision being taken. The appeal lodged by the fourth person convicted, Mr. M, was dismissed by the Federal Court on July 1982 as being manifestly ill-founded. The Essen Regional Court found against Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff. She requested the Regional Court to adjourn a decision on her applications until such time as the Federal Court of Justice had given judgment on the appeal brought by the co-defendant Mr. M. The decision read as follows: “... The applications are admissible ... but ill-founded. Where proceedings are terminated by reason of a defendant’s death, his necessary costs and expenses are normally borne by the Treasury. This does not apply where, were it not for this technical bar, the defendant would almost certainly have been convicted or his conviction almost certainly has been upheld" The court declines to award compensation for the time spent in detention on remand, pursuant to section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. The court does not consider it necessary to defer judgment until a decision has been given on the co-defendant M’s appeal on points of law. The applicant appealed to the Hamm Court of Appeal against that decision on 11 March 1982. In written pleadings dated 18 March, she challenged, inter alia, the Regional Court's finding that, had her husband not died, he “would almost certainly have been convicted or his conviction almost certainly would have been upheld’. The Regional Court likewise disregarded the presumption of innocence in stating that the grounds of appeal afforded no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted. It was as if it were sought to obtain a final (abschliessend) conviction of the deceased by a side wind in the form of a decision as to costs. The court should have known that vital points in Mr. Nölkenbockhoff’s appeal were also relied on by the co-defendant M. The applicant pointed out in addition that from the outset her husband had denied having committed any offences and had indeed been acquitted on several counts. Since criminal law was based on the principle of individual guilt, it was quite simply unacceptable - and, once again, contrary to Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) - to judge the deceased. The Hamm Court of Appeal dismissed the action on 14 July 1982. It left open the question whether, in the event of a defendant’s death before the final conclusion (rechtskräftiger Abschluss) of criminal proceedings, a decision such as that sought by Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff could be taken, by analogy, under Article 467 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act (see paragraphs 24-26 below) The Bochum public prosecutor submitted that there was every likelihood (hohe Wahrscheinlichkeit) that the conviction would have been upheld. The decision on the claim for compensation is based on section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. Both provisions, whose conformity with the Constitution cannot be doubted, confer on the courts a degree of discretion. There is nothing to suggest that the courts exercised their discretion in a manner contrary to the Constitution. Admittedly, the decisions being challenged make a prediction of the probable outcome of the proceedings. That does not mean, however, that in every case costs must be reimbursed where the proceedings are terminated without guilt having been established (Schuldnachweis) ... The decision to uphold the conviction of co-defendant M. (zutreffend) has been upheld. The judge ruled that a conviction would have been more likely than an acquittal had the proceedings been continued. The judge said that such an assessment does not amount to a finding of guilt but merely to aFinding of a continuing state of suspicion. The courts’ reference to the lack of success of the appeal proceedings instituted by the co-defendant M and to the withdrawal of the appeals on points of law entered by the other defendants is clearly to be regarded merely as an additional argument, and the impugned decisions are not based on it. The court ruled that the decision not to continue the proceedings was not arbitrary in nature. The decision was made on the basis of the fact that the deceased defendant was convicted of each of the offences of which he was convicted.

Grosse Strafkammer) They lasted until 11 July 1980, two or three hearings being held each week. The applicant’s husband was defended by two counsel, one of whom was assigned by the court. That does not mean, however, that in every case costs must be reimbursed where the proceedings are terminated without guilt having been established (Schuldnachweis) ... The reasons given for the contested decision, which are valid (zutreffend), have been upheld. The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 28 January 1986. It originated in an application (no. 10300/83) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 (art.) 6-2. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Lutz and Englert cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The Government and Commission had until 1 July 1986 to file memorials. The President twice extended the first of these time-limits - on 3 July until 31 October, and on 10 November until 21 November 1986. On 29 November, the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government, by. Mr. Weitzel for the Commission and by Mr. Bergemann for the applicant, as well as their replies to its. questions. Martha Nölkenbockhoff is the widow and heir of Mr. Theodor Nölbockhoff. Her husband was a senior manager in a holding company, Stumm AG, whose trading activities centred on iron, steel and fuel, including motor fuel. On 13 November 1974 he was arrested under a warrant issued by the Essen District Court. He was suspected among other things of bankruptcy offences. Other senior managers in the company were also arrested. The trial hearings began on 29 October 1976 before the 6th Criminal Chamber (6. Grosse Strafkammer) and lasted until 11 July 1980. In respect of a series of fraud charges, the Regional Court stayed the proceedings under Article 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Mr. Nölkenbockhoff entered an appeal on points of law on the same day that judgment was given. The Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof) had not given a decision by the time he died on 13 November. Three of the co-defendants, who had likewise challenged the Regional Court’s judgment, later withdrew their appeals. The appeal lodged by the fourth person convicted, Mr. M, was dismissed by the Federal Court on 7 July 1982 as being manifestly ill-founded. The applicant sought orders that the Treasury should bear the necessary costs and expenses (notwendige Auslagen) incurred by her late husband in connection with his conviction. Essen Regional Court found against Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff. Decision read as follows: “... The applications are admissible ... but ill-founded” The defendant had already been found guilty, in a judgment that had not become final, after lengthy court proceedings in a trial (Hauptverhandlung) lasting more than three and a half years. The judgment convicting the three co-defendants ..., who were likewise sentenced to several years’ imprisonment, has become final. The defence’s submissions again provide nothing to support the hypothesis that the proceedings were moving towards an acquittal. The fact that [three of] the defendants ... have withdrawn their appeals on points of law, thereby confirming the judgment against them, argues decisively in favour of the correctness of the judgment. The court does not consider it necessary to defer judgment until a decision has been given on the co-defendant M’s appeal on points of law. In view of the reasons given for the judgment, it was much more likely, having regard to the adverse financial position of the Stumm holding company, that if the proceedings had continued, the defendant would have been convicted on the counts in question. Nor, to the extent that the proceedings were provisionally stayed under Article 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure [see paragraph 23 below], are there any grounds for ordering the Treasury to pay the defendant's necessary costs and expenses. The court declines to award compensation for the time spent in detention on remand. The Regional Court disregarded the presumption of innocence in stating that the grounds of appeal afforded no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted. It was as if it were sought to obtain a final (abschliessend) conviction of the deceased by a side wind in the form of a decision as to costs. The applicant had requested an adjournment to await the judgment of the Federal Court of Justice in the appeal proceedings brought by one of the co-defendants. Since criminal law was based on the principle of individual guilt, it was quite simply unacceptable - and, once again, contrary to Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) - to judge the deceased. The Hamm Court of Appeal dismissed the action on 14 July 1982. It left open the question whether, in the event of a defendant’s death before the final conclusion (rechtskräftiger Abschluss), a decision such as that sought by Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff could be taken, by analogy, under Article 467 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act (see paragraphs 24-26 below). The applicant, inter alia, stated that there were considerable dissimilarities between M and her husband as regards the charges against them, their behaviour and the grounds of their appeals. Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff claimed a breach of Article 1 (protection of the dignity of man), Article 14 (the right of property) and Article 20 (principle of the rule of law) of the Basic Law. A bench of three judges of the Constitutional Court refused to entertain the constitutional complaint because it considered that the complaint did not have sufficient prospects of success. The court's decision on the claim for compensation is based on section 6(1)(2), sub-paragraph 2, of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court of Appeal rejected the objections (Gegenvorstellungen) which the applicant had lodged against the judgment of 14 July 1982. The courts’ reference to the lack of success of the appeal proceedings instituted by the co-defendant M and to the withdrawal of the appeals on points of law entered by the other defendants is clearly to be regarded merely as an additional argument, and the impugned decisions are not based on it. It was as if it were sought to obtain a final (abschliessend) conviction of the deceased by a side wind in the form of a decision as to costs. The Regional Court’s opinion that, had the proceedings been continued, a conviction would have been more likely than an acquittal ... ... ....“ Neither the alleged defects ... in the judgment convicting the defendant nor the grounds of the appeal on points of law make it possible to dismiss as untenable the conclusion reached in the contested decisions that a (subsequent) acquittal was unlikely in respect of each of the offences of which the deceased defendant had been convicted. name: Eie Enhorn
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56529/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5 of the convention. In 1994 it was discovered that he was infected with the HIV virus and had transmitted the virus to a 19-year-old man with whom he had first had sexual contact in 1990. The application was initially allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) By a decision of 10 December 2002, the Chamber declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) The applicant kept three appointments with the county medical officer in September 1994 and one in November 1994. He failed to appear as summoned five times during October and November 1994 and was ordered to be in compulsory isolation in a hospital. The applicant is prohibited from giving blood and donating organs or sperm. The court's record of the applicant's statement reads, inter alia, as follows: “After learning about his HIV infection he had hardly had any sexual relationships. Henceforward he would only have sexual relations with other HIV infected persons. also tell his dentist [about it]. Moreover, the applicant is to visit his consulting physician again and to keep appointments fixed by the countymedical officer.” The applicant absconded from the hospital several times, first on 25 April 1995. The County Administrative Court ordered that the applicant should be kept in compulsory isolation for up to three months pursuant to section 38 of the 1988 Act. The order took effect immediately, but the applicant failed to report to the hospital. He ran away for the fourth time on 26 February 1997 and was not returned until 26 February 1999. During the period from 26 February until 2 March 1999 the applicant was detained in his room. The applicant explained that before 1994 he had ten to twelve sexual relations per year. His partners were partly old acquaintances, partly new ones, whom he met in parks and so on. The applicant had taken precautions against spreading the disease. He had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant had a healthy liver. It was noted that subsequent to his return the applicant returned to Stockholm or Norrköping on a few occasions in order to deal with money matters. The owner of the farm hostel could hardly imagine that [the applicant] had had any sexual relations while living at the hostel. A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N., connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. After the applicant's involuntary return, he had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. The county medical officer, who gave evidence before the court, is recorded, inter alia, as follows: “During the last two years when he was on the run, [the applicant] sought medical treatment twice and it has been established that both times he said that he had the HIV virus’. “The chances of eliminating or limiting the continuous risk of the infection being spread by means of a prolonged placement in isolation are deemed – all facts considered – to have not yet completely vanished.” The County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has during this period absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years. During these two years he has used a false name and has been living a very secluded life, obviously owing to the risk of being discovered. A life at liberty makes great demands upon the person carrying the infection. During [the applicant's] contact with the doctors in question, they did not discuss therisk of spreading the disease at all. A treatment plan was not formally signed [by the applicant]” The Court finds that there is good reason to suppose that, if he remains free, [the applicant] will not comply with the practical instructions issued and that this entails a risk of the infection spreading. The applicant again absconded, leaving his whereabouts unknown. The case originated in an application (no. 56529/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5 of the convention. The application was initially allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits. This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The county medical officer petitioned the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) for a court order that the applicant be kept in compulsory isolation in a hospital for up to three months. The court's record of the applicant's statement reads, inter alia, as follows: “After learning about his HIV infection he had hardly had any sexual relationships. Henceforward he would only have sexual relations with other HIV infected persons. also tell his dentist [about it]. Moreover, the applicant is prohibited from giving blood and donating organs or sperm. Finally, he is to visit his consulting physician again and to keep appointments fixed by the county medical Officer.” The applicant's lack of social contact and his feeling of being an outsider, in combination with possible alcohol abuse, could increase the risk of destructive sexual relations. He has had periods of extensive [alcohol] abuse as a consequence of learning that he was infected with HIV but also when he lost his job. While being isolated the applicant had the opportunity to go outdoors every day together with members of the hospital staff, but not on his own. The boy, who was 15 years old when they met, took the initiative both emotionally and sexually. Today [the applicant] realises that he infected the boy, which he finds very regrettable. During his period at large, the applicant had no sexual relations. He had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that he had a healthy liver. It was noted that subsequent to his return the applicant returned to Stockholm and lived under a pseudonym. The owner of the farm hostel could hardly imagine that [the applicant] had had any sexual relations while living at the hostel ...” A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N., connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. After the applicant's involuntary return, he had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. He claimed that on the latest occasion, in March 1999, the applicant made a lunge at him. The applicant is considered to be completely devoid of any sense of being ill and also lacks awareness. The chances of eliminating or limiting the continuous risk of the infection being spread by means of a prolonged placement in isolation in accordance with the Act are deemed – all facts considered – to have not yet completely vanished. The County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has during this period absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years. During these two years he has used a false name and has been living a very secluded life, obviously owing to the risk of being discovered. A life at liberty makes great demands upon the person carrying the infection.” “In conclusion, in the county medical officer's opinion, [if released the applicant] will not voluntarily comply with the instructions given or limit the spreading of the disease” On 12 June 1999 the applicant again absconded, leaving his whereabouts unknown. In the meantime, he had appealed against the above judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal. He relied on an opinion of 14 May 1999 by the aforementioned chief physician and specialist in psychiatry, C.G., which stated, inter alia, that he was a man with a paranoid personality disorder, who misused alcohol. This diagnosis is to be distinguished from alcohol dependency, which means a compulsive use of alcohol with abstinence and social complications. The diagnosis 'paranoid personality disorder' is defined as a pervading suspiciousness and lack of trust in other people, whose motives are consistently perceived as malicious. The applicant showed empathy as far as other people from those years were concerned. He was partly able to shoulder responsibility for his own mistakes, without blaming others. His attitude towards the county medical officer and the staff at the infection ward, whom he believed had kept harassing him unjustly, was almost hateful. From 1996, he had not experienced feelings of persecution, inter alia since he had secured his own liberty. With regard to sexual relations, [the applicant] has stated that he preferred sexual contact with boys around the age of 17. He had been celibate since 1996 and had no longer any particular sexual desires or fantasies. The applicant could be described in everyday terms as an odd person, but not as mentally ill. Several applications for an extension of the applicant's compulsory isolation were submitted by the county medical officer after June 1999 and granted. On 12 December 2001 an application was turned down by the County Administrative Court, which referred to the fact that the applicant’s whereabouts were unknown and that therefore no information was available regarding his behaviour, state of health and so on. It appears that since 2002 the. applicant's whereabouts have been known, but that the competent county medical. officer has made the assessment that there are no grounds for the applicant.'s further involuntary placement in isolation. The application was dismissed on 5 October 1999, and the application was again turned down in December 2001.

name: Janusz Krawczak
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the excessive length of proceedings. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike out the application. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The application was dismissed and the case returned to the Polish Supreme Court for review. The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights and Human Rights Protection (ECHPRH) on 13 November 2010. The hearing was adjourned until 15 December 2010. On 24 November 2005 the Gdańsk Regional Court severed the bill of indictment and ordered that cases against fifteen other co‑accused be tried in separate proceedings. The applicant lodged a complaint about the undue length of the criminal proceedings under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004. The court observed that the 2004 Act had entered into force on 17 September 2004 and could not be applied to the proceedings before that date. This meant that the proceedings had to be restarted. The proceedings are still pending. The judge rapporteur is still waiting for a new bench to be appointed. The case is still pending at the Polish Court of Appeal.

The case originated in an application (no. 40387/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the excessive length of proceedings. He also alleged a violation of Article 6 read in conjunction with Article 13 of the. Convention in that he had been deprived of his right to have the remedy examined by an impartial court. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike out the application. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The proceedings under the 2004 Act are still pending. The applicant lodged a complaint about the undue length of the criminal proceedings under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004. He requested just satisfaction of PLN 10,000. The Gdańsk Court of Appeal dismissed his complaint on the ground that no undue delays in the proceedings could be discerned, the proceedings having been conducted with due diligence and within a reasonable time. The application was dismissed again on 23 March 2006. The proceedings were restarted on 24 November 2005 when the bill of indictment was severed. This meant that the proceedings had to be restarted. A judge rapporteur, a new bench should be appointed.

name: Gülşen Ketenoğlu
train_texts: The case was brought against the Republic of Turkey under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of their conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court which lacked independence and impartiality. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. In 2001, the Chamber decided to join the applications and declared them admissible. The Government and the applicants each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The application was settled in favour of the applicants in May 2002. The applicants were accused of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the Dev-Yol. The applicants were released pending trial by the Ankara Martial Law Court. In May 1989 the applicants both fled the country and settled in Germany. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) and the case was transmitted to it. On 27 December 1995 the Court ofCassation quashed the applicants’ conviction. It held, under Article 102 of the Turkish Criminal Code, that the criminal proceedings against Mrs Ketenoğlu should be discontinued since the prosecution was time‑barred. It therefore referred the case to the 6th Chamber of the Ankara Assize Court.

Case was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against them had not been concluded within a “reasonable time” and that their right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of their conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 11 January 2001, the Chamber decided to join the applications and declared them admissible. The applicants were accused of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The applicants both fled the country and settled in Germany. In 1995 the Court of Cassation quashed the applicants’ conviction. The case is still pending at the 6th Chamber of the Ankara Assize Court where the criminal proceedings are still pending. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the case was not a criminal one and that the prosecution had not been successful.

name: Aziz Canpolat

Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the Application at the. same time as its admissibility. The Diyarbakır State Security Court convicted the applicant and his co-accused and sentenced them to six years and three months' imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance court's judgment, holding that the applicant's defence rights had not been respect as they were not informed about the date of the hearing. On 20 April 2000 the Court ofCassation upheld the judgment of the first‑instance court. The applicant was released from prison on 21 May 2000. He is currently serving a six-year prison sentence for a charge of attempted murder. The case is still pending before the Turkish Supreme Court of Justice.

name: Şükran Yıldız
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4661/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the applicant’s detention on remand to the Government. The applicant was brought before the Diyarbakır public prosecutor and subsequently before the investigating judge and denied the allegations against her. She was represented by Mr Beştaş, a lawyer practising in Diyartsar. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The Diyarbakır State Security Court concluded that the woman was a member of the PKK. The court refused to release the woman on account of the nature of the alleged offence and the state of evidence. The Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance court's decision and released the woman in August 2001. On 9 April 2002 the court rendered its judgment and sentenced the woman to eight years and four months’ imprisonment pursuant to Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code. The woman was released in August 2002 and the case was dismissed. The conviction was overturned on 7 October 2002. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the applicant’s detention on remand, the right to have the lawfulness of her detention decided by a court to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant, who was sixteen years old at the time, was taken into custody by policemen from the Diyarbakır Security Directorate on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation. name: Milenko Stojakovic
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained about the lack of a public oral hearing before a tribunal. Since 1984 the applicant was the head of the Federal Bacteriological Serological Research Institute (Bundesstaatiche bakteriologisch-serologische Untersuchungsanstalt) in Linz. According to the activity profile submitted by the Government, the tasks of the Institute involved carrying out various examinations. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The head of the Institute was responsible for all tasks entrusted to it. He was further responsible for certain matters concerning the regulation of its service. The applicant was found guilty of having violated his professional duties under the Non-Discrimination Act and sentenced to a fine of approximately 2,400 euros (EUR) The Federal Minister for Work, Health and Social Affairs recalled the applicant from his post with immediate effect (Abberufung mit sofortiger Wirkung) and transferred him to a post with a lower grade, namely a referee post at the Ministry for work, health and social affairs in Vienna. In 2003 the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's complaint. The applicant appealed against his transfer. The Appeals Commission dismissed the appeal without holding a hearing. The applicant filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant's complaint on 26 November 2001. The Court found that rights and obligations which resulted from an employment as a civil servant could not be considered as part of the transfer process. It noted that the authority deciding on the transfer did not necessarily need to wait for the outcome of pending disciplinary proceedings. It confirmed the Federal Minister's finding that the applicant could no longer be trusted to perform the tasks of a head of the Institute. In particular, there was an important official interest which made his transfer to another post necessary. It followed that Article 6 was not applicable to the applicant's case. It further found that there was no indication of arbitrariness in the proceedings at issue. This decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 13 February 2002. It followed that it was not relevant to Article 6 of the Convention. It also followed that the applicant was not entitled to ‘civil rights’ within the meaning of Article 6. “Civil rights” within themeaning of Article 4 of the convention means ‘freedom of speech’, ‘privilege of expression’ and ‘the right to assemble’.

The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's complaint on 4 September 2003. The applicant was transferred to a referee post at the Ministry for work, health and social affairs in Vienna. It confirmed the Federal Minister's finding that the applicant could no longer be trusted to perform the tasks of a head of. the Institute. name: Eugeniusz Ludwiczak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 31748/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was made by a Polish national, Mr Eugeniusz Ludwiczak (‘the applicant’), on 17 July 2006. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The trial was adjourned 11 times on procedural grounds, such as, for example, the appointment of the defendant’s attorney. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The applicant lodged a complaint with the Warszawa Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The applicant sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before theWarszawa District Court had been excessive. The appeal was rejected on procedural grounds, i.e. failure to pay the so-called “basic court fee” (opłata podstawowa). The court examined the course of the impugned proceedings and held that there had been no delays for which the Court could be held responsible, although it admitted the proceedings had been lengthy.

name: Mobin Ahmed
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 9 July 1997. It originated in an application (no. 22954/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality. Liberty, a non-governmental organisation based in London, was granted leave to submit written comments on the case. No observations were submitted. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 April 1998. The applicants were all British citizens, born in 1941, 1948, 1947 and 1932 respectively. At the relevant time they were each permanently employed in different capacities by various local authorities. Their precise status and functions are described in Section C below. The background to their complaints to the Convention institutions is constituted by the enactment and implementation of legislative measures designed to limit the rights of people living in England and Wales. The Court heard addresses by the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent and Mr J. Morris QC, Attorney-General. The history of the enactment of the relevant measures as well as their purport and scope are described in Section B below. The impact of the measures on the applicants, all persons considered holders of politically restricted posts within the meaning of the applicable legislation, is described in Sections C and D. The adoption of the Local Government Officers (Political Restrictions) Regulations 1990 is referred to as the ‘Widdicombe Committee’ report. The report concludes that ‘the overwhelming view in the evidence we have received has been that officers (subject to very limited and closely defined exceptions) should continue to serve the council as a whole’. The Local Government Officers (Political Restrictions) Regulations 1990 (“the Regulations”) were made under section 1(5) of the Act on 4 April 1990. They were laid before Parliament the following day and came into force on 1 May 1990. The Regulations applied to all persons holding a politically restricted post. This term covers three broad categories of local government officials: the most senior post-holders in. local government and senior members of a political party. The regulations apply to officers at the rank of principal officer and above. These include those who are standing for, and holding, public elected office. They are also prohibited from speaking or writing in public in a way that might be regarded as engaging in party political debate. Local government officials in three categories were deemed to be subject to the Regulations. A local government officer in the second and third categories could apply to an independent adjudicator to have his or her post removed from the list of posts to which the Regulations applied. Mr Ahmed was a solicitor employed by the London Borough of Hackney. Mr Perrin was Principal Valuer with the Devon County Council (a category three officer). He was responsible for leading, leading, the Housing Benefits Review Board and the Environmental Sub-Committee. The Council did not provide a certificate stating that he did not give advice regularly. The adjudicator replied to the Council on 30 March 1990 that Mr Ahmed’s application for exemption could not therefore be granted. Mr Perrin's post required him to give regular advice to the Council’s committees, including strategy advice on key estate management issues. His application for exemption was refused on 20 March 1990. Mr Perrin had to give up his position as Vice-Chair and Property Officer of the Exeter Constituency Labour Party. He also had to refrain from supporting and assisting Labour candidates in Exeter City Council elections, including his wife, who was a candidate in May 1990 and May 1991. Mr Bentley's post was classified as politically sensitive and appropriately subject to political restrictions. He was also restricted in canvassing for his wife who stood as the only Labour Councillor for West Devon Borough Council. Mr Bentley applied for exemption from political restrictions. Mr Brough is employed by Hillingdon Borough Council as the head of its Committee Services Department. He can no longer act as Parliamentary Chairman of his party in Harrow East and is prevented from speaking at public meetings on issues such as housing and the health service. Judicial review proceedings challenging the validity of the Regulations were dismissed on 20 December 1991. The judge, Mr Justice Hutchison, considered that he was bound by the recent decision of the House of Lords in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Brind and Others regarding the status of the post. The judge referred to an affidavit submitted by Mr Simcock, a senior civil servant at the Department of the Environment. He explained how the Widdicombe Committee had been set up in 1985 to inquire into local authority practices and procedures with particular reference to the respective roles of elected members and officers. The judge continued: “... I preface my summary by pointing out that some of [the applicants’ complaints] reflect the applicant’s root and branch opposition to the whole concept of restricting the political activities of local government employees’” The judge added that the Regulations were ‘unreasonable’ and ‘contrary’ to Article 10 of the Convention. The Regulations go too far in prohibiting conduct undertaken with apparent intention, etc., or likely to create the impression of support, etc. They should, at most, have proscribed actual political activities. The width of the language used means that many non-party political activities, including trade unions and charitable activities, are prohibited. The terms are imposed on existing employees, who entered into their contracts of employment on a different basis. The restrictions may have an adverse effect on recruitment and lead to resignations by skilled staff. The arguments summarised in (a) to (h) above are essentially arguments against the whole concept of restricting such activities, and in the circumstances cannot found an attack on Wednesbury grounds. An appeal to the Court of Appeal was dismissed on 26 November 1992. Lord Justice Neill found that the provisions of Article 10 of the Convention did not assist NALGO and the applicants. The other judges, Lords Justices Russell and Rose, agreed. The House of Lords refused leave to appeal to it on 24 March 1993. The Regulations were not ‘Wednesbury unreasonable’ or ultra vires, Lord Neill said. He also agreed with the first-instance judge as to legitimate expectation. The argument mentioned in (f) is in my view misconceived: the Regulations do not prohibit the kind of activities there mentioned.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 9 July 1997. It originated in an application (no. 22954/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). Liberty, a non-governmental organisation based in London, submitted written comments on the case on 2 September 1997. These were received on 12 January 1998 and subsequently communicated to the Agent of the Government, the representative of the applicants and the Delegate of the Commission for possible observations. No observations were submitted. The Government’s responses to the applicants’ claims were filed with the registry on 21 April and 18 May 1998. The applicants filed observations in reply on 29 May 1998 and the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 April 1998. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Morris QC, Attorney-General, Mr. J. Eadie, Barrister-at-Law, Counsel, Mr I. MacLeod, Legal Secretariat to the Law Officers and Mr P. Rowsell, Department of the Environment, Transport and the Regions. History of the enactment of the relevant measures as well as their purport and scope are described in Section B below. The impact of the measures on the applicants, all persons considered holders of politically restricted posts within the meaning of the applicable legislation, is described in the Section C below. Section C: The adoption of the Local Government Officers (Political Restrictions) Regulations 1990 is described as the ‘political background’ to the adoption of these Regulations. The Committee firmly endorsed the continuation of the tradition of politically impartial local government officers having regard in particular to the roles of senior officers as managers, advisers and arbitrators in the day-to-day functioning of local government. Widdicombe Committee recommended that senior officers continued to discharge their functions in a manner which was impartial from both a subjective and an objective point of view. The Local Government Officers (Political Restrictions) Regulations 1990 (“the Regulations”) were made under section 1(5) of the Act on 4 April 1990. They were laid before Parliament the following day and came into force on 1 May 1990. The Regulations applied to all persons holding a politically restricted post. This term covers three broad categories of local government officials: the most senior post-holders in the local authority, and those who are councillors or standing for election. Local government officials employed in these categories at the time of the entry into force of the Regulations were deemed, according to regulation 3(1), to be subject to the measures. A more detailed analysis of the contents of the Act and the Regulations is set out at paragraphs 26–33 below. Mr Ahmed was a solicitor employed by the London Borough of Hackney. Mr Perrin was Principal Valuer with the Devon County Council (a category three officer). He was responsible for leading, leading, the Housing Benefits Review Board and the Environmental Sub-Committee. The Council confirmed that Mr Ahmed had not attended committees during the previous twelve months, but stated that he would be involved in giving advice in future. Mr Perrin applied for exemption from political restrictions on the ground that although he advised the Council and spoke to the media, the advice was ‘factual valuation information regarding the acquisition, disposal and management of property’ His application for exemption was refused on 20 March 1990. Mr Perrin had to give up his position as Vice-Chair and Property Officer of the Exeter Constituency Labour Party. He also had to refrain from supporting and assisting Labour candidates in Exeter City Council elections, including his wife, who was a candidate in May 1990 and May 1991. Mr Bentley was head of the Council’s corporate policy unit, and his post was responsible for policy analysis and research. Mr Bentley applied for exemption from political restrictions. Mr Brough is employed by Hillingdon Borough Council as the head of its Committee Services Department. He can no longer act as Parliamentary Chairman of his party in Harrow East and is prevented from speaking at public meetings on issues such as housing and the health service. Judicial review proceedings challenging the validity of the Regulations were dismissed on 20 December 1991. The judge, Mr Justice Hutchison, considered that he was bound by the recent decision of the House of Lords in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Brind and Others regarding the status of the post. The judge referred to an affidavit submitted by Mr Simcock, a senior civil servant at the Department of the Environment. The affidavit explained how the Widdicombe Committee had been set up in 1985 to inquire into local authority practices and procedures. Mr Sim Cock also described the consultation process between the publication of the WIDDICOMbe Report and the making of the Regulations, in which NALGO was involved. The judge continued: “... I preface my summary by pointing out that some of [the applicants’ complaints] reflect the applicant’s root and branch opposition to the whole concept of restricting the political activities of local government employees” Some of these points will have to be considered individually when I come to deal with further arguments advanced by the applicants under quite different heads, but in the context of Wednesbury unreasonableness I propose only to say that they do not in my judgment come near to establishing a case of perversity. I have already briefly referred to the genesis of the Act and the Regulations in the Widdicombe Report, and to the consultative processes that followed it. The Government’s Command Paper in July 1988 spelt out the essential aim that: ‘it was important that the post-holder should be seen to be politically impartial but otherwise, local government employees should not be subject to restrictions on their political activity’ The Regulations did not go beyond the policy and purpose of the Act, and rejected an argument that the applicants had a ‘legitimate expectation’ that the Government would not interfere with trade union activities. Lord Justice Neill found that the provisions of Article 10 of the Convention did not assist NALGO and the applicants. The other judges, Lords Justices Russell and Rose, agreed. An appeal to the Court of Appeal was dismissed on 26 November 1992. The House of Lords refused leave to appeal to it on 24 March 1993. The case was settled in favour of the applicants in November 1992, and the case was heard at a first-instance court in January 1993.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 9 July 1997. It originated in an application (no. 22954/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality. Liberty was granted leave to submit written comments on the case on 2 September 1997. No observations were submitted. A schedule to the applicants’ memorial setting out details of their claims under Article 50 of the Convention was received on 22 January 1998. An amended schedule of claims was filed with the registry on 27 April 1998. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 April 1998, and the Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza, Mr Goudie and Mr Morris. The applicants live in London, Yelverton, Edgware and Exeter respectively. At the relevant time they were each permanently employed in different capacities by various local authorities. The history of the enactment of the relevant measures as well as their purport and scope are described in Section B below. The impact of the measures on the applicants, all persons considered holders of politically restricted posts within the meaning of the applicable legislation, is described in Sections C and D. The adoption of the Local Government Officers (Political Restrictions) Regulations 1990 is described as one of the main reasons for their development. The regulations aim to prevent the. involvement of certain categories of local government officials, such as themselves, in political. activities. They are also intended to protect the interests of the public from the. influence of politicians. The Local Government Officers (Political Restrictions) Regulations 1990 (“the Regulations”) were made under section 1(5) of the Act on 4 April 1990. They were laid before Parliament the following day and came into force on 1 May 1990. The Regulations applied to all persons holding a politically restricted post. This term covers three broad categories of local government officials: the most senior post-holders in. the council, those at the rank of principal officer and above, and those who hold office in a political party. The regulations were introduced after the Widdicombe Committee recommended they should be included in the terms and conditions of officers. Local government officials in three categories were deemed to be subject to the Regulations. A local government officer could apply to an independent adjudicator to have his or her post removed from the list of posts to which the Regulations applied. A more detailed analysis of the contents of the Act and the Regulations is set out at paragraphs 26–33 below. The effect of the Regulations on the applicants is outlined at the bottom of this article. Mr Ahmed was a solicitor employed by the London Borough of Hackney. Mr Perrin was Principal Valuer with the Devon County Council (a category three officer). He was responsible for leading, leading, the Housing Benefits Review Board, the Environmental Sub-Committee and the Housing Development Committee. Mr Perrin's post required him to give regular advice to the Council’s committees, including strategy advice on key estate management issues. His application for exemption was refused on 20 March 1990. Mr Perrin had to give up his position as Vice-Chair and Property Officer of the Exeter Constituency Labour Party. He also had to refrain from supporting and assisting Labour candidates in Exeter City Council elections, including his wife, who was a candidate in May 1990 and May 1991. Mr Bentley's post was classified as one that was politically sensitive (a category one post) and appropriately subject to political restrictions under section 2(3) of the Act. Mr Bentley applied for exemption from political restrictions. Mr Brough is employed by Hillingdon Borough Council as the head of its Committee Services Department. He can no longer act as Parliamentary Chairman of his party in Harrow East and is prevented from speaking at public meetings on issues such as housing and the health service. Judicial review proceedings challenging the validity of the Regulations were dismissed on 20 December 1991. The judge, Mr Justice Hutchison, considered that he was bound by the recent decision of the House of Lords in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Brind and Others regarding the status of the post. The judge referred to an affidavit submitted by Mr Simcock, a senior civil servant at the Department of the Environment. The affidavit explained how the Widdicombe Committee had been set up in 1985 to inquire into local authority practices and procedures with particular reference to the respective roles of elected members and officers. The judge continued: “... I preface my summary by pointing out that some of [the applicants’ complaints] reflect the applicant’s root and branch opposition to the whole concept of restricting the political activities of local government employees’” NALGO was involved in the making of the Regulations, in which NALSO was involved. The Regulations go too far in prohibiting conduct undertaken with apparent intention, etc., or likely to create the impression of support. The width of the language used means that many non-party political activities, including trade unions and charitable activities, are prohibited. The terms are imposed on existing employees, who entered into their contracts of employment on a different basis. The restrictions may have an adverse effect on recruitment and lead to resignations by skilled staff. Some of these points will have to be considered individually when I come to deal with further arguments advanced by the applicants under quite different heads. I propose only to say that they do not in my judgment come near to establishing a case of perversity. An appeal to the Court of Appeal was dismissed on 26 November 1992. The House of Lords refused leave to appeal to it on 24 March 1993. Lord Justice Neill found that the provisions of Article 10 of the Convention did not assist NALGO and the applicants. He also agreed with the first-instance judge as to legitimate expectation. The other judges, Lords Justices Russell and Rose, agreed. Leave to appeal  to the House of Lords was refused. The Court of appeal ruled that the Regulations were not “Wednesbury unreasonable” or ultra vires. It also ruled that it was not open to the courts below the House of Lords to depart from the traditional Wednesbury grounds.

name: Arthur Hutchinson
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 57592/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. In 1983 the applicant broke into a family home, stabbed to death a man, his wife and their adult son and repeatedly raped their 18 year‑old daughter. On 14 September 1984, at Sheffield Crown Court, he was convicted of aggravated burglary, rape and three counts of murder. The trial judge sentenced the applicant to a term of life imprisonment and recommended a minimum tariff of 18 years. On 10 July 2013 the complaint under Article 3 was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. Tugendhat J handed down judgment in the applicant’s case on 16 May 2008. The seriousness of the offences alone was such that the starting point was a whole life order. There were no mitigating factors. On 6 October 2008, the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal. The applicant was sentenced to a life. term of imprisonment. The sentence was suspended for 20 years and a fine of £50,000. The victim was given a 12-month suspended sentence and a £40,000 fine. The application was rejected on the grounds that the sentence was too lenient. The appeal was dismissed on 6 October 2009.

The case originated in an application (no. 57592/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his whole life sentence gave rise to a violation of Article 3 of the convention. The complaint under Article 3 was communicated to the Government on 10 July 2013 and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The application was brought by Mr Arthur Hutchinson, a British national detained in Her Majesty’s Prison Durham. He stabbed to death a man, his wife and their adult son and repeatedly raped their 18 year‑old daughter, having first dragged her past her father's body. Tugendhat J handed down judgment in the applicant’s case in May 2008. He found that there was no reason for deviating from the Secretary of State's decision. On 6 October 2008, the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal. There were no mitigating factors, he said. The seriousness of the offences alone was such that the starting point was a whole life order. In addition, there were a number of very serious aggravating factors. The surviving victim described “sadistic as well as sexual conduct’. The judge said that the victim had made an impact statement that was ‘sadistically and sexually oriented’
