name: Tayfun Koç
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 50934/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Ms O. E. Ataman, a lawyer practising in İstanbul. The first applicant is the owner of the monthly magazine “Revolution for Equality, Liberty and Peace” and the second applicant is its editor-in-chief. In the fifth and sixth issue of the magazine, three articles written by Mr C.K. were published entitled “The Kurdish problem in Turkey and the peace process 2 and 3” Kurdish people are crushed. An inevitable imperative for the salvation of crushed people is the integration of the social revolution with the right to self determination. The objective revolutionary feature of the PKK is not an excuse to dispense it from criticism. A “democratic peace” struggle is not only to ask for the end of the ongoing war in the region. Of course, a ceasefire is the first and the compulsory step to peace. (...) The request for peace of the oppressed people and proletarians is part of the struggle against imperialism and oligarchy.” “The butcher of justice is once again at work” read, inter alia, as follows: “Oltan Sungurlu, taking behind him a registry tainted by blood, became the Minister of Justice of the MGK Government’ Sungurlu: The main policy of pressure, targeting particularly political prisoners, is the usurpation of their right to communication and to receive information. He is trying to legitimise cell-type prisons by [pointing to] the recent bloodshed in Bayrampaşa prison and the quarrels between prisoners. 60-70 people are imprisoned in dormitories of a capacity of 30-35. The medical assistance to ill prisoners and suspects are arbitrarily obstructed or delayed. The Kurdish problem has taken the shape of an open war for the past thirteen years. It must be firstly stated that the war waged by the State is a dirty war and that the Kurdish national struggle is a Kurdish problem. The court held that with the first two articles, the applicants spread propaganda against the indivisibility of the State. As regards the third article, the court found that the article in question referred to the Minister of Justice as a ‘butcher of justice’ and, as a result, designated him as a target for terrorist organisations. The court decided to suspend the execution of the applicants’ sentences, for a period of three years, on 24 November 1999 and 14 January 2000 respectively. At no time during the criminal proceedings were the applicants detained. The applicants had not committed any intentional offence during the three years since the date of deferment. An additional judgment (ek karar) dated 6 June 2003, the İstanbul State Security Court, nullified the applicants' condemnation.

The case originated in an application (no. 50934/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two Turkish nationals, Mr Tayfun Koç and Mr Musa Tambaş (“the applicants”), made the application on 3 August 1999. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Ms O. E. Ataman, a lawyer practising in İstanbul. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The request for peace of the oppressed people and proletarians is part of the struggle against imperialism and oligarchy. The applicants claimed that the content of the articles remained within the limits of freedom of expression. They were fined 150,000,000 Turkish Liras (TRL) (approximately 500 euros (EUR) and TRL 75,900,000 (approximately EUR 252) respectively. The Kurdish problem has taken the shape of an open war for the past thirteen years. It must be firstly stated that the war waged by the State is a dirty war and that the Kurdish national struggle is a Kurdish problem. name: Bayram Güçlü
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 31535/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1966 and is currently serving a prison sentence in Samsun. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. On 10 October 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. The application was filed by a Turkish national, Mr Bayram Güçlü (“the applicant”), on 23 June 2004. On 14 July 1999 the Istanbul State Security Court issued an order in respect of the applicant, in absentia, for him to be arrested on suspicion of trafficking illegal drugs. In the absence of a lawyer, the applicant admitted some of the allegations made against him. On 26 February 2003 the Istanbul State Security Court found the applicant guilty of trafficking cocaine and sentenced him to thirty-six years’ imprisonment. In convicting the applicant, it relied on his statements, the statements made by the other members of the criminal organisation, and forensics reports on the drugs that had been seized. The court deducted the thirty-three months the applicant had already served in the Netherlands from his total sentence. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court on 6 November 2003. That decision was deposited with the latter’s registry on 9 January 2004.

The court deducted the thirty-three months the applicant had already served in the Netherlands from his total sentence.

name: Günther Paul Litwin
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been denied access to the appeal courts. The court, following a proposal made by the applicant’s counsel, promised a penalty of nine‑and‑a‑half years’ imprisonment in exchange for his right to appeal. The Government did not take part in the agreement reached, the public prosecutor did not call for further evidence, and the content of which is in dispute between the parties. The application was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Fulda Regional Court convicted the applicant of aggravated extortion, aggravated robbery and attempted aggravated robbery (two counts of each offence) and dangerous bodily injury (one count) and sentenced him to nine-and-a-half years’ imprisonment. The court considered the fact that the applicant had eventually waived his right to the confiscated assets and had thus delivered a major proportion of his criminal profits as a mitigating factor. The applicant complained that the negotiated agreement had not complied with the requirements of the Federal Court of Justice’s case-law. He applied for restitution of the status quo ante and lodged an appeal on points of law, arguing that the waiver of the right to appeal was invalid. The Second Chamber of the Federal Court of Justice dismissed the applicant’s request for restitution of the status quo ante and rejected his appeal on points of law as inadmissible. Relying on its own settled case-law, the court observed that a waiver of the right to appeal could not be revoked, rescinded or withdrawn. The court did not find it necessary to establish whether the waiver had been part of a negotiated agreement, as this fact did not call into question the validity of the waiver as such. The only decisive factor was whether the accused had been unduly influenced when waiving hisright to appeal. In the present case, there was no indication that there had been such undue influence. The applicant claimed that he had been unduly influenced when waiving his right to appeal in exchange for a maximum penalty of nine-and-a-half years’ imprisonment. The Federal Constitutional Court (file no. 2 BvR 1339/01), relying on the relevant provisions of its rules of procedure, refused to admit the constitutional complaint for examination without giving further reasons. This decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 4 December 2003. The applicant's wife had also been asked to waive any rights she had to the confiscated assets. This procedural method had been arbitrary, had not been in accordance with the statutory provisions governing the confiscation of assets in criminal proceedings and constituted a violation of the right to an effective remedy.

name: Hasan Demirkaya
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, namely the PKK (Kurdistan Workers' Party) On 18 January 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the applicant's application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant admitted that he had aided and abetted the PKK and acted as courier for the organisation, but denied all the charges against him. Izmir State Security Court charged the applicant and fifteen others with aiding and abetting an illegal organisation. The charges were brought under Article 169 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of Law no. 3713 (the anti-terrorist law) The applicant denied any connection with the PKK. On 20 June 2002 the Izmir State security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to three years and nine months' imprisonment. On 10 October 2003 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's appeal. The applicant was sentenced to three-and-a-half years in prison. The sentence was suspended on appeal and the applicant was released in March 2004.

He was taken into police custody on suspicion of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, namely the PKK (Kurdistan Workers' Party) On 18 January 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The case was decided in favour of the applicant on 13 May 2002. Izmir State Security Court charged the applicant and fifteen others with aiding and abetting an illegal organisation. The charges were brought under Article 169 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of Law no. 3713 (the anti-terrorist law). During the trial, the applicant denied any connection with the PKK. N.S., one of the co-defendants, admitted to being a PKK member before the court, but stated that although he had stayed at the applicant's house when he had come to Izmir, he did not know that he was a PKK members. On 20 June 2002 the Izmir State security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to three years and nine months' imprisonment. The applicant's appeal was dismissed on 10 October 2003.

name: Iradj Kuhlen-Rafsandjani
train_texts: The case originated in three applications (nos. 21980/06, 26944/07 and 36948/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of two sets of proceedings concerning custody of his children had been excessive. He was granted contact with his children every second and fourth weekend of the month from 6 p.m. Friday to 6p.m Saturday. The German Government was represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, Federal Ministry of Justice. The proceedings concerning custody of the children and the applicant's contact rights began on 31 August 1998. The parties agreed to the commissioning of an expert opinion on a possible regulation of custody and contact rights. They further agreed that until the completion of the expert opinion the contact of the applicant with his children should be provisionally regulated by the acting judge in cooperation with the Kleve child protection agency (Kinderschutzbund). On 28 April 1999 the judge ruled in favour of the application. The proceedings were to a large extent conducted jointly until the. applicant's former wife's petition for divorce was granted by a judgment dated 29 November 2001. Father and children had been living with the mother for a considerable time. Mother requested sole custody of the children for the duration of the separation of the spouses. District Court ordered an expert opinion on the question of what attribution of custody rights and – should sole custody be awarded to the mother – what contact with their father would be in the children's best interest. The expert opinion was finalised on 31 August 2000. The mother had previously cancelled appointments for appraisals in connection with the drawing up of the expert opinion, thereby delaying its completion. Nevertheless, it appears that regular contact between the father and the children ceased temporarily during the year 2000. In the meantime the applicant had supervised contact in cooperation with the Kleve child protection agency. In 2000, the applicant asked to be granted contact rights in accordance with his request as reformulated on 18 October 2000. The curator ad litem emphasised, in particular, that the son's apparent rejection of his father was due to the influence of the mother and the grandparents. The Düsseldorf Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's request for legal aid in the appellate proceedings on the ground that his claim was devoid of any prospect of success. In view of the tensions and lack of cooperation between the parents, the transfer of sole custody of the children to the mother was in the children's best interest. By transferring the right to determine the children’s place of residence to the Kleve District Youth Welfare Office, the District Court had set the stage for implementing regular contact between the father and his children. The case began in November 2000 in Düsseldorf, Germany. The applicant's contact rights were to be decided by a court decision after consultation with the guardian. The children were summoned to a hearing in May 2002, but did not hear. The application was dismissed by the Court of Appeal in August 2002. The mother was granted sole custody of the children in March 2002. Her children were not heard at the appeal hearing. The case was heard by the Federal Constitutional Court in October 2002. In March 2002 the applicant appealed to be granted joint custody with the mother and to leave the right to determine the children's place of residence with the District Youth Welfare Office. Following the divorce the parties continued to argue about the applicant's contact rights. The parties, the children's guardian and their curator ad litem were heard. The applicant was granted the right to visit the children at their mother's house on the occasion of the Iranian public holidays at a time to be previously agreed with the mother. On 2 April 2004 the Düsseldorf Court of Court of Appeal ruled that the applicant should have contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays or Sundays from 2 p.m. in the mother's presence and by prior agreement with her. On 28 August 2003 the District Court rejected the applicant’s further application for a decision on his contact rights since the court settlement of 5 September 2002 constituted a binding agreement between the parties in this regard. The father applied to have contact with his children for part of the Easter and Christmas holidays. The children objected to spending holidays alone with their father. Appeal dismissed and confirmed that the settlement was neither invalid nor void. The father was granted unaccompanied contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays or Sundays from 10.00 a.m. to 6.00 p.m., but refrained from regulating the applicant's contact rights for the holidays since at the hearing of 11 March 2005 the children had objected to being left alone. The court further found that there was no evidence that the. children had been manipulated by their grandparents. It specified that in reaching its conclusion it could not rely on an expert opinion because the father had refused to be examined by the appointed expert. The case involved a request to spend summer holidays with his children at his home in Heidelberg from 23 July to 3 August 2008. By a decision of 6 June 2008 the District Court rejected the request since the children had objected to spending the holidays with him; the request therefore could not be regarded as being in their interest. On 19 August 2008 the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal dismissed an appeal against that decision, since because of the passage of time a decision in the matter was no longer required. The decisions of the Federal Constitutional Court (file no. 5 F 283/98) 42. The applicant challenged the provisional attribution of sole custody to the mother. The decision was served on the applicant on. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint regarding the attribution of sole custody to the mother as an ancillary matter to the divorce proceedings. The court held that the courts had an obligation to take the child's wishes into account when taking decisions on custody. It was questionable in the case at hand whether the proceedings had satisfied these requirements since the lower courts had not given any convincing reasons why the children had not been heard. The applicant could not claim to have suffered a particularly serious disadvantage since his complaint did not have any prospect of success even if remitted to lower courts. It had been difficult for years to regulate the father's contact rights with his children. At a hearing that had taken place in those proceedings it had transpired that the children were rather opposed to an extension of the applicant. The applicant had already lodged a similar application in previous proceedings (5 F 155/99), which had been rejected by a decision of the District Court dated 9 November 2000. The applicant argued that the grandparents were setting the children against him and obstructing the exercise of his contact rights. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint (File no. 1 BvR 2127/01) in December 2005. The German Civil Code in its current version was unconstitutional, the Constitutional Court ruled in November 2001. The case was dismissed by the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal on 7 November 2001, and by the Emmerich District Court on 4 July 2001. The case was heard by the Düsseldorf District Court in 2001. The court ruled that a ban on contact between the children and their grandparents was neither practicable nor in the children's best interest. The Court of Appeal rejected the applicant's request for legal aid for the appellate proceedings since his appeal was devoid of any prospect of success. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant’s constitutional complaint that his parental rights had been violated by the decisions of the lower courts. It held that the right to determine the contact of the children with third persons was part of the right of custody which had been awarded solely to the mother. The applicant's parental rights could therefore not be directly affected.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of two sets of proceedings concerning custody of his children had been excessive. On 9 December 2009 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applied at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant was granted legal aid and was represented by Ms C. Krüger-Rauch. The applicant filed an application with the Emmerich District Court to be granted contact with his children in accordance with the aforementioned decision of 23 July 1998. The proceedings were instituted under file no. 5 F 272/98. At approximately the same time custody proceedings were opened before the same court. The parties agreed to the commissioning of an expert opinion on a possible regulation of custody and contact rights. They further agreed that until the completion of the expert opinion the contact of the applicant with his kids should be provisionally regulated by the acting judge in cooperation with the Kleve child protection agency (Kinderschutzbund). On 28 April 1999 the applicant and his wife agreed to a settlement that was never accepted by the applicant, and he later challenged it. Father had supervised contact in cooperation with the Kleve child protection agency. He revoked his approval of the supervised contacts and applied to the District Court for contact in accordance with the regulations set out in the court's decision of 23 July 1998. The mother requested sole custody of the children for the duration of the separation of the spouses. Expert opinion recommended that sole custody be transferred to her. However, finding that the mother and grandparents were influencing the children against their father, she proposed that the question of where the children should reside (Aufenthaltsbestimmungsrecht) be referred to the Rees Youth Welfare Office (Jugendamt) In 2000, in separate custody proceedings, the District Court decided to provisionally grant sole custody of the children to the mother. relations between the parents had deteriorated to the extent that joint custody was no longer in the children's best interest. The children's main focal point and familiar environment remained with the mother it was in their interest that sole custody be awarded to her. The District Court deprived the mother of the right to determine the children’s place of residence because she was not willing to accept regular contact between the father and his children. By a joint judgment (Verbundurteil) of 29 November 2001 the District Court granted the wife's petition for divorce and transferred sole custody of the children to her. The applicant appealed on 18 February 2002 and requested to be granted joint custody with the mother and to leave the right to determine the children's place of residence with a guardian. The applicant and his former wife entered into a court settlement (Prozessvergleich) stipulating that the applicant should have contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays or Sundays from 2 p.m. in the mother's presence and by prior agreement with her. The parties further agreed that with effect from 2003 they would plan at least one holiday per year with theChildren at approximately the same place and time. The applicant was further granted the right to visit the children at their mother's house on the occasion of the Iranian public holidays at a time to be previously agreed with the mother. The applicant was granted unaccompanied contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays and Sundays for the period until finalisation of the expert opinion. The court held that the parental rights as guaranteed by the Basic Law included an obligation for the courts to conduct custody proceedings in such a way as to obtain a reliable basis for a decision founded on the child's wellbeing. The applicant could not claim to have suffered a particularly serious disadvantage since his complaint did not have any prospect of success even if remitted to the lower courts, the court held. The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The proceedings concerning custody of the children and the applicant's contact rights began in 1998. The parties agreed to the commissioning of an expert opinion on a possible regulation of custody and contact rights. They further agreed that until the completion of the expert opinion the contact of the applicant with his children should be provisionally regulated by the acting judge in cooperation with the Kleve child protection agency (Kinderschutzbund). On 28 April 1999 the judge ruled in favour of the mother and the application was dismissed. The application was appealed and the case was settled out of court in 2002. The case was decided by the European Court of Human Rights in March 2007. The court ordered an expert opinion on the question of what attribution of custody rights and – should sole custody be awarded to the mother – what contact with their father would be in the children's best interest. In view of the repeated disputes between the parents and the fact that the children had been living with the mother for a considerable time and were settled, the expert recommended that sole custody of the children be transferred to her. The mother had previously cancelled appointments for appraisals in connection with the drawing up of the expert opinion, thereby delaying its completion. Nevertheless, it appears that regular contact between the father and the children ceased temporarily during the year 2000. In 2000, the District Court decided to provisionally grant sole custody of the children to the mother. relations between the parents had deteriorated to the extent that joint custody was no longer in the children's best interest. The applicant appealed against the attribution of sole custody and requested legal aid for the appeal proceedings. The Düsseldorf Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's request for legal aid in the appellate proceedings on the ground that his claim was devoid of any prospect of success. By transferring the right to determine the children’s place of residence to the Kleve District Youth Welfare Office, the Court had set the stage for implementing regular contact between the father and his children. The wife filed for divorce and the children were transferred to their mother. The court found that joint custody was not an option in view of the lack of cooperation between the parents. The children attended the hearing but were not heard by the Court of Appeal. The applicant appealed on 18 February 2002 and requested to be granted joint custody with the mother and to leave the right to determine the children's place of residence with a guardian. By a decision of 26 June 2002 the Düsseldorf Court of appeal partially partially granted the applicant's request for joint custody. The application was dismissed by the Federal Constitutional Court in October 2002. The case continues. The parties continued to argue about the applicant's contact rights following the divorce. The applicant and his former wife entered into a court settlement stipulating that the applicant should have contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays or Sundays from 2 p.m. in the mother's presence and by prior agreement with her. The parties further agreed that with effect from 2003 they would plan at least one holiday per year with theChildren at approximately the same place and time, so as to enable the applicant to meet the children regularly for a period of several days during the holidays. On 2 April 2004 the Düsseldorf Court of Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the applicant. The father applied to spend holidays with his children at his home in Heidelberg. Appeal dismissed the appeal and confirmed that the settlement was neither invalid nor void. For the period until finalisation of the expert opinion the applicant was granted unaccompanied contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays or Sundays from 10.00 a.m to 6 p.m. The father had refused to be examined by the appointed expert. The court further found that there was no evidence that the children had been manipulated by their grandparents. The applicant objected to the new expert on the ground that she did not have the necessary professional qualifications. An expert opinion could therefore not be established. The applicant filed a request to spend summer holidays with his children at his home in Heidelberg from 23 July to 3 August 2008 (file no. 5 F 33/08). A hearing took place on 21 May 2008, during which the parents and the children were heard. By a decision of 6 June 2008 the District Court rejected the request since the children had objected to spending the holidays with him; the request therefore could not be regarded as being in their interest. The child had been given the opportunity to disclose its personal relations with the other family members during the proceedings. The court pointed out that it was questionable in the case at hand whether the proceedings had satisfied these requirements since the lower courts had not given any convincing reasons why the children had not been heard. But there was no need to take a decision because in any event the applicant could not claim to have suffered a particularly serious disadvantage since his complaint did not have any prospect of success. The applicant filed an application with the Emmerich District Court on behalf of and in the name of his children for the regulation of the children's contact rights with respect to their father. On 4 July 2001 the District Court dismissed his request as inadmissible. On 10 September 2001 he was informed by the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal that there existed doubts as to his entitlement to represent his children in the proceedings. By a decision of 7 December 2005 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint (File no. 1 BvR 2127/01) The applicant argued that the grandparents were setting the children against him and obstructing the exercise of his contact rights. District Court rejected the application on 22 March 2001. Düsseldorf Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 3 June 2002. Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint that his parental rights had been violated by the decisions of the lower courts. It held that the right to determine the contact of the children with third persons was part of the right of custody which had been awarded solely to the mother. The applicant's parental rights could therefore not be directly affected by the contact. of his children withthird persons and his own contact rights could be affected only indirectly. In view of the close relationship between the mother, children and the grandparents and the fact that the grandparents assumed a considerable part of child care, a prohibition of contact was neither practicable nor in the children's best interest.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 17912/05) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 10 May 2005. The applicant complained, in particular, about a breach of Article 6 of the. Convention on account of unreasonably lengthy proceedings in which no oral hearing. before a tribunal was held. On 10 April 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of. the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The Vorarlberg Regional Planning Act provided an exemption only for a small-sized project of around 25 square meters. The Mayor observed that for the construction of the two other buildings there had been proceedings for re-designation of the concerned land. The applicant had then promised to demolish the already existing roofing which had been built without the authorities' consent and the relating demolition order had not been challenged by the applicant. He filed two complaints with the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) in 2001 and 2004. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant's complaint as it had no prospect of success. In his second complaint, of 20 November 2001, the applicant submitted that an exemption should have been granted as his project was small. The Administrative Court found that there was no need for a hearing as the applicant's complaints concerned only legal questions of no particular complexity. The question of the lawfulness of the area zoning plan had been considered by the Constitutional Court, which had no doubts as to its lawfulness. The applicant did not pursue these proceedings any further. In the meantime, on 29 June 2000, the Municipal Council dismissed the applicant’s request for re-designation of the land concerned. In November 2004, the Administrative Court served a decision to the applicant. which it had joined. This decision was served on the applicant 's counsel on 11 November 2004.

The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant is the owner of a farm in Frastranz. He asked the Mayor (Bürgermeister) of Frastanz to grant him a permit for the building of roofing between two buildings in order to create a tool shed on his farm. The Mayor, acting as building authority of first instance, dismissed this request as the project was contrary to the relevant area zoning plan. The Vorarlberg Regional Planning Act provided such an exemption only for a small-sized project of around 25 square meters. The applicant filed two complaints with the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) In the first complaint, of 24 September 2001, he submitted that the refusal to grant him a building permit had been unlawful as the actual designation of the land concerned was not clear and the underlying area zoning plan was unlawful. In the second complaint he submitted he should have been granted an exemption as his project was small. In both complaints the applicant asked the Administrative court to hold a hearing. The Administrative Court dismissed both complaints on 21 October 2004. The Administrative Court found that there was no need for a hearing as the applicant's complaints concerned only legal questions of no particular complexity. The question of the lawfulness of the area zoning plan had been considered by the Constitutional Court, which had no doubts as to its lawfulness either. The applicant did not pursue these proceedings any further. In the meantime, on 29 June 2000, the Municipal Council dismissed the applicant’s request for re-designation of the land concerned. This decision was served on the applicant and its counsel on 11 November 2004. The Administrative Court ruled in favour of the applicant. which it had joined.

train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 38414/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he did not receive a fair and public hearing, as he was not informed promptly of the accusation against him. The Government filed observations on the admissibility and merits on 30 May 2006. On 19 October 2006 the President of the Third Section refused to include in the case file the applicant's observations in reply to Government's observations and his just satisfaction claims which were filed outside the time-limit (Rule 38 § 1). The applicant challenged the decision of the İzmir Magistrate's Court. He argued that he had been deprived of his right of defence in violation of Article 6 of the Convention. The applicant paid the relevant charge on 26 November 2002. He was warned that in case he failed to pay the due amount, the fine would be converted into prison sentence. The application was rejected by the Supreme Court of Turkey in 2007. The court ruled that the decision was in accordance with the law and procedure. The Court of Appeal ruled that there was insufficient evidence to support the applicant's claim that he was deprived of the right to defend himself. The appeal was dismissed and the applicant was ordered to pay a fine.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4789/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant alleged, in particular, that there had been a violation of Article 8 of the. Convention, on account of the refusal by the national authorities to. indicate her forename in the civil register of births as that of the mother of. her adopted child. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Justice (‘the Court’) on 12 January 2010. The applicant was represented by Ms Habibe Y Turkey Kayar, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government were represented by their Agent. The court dismissed the applicant’s request on the ground that it had no legal basis. On 14 April 2008 the applicant appealed on points of law. On 15 March 2009 a new regulation entered into force entitled ‘Regulation on the implementation of mediation services for the adoption of minors’ (“the Regulation’) On 9 November 2010 she applied to the registry office for the registration of her forename as that of the mother of E., relying on Article 20 § 4 of the new Regulation. That request was granted on the same day and the record entries concerning the child were consequently amended with immediate effect. On 5 November 2009 the Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the court below.

The case originated in an application (no. 4789/10) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that there had been a violation of Article 8 of the convention on account of the refusal by the national authorities to indicate her forename in the civil register of births as that of the mother of her adopted child. She argued that in relation to single-parent adoptions there was a lacuna in the Civil Code which required the court to make provision for such a situation. The court ruled in favour of the applicant. The applicant's request was dismissed on the ground that it had no legal basis. On 14 April 2008 the applicant appealed on points of law. On 15 March 2009 a new regulation entered into force entitled “Regulation on the implementation of mediation services for the adoption of minors’ (“the Regulation”) enabling a single adoptive parent to have his or her forename registered in the place of that of the biological parent. On 9 November 2010 she applied to the registry office for the registration of her fore Name. That request was granted on the same day and the record entries concerning the child were consequently amended with immediate effect.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been denied access to a lawyer while in police custody and that his police statements had been relied on by the trial court to convict him. The application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. On 7 October 2016 the Vice-President of the Second Section invited the Government to submit further observations, if they so wished, following the judgment in Ibrahim and Others v the United Kingdom ([GC], nos. 50541/08 and 3 others, 13 September 2016). The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The applicant's lawyer appealed against the judgment, arguing that the applicant had been convicted on the basis of statements taken under duress. On 3 March 2010, the Court of Appeals upheld the judgement. The appeal was dismissed on appeal on the grounds of the applicant's claim that the statements were made under du pressure. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the application on 2 March 2010. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Justice on 27 May 2009. The judge ruled in favor of the appeal on 7 June 2009, but the appeal was upheld on 1 December 2009.

name: Jane Smith
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25154/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by a British citizen, Mrs Jane Smith (“the applicant”), on 4 May 1994. The applicant alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against her in respect of her occupation of her land in her caravans violated her right to respect for home, her family and private life. The case was referred to the Court, in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 May 2000. The applicant and the Government each filed a memorial. Third-party comments were also received from the European Roma Rights Centre. The judge elected in respect of the United Kingdom, who had taken part in the Commission’s examination of the case, withdrew from sitting in the Grand Chamber (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Lord Justice Schiemann to sit as an ad hoc judge in his place. The Court heard addresses by Mr Drabble, Mr Pannick and Mr Llewellyn. On 29 November 2000, Mr Makarczyk, who was unable to take part in further consideration, was replaced by Mr Bonello. The applicant and her husband applied repeatedly throughout the years for places on many of the local private and official sites in Surrey. Their applications proved unsuccessful as all the sites were full with long waiting lists. They were required to move from roadside to roadside on innumerable occasions. In March 1993, the applicant bought land known as 111A Almners Road, Runnymede. It was a portion of a garden in a Green Belt area where there was already some residential development. The applicant moved a mobile home onto the land and took up residence with her family. In June 1989, the High Court had granted a declaration that Surrey County Council was in breach of its duty under section 6 of the Caravan Sites Act 1968. The previous owner of 111A Almners Road, also a gypsy, had been refused planning permission in January 1993 to live on the land in a caravan. The Council considered that the stationing of a caravan would be detrimental to the character of the Green Belt. The applicant was aware of this situation and the fact that the previous owner had appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment against the refusal of planning permission and the enforcement order. When the applicant purchased the land, she was advised that there was a special concession for granting planning permission to gypsies in Green Belt areas under Circular 28/77. An Inspector appointed by the Department of Environment heard evidence and representations from the applicant and the Council. The appeals site lies within the south west sector of the Metropolitan Green Belt. The application conflicts with the second and third objectives of government green belt policy listed in PPG2. The mobile home is set behind the front of the adjoining house and its range of visibility from the other direction on Almners Road is limited by conifers on its western boundary. It is significantly different to the character of the touring caravans that are parked in some of the nearby gardens, which are incidental to the enjoyment of the residential curtilages within which they stand. … In light of this and its particular impact on the aims of green belt Policy, I conclude … that the use of the land for a residential caravan site for a mobile home and associated operational development is not appropriate to this part of the Met. There is no reason why the site should not be used for the development of a new school. The site is located in an area of the town that has been designated as a national park. It is intended to be part of a wider national park that will be developed for the benefit of the local community. There are no plans to change the name of the site, just the location of the school. It will be open to the public to see if the site is used for school or for other purposes, such as for housing, as long as it is in the same place as the other sites in the town. There is no plan to alter the site’s name to make the area more accessible to people in need of it. The applicant applied to the Council for planning permission to build a bungalow. The Council refused planning permission. The applicant appealed this decision by written statement as she could not afford a public enquiry. On 29 November 1993, an Inspector appointed by the Department of the Environment dismissed the appeal. On 5 September 1994, the Council obtained an injunction in the High Court requiring the applicant and her family to move off their land immediately. In light of the new Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, which came into force on 3 November 1994,. the applicant, in fear of being on the roadside, applied to be placed on the local authority homeless list on 4 August 1994. The application was made on behalf of a family living in a caravan site near Runnymede, Surrey. The family has applied for accommodation in a more natural environment but no offer has yet been made. The Council had previously offered three alternative pieces of land which were subsequently withdrawn due to a methane gas leak, boggy ground and vicinity to a rubbish dump. The local authority has stated that, in the event that the applicant is forced to leave the site, the authority will provide temporary accommodation for her until permanent accommodation becomes available. However, in view of the restrictions on development within the Green Belt, all accommodation offered will be in urban areas. The applicant stated that in May 1997 the local authority decided to institute proceedings against her. The applicant submitted that all the area of the Council was in the Metropolitan Green Belt area. The Government stated that only a large part of it was. The diagram and materials submitted from the Surrey Structure Plan 1994 indicates that 70% of the County was Green Belt, 20% urban and 10% countryside beyond the Green Belt. According to the diagram, the Runnymede area consists entirely of Green Belt and urban centres. AONB and ADLV areas account for 40% of Surrey and include areas of outstanding natural beauty (AONB) or designated landscape value (ADLV) which are also classed as Green Belt areas.

name: Halil Kaya
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22922/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the lack of legal assistance to the applicant during his police custody. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment. In convicting the applicant, the court had regard to the. applicant’s statements to the police and the public prosecutor, which were taken in the absence of a lawyer. On 21 August 2002 the applicant was sent to prison to serve his sentence. On 30 July 2003 Law no. 4963 entered into force, which amended Article 169 of the Criminal Code. Relying on the fact that the new law provided more favourable provisions for the applicant, on 29 August 2003 the applicant’s lawyer requested the re-opening of the proceedings. On 15 September 2003 the Adana Criminal Court decided to re-open the case. On 7 October 2004 the applicant appealed. On 8 May 2006 the court found the applicant guilty and sentenced him to twenty five days’ imprisonment. The court further converted the sentence to a fine.

The case originated in an application (no. 22922/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the lack of legal assistance to the applicant during his police custody. The court also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal, without holding a hearing on the merits. The decision dated 8 July 2002 was deposited with the registry of the Adana State. The applicant was sentenced to three months and ten days’ imprisonment by the Security Court on 21 August 2002. The Adana Criminal Court decided to re-open the case and ordered the applicant’s release from prison on 15 September 2003. On 7 October 2004 the court held that the applicant should not be convicted under Article 169 but under Article 312. The court further converted the sentence to a fine and, pursuant to Law no. 5395 on Juvenile Protection, it decided to defer adjudication of the sentence. This decision was upheld by the Adana Assize Court on 20 June 2007. The applicant appealed the decision. Finally, on 8 May 2006 the court found the applicant guilty under Article 215 of Law. no. 5326 and sentenced him to twenty five days' imprisonment.

name: Raisa Wróblewska

Mrs Raisa Wróblewska (“the applicant”) was born in 1941 and lives in Białystok. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The court held hearings on 1 and 15 February and 1 March 1994. The Białystok District Court delivered a judgment excluding the applicant from the succession. She appealed. The Supreme Court refused to accept the cassation appeal for examination. The court admitted an additional opinion of an expert land surveyor and an expert in building matters on 20 December 1995. The opinion was submitted on 21 January 1996. A hearing on 22 September 1997 was adjourned in order to hear an expert. Another hearing was scheduled for 27 October 1997. The appeal was dismissed on 20 October 1998. On 31 May 2001, the Supreme Court rejected the appeal.

name: Marcin Bereza
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38713/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention had exceeded a “reasonable time’ within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was made by a Polish national, Mr Marcin Bereza (‘the applicant’), on 18 September 2006. On 17 October 2005 a bill of indictment was lodged with the Warsaw Regional Court. There were 57 defendants in the case, all charged with numerous counts of attempted murder, extortion, robbery, drug trafficking, theft, illegal possession of firearms, battery and forgery committed in an organised criminal group. The courts repeated the grounds previously given for the applicant’s continued detention. They relied especially on the complexity of the case and the large number of co-accused. In September 2006 the applicant made a written request for the appointment of a new lawyer on the ground that he did not ‘trust’ G.R, his court-appointed defence counsel.

On 4 March 2008 the applicant was released from Detention Centre. The proceedings before the Warsaw regional Court are still pending.

name: Engin Erkol
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 50172/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that despite the suspension of criminal proceedings against him, wording employed subsequently by a number of domestic courts had breached his right to the presumption of innocence. The President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The decision was made on 27 May 2009. The applicant's contract of employment was terminated by the bank on 24 August 1998. The Trabzon Labour Court ordered the applicant and his two colleagues to repay the bank the missing money, with the ‘highest rates of interest applicable’ The applicant appealed against the Assize Court decision, arguing that if the proceedings had not been suspended his innocence would have been proved. The Court of Cassation decided that the decision was not appealable, because it was not a decision containing a definitive conclusion. It considered, however, that the applicant's appeal could be examined as an ‘objection’ and forwarded it to the prosecutor for the necessary action to be taken. The applicant and his two colleagues brought a case against the bank before the Trabzon Labour Court, claiming compensation for their dismissal. The applicant appealed against the decision, submitting that the criminal proceedings against him had been suspended by the Istanbul Assize Court. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision in so far as it concerned the applicable rate of interest. An appeal lodged against this decision by the applicant was rejected by the Court ofCassation on 26 September 2005. The bank brought proceedings to enforce the decision with a view to recovering the money. The case was settled out of court in July 2004. On 26 May 2005 the Court of Cassation quashed the Labour Court decision of 21 September 2004. The Labour Court had erred in rejecting the applicant's claim without hearing any of the witnesses proposed by him or obtaining expert reports. The Trabzon Labour Court repeated the decision on 13 October 2005. On 24 May 2006 an appeal lodged by the applicant against the Labour court decision was rejected. This decision was communicated to the applicant on 1 August 2006. The applicant is now appealing against the decision of the Trabzon Labour Court.

name: David Gregory
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 2 December 1995. It originated in an application (no. 22299/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr David Gregory, a British citizen, on 7 July 1993. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality. The applicant, who is black, is a British citizen born in 1966 and currently living in Manchester, England. He was tried for robbery at Manchester Crown Court between 26 and 28 November 1991. No comments were received. The trial was adjourned until 21 October 1996. The jury retired to consider their verdict. An hour and three quarters later a note was passed by the jury to the judge. It read: “JURY SHOWING RACIAL OVERTONES 1 MEMBER TO BE EXCUSED.” The Court heard addresses by Mr Ress, Mr Mansfield and Mr Garnham. The applicant was legally represented at the trial. Defence counsel seems to recall that he did in fact ask the trial judge to discharge the jury in the circumstances. Defence counsel based his recollection on the grounds of appeal and advice on appeal which he drafted shortly after the trial on 10 December 1991. Prosecution counsel recalls that defence counsel did not raise strong objections to the approach which the judge indicated he intended to pursue. The jury were recalled at 12.47 p.m. and instructed to return a verdict on the basis of the evidence alone. Judge: “You are brought here as twelve people from your various walks of life, your various backgrounds. You decide this case on evidence. Do you understand that, members of the jury? The jury then retired at 12.50 p.m. and were recalled by the judge. He informed them that the time had come when he could accept a verdict of at least a majority of ten. The jury were still undecided and they were called back again. At 4.06 p.M. the jury returned and delivered a ten to two majority verdict finding the applicant guilty. The applicant was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment. The appeal proceedings were heard at the Court of Appeal in London. The application was dismissed on the grounds of racial prejudice, but the appeal was heard again at the High Court in London on the merits.  leave to appeal was refused by the single judge on 28 February 1992. The applicant renewed his application to the full Court of Appeal. On 19 January 1993 the application was dismissed. The Court of appeal noted that the trial judge “... took the view and this Court agrees with it, that the nature of the jury’s anxiety was that one member of the Jury felt that there was a general overtone of racial comment which was unacceptable’. The court continued: “The jury system does require an element of give and take after proper directions from the judge. In our judgment His Honour Judge Hammond dealt with this matter sensitively, sensibly and correctly’

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 2 December 1995. It originated in an application (no. 22299/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr David Gregory, a British citizen, on 7 July 1993. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The applicant, who is black, is a British citizen born in 1966 and currently living in Manchester, England. He was tried for robbery at Manchester Crown Court between 26 and 28 November 1991 and was legally represented at the trial. The trial ended on the final day of the trial, at 10.46 a.m., the jury retired to consider their verdict. An hour and three quarters later a note was passed by the jury to the judge. It read: “JURY SHOWING RACIAL OVERTONES 1 MEMBER TO BE EXCUSED.“ On 13 June 1996 the President of the Chamber at the time, Mr Bernhardt, granted leave to Rights International, a non-governmental human rights organisation based in New York, to submit written comments. These were received on 28 August 1996 and forwarded to the Delegate of the Commission, the applicant’s representative and the Agent of the Government for comment. No comments were received. Judge showed the note to counsel for the prosecution and defence and consulted them on the appropriate response to it. Defence counsel seems to recall that he did in fact ask the trial judge to discharge the jury in the circumstances, but his application was refused. Prosecution counsel recalls that defence counsel did not raise strong objections to the approach which the judge indicated he intended to pursue, namely to recall the jury and give clear directions on their duty to return a verdict on the basis of the evidence alone. “You are brought here as twelve people from your various walks of life, your various backgrounds. Everybody has preconceived ideas and thoughts but you are brought. here from twelve different backgrounds expecting to apply your twelve different minds to the problems that are put before you,” said the judge. The jury retired at 12.50 p.m. and were recalled at 2.21pm. At 3.27pm the jury were still undecided and they were called back again. At 4.06pm they returned and delivered a ten to two majority verdict finding the applicant guilty. The applicant was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment. The appeal proceedings were heard at the Court of Appeal. The judge ruled that the trial judge had wrongly failed to make any enquiry into the note with a view to determining whether one of the members of the jury should be discharged on the grounds of racial prejudice and that this failure gave rise to the appeal. Leave to appeal was refused by the single judge on 28 February 1992. The applicant renewed his application to the full Court of Appeal. On 19 January 1993 the application was dismissed. The court continued: “Matters of this kind raise delicate issues. The jury system does require an element of give and take after proper directions from the judge’s. In our judgment His Honour Judge Hammond dealt with this matter sensitively, sensibly and correctly, and cannot be faulted for a conclusion that the jury should continue the deliberations which they had given their oath to undertake. We, therefore, find no ground for complaint and we dismiss this application.“

name: Göran Ravnsborg
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 19 February 1993. It originated in an application (no. 14220/88) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swedish national, Mr Göran Ravnsborg, on 2 July 1988. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The President granted him leave to present his own case (Rule 30). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 October 1993. The Court heard addresses by Ms Jagander, Mr Gaukur Jörundsson and Mr Ravnsborg. There appeared before the Court: Ms E. Jagander for the Government, Ms C. Renfors for the Ministry of Justice and Mr G. Ravns Borg for the Commission. The applicant applied under Article 50 (art. 50) of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and the hearing was adjourned until later in the year. The ECHR ruled in favour of the applicant and dismissed the case. The applicant was ordered by the relevant courts to pay fines for improper statements made in his written observations. The orders were made in the form of decisions (beslut) He appears to have paid the fines. The first fine was a fine of 1,000 Swedish kronor. The applicant appealed from the above decision to the Court of Appeal for Western Sweden (Hovrätten för Västra Sverige) He asked for an oral hearing and complained of not having had the possibility to defend himself orally before the District Court. The Court of Appeal confirmed the decision and ordered the applicant to pay a further fine of 1,000 kronor. The applicant then applied to the Supreme Court for leave to appeal, alleging that the lower and appellate courts had not only denied him a fair trial but had also violated his right to freedom of expression. Such leave was refused on 5 January 1988. The third fine for improper remarks in his appeal was also ordered to be paid. The case was heard by the U.N. Human Rights Committee in Geneva. The appeal was settled out of court by a settlement of around £100,000. name: Paweł Kurczewski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18157/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the excessive length of the applicant's detention to the Government. The applicant was born in 1979 and lives in Gdańsk, Poland. He was arrested on suspicion of having committed robbery on 16 April 2002 and remanded in custody until 16 July 2002. The court considered that keeping the applicant in detention was justified by the existence of strong and substantial evidence, in particular testimonies of a victim and witnesses. The applicant was indicted before the Gdańsk District Court on 25 March 2003. He was charged with robbery and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. The bill of indictment concerned five defendants and, in all, twelve charges were brought against them. Hearings scheduled for 9 October and 11 December 2003 were cancelled due to, among other things, the failure to bring the co-accused to trial from prison. On 28 July 2004 the GDAńk District Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to four years' imprisonment. The applicant appealed on 7 December 2004. His detention was subsequently extended on several occasions. In all those decisions the courts stated that the grounds originally given for the applicant's detention were still valid. Appeal hearings scheduled for 12 October and 12 December 2005 and 2 February 2006 were cancelled for various reasons, such as illness or absence of defence lawyers, and the need to obtain evidence. On 3 February 2006 the Gdańsk Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) quashed the applicant's detention order. He was released on the same date. It appears that the first-instance judgment was upheld on 11 July 2007. The application for bail was denied by the judge on the case and he was sentenced to 10 years in prison. The appeal was denied and the judge sentenced the applicant to 10 months in prison, but the sentence was later overturned.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42234/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was represented by Mr A.T. Ocak, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The events of 14 October 2001 are described as follows: The crowd was shouting out slogans like “Yankee go home”, “No to imperialist and colonial war’ and “Terrorist America”. The applicant went to the office of the Kadıköy prosecutor and made an official complaint about the treatment to which he had been subjected by police officers. He submitted that he had received blows to his back and had been kicked. The applicant claimed that since the police officers had masks it was not possible for him to identify the perpetrators. On 22 October 2001 a doctor who examined the applicant’s X‑rays noted that the applicant had a closed fracture on the right eleventh costal cartilage. On the same day the applicant was examined by a doctor at the Numune hospital who found 3 x 15 cm of hyperaemia (increases of blood flow in tissue) and sensitivity in the right femur. He was transferred to an orthopaedist who noted ecchymotic regions on his right arm and back. The applicant was allegedly ill-treated by police officers in November 2001. A doctor found that the applicant was suffering from lumbago and recommended ten days’ rest. name: Douglas Gary Vinter
train_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Since the abolition of the death penalty in England and Wales, the sentence for murder has been a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment. When such a sentence is imposed, it is the current practice, in the majority of cases, for the trial judge to set a minimum term of imprisonment which must be served before the prisoner is eligible for release on licence. Exceptionally, however, “a whole life order” may be imposed by the trialJudge instead of a minimum. This has the effect that the prisoner cannot be released other than from prison. The power of the Secretary of State to release a prisoner is provided for in section 30(1) of the Crime (Sentences) Act 1997. All three applicants maintain that these whole life orders, as they apply to their cases, are incompatible inter alia with Articles 3 and 5 § 4 of the Convention. The cases concern three applicants who, having been convicted of murder in separate criminal proceedings in England and Wales, are currently serving mandatory sentences of life imprisonment. The application was made by Mr Vinter, Mr Hindley and Mr Brown. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal on 29 June 2012. The judge ruled in favour of all three applicants. The first applicant pleaded guilty to murder and instructed his counsel not to make any submissions in mitigation lest it add to the grief of the victim’s family. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 25 June 2009. It considered the general principles for determining the minimum term of a mandatory life sentence (as set out in schedule 21 to the 2003 Act) for the murder of a work colleague. It found that, given the circumstances of the offence, there was no reason whatever to depart from the normal principle enshrined in the. normal principle of the law. The first applicant was sentenced to a minimum of 10 years in prison with a maximum of life. He was released on licence on 4 August 2005. Mr Bamber's parents, his adoptive sister and her two young children were shot and killed in 1985. The second applicant was subsequently charged and convicted of the murders. In 1988, the Secretary of State imposed a whole life tariff. In 2008, following the entry into force of section 276 and schedule 22 to the 2003 Act, the second applicant applied to the High Court for review of the whole life order. The High Court found that there was no reason to depart from the views of the Lord Chief Justice and the Secretary Of State. It therefore imposed a entire life order on Mr Bamber. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 14 May 2009. The Court of Appeal also found that the whole life order imposed by the High Court was not only correct but, for the purposes of punishment and retribution, fully justified. The review procedure created by the 2003 Act was compatible with Article 7 of the Convention as, properly construed, the relevant statutory provisions meant a prisoner could not be disadvantaged by the outcome of the review. The second applicant applied to the Court of appeal to certify that its judgment concerned a point of law of general public importance which ought to be considered by the House of Lords. That application was refused on 23 June 2009. The third applicant was convicted in 1996 of four counts of murder. The High Court found that, since the case involved the murder of two or more persons, sexual or sadistic conduct and a substantial degree of premeditation, under schedule 21 the starting point was a whole life order. There were no mitigating features and even the Lord Chief Justice, in recommending a minimum term of thirty years, had shared the trial judge’s view that it might never be safe to release the third applicant. The High Court added that no issue of arbitrariness arose and whether such a sentence was disproportionate depended on the facts of each case. The court also found that a wholeLife order would be compatible with Articles 3 and 5 of the Convention. The Court of Appeal dismissed the third applicant’s appeal, finding that the High Court was not only entitled, but clearly right, to conclude that a whole life order was appropriate. The third applicant, in order to allow him to appeal to the House of Lords, then applied to the Court of appeal to certify that its judgment concerned a point of law of general public importance. On 14 August 2009, he was informed that, because the Court. of Appeal had refused his application for permission to appeal against sentence, an application to certify a point. of law for the House. of Lords could not be made. The appeal was dismissed on 26 February 2009.

The case originated in an application (no. 52479/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. On 9 October 2007 the Court declared admissible the applicant’s complaints relating to the excessive length of his detention and the lack of unsupervised contacts with his lawyer at the investigation stage of the proceedings, and the remainder of the application inadmissible. The applicant’s detention was prolonged twice, on 1 August, until 31 October 1996. On 23 December 1996 the prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and his co-accused with the Wrocław Regional Court. The first hearing in the case was held on 21 March 1997. The court held subsequent hearings on 11 and 12 September and 18 November 1997, and 10 February and 3 March 1998. On 16 April 1998 the court heard evidence from two anonymous witnesses who answered questions which had been formulated in writing by the applicant's lawyers. On 25 March 1998 they submitted to the court a list of further questions to be put to one of those witnesses. The applicant’s lawyer challenged the credibility of the evidence against the applicant. He disputed the finding that the accused persons had substantially contributed to the length of the proceedings. He stated that the proceedings were lengthy because of the long intervals between the hearings. The Supreme Court found that apart from the reasonable suspicion that he and the two co-accused persons had committed the offence at issue, there existed an actual risk that they would obstruct the proceedings if released. The judge recommended that the trial court should “schedule the hearings in a more rational way so as to avoid further intervals of several months in the instant case”. The court ruled that the other premises for detention remained valid. The Wrocław Regional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal on 15 July 1996. The court noted that the applicant could at that time see his lawyer whenever he requested. The restrictions imposed on his contacts with his lawyer did not impair his defence rights. The fact that a prosecutor was to be present during these visits did not affect the applicant’s defence rights at that stage, the more so as the restriction was to apply only during the investigations. A court further stated that the defence strategy could also be discussed in accordance with the law in the presence of a person appointed by the prosecutor.

name: Franz Steininger
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Austrian Government was represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. The applicant company, which has its seat of business in Ernstbrunn (Austria), carries out cattle and pig slaughter, and is therefore liable to agricultural marketing charges. It was ordered to pay outstanding contributions for the period of December 2005 and January 2006 in the amount of 11.730,05 euros (EUR) and a surcharge for failure to pay, amounting to 60% of the unpaid contributions. The European Commission had expressed that it had no objection to the AMA Quality programmes and quality mark registered as state aid NN 34A/2000. The applicant company lodged complaints with the Constitutional Court and the Administrative Court against the Federal Minister’s decision. AMA dismissed the request for suspension of the enforcement on 25 July 2006. The Federal Minister found that it was not necessary to hold a hearing because a hearing was only held if a decision was taken by a panel on an appeal against the decision of a tax office or a regional directorate of finance, which was not the case here. It also held that the levying of AMA contributions was in accordance with the relevant provisions of EU law. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant company’s complaint under Article 144 of the Federal Constitution for lack of prospect of success. As the authorities imposing the surcharges had failed to hold an oral hearing, the applicantCompany asked the Administrative Court for a public hearing. The Administrative Court dismissed the complaint on 30 January 2007 and held as follows: “The present case does not differ in the questions of relevance to the decision from the one decided on 20 March 2006, no. 2005/17/230. Pursuant to Section 43(2) of the Administrative court Act reference is made to it. For the reasons set out in that decision the breach of law complained of by the applicantcompany also does not exist in view of the present complaint.”

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that no tribunal had decided on the imposition of surcharges for unpaid contributions to the Austrian Agricultural Marketing Association. The Federal Minister of Agriculture, Forestry, Environment and Water, acting as the appeal authority, dismissed the applicant company’s appeal on 17 July 2006 without holding a hearing. The case was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). It was decided that the application was not admissible. The decision was made to dismiss the appeal and uphold the payment order. The Federal Minister found that after the decision of the European Commission of 30 June 2004 (C(2004)2037), the applicant company was in a position to know precisely which charges it had to pay. The Federal Minister referred further to the Administrative Court’s decision of 20 March 2006, no. 2005/17/230, according to which also the levying of AMA contributions was in accordance with the relevant provisions of EU law. On 25 July 2006 AMA dismissed the request for suspension of the enforcement. The applicant company lodged complaints with the Constitutional Court and the administrative court against the Federal Minister's decision. It complained that no public hearing had been held and that no impartial tribunal established by law decided on the criminal charge against it. The authorities imposing the surcharges had failed to hold an oral hearing, the applicant company asked the Administrative Court for a public hearing. By a decision of 18 October 2001, the Chamber declared the application admissible. In 1992 the applicant, represented by counsel, brought an action with the Berlin Regional Court against a German health insurance company. Having been affiliated to this company since 1975, she claimed reimbursement of pharmaceutical expenses for hormone treatment. She also requested a declaratory judgment to the effect that the defendant company was liable to reimburse 50% of the expenses for gender reassignment operations.
