Expert concluded that the gender reassignment operation formed part of the curative treatment of a mental disease. The court considered that under the relevant provisions of the General Insurance Conditions, the applicant was not entitled to reimbursement of medical treatment regarding her transsexuality. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Berlin Court of Appeal. In its reasoning, the court, having regard to the opinion prepared by Dr H. and to the expert opinions prepared in the proceedings before the Schöneberg District Court, considered that the applicant is a male-to-female transsexual and that her condition had to be regarded as a disease. The Court of Appeal valued the claims at stake at 28,455.92 German marks. The applicant objected to the findings of the Regional Court in so far as they denied the necessity of gender reassignment measures. According to the opinion of the expert Dr H., her transsexuality constituted a disease, a matter not in dispute between the parties to the proceedings. The Court of appeal found that, with this cautious formulation, the expert had not clearly affirmed the necessity. of an operation. The. applicant had therefore failed to prove that the conditions for reimbursement of medical treatment were met in her. case, the Court of. Appeal said. The Court of Appeal considered that the applicant had continued to live as a man. In its view, the applicant’s “fear of bigger boys” at school was not gender-specific. The applicant was not entitled to reimbursement under clause 5.1(b) of the General Insurance Conditions on the ground that she had herself deliberately caused the disease, as argued by the defendant in earlier submissions. In any event, the Court of appeal further considered that, in any event,. the applicant wasnot entitled to reimbursing the NHS for the treatment of her transsexuality as long as she did not claim that she was a female. The German Transsexuals Act (Gesetz über die Änderung der Vornamen und die Feststellung der Geschlechtszugehörigkeit in besonderen Fällen) of 10 September 1980 (Federal Gazette I, p. 1654) was adopted following a decision of 11 October 1978 of the Federal Constitutional Court. The Federal Social Court, in a decision of 6 August 1987 (Reports of Decisions, BSGE 62, pp. 83 et seq.), confirmed the lower social courts’ decisions. The basic rules for private health insurance, as for any other private insurance, are laid down in the Insurance Contract Act (Gesetz über den Versicherungsvertnung) The German health insurance system has been governed by the Social Security Act, Book V, Health Insurance (Sozialgesetzbuch, Fünftes Buch) since 1989. Private health insurance covers expenses for curative treatment which is medically necessary on account of a disease or injuries suffered as a result of an accident. The insurer is exempted from liability if the insured person has deliberately caused his or her own disease or accident (section 178.l). The contractual relations are standardised in general insurance conditions. The Federal Court of Justice, in a decision of 11 April 1994 (Versicherungsrecht 1995, pp. 447 et seq.), endorsed the lower court’s finding that gender reassignment surgery had to be considered as necessary medical treatment. In its judgment of 17 February 1998, in Lisa Jacqueline Grant v. South-West Trains Ltd (C-249/96, Rec. I-621), the ECJ clarified the resulting position as follows “... [w]here a person is dismissed on the ground that he or she intends to undergo or has undergone gender. reassignment, he or. she is treated unfavourably by comparison with persons of the sex to which he/she was deemed to belong” ECJ: Community law as it stands at present does not cover discrimination based on sexual orientation. The Court of appeal added that, while the expert had mentioned that the gender. was not the only possible curative treatment, but recommendable from a psychiatric-psychotherapheutic point of view in order to improve the applicant’s social situation, the Court of. Appeal found that, with this cautious formulation, the Expert had not clearly affirmed the necessity of an operation. The Court of Appeal concluded that the applicant had failed to prove the necessity of her treatment. In its view, the applicant’s ‘fear of bigger boys’ at school was not gender-specific. applying to join the armed forces did not indicate female feelings, and she had left the armed Forces not because of the feeling that she was a ‘woman’ but because she had experienced degrading treatment. The applicant was not entitled to reimbursement under clause 5.1(b) of the General Insurance Conditions on the ground that she had herself deliberately caused the disease, as argued by the defendant in earlier submissions. The ‘turning-point’, as stated by the applicant, had been the moment when, after an unsuccessful operation in 1986, she had realised she was infertile. The German Transsexuals Act (Gesetz über die Änderung der Vornamen and die Feststellung der Geschlechtszugehörigkeit in besonderen Fällen) of 10 September 1980 (Federal Gazette I, p. 1654) was adopted following the decision of 11 October 1978. On 25 October 1996 the Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint. The case was heard at the Federal Court of Appeal in Berlin, and the decision was made to uphold the Transsexual Act. The plaintiff, who was infertile, argued that she wanted to be a woman and to look like one, although it was biologically impossible. The German health insurance system has been governed by the Social Security Act, Book V, Health Insurance (Sozialgesetzbuch, Fünftes Buch, Gesetzliche Kranken-versicherung) since 1989. Under the relevant provisions, persons insured under the health system are entitled to medical treatment which is necessary in order to diagnose or to cure a disease. Under section 1, persons may request that their forenames be changed if, on account of their transsexual orientation, they no longer feel they belong to the sex recorded in the register of births. The competent civil courts have to obtain two medical expert opinions to establish whether the medical conditions are met (section 4). Private health insurance covers expenses for curative treatment which is medically necessary on account of a disease or injuries suffered as a result of an accident. The insurer is exempted from liability if the insured person has deliberately caused his or her own disease or accident (section 178.l). The contractual relations are standardised in general insurance conditions. The European Court of Justice (ECJ) found that discrimination arising from gender reassignment constituted discrimination on grounds of sex and, accordingly, Article 5 § 1 of Council Directive 76/207/EEC of 9 February 1976, precluded dismissal of a transsexual for a reason related to a gender reassignment. ECJ: Community law as it stands at present does not cover discrimination based on sexual orientation. The refusal by an employer to allow travel concessions to the person of the same sex with whom a worker has a stable relationship does not constitute discrimination prohibited by Article 119 of the Treaty or Directive 75/117. reasoning, which leads to the conclusion that such discrimination is to be prohibited just as isdiscrimination based on the fact that a person belongs to a particular sex, is limited to the case of a worker’s gender reassignment and does not therefore apply to differences of treatment based on a person's sexual orientation, the ECJ said.

name: Ludwig Weh
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38544/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, inter alia, that the first applicant's right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself had been breached in criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Government filed observations on the admissibility and merits. By a decision of 4 July 2002 the Court declared the application partly admissible, namely as regards the firstApplicant's complaint that his right to remains silent and to not incriminate itself had been breach. The applicant, Mr W. Weh, was born in 1952 and lives in Bregenz. He was convicted of exceeding the city area speed limit by 21 km/h. The applicant did not comply with the anonymous order and the order became invalid. He appealed to the Vorarlberg Independent Administrative Panel (Unabhängiger Verwaltungssenat) The panel dismissed the appeal on 15 April 1996 and ordered him to pay a fine of ATS 90 by way of contribution to the costs of the proceedings. The appeal was dismissed on 16 April 1996. The case was decided in favour of the applicant. The applicant was ordered to pay ATS 180 by way of contribution to the costs of the appeal proceedings. He raised various issues regarding the tribunal quality of the Independent Administrative Panel and the fairness of the proceedings. The Administrative Court refused to deal with the applicant's complaint pursuant to section 33a of the Administrative Court Act (Verwaltungsgerichtshofgesetz) Since the amount of the penalty did not exceed ATS 10,000, and no important legal problem was at stake, the applicant was not prosecuted for exceeding the speed limit. The applicant did not raise the issue of his right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself.

The panel dismissed the appeal and ordered the applicant to pay a fine of ATS 90 by way of contribution to the costs of the proceedings. The appeal was dismissed on 17 April 1998 and the applicant was sentenced to 54 hours' imprisonment in default. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) on 3 June 1996. He raised various issues regarding the tribunal quality of the Independent Administrative Panel and the fairness of the proceedings. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the applicant's complaint for lack of prospects of success. The applicant was not prosecuted for exceeding the speed limit. The Administrative Court ordered the applicant to pay ATS 180 by way of contribution to the costs of the appeal proceedings. He was found not guilty of any offence under section 103 of the Motor Vehicles Act. The case was dismissed by the Administrative Court on 27 June 1997.

name: Johann Ferihumer
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30547/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been violated in his right to freedom of expression under Article 10. The Court declared the application admissible on 14 February 2006. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal from 2-8 February 2007. The jury found the applicant's case not to be proved and the appeal was dismissed. The application was brought by Johann Ferihumer, the father of a pupil of a secondary school in Grieskirchen. He was the vice-chairman and recording clerk of the parents' association at this school. The majority of teachers of the Grieskirchen secondary school brought proceedings against the applicant for insult and damage to their reputation. The Peuersbach District Court heard the applicant, the teachers, the spokesperson of the pupils, the chair of the parents' association and several other witnesses. It ordered the applicant to refrain from repeating the statement that the teachers were applying pressure on the pupils and parents to an intolerable extent and that this amounted in fact to an abuse of their authority. The applicant had to accept the most unfavourable interpretation of this statement which meant the teachers had used unlawful and unobjective means to make parents and pupils agree to the boycott measures. The court further observed that the conflicting interests of teachers, parents and pupils in regard to the boycott measures naturally caused tensions. There was, however, no indication that the teachers had used unlawful and unobjective means, such as, for example, the use of their authority to assign marks. It was, on the contrary, because of the teachers' unbending attitude that pupils and parents had finally resigned and agreed to the compromise. The injunction at issue did, therefore, not violate the applicant's right to freedom of expression. The court further ordered the applicant to pay the costs of the proceedings. This decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 13 March 2003.

name: Stephen Andrew Benham
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 23 January 1995 by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) and on 26 January 1995. It originated in an application (no. 19380/92) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 20 September 1991. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 5 and 6 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The case was heard by the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg on 22 November 1995. The Court heard addresses from the Government, the Commission and the applicant. The Grand Chamber decided that it was not necessary to hold a further hearing following the relinquishment of jurisdiction by the Chamber. The case was decided in favour of Mr Benham, and he was ordered to pay a community charge of £325. The trial was adjourned until April 1996, when the case was returned to the Court of Appeal for a new hearing. The hearing was held on 22 April 1996. The jury returned a unanimous verdict in favor of the applicant, and the appeal was dismissed. Poole Magistrates' Court ordered the issue of a liability order in 1990. Mr Benham did not pay the amount owed. Bailiffs visited his parents' house but were told that he had no goods of any value there or elsewhere which could be seized by them and sold in order to pay the debt. On the basis of this evidence, the magistrates concluded that his failure to pay was due to his culpable neglect, “as he clearly had the potential to earn money to discharge his obligation to pay“. They decided that he ought to be sent to prison for thirty days unless he paid what was owing. He was taken to Dorchester prison on the same day. Mr Benham appeared without payment before the magistrates on 28 March 1991 to apply for bail, but he was unsuccessful. His solicitor lodged a notice of appeal by way of case stated and an application for bail pending appeal. Legal aid was obtained for the appeal, but not for the bail application, because it is not available for such proceedings. Bail was granted on 5 April 1991 and Mr Benham was thus released from prison, having served eleven days. Mr Justice Potts in the Divisional Court held that the Magistrates had been mistaken in concluding that the failure to pay the community charge had been due to culpable neglect. Mr Benham was not able to apply for compensation in respect of the time he spent in prison. He was unable to show bad faith on the part of the magistrates, as was required by section 108 of the Courts and Legal Services Act 1990. Mr Benham had to wait until after the hearing before the Magistrates before he could apply for release. The magistrates did not consider the alternatives to immediate detention provided for by the Regulations. They could have suspended the term of imprisonment subject to such conditions as they thought fit, or refused to issue a warrant. The local authority could have renewed their application at a later date if Mr Ben Ham's circumstances had changed (see paragraph 19 below).

name: Abdisamad Adow Sufi
train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 8319/07 and 11449/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that if returned to Somalia they would be at real risk of ill-treatment contrary to Article 3 and/or a violation of Article 2. The cases were adjourned on 7 October 2008 pending the decision of the Court of Appeal in HH (Somalia), AM (S Somalia) and J (S Somalia) (2010) EWCA Civ 426. The adjournment was lifted when the court of Appeal delivered its judgment on 23 April 2010. The first applicant, Mr Abdisamad Adow Sufi, is a Somali national who was born in 1987. On 3 October 2003 he claimed asylum on the ground that as a member of the Reer-Hamar, a sub-clan of the minority Ahansi clan, he had been subjected to persecution by Hawiye militia. On 15 April 2005 the Secretary of State for the Home Department refused the first applicant’s asylum application, finding, inter alia, that the fact he had remained in Somalia until 2003 undermined his claim to be a minority clan. On 29 June 2005 both the asylum appeal and the human rights appeal were dismissed by an Adjudicator who found that his account of what had happened to him in Somalia was not credible. He was later sentenced to three months’ imprisonment following a conviction for indecent exposure in October 2007. The second applicant, Mr Abdiaziz Ibrahim Elmi, is a Somali national who was born in 1969 and is currently detained in an Immigration Detention Centre. His father, a high-ranking officer in the army during the Barré regime, was appointed to the Somali Embassy in London as a military attaché in 1988. On 1 March 1989 his father died. On 26 April 1989 the second applicant made an application for asylum based on his father’s position in the Somali army and the beginning of the civil war in Somalia. On 31 October 1989 he was recognised as a refugee and granted leave to remain until 31 October 1993. On 7 January 1994 he was granted Indefinite Leave to Remain in the United Kingdom. The second applicant was convicted of supplying class A drugs (cocaine and heroin) and was sentenced to 42 months’ imprisonment. On 21 June 2006 a decision was made to issue a deportation order by virtue of section 3(5) of the Immigration Act 1971. He accepted that he was a drug addict but submitted that he did not constitute a danger to the community because he had made efforts to overcome his addiction and had recognised his past wrongdoings. On 4 September 2006 the Secretary of State for the Home Department found that he had failed to demonstrate that he would not constitute such a danger. In respect of his rights under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention, he was found not to be at risk on return to Somalia as he was member of the Isaaq, a majority clan. A deportation order against the second applicant was signed on 8 January 2007 and on 6 March 2007 he was served with removal directions. On 3 March 2008 he was convicted of possession of a Class A controlled drug with intent to supply and was sentenced to eighteen months’ imprisonment. On 8 July 2010 he was again charged with possession ofA Class A drug withintent to supply. A hearing has not yet taken place. The second applicant requested, and was granted, interim measures under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court to prevent his removal before his application was considered by the Court. Finally, the AIT noted that the sale of drugs posed a danger to the community and there was a real likelihood of theSecond applicant re‑offending.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25166/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a German national, Mr Jürgen Schneider. The applicant was represented by Mr J. Postlmayr, a lawyer practising in Mattighofen. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador F. Trauttmansdorff, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The German Government did not make use of their right to intervene under Article 36 § 1 of the convention. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The applicant was convicted of four traffic offences, namely speeding, breaching the requirement to drive in the right-hand lane, unjustified use of fog-lights and failure to carry his driving licence with him. He did not appeal against his conviction for failing to carry a driving licence. The applicant alleged in particular that the Independent Administrative Panel had failed to hold a hearing. On 23 July 2004 the Administrative Court partly quashed the decision. It (a) upheld the conviction as upheld by the Court of Appeal for Lower Austria. The case was heard by the court of appeals in Vienna, Austria, on 15 September 2004. The appeal was dismissed on 17 November 2004. The case was heard by the Independent Administrative Panel on 30 September 2004. The hearing was held in the absence of the defence counsel. The decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 30 December 2004. It was dismissed on 13 December 2004 by the Independent Administrative Panel. The applicant did not lodge a complaint with the Administrative Court or the Constitutional Court. The case was settled at a hearing held on 7 September 2004 in the presence of the two police officers who had been called as witnesses. The application was dismissed as there was no evidence of a breach of the terms of the Criminal Offences Act. The appeal was dismissed and the case returned to the Administrative Court.

name: Piotr Rachwalski
train_texts: The application was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 18 October 1998. The applicants alleged that they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment and that the police had used excessive and unjustified force towards them. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The parties do not fully agree about the facts of the case, which may be summarised as follows. 1. The case was brought by two Polish nationals. The applicants were subjected to abuse by police who called them 'scum' and 'slobs' The applicants were examined by a forensic medicine specialist. It was established that the first applicant had two long bruises on his left arm, and other bruises on the palm of his hand. The second applicant had a blue mark on her bottom (13 by 9 cm) It was stated that these bruises could have been caused by the use of police truncheons. The applicants requested to be examined by an independent medical specialist. The applicant and her friend D. S. lived in the house with the owner’s permission. They often received young visitors from all over the country. The owner of the car gave the police the keys and documents to the car. As D. S. was unruly and continued to express objections, the policemen decided to arrest him. While he was being taken into custody by the police, he hit one of them in the face. Thereupon truncheons were used against him. The applicants requested the Wrocław District Prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of authority. On 23 December 1997 the prosecutor refused to do so. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The police could have reasonably suspected that the unlocked car had been stolen, even though it had not been reported as such. D. S. had objected in a loud voice to the police intervention. He had insisted that the intention of the police was to harass the persons in the house. As he had not obeyed the police requests to calm down and the verbal exchange between him and the police officer A. C. had become increasingly heated, it had been decided that he should be taken to a police car. The first applicant appealed. He argued that the police brutality and aggression had been totally unjustified. Nothing in the behaviour of the persons present had justified the use of force. The prosecutor concluded that the measures taken by the police had been proportionate to the situation. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. He had not given any reason to be beaten, verbally insulted and humiliated just at the whim of the police. The Wrocław Regional Prosecutor upheld the contested decision. He considered that the police intervention had been justified in so far as they wanted to verify the identity of the owner of the car. Regardless of whether he had intended to hit A. C. in the face or not, his behaviour could have been perceived as an intentional assault. The findings of the inquiry had not established that the students had been insulted verbally by the police, as the policemen consistently denied this.

The applicant and her friend lived in the house with the owner’s permission. They often received young visitors from all over the country. It was established that the first applicant had two long bruises on his left arm, and other bruises on the palm of his hand. The second applicant had a blue mark on her bottom (13 by 9 cm) It was stated that these bruises could have been caused by the use of police truncheons. He had not given any reason to be beaten, verbally insulted and humiliated just at the whim of the police. The police should not intervene in private property at night and hit, insult and humiliate people just because they looked, or lived, differently. name: Gerhard Klass
train_texts: The case originated in an application against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission on 11 June 1971. Five German citizens, namely Gerhard Klass, Peter Lubberger, Jürgen Nussbruch, Hans-Jürgen Pohl and Dieter Selb. The Commission’s request, which referred to Articles 44 and 48, paragraph (a) (art. 44, art. 48-a), was lodged. with the registry of the Court on 15 July 1977. The purpose of the request is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 para. 1, 8 and 13. The Government filed their memorial on 28 November 1977. On 27 January 1978, a memorial by the Principal Delegate of the Commission was received at the registry. The Secretary to the Commission advised the Registrar that the Delegates would reply to the Government’s memorial during the oral hearings. The oral hearings took place in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 10 March. The Court granted a request presented by the Government to address the Court in German at the hearings, the Government undertaking responsibility for the interpretation into French or English of their oral arguments or statements. In addition, the Court also authorised Mr. Pohl to speak in German (Rules 29 para. 1 in fine and 27 para. 3). The applicants, who are German nationals, are Gerhard Klass, an Oberstaatsanwalt, Peter Lubberger, a lawyer, Jürgen Nussbruch, a judge, Hans-Jürgen Pohl and Dieter Selb. All five applicants claim that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law (Grundgesetz) and a statute enacted in pursuance of that provision are contrary to the Convention. They do not dispute that the State has the right to have recourse to the surveillance measures contemplated by the legislation. They challenge this legislation in that it permits those measures without obliging the authorities to notify the persons concerned after the event. The Government of the Federal Republic of Germany were prompted by this judgment to propose amendments to the G 10, but the parliamentary proceedings have not yet been completed. At no time have surveillance measures provided for by the Act enacted in pursuance of Article 10 of the Basic Law been ordered or implemented against the applicants. There is also no question of the applicants’ having been indirectly involved in a surveillance measure directed against another person - at least, not in any fashion which would have permitted their identification. Finally, there is no question that the applicants' having been subjected to surveillance by mistake - for example through confusion over a telephone number -. After the end of the Second World War, the surveillance of mail, post and telecommunications in Germany was dealt with by the occupying powers. Neither the entry into force on 24 May 1949 of the Basic Law nor the foundation of the State of the Federal Republic altered this situation which continued even after the termination of the occupation régime in 1955. The Government wished to substitute the domestic law for the rights exercised by the Three Powers and to place under legal control interferences with the right to respect for correspondence. in such cases the person concerned is notified of the surveillance measure.“ The contested legislation was adopted on 24 June and 13 August 1968 respectively. Law guaranteed the secrecy of mail, post and telecommunications with a proviso that restrictions could be ordered only pursuant to a statute. As amended by the Act of 24 June 1968, it now provides: “(1) Secrecy of the mail,post and telecommunications shall be inviolable. (2) Restrictions may be orderedOnly pursuant to an Act of Parliament.“ The G 10, adopting the solution contemplated by the second sentence of paragraph 2 of the above-quoted Article 10, specifies (in Article 1 para. 1) the cases in which the competent authorities may impose the restrictions provided for in that paragraph, that is to say, may open and inspect mail and post, read telegraphic messages, listen to and record telephone conversations. The measures are ordered, on written application giving reasons, either by the supreme Land authority in cases falling within its jurisdiction or by a Federal Minister empowered for the purpose by the Chancellor. Measures ordered must be immediately discontinued once the required conditions have ceased to exist or the measures themselves are no longer necessary. The measures remain in force for a maximum of three months and may be renewed only on fresh application. The G 10 Commission may direct the Minister to inform the person concerned that he has been subjected to surveillance measures. The person concerned is not to be notified of the restrictions affecting him. However, since the Federal Constitutional Court’s judgment of 15 December 1970 (see paragraph 11 above), the competent authority has to inform him as soon as notification can be made. The G 10 Commission decides, ex officio or on application by a person believing himself to be under surveillance, on both the legality of and the necessity for the measures. If the Commission declares any measures to be illegal or unnecessary, the Minister must terminate them immediately. Although not required by the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 15 December 1970, the Commission has, since that judgment, also been called upon when decisions are taken on whether the person concerned should be notified of the measures affecting him (see paragraph 19 above). The Commission members are appointed for the current term of the Bundestag by the above-mentioned Board of five Members of Parliament after consultation with the Government. The surveillance of the post and telecommunications of a certain person can serve a useful purpose only if the person concerned does not become aware of it. For this reason, notification to this person is out of the question. For the same reason, it must be avoided that a person who intends to commit, or who has committed, the offences enumerated in the Act can, by using a legal remedy, inform himself whether he is under surveillance. The Bill presented during the 4th legislative session ... provided for the ordering (of such measures) by an independent judge. The Federal Government abandoned this solution in the Bill amending Article 10 of the Basic Law, introduced as part of the Emergency Legislation. If the person concerned is notified, after the measures have been discontinued, that he has been subject to surveillance, several legal remedies against the interference with his rights become available to him. The authorities are bound to reply to such a request even if the information asked for is secret. It is then for the Constitutional Court to decide whether the information and documents so obtained can be used. The Court may decide by a two-thirds majority that their use is incompatible with State security and dismiss the application on that ground. The Agent of the Government admitted that this remedy might be employed only on rare occasions. The persons concerned are informed of the measures taken in their respect as soon as notification can be made without jeopardising the purpose of the investigation. In. June 1971, the applicants alleged that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law and the G. 10 violate Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. On 18 December 1974, the Commission declared the application admissible. In view of this particularity of the case the applicants have to be considered as victims for the purpose of Article 25 (art. 25) of the convention. The Commission then expressed the opinion:by eleven votes to one with two abstentions, that the present case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 6-1. The Delegates of the Commission made the following concluding submissions to the Court: “May it please the Court to say and judge whether, having regard to the circumstances of the case, the applicants could claim to be ‘victims’ of a violation of their rights guaranteed by the Convention’“

The case of Klass and others was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (hereinafter called “the Commission’). The case originated in an application against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission on 11 June 1971 under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The purpose of the request is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 para. 1, 8 and 13 ( art. 6-1, art. 8) of. the Convention. The Government filed their memorial on 28 November. On 27 January 1978, a memorial by the Principal Delegate of the Commission was received at the registry. On 18 November in Strasbourg, the Chamber decided under Rule 48 to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The Court held a preparatory meeting on 10 March, immediately before the opening of the hearings. Five applicants claim that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law (Grundgesetz) and a statute enacted in pursuance of that provision, namely the Act of 13 August 1968 on Restrictions on the Secrecy of the Mail, Post and Telecommunications, are contrary to the Convention. They challenge this legislation in that it permits those measures without obliging the authorities in every case to notify the persons concerned after the event. The Government of the Federal Republic of Germany were prompted by this judgment to propose amendments to the G 10, but the parliamentary proceedings have not yet been completed. The applicants did not know whether the surveillance measures had actually been applied to them. There is no question of the applicants’ having been subjected to. surveillance by mistake - for example through confusion over a telephone number -, since. they were not involved in a surveillance measure directed against another person - at least, not in. any fashion which would have permitted their identification. After the end of the Second World War, the surveillance of mail, post and telecommunications in Germany was dealt with by the occupying powers. Neither the entry into force on 24 May 1949 of the Basic Law nor the foundation of the State of the Federal Republic altered this situation which continued even after the termination of the occupation régime in 1955. The contested legislation sought to substitute the domestic law for the rights exercised by the Three Powers and to place under legal control interferences with the right to respect for correspondence. in such cases the person concerned is notified of the surveillance measure.“ The Government introduced two Bills as part of the Emergency Legislation. The first sought primarily to amend Article 10 para. 2 of thebasic law; the second was designed to limit the right of secrecy. Law guaranteed the secrecy of mail, post and telecommunications with a proviso that restrictions could be ordered only pursuant to a statute. As amended by the Act of 24 June 1968, it now provides: “(1) Secrecy of the mail,Post and telecommunications shall be inviolable. (2) Restrictions may be orderedOnly pursuant to the law of the State or of the Federation or of a Land.“ “The G 10, adopting the solution contemplated by the second sentence of paragraph 2 of the above-quoted Article 10, specifies (in Article 1 para. 1) the cases in which the competent authorities may impose restrictions. An application for surveillance measures may be made only by the head, or his substitute, of one of the following services: the Agencies for the Protection of the Constitution of the Federation and the Länder, the Army Security Office (Amt für Sicherheit der Bundeswehr) and the Federal Intelligence Service (Bundesnachrichtendienst) The measures are ordered, on written application giving reasons, either by the supreme Land authority in cases falling within its jurisdiction or by a Federal Minister empowered for the purpose by the Chancellor. Measures ordered must be immediately discontinued once the required conditions have ceased to exist or the measures themselves are no longer necessary. The G 10 Commission decides, ex officio or on application by a person believing himself to be under surveillance, on both the legality of and the necessity for the measures. The Commission members are appointed for the current term of the Bundestag by the above-mentioned Board of five Members of Parliament after consultation with the Government. They are completely independent in the exercise of their functions and cannot be subject to instructions. The Government, moreover, intend proposing to Parliament to amend the G 10 so as to make such prior consent obligatory. For the Länder, their legislatures lay down the parliamentary supervision to which the supreme authorities are supreme. The surveillance of the post and telecommunications of a certain person can serve a useful purpose only if the person concerned does not become aware of it. For this reason, notification to this person is out of the question. For the same reason, it must be avoided that a person who intends to commit, or who has committed, the offences enumerated in the Act can, by using a legal remedy, inform himself whether he is under surveillance. The Bill presented during the 4th legislative session ... provided for the ordering (of such measures) by an independent judge. It may also request the Government concerned to supply it with information or to produce documents to enable it to verify for itself the individual’s allegations. name: Axel Springer AG
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48311/10) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant company alleged that an injunction prohibiting it from further publication of two sentences was in breach of Article 10 of the convention. The Media Legal Defence Initiative, a non-governmental organisation, was granted leave to submit written comments. The case was dismissed by the Federal Constitutional Court, which, by a majority, dismissed the case by the end of 2012. The application was brought by Axel Springer AG, the publisher of the mass-circulation daily newspaper Bild.  Schröder was appointed chairman of the supervisory board of the German-Russian consortium NEGP (Konsortium Nordeuropäische Gaspipeline) The aim of the consortium, which had its registered office in Switzerland and was controlled by the Russian company Gazprom, was to build a gas pipeline to supply Russian gas to western Europe. The agreement on the principle of building the pipeline had been signed on 11 April 2005 by the German company BASF and Gazprom. The signing of the contract itself, initially scheduled for mid-October at an energy summit in Moscow, had taken place on 8 September 2005 – ten days before the early elections. Bild says Thiele had wondered whether Schröder had already spoken to the Russians about a lucrative position before calling the early elections in May 2005. Lower Saxony Prime Minister Christian Wulff told Bild: ‘Through his behaviour Gerhard SchröDer has seriously damaged the reputation of politics in Germany.’ The impugned article was published in the 12 December 2005 edition of the German newspaper Bild. The former Chancellor is to head the supervisory board of a business seeking to build a four-billion-euro gas pipeline through the Baltic Sea from Russia to Germany. While he was Chancellor, he pushed this project through despite considerable resistance. Insiders reckon that Schröder is pocketing more than a million dollars a year for his gas job. Five supervisory board members of the Russian company Northgas, a Gazprom subsidiary, have received payments totalling seven million dollars. On 11 April the Russian energy giant Gazprom and the German [company] BASF signed a memorandum in Hanover for the joint exploitation of a Russian gas field. Following the signing, the two government leaders stayed up late drinking red wine together. Was Schr Öder’s recruitment to the multinational gas company already being discussed at that time – six weeks before he called the early elections? The vice-chairman of the FDP parliamentary group, Carl-Ludwig Thiele, said: ‘That”s a question we need to ask!’ The appointment of Gerhard Schröder as chairman of the NEGP supervisory board gave rise to public debate and was reported in the media and discussed in the German Parliament. In April 2006 it emerged that in late October 2005, while government business was still being conducted on an interim basis by the outgoing government, guarantees had been signed. The German government agreed to underwrite a loan of one billion euros from two German banks in favour of Gazprom and part of the pipeline. In 2006, the German government sought an injunction in the Hamburg Regional Court prohibiting any further publication of the passage of the article. The Regional Court’s judgment held that the quotation was neither a factual allegation nor a value judgment but mere speculation in the form of questions. Hamburg Court of Appeal upheld the Regional Court’s judgment. Publication breached Article 823 of the Civil Code and the right to protection of personality rights. It suggested to readers of the newspaper that Chancellor Schröder had taken the decision to hold early parliamentary elections on the basis of private considerations motivated by self-interest. The Court of appeal found it unnecessary to determine whether the quotation in issue amounted to a genuine (open) question or a factual allegation in the form of a question. The Regional Court had thus been correct in applying the criteria for reporting on suspicions. The article had begun by saying that Mr Schr Öder and the Russian President Putin had met in April 2005, and had then asked whether Chancellor Schräder's activities on behalf of Gazprom had been discussed. The Court of Appeal observed that the principles for reporting on suspicions applied to the case before it. The applicant company had conveyed a suspicion entailing a serious and damaging accusation against the former Chancellor. The article had suggested that he had misled the general public and the electorate about the true reasons for his decision to call early elections. The Court of appeal considered that this was one of the most serious accusations that could be levelled against a person who had formerly held a State office. It added that the quotations confirmed the seriousness of the accusation by using the phrase “monstrous suspicion”. According to these principles, any such reports had to concern a matter of justifiable public interest, have a minimum factual basis and set out the facts objectively. Court of Appeal asked how Mr Schröder could have secured a very well-paid post in a consortium controlled by Gazprom. The Court of Appeal added that the impugned publication had lacked objectivity and balance. It pointed out that the version of events set out in a report should not amount to a prejudgment (Vorverurteilung) of the person concerned. The report did not mention that the May election defeat in North Rhine-Westphalia had considerably weakened the authority of the government majority at federal level and could have constituted a valid reason for asking the electorate, by means of early elections, whether it still supported this majority. Court of Appeal emphasised that the applicant company was not prevented from criticising Mr Schröder. The applicant company had no basis for arguing that these circumstances were so well known to readers that there was no need to reiterate them in the report. The Court of Appeal concluded that this duty had been all the more compelling in the case before it, in view of the especially serious nature of the allegation being made. Decision of the Federal Court of Justice in a decision of 13 January 2009 refused the applicantCompany leave to appeal on points of law, holding that the case did not raise a question of fundamental importance and was not necessary for the development of the law. The Federal Constitutional Court decided not to accept for adjudication a constitutional appeal by the applicant company (no. 1 BvR 368/09) It declined to give reasons for its decision. The court has not ruled on any other appeals since the case was brought to the court. The case-law.com site says the court did not consider the appeal because it was not related to the case at hand. The company said the appeal was not relevant to its business practice and that the court should not have accepted it. For more information on the case, go to: http://www.cnn.com/2010/02/18/technology/index.html#storylink=cpy. The Court refused to rule on the appeal.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant company alleged that an injunction prohibiting it from further publication of two sentences was in breach of Article 10 of the convention. On 21 July 2005 Federal President Horst Köhler dissolved the Bundestag. This means of securing the dissolution of Parliament prompted discussions in public and among members of parliament, and was also the subject of appeals to the Federal Constitutional Court, which, by a majority, dismissed the appeals. The case was heard by the Federal Court of Appeal on 2 March 2012. The elections were held on 18 September 2005. None of the main political parties emerged victorious with a sufficient majority. The parties forming the outgoing Schröder government (the SPD and the Greens) lost their majority. Subsequently, the conservative parties (the CDU and CSU) and the SPD agreed to form a coalition headed by Ms Angela Merkel. On 22 November 2005, Ms Merkel was elected as the new Federal Chancellor. The aim of the consortium, which had its registered office in Switzerland and was controlled by the Russian company Gazprom, was to build a gas pipeline to supply Russian gas to western Europe. The agreement on the principle of building the pipeline had been signed on 11 April 2005 by the German company BASF and Gazprom. The signing of the contract itself, initially scheduled for mid-October at an energy summit in Moscow, had taken place on 8 September 2005 – ten days before the early elections. Bild published an article in December 2005 asking whether Schröder had spoken to the Russians about a lucrative position before calling the early elections in May 2005. Lower Saxony Prime Minister Christian Wulff (CDU) called on SchröDer to act, either by declining the chairmanship of the NEGP consortium’s supervisory board, or by revealing all his income from his Russian job. The impugned article read as follows: “The ex-Chancellor and Russian gas: there is growing outrage among all political parties.” On page 2 of the newspaper, under the headline “Russian salary – will Schröeder earn more than a million a year?” the article read: ‘What does he really earn from the pipeline project? Schr Öder must reveal his Russian salary’ Insiders reckon Schröder is pocketing more than a million dollars a year for his gas job. Five supervisory board members of the Russian company Northgas, a Gazprom subsidiary, have received payments totalling seven million dollars. The early election gambit should ‘now be seen in a new light’, said the vice-chairman of the FDP parliamentary group, Carl-Ludwig Thiele. ‘Did he have personal motives in deciding to call early elections in a politically desperate situation?’ said the CDU’s Wolfgang Bosbach. The former Chancellor should now lay his cards on the table and say whether these agreements had already been reached while he was in office, he added. Gerhard Schröder’s appointment as chairman of the supervisory board gave rise to public debate and was reported in the media and discussed in the German Parliament, in particular on 15 December 2005. In April 2006 it emerged that in late October 2005, while government business was still being conducted on an interim basis by the outgoing government, guarantees had been signed whereby the German government agreed to underwrite a loan of one billion euros from two German banks in favour of Gazprom and part of the pipeline. In June 2005 the Hamburg Regional Court granted the injunction against Focus magazine. It held in particular that the quotation in issue was neither a factual allegation nor a value judgment but mere speculation in the form of questions. Court of Appeal upheld the Regional Court’s judgment. The Court of Appeal observed that the report published by the applicant company did not merely reproduce what Mr Thiele had said, but the quotation had formed part of a significantly longer article intended to steer readers in a certain direction. It added that the article had begun by saying that Mr Schröder and the Russian President Putin had met in April 2005, and had then asked whether Chancellor Schr Öder’‘s activities on behalf of Gazprom had been discussed on that occasion’. In the court's view, this encouraged readers to believe that it was possible that an agreement had been reached for Mr Schrøder to take up a private-sector post. The Court of Appeal found that the applicant company had conveyed a suspicion entailing a serious and damaging accusation against the former Chancellor. The article had suggested that he had misled the general public and the electorate about the true reasons for his decision to call early elections. According to the Court, the quotation in issue confirmed the seriousness of the accusation by using the phrase “monstrous suspicion’. The applicant company added that it had not had due regard to the principles established for reporting on suspicions. These principles include that reports had to concern a matter of justifiable public interest, have a minimum factual basis, set out the facts objectively and be the result of research satisfying requirements of journalistic rigour. The Court of Appeal added that the impugned publication had lacked objectivity and balance. It pointed out that the version of events set out in a report should not amount to a prejudgment (Vorverurteilung) of the person concerned. This was not only the case where the report gave the impression that the person had in fact done what he or she was suspected of doing, but also when a report was intentionally biased and distorted the facts for sensationalist purposes, the court said. The Court also found that at the time of the article’s publication there had been no information from anyone close to Mr Schröder to suggest that he had based his decision to call early elections on grounds that were spurious. Court of Appeal emphasised that the applicant company was not prevented from criticising Mr Schröder. However, in view of the extremely serious accusation being made, it could have been expected to indicate that the facts had yet to be established. The applicant company had not carried out sufficient research before publishing the article. It considered that irrespective of whether the politician quoted in the article should have been required to conduct his own research before raising his questions, the applicantCompany had had a duty to clarify the facts further before publicly reproducing those questions.
